title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning: Exercises
text:
Preface
This is the exercise book of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning. It has one page for each chapter of the full edition, numbered like that chapter, and each page has the chapter’s exercises with a worked solution for each.
Every exercise names in italics the technique it practises, and most give a check value, so you know when you have the answer. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The solutions use the notation of their chapter, and a reference to an equation, section, figure or table of the chapter links to it in the full edition.
The numbers the solutions quote are computed by scripts in the repository’s code/ directory, one per chapter, named solutions_<script>.py, and the tests in tests/ check each of them.

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
1.1 Binomial variance from the PMF
Exercises for Probability distributions, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The numbers come from code/solutions_distributions.py; run it from the repository root with uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_distributions.py.
The solutions work with the probability mass function (PMF) and the moment generating function (MGF) of each family, exactly as the chapter defines them.

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
Exercise 1. Binomial variance from the PMF. Compute \(\mathbb E[S(S-1)]\) for \(S \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, p)\) directly from the PMF, and recover \(\operatorname{Var}S = np(1-p)\). Compare the effort with the decomposition argument. (Binomial)







TipSolution





Write \(q = 1 - p\).

Write the expectation as a sum over the PMF. The terms \(k = 0\) and \(k = 1\) vanish because \(k(k-1) = 0\): \[\mathbb E[S(S-1)] = \sum_{k=2}^n k(k-1)\binom nk p^kq^{n-k}. \tag{1.1}\]
Absorb \(k(k-1)\) into the binomial coefficient. For \(k \ge 2\), \[k(k-1)\binom nk = \frac{n!}{(k-2)!\,(n-k)!} = n(n-1)\binom{n-2}{k-2}. \tag{1.2}\]
Pull out \(n(n-1)p^2\) and re-index with \(j = k - 2\): \[\mathbb E[S(S-1)] = n(n-1)p^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{j}p^jq^{(n-2)-j}. \tag{1.3}\]
The remaining sum is a whole PMF. It is the sum of the \(\mathrm{Bin}(n-2, p)\) PMF over all its values, which is 1 (equivalently, \((p + q)^{n-2} = 1\) by the binomial theorem). So \[\mathbb E[S(S-1)] = n(n-1)p^2. \tag{1.4}\]
Recover the variance. \(\mathbb E S^2 = \mathbb E[S(S-1)] + \mathbb E S\), and the same trick with one factor \(k\) gives \(\mathbb E S = np\). So \[\operatorname{Var}S = n(n-1)p^2 + np - n^2p^2 = np - np^2 = np(1-p). \tag{1.5}\]

A small case. For \(n = 3\), Table 1.1 lists every term of the sum in step 1.

The total is \(6p^2q + 6p^3 = 6p^2(q + p) = 6p^2 = n(n-1)p^2\), as step 4 says. Summed numerically over the PMF, the script gets \(\mathbb E[S(S-1)] = 34.2000\) and \(\operatorname{Var}S = 4.2000\) for \(\mathrm{Bin}(20, 0.3)\), and \(2497.5000\) and \(47.5000\) for \(\mathrm{Bin}(1000, 0.05)\), matching \(n(n-1)p^2\) and \(np(1-p)\).
The effort. The PMF route needs the factorial moment \(\mathbb E[S(S-1)]\) (not \(\mathbb E S^2\), which does not telescope), an identity for the coefficient, a re-index, and the fact that a PMF sums to 1. The decomposition \(S = X_1 + \dots + X_n\) in the proof of Proposition 1.3 needs one line: each Bernoulli has variance \(p(1-p)\), and independent variances add by Lemma 1.1.
Factorial moments are the moments that a PMF with factorials sums easily, but decomposing into independent pieces is shorter.

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
1.2 Poisson thinning

Exercise 2. Poisson thinning. \(N \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\) events occur, and each is kept independently with probability \(q\). Show the number kept is \(\mathrm{Poisson}(q\mu)\). Hint: condition on \(N\) and use the MGF. (Poisson)







TipSolution





Let \(K\) be the number kept.

Given \(N\), the count kept is binomial. If \(N = n\), then \(K\) counts the successes in \(n\) independent \(\mathrm{Bern}(q)\) trials, so \(K \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, q)\). Its MGF is the binomial MGF of Proposition 1.3: \[\mathbb E[e^{\lambda K} \mid N = n] = \big(1 + q(e^\lambda - 1)\big)^n. \tag{1.6}\]
Average over \(N\). The MGF of \(K\) is the average of these conditional MGFs, weighted by \(\Pr[N = n]\): \[M_K(\lambda) = \sum_{n\ge0}\Pr[N = n]\,\big(1 + q(e^\lambda - 1)\big)^n = \mathbb E\big[c^N\big], \qquad c = 1 + q(e^\lambda - 1). \tag{1.7}\]
Recognize the Poisson MGF. Write \(c^N = e^{N\ln c}\), so \(\mathbb E[c^N] = M_N(\ln c)\), which by Proposition 1.4 is \(\exp\big(\mu(e^{\ln c} - 1)\big) = \exp\big(\mu(c - 1)\big)\). Substituting \(c - 1 = q(e^\lambda - 1)\), \[M_K(\lambda) = \exp\big(q\mu(e^\lambda - 1)\big). \tag{1.8}\]
Identify the distribution. This is the \(\mathrm{Poisson}(q\mu)\) MGF, for every \(\lambda\). Two distributions with the same MGF around 0 are the same (Theorem 1.1), so \(K \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(q\mu)\).

Step 2 on a small case. Take the outcome \(N = 2\). The two events are kept or dropped independently, so Table 1.2 lists the four possibilities.

The conditional average is \((1-q)^2 + 2q(1-q)e^\lambda + q^2e^{2\lambda} = \big((1-q) + qe^\lambda\big)^2 = \big(1 + q(e^\lambda - 1)\big)^2\), which is step 1 with \(n = 2\). Step 2 does this for every \(n\) and weights the results by \(\Pr[N = n]\).
As a check, the script draws \(N \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(4)\) a million times and keeps each event with probability \(q = 0.3\). The kept count has mean 1.198 and variance 1.200, against \(q\mu = 1.200\) for both, as a Poisson needs.
Randomly discarding events from a Poisson count leaves a Poisson count, with the mean scaled by the sampling rate \(q\).

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
1.3 Quality of the Poisson approximation

Exercise 3. Quality of the Poisson approximation. For \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, 5/n)\), compute the total variation distance \(\frac12\sum_k|\Pr[S = k] - \Pr[N = k]|\) to \(\mathrm{Poisson}(5)\) for \(n = 10, 100, 1000\) using the functions in the script. Check: it shrinks roughly like \(1/n\). (Poisson limit)







TipSolution






Split the sum at \(n\). The binomial puts no mass above \(n\), so for \(k > n\) each term is \(\Pr[N = k]\), and those terms add up to \(\Pr[N > n]\): \[\frac12\sum_k\big|\Pr[S = k] - \Pr[N = k]\big| = \frac12\left(\sum_{k=0}^n\big|\Pr[S = k] - \Pr[N = k]\big| + 1 - \sum_{k=0}^n\Pr[N = k]\right). \tag{1.9}\]
Evaluate with the chapter’s functions. binomial_poisson_tv in the solutions script computes this with binomial_pmf and poisson_pmf from distributions.py. Table 1.3 gives the results.




Table 1.3: Total variation distance between \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, 5/n)\) and \(\mathrm{Poisson}(5)\).





\(n\)
Total variation distance
\(n \times\) distance




10
0.171835
1.7184


100
0.012598
1.2598


1,000
0.001228
1.2276







Read off the rate. Each tenfold increase in \(n\) cuts the distance by about ten, and \(n\) times the distance settles near 1.23. So the distance is roughly \(1.23/n\), which confirms the check.

Why \(1/n\). The two distributions have the same mean \(\mu = 5\), but the binomial variance is \(np(1 - p) = \mu - \mu^2/n\), smaller than the Poisson’s \(\mu\) by \(\mu^2/n = 25/n\). The binomial is narrower by an amount of order \(1/n\), which is the gap Figure 1.1 shows at \(n = 10\).
(The chapter’s binomial_pmf evaluates \(\binom nk\) as an exact integer and then converts it to a float. That conversion overflows once \(n\) is a little above 1,000, so going further, to \(n = 10{,}000\), would need the PMF in log space, as poisson_pmf already does.)
The Poisson approximation to \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, \mu/n)\) is off by an amount of order \(1/n\), because the two variances differ by \(\mu^2/n\).

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
1.4 Median from absolute loss

Exercise 4. Median from absolute loss. Show that \(\sum_i|y_i - m|\) is minimized at any median of \(y_1, \dots, y_n\). Hint: look at the slope in \(m\). (Laplace)







TipSolution





Let \(f(m) = \sum_i|y_i - m|\). A median is any \(m\) with at most half the points strictly below it and at most half strictly above it: \(\#\{i : y_i < m\} \le n/2\) and \(\#\{i : y_i > m\} \le n/2\).

Slope of one term. As a function of \(m\), \(|y_i - m|\) has slope \(-1\) for \(m < y_i\) and \(+1\) for \(m > y_i\).
Slope of the sum. At any \(m\) that is not one of the \(y_i\), add the slopes: \[f'(m) = \#\{i : y_i < m\} - \#\{i : y_i > m\}. \tag{1.10}\]
The slope never decreases. As \(m\) moves right past a data point, that point moves from the “above” count to the “below” count, so the slope rises by 2 (more if several points coincide). So \(f\) is continuous and piecewise linear, with slopes that only increase: it is convex.
Where the minimum is. A convex piecewise-linear function is minimal exactly at the points where the slope just to the left is \(\le 0\) and the slope just to the right is \(\ge 0\). At \(m\), those one-sided slopes are \[f'(m^-) = \#\{y_i < m\} - \#\{y_i \ge m\}, \qquad f'(m^+) = \#\{y_i \le m\} - \#\{y_i > m\}. \tag{1.11}\]
Translate the two conditions. Since \(\#\{y_i \ge m\} = n - \#\{y_i < m\}\), the condition \(f'(m^-) \le 0\) says \(\#\{y_i < m\} \le n/2\). Since \(\#\{y_i \le m\} = n - \#\{y_i > m\}\), the condition \(f'(m^+) \ge 0\) says \(\#\{y_i > m\} \le n/2\). Together they are the definition of a median. So \(f\) is minimized exactly at the medians.

A small case. Take the data \(1, 2, 7\), and then add a fourth point, 10. Table 1.4 gives the slope of \(f\) on each interval.



Table 1.4: Slope of \(f(m) = \sum_i|y_i - m|\) between the data points, for three and for four data points.





Interval of \(m\)
Slope for \(1, 2, 7\)
Slope for \(1, 2, 7, 10\)

\(-4\)


\(1 < m < 2\)
\(-1\)

With three points the slope changes sign at \(m = 2\), the middle value, where \(f(2) = 1 + 0 + 5 = 6\). With four points the slope is 0 on \([2, 7]\), so every \(m\) there is a minimizer with \(f(m) = (m - 1) + (m - 2) + (7 - m) + (10 - m) = 14\), and every such \(m\) is a median. Now replace 10 by 1,000. No slope in the first three rows changes sign, so the minimizers are still \([2, 7]\), while the mean jumps from 5 to 252.5. This is the robustness that Example 1.6 describes.
Minimizing absolute error balances the count of points on each side, not their distances, so a median is the minimizer.

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
1.5 Laplace kurtosis

Exercise 5. Laplace kurtosis. Show that \(\mathbb E X^4/(\mathbb E X^2)^2\) is 6 for the Laplace and 3 for the normal. What does the larger value say about the shape? (Laplace, normal)







TipSolution





The ratio is the same for every location-0 member of each family, since scaling \(X\) by \(c\) multiplies both numerator and denominator by \(c^4\). Take location 0.
Laplace. Let \(X \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\).

Use \(|X| \sim \mathrm{Exp}(b)\). By Proposition 1.8 the size \(|X|\) is \(\mathrm{Exp}(b)\). Even powers do not see the sign, so \(\mathbb E X^4 = \mathbb E|X|^4\) and \(\mathbb E X^2 = \mathbb E|X|^2\).
Exponential moments. By Proposition 1.6, \(\mathbb E Y^k = k!\,b^k\) for \(Y \sim \mathrm{Exp}(b)\). So \(\mathbb E X^4 = 4!\,b^4 = 24b^4\) and \(\mathbb E X^2 = 2b^2\).
Divide. \(\mathbb E X^4/(\mathbb E X^2)^2 = 24b^4/(4b^4) = 6\).

Normal. Let \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and write \(X = \sigma Z\) with \(Z\) standard normal.

The moments of \(Z\). Step 2 of the proof of Proposition 1.13 reads \(\mathbb E Z^4 = 3\) off the MGF \(e^{\lambda^2/2}\), and \(\mathbb E Z^2 = 1\).
Scale. So \(\mathbb E X^4 = 3\sigma^4\) and \(\mathbb E X^2 = \sigma^2\), and \(\mathbb E X^4/(\mathbb E X^2)^2 = 3\sigma^4/\sigma^4 = 3\).

What the larger value says. The fourth power weighs values far from 0 much more heavily than the square does. At equal variance, a ratio of 6 against 3 means the Laplace puts more of its mass far out. To keep the same variance it must then also put more mass near 0, and less in the shoulders in between. That is the sharp peak and fat tails of Figure 1.4. The chapter’s comparison in Section 1.6 shows the tail side: \(\Pr[|X| \ge 3b] = e^{-3} \approx 0.050\) for the Laplace against about 0.034 for the normal with the same variance.
A larger fourth-moment ratio at the same variance means heavier tails and a sharper peak.

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
1.6 Maximum of normals

Exercise 6. Maximum of normals. For \(Z_1, \dots, Z_k \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) (not necessarily independent), show \(\mathbb E\max_i Z_i \le \sqrt{2\ln k}\). Hint: \(e^{\lambda\mathbb E\max} \le \mathbb E e^{\lambda\max} \le \sum_i\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z_i} = ke^{\lambda^2/2}\), then optimize \(\lambda\). (Normal MGF)







TipSolution





Take \(k \ge 2\) and any \(\lambda > 0\). Write \(M = \max_i Z_i\).

Jensen. \(u \mapsto e^{\lambda u}\) is convex, so \(e^{\lambda\mathbb E M} \le \mathbb E e^{\lambda M}\). (This is the same inequality the chapter uses for the norm, with a convex function instead of a concave one.)
Replace the max by a sum. Since \(\lambda > 0\), \(e^{\lambda M} = \max_i e^{\lambda Z_i}\). Every term is positive, so the maximum is at most the sum: \(e^{\lambda M} \le \sum_i e^{\lambda Z_i}\).
Take expectations. Linearity, which needs no independence, gives \(\mathbb E e^{\lambda M} \le \sum_i\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z_i}\). Each \(Z_i\) is \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), with MGF \(e^{\lambda^2/2}\) by Proposition 1.10, so the sum is \(ke^{\lambda^2/2}\).
Take logs and divide by \(\lambda\). From steps 1 to 3, \(\lambda\mathbb E M \le \ln k + \lambda^2/2\), so \[\mathbb E M \le \frac{\ln k}{\lambda} + \frac\lambda2 \qquad\text{for every } \lambda > 0. \tag{1.12}\]
Optimize \(\lambda\). The derivative of the right side is \(-\ln k/\lambda^2 + 1/2\), which is zero at \(\lambda = \sqrt{2\ln k}\) (positive because \(k \ge 2\)). There the two terms are equal, each \(\sqrt{2\ln k}/2\), so \[\mathbb E\max_i Z_i \le \sqrt{2\ln k}. \tag{1.13}\]

For \(k = 1\) the claim reads \(\mathbb E Z_1 \le 0\), which holds with equality.
How good is it? Only step 3 used the distribution, and only one \(Z_i\) at a time, so the bound holds whatever the dependence. When the \(Z_i\) are all the same variable, \(\mathbb E M = \mathbb E Z_1 = 0\), and the bound is far off. When they are independent, Table 1.5 compares it with simulation.



Table 1.5: Mean of the maximum of \(k\) independent \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) variables over 10,000 draws (seed 0), against the bound.

The \(k = 2\) row has an exact answer. \(\max(Z_1, Z_2) = \frac{Z_1 + Z_2}{2} + \frac{|Z_1 - Z_2|}{2}\), and \(Z_1 - Z_2 \sim \mathcal N(0, 2)\), so \(\mathbb E|Z_1 - Z_2| = \sqrt2\cdot\sqrt{2/\pi}\) and \(\mathbb E\max = 1/\sqrt\pi = 0.564\), consistent with the simulated 0.557. The bound is loose by a factor of about 2 at \(k = 2\), but the ratio climbs toward 1 as \(k\) grows: for independent normals, \(\sqrt{2\ln k}\) is the right growth rate.
The maximum of \(k\) standard normals grows only like \(\sqrt{2\ln k}\), whatever their dependence, because the normal MGF is \(e^{\lambda^2/2}\).

title: 1  Exercises: Probability distributions
text:
1.7 Random vectors are nearly orthogonal

Exercise 7. Random vectors are nearly orthogonal. For independent \(X, Y \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\), show \(\langle X, Y\rangle/(\|X\|\|Y\|)\) is of order \(1/\sqrt d\). Check by simulation for \(d = 10, 1000\). (Rotation invariance, norm concentration)







TipSolution





Let \(\rho = \langle X, Y\rangle/(\|X\|\|Y\|)\), the cosine of the angle between \(X\) and \(Y\).

Fix \(Y\). Condition on \(Y\) and let \(u = Y/\|Y\|\), a fixed unit vector. Since \(X\) is independent of \(Y\), \(X\) is still \(\mathcal N(0, I_d)\), and \[\rho = \frac{\langle u, X\rangle}{\|X\|}. \tag{1.14}\]
Numerator: rotation invariance. By Proposition 1.12, \(\langle u, X\rangle \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) for any unit \(u\). Its distribution does not depend on \(u\), so it does not depend on \(Y\) either.
Denominator: norm concentration. By Proposition 1.13, \(\|X\|^2/d\) has mean 1 and standard deviation \(\sqrt{2/d}\), so \(\|X\| = \sqrt d\,\big(1 \pm O(1/\sqrt d)\big)\).
Combine. \(\rho \approx \langle u, X\rangle/\sqrt d\): a standard normal divided by \(\sqrt d\). So \(\rho\) is typically of size \(1/\sqrt d\).

The exact standard deviation. Steps 3 and 4 are approximate, but the second moment is exact.

Turn \(u\) into the first coordinate. The \(\mathcal N(0, I_d)\) density \((2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|x\|^2/2}\) depends on \(x\) only through \(\|x\|\). A rotation \(R\) that maps \(u\) to \(e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0)\) preserves norms and inner products, so \(RX\) has the same distribution as \(X\), and \(\rho = \langle Ru, RX\rangle/\|RX\| = \langle e_1, RX\rangle/\|RX\|\). So \(\rho\) has the same distribution as \(X_1/\|X\|\). In \(d = 2\), for example, \(R\) turns the plane until \(u\) points along the first axis, and the circular contours of the density don’t move.
Symmetry among coordinates. The coordinates of \(X\) are independent and identically distributed, so \(\mathbb E[X_i^2/\|X\|^2]\) is the same for every \(i\). These \(d\) numbers add up to \(\mathbb E[\sum_iX_i^2/\|X\|^2] = 1\), so each is \(1/d\).
Mean and standard deviation. \(X\) and \(-X\) have the same distribution, so \(\mathbb E \rho = 0\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\rho) = \mathbb E \rho^2 = 1/d\). The standard deviation of \(\rho\) is exactly \(1/\sqrt d\).

Simulation. Table 1.6 reports 10,000 pairs for each \(d\).

2.1 Tightness of Markov
Exercises for Concentration inequalities, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
Exercise 1. Tightness of Markov. For given \(\mu\) and \(a\), construct the distribution attaining \(\Pr[X \ge a] = \mu/a\), and explain why no variable with mean \(\mu\) can do worse. (Markov)







TipSolution





Take \(0 < \mu \le a\). (If \(\mu > a\), the bound \(\mu/a\) exceeds 1 and says nothing; the constant \(X = \mu\) has \(\Pr[X \ge a] = 1\).)
The construction.

Let \(X = a\) with probability \(\mu/a\) and \(X = 0\) otherwise. This is a valid distribution because \(\mu/a \le 1\), and \(X \ge 0\).
Its mean is \(a \cdot \mu/a + 0 = \mu\).
\(X \ge a\) happens exactly when \(X = a\), so \(\Pr[X \ge a] = \mu/a\), which is Markov’s bound.

Why no variable can do worse. The proof of Theorem 2.1 used nothing about \(X\) except \(X \ge 0\) and \(\mathbb E[X] = \mu\). So every non-negative \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) has \(\Pr[X \ge a] \le \mu/a\), and the two-point variable reaches that ceiling.
Why this variable, and only this one. The only inequality in that proof is step 1, \(a\,\mathbf 1[X \ge a] \le X\). Equality after averaging needs equality on every outcome (up to probability zero), so \(X\) must equal \(a\) where \(X \ge a\) and \(0\) where \(X < a\). Take \(\mu = 1\) and \(a = 4\) and compare the two rows, as in Table 2.1:



Table 2.1: The scaled indicator and the variable agree on every outcome of the two-point distribution with \(\mu = 1\), \(a = 4\), so Markov loses nothing.





Outcome
\(X = 0\) (prob. \(3/4\))
\(X = 4\) (prob. \(1/4\))
Average




\(4\cdot\mathbf 1[X \ge 4]\)
0
4
\(4\Pr[X \ge 4] = 1\)


\(X\)
0
4
\(1\)






The two rows of Table 2.1 are identical. On the die, by contrast, every roll except 5 had slack. Any mass strictly between 0 and \(a\), or strictly above \(a\), creates slack, because it adds to the mean without adding to \(\Pr[X \ge a]\) at the full rate.
Non-negativity matters. Without it, \(X = a\) with probability \(1 - \xi\) and \(X = -(a(1-\xi) - \mu)/\xi\) otherwise has mean \(\mu\) and \(\Pr[X \ge a] = 1 - \xi\), as close to 1 as you like.
Markov is the best bound that uses only the mean: its worst case puts all the mass at \(0\) and \(a\).

title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
2.2 Cantelli’s inequality

Exercise 2. Cantelli’s inequality. Show that \(\Pr[X - \mu \ge t] \le \sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + t^2)\). Hint: apply Markov to \((X - \mu + u)^2\) for \(u > 0\), then optimize \(u\). (Generalized Markov)







TipSolution





Let \(Y = X - \mu\), so \(\mathbb E[Y] = 0\) and \(\mathbb E[Y^2] = \sigma^2\). Take \(t > 0\) and any \(u > 0\).

Event inclusion. If \(Y \ge t\), then \(Y + u \ge t + u > 0\), and squaring two positive numbers keeps the order: \((Y + u)^2 \ge (t + u)^2\). So \(\Pr[Y \ge t] \le \Pr[(Y + u)^2 \ge (t + u)^2]\). (The function \((y+u)^2\) is not increasing everywhere, so this is only an inclusion, not an equality. That is enough.)
Markov on the non-negative variable \((Y + u)^2\) with threshold \((t+u)^2\): \[\Pr[Y \ge t] \le \frac{\mathbb E[(Y + u)^2]}{(t + u)^2} = \frac{\sigma^2 + 2u\,\mathbb E[Y] + u^2}{(t + u)^2} = \frac{\sigma^2 + u^2}{(t + u)^2}. \tag{2.1}\]
Optimize \(u\). The log of the right side is \(\ln(\sigma^2 + u^2) - 2\ln(t + u)\), with derivative \(\frac{2u}{\sigma^2 + u^2} - \frac{2}{t + u}\). It vanishes when \(u(t + u) = \sigma^2 + u^2\), that is, at \(u = \sigma^2/t > 0\). The derivative is negative below this point and positive above it, so it is the minimum.
Substitute \(u = \sigma^2/t\). The numerator is \(\sigma^2 + \sigma^4/t^2 = \sigma^2(t^2 + \sigma^2)/t^2\), and the denominator is \((t + \sigma^2/t)^2 = (t^2 + \sigma^2)^2/t^2\). Their ratio is \[\Pr[X - \mu \ge t] \le \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + t^2}. \tag{2.2}\]

How it compares with Chebyshev. Setting \(u = 0\) in step 2 gives back \(\sigma^2/t^2\). The shift \(u\) helps because a one-sided event lets you move the centre of the square towards the side you don’t care about. At \(t = \sigma\), Chebyshev gives 1 and Cantelli gives \(1/2\). For a standard normal at \(t = 3\), Cantelli gives \(1/10 = 0.1\) against Chebyshev’s \(0.111\) (Table 2.3): the gain fades for large \(t\), where both decay like \(\sigma^2/t^2\).
It is tight. Let \(Y = t\) with probability \(p = \sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + t^2)\) and \(Y = -\sigma^2/t\) otherwise. Its mean is \(tp - (\sigma^2/t)(1 - p) = \frac{t\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 t}{\sigma^2 + t^2} = 0\), its variance is \(t^2 p + (\sigma^4/t^2)(1-p) = \frac{t^2\sigma^2 + \sigma^4}{\sigma^2 + t^2} = \sigma^2\), and \(\Pr[Y \ge t] = p\).
A one-sided question deserves a one-sided bound: shifting before squaring buys up to a factor of 2 over Chebyshev.

title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
2.3 A direct Hoeffding lemma

Exercise 3. A direct Hoeffding lemma. For \(X = \pm1\) with probability \(\frac12\) each, show that \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}] = \cosh\lambda \le e^{\lambda^2/2}\). Hint: compare Taylor series term by term, using \((2k)! \ge 2^k k!\). (Sub-Gaussian)







TipSolution






The moment generating function (MGF). \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}] = \frac12 e^{\lambda} + \frac12 e^{-\lambda} = \cosh\lambda\).
Its series. Add the series of \(e^\lambda\) and \(e^{-\lambda}\) and halve. Odd powers cancel and even powers survive: \(\cosh\lambda = \sum_{k \ge 0}\frac{\lambda^{2k}}{(2k)!}\).
The series of the bound. Substitute \(\lambda^2/2\) into \(e^x = \sum_k x^k/k!\): \(e^{\lambda^2/2} = \sum_{k \ge 0}\frac{\lambda^{2k}}{2^k k!}\).
The factorial inequality. Group \((2k)!\) into \(k\) pairs of consecutive factors: \[(2k)! = \prod_{i=1}^{k}(2i - 1)(2i) \ge \prod_{i=1}^{k} 2i = 2^k k!, \tag{2.3}\] since each odd factor \(2i - 1\) is at least 1.
Compare term by term. Both series have the same powers \(\lambda^{2k} \ge 0\). By step 4 each coefficient of \(\cosh\lambda\) is at most the matching coefficient of \(e^{\lambda^2/2}\). Summing gives \(\cosh\lambda \le e^{\lambda^2/2}\) for every real \(\lambda\).

Table 2.2 shows the first four terms.

So \(X\) is 1-sub-Gaussian. Hoeffding’s lemma (Lemma 2.2) on \([l, u] = [-1, 1]\) gives the same constant, \((u - l)/2 = 1\): this fair coin on the endpoints is exactly the lemma’s worst case. The series comparison reaches the same constant without the convexity argument.

title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
2.4 Sample size for a mean

Exercise 4. Sample size for a mean. How many samples in \([0, 1]\) does Hoeffding need to estimate a mean to within \(\pm0.01\) with probability 0.99? Check: \(n \ge \ln(200)/(2\times10^{-4}) \approx 26{,}500\). (Hoeffding, inverting a tail bound)







TipSolution






Two-sided Hoeffding (Theorem 2.5) for the mean of \(n\) independent variables in \([0, 1]\), so \(u - l = 1\): \(\Pr[|\bar X_n - \mu| \ge t] \le 2e^{-2nt^2}\) (the one-sided bound, doubled for the lower tail).
Set the failure probability to \(\beta = 1 - 0.99 = 0.01\) and require \(2e^{-2nt^2} \le \beta\).
Solve for \(n\) (Lemma 2.1): take logs, \(-2nt^2 \le \ln(\beta/2)\), so \[n \ge \frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2t^2} = \frac{\ln 200}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = 26{,}491.6. \tag{2.4}\]
\(n\) is an integer, so \(n = 26{,}492\) samples suffice. This matches the check value.

For comparison, Chebyshev with the largest possible variance on \([0, 1]\), \(\sigma^2 \le 1/4\), needs \(n \ge \sigma^2/(t^2\beta) = 0.25/(10^{-4} \times 0.01) = 250{,}000\): almost ten times more. The \(\ln(1/\beta)\) in Hoeffding against the \(1/\beta\) in Chebyshev is the whole difference.
Halving the error multiplies \(n\) by 4; dividing the failure probability by 10 only adds \(\ln 10/(2t^2)\).

title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
2.5 Noisy argmax

Exercise 5. Noisy argmax. You add independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise to each of \(k\) scores and pick the largest noisy score. Show that with probability at least \(1-\beta\), the true score of the item you pick is within \(2b\ln(k/\beta)\) of the true maximum. (Laplace tail + union bound)







TipSolution





Write \(u_1, \dots, u_k\) for the true scores, \(Z_1, \dots, Z_k\) for the noise, \(i^*\) for an item with the largest true score, and \(\hat\imath\) for the item with the largest noisy score \(u_i + Z_i\). Let \(\tau = b\ln(k/\beta)\).

One draw (Laplace tail, Proposition 2.3). For each \(i\), \(\Pr[|Z_i| \ge \tau] = e^{-\tau/b} = \beta/k\).
All draws at once (union bound, Lemma 2.3). \(\Pr[\text{some } |Z_i| \ge \tau] \le k \cdot \beta/k = \beta\). So the event \(G\) = “every \(|Z_i| < \tau\)” has probability at least \(1 - \beta\).
The choice. \(\hat\imath\) maximizes the noisy score, so in particular \(u_{\hat\imath} + Z_{\hat\imath} \ge u_{i^*} + Z_{i^*}\).
Rearrange: \(u_{i^*} - u_{\hat\imath} \le Z_{\hat\imath} - Z_{i^*}\).
On \(G\), both noise terms are below \(\tau\) in absolute value, so \(Z_{\hat\imath} - Z_{i^*} < 2\tau\). Hence \(u_{i^*} - u_{\hat\imath} < 2b\ln(k/\beta)\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).

Why step 2 needs the union bound. The picked item \(\hat\imath\) depends on the noise: it tends to be an item whose noise came out large. So you can’t apply the one-draw bound to \(Z_{\hat\imath}\) as if \(\hat\imath\) were fixed in advance. Bounding all \(k\) noise terms at once covers whichever item gets picked.
Size. With \(k = 100\), \(b = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\), the guarantee is \(2\ln 2000 = 15.20\), twice the maximum-of-Laplace bound 7.60 of Table 2.3. It grows only like \(\ln k\). It is loose, because it charges the worst case on both sides: the picked item’s noise at \(+\tau\) and the best item’s at \(-\tau\).
Selecting with noise costs at most twice the largest noise, and the largest of \(k\) noises costs only \(\ln k\).

title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
2.6 Chernoff for a Poisson

Exercise 6. Chernoff for a Poisson. For \(N \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\), show that \(\Pr[N \ge (1+r)\mu]\) satisfies exactly the same bound as the Bernoulli sum. Why is that no coincidence? (Chernoff)







TipSolution






The MGF. \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda N}] = \exp(\mu(e^\lambda - 1))\) (Probability distributions).
The Chernoff bound (Theorem 2.3) with \(t = (1 + r)\mu\) and \(\lambda > 0\): \(\Pr[N \ge (1+r)\mu] \le \exp\big(\mu(e^\lambda - 1) - \lambda(1+r)\mu\big)\).
This is the Bernoulli expression. Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 2.4 reached exactly this exponent. Steps 4 and 5 there worked on that exponent alone, without going back to the Bernoullis. So they apply verbatim: \(\lambda = \ln(1 + r)\) gives \[\Pr[N \ge (1+r)\mu] \le \exp\big(-\mu[(1+r)\ln(1+r) - r]\big) \le \exp\left(-\frac{r^2\mu}{2+r}\right). \tag{2.5}\] The lower tail works the same way: step 6 of that proof also reduced to \(\exp(\lambda s + \mu(e^{-\lambda} - 1))\), which is the Poisson MGF at \(-\lambda\).

Why it is no coincidence. Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 2.4 replaced each factor \(1 + p_i(e^\lambda - 1)\) by \(\exp(p_i(e^\lambda - 1))\), the MGF of a \(\mathrm{Poisson}(p_i)\). The product of those is the MGF of a sum of independent Poissons, which is \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\). So the Bernoulli-sum bound is the Chernoff bound of \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\), used as an upper bound on the MGF of the sum. For the Poisson itself, that step is an equality and nothing is lost. The Poisson is the worst case among sums of independent Bernoullis with mean \(\mu\), as far as the MGF can tell. It is also their limit as every \(p_i \to 0\), so a bound that depends only on \(\mu\) and holds for all Bernoulli sums has to hold for the Poisson anyway.
How tight. For \(\mu = 10\) and \(r = 1\), the exact tail \(\Pr[N \ge 20]\) is \(3.45\times10^{-3}\). The optimized bound gives \(2.10\times10^{-2}\) and the simplified one \(3.57\times10^{-2}\): about 6 and 10 times too large. The exponent is right (Cramér’s theorem); what the bound misses is a prefactor of order \(1/\sqrt\mu\).

title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
2.7 Azuma for the coin game

Exercise 7. Azuma for the coin game. Modify the script to use a different adaptive rule (for example, pick the 0.7 coin after two heads in a row). Check that the Azuma bound still holds and explain why the rule does not matter. (Azuma)







TipSolution





The modification. Make the rule a parameter. A rule sees only the past (the last two flips and the running martingale) and says, for each simulated game, whether the next flip uses the 0.7 coin:
Rule = Callable[[BoolArray, BoolArray, FloatArray], BoolArray]

def rule_after_two_heads(last: BoolArray, before: BoolArray, m: FloatArray) -> BoolArray:
    return last & before

def adaptive_martingale(rng, rule: Rule, n: int, p_low: float, p_high: float, trials: int) -> FloatArray:
    m = np.zeros(trials)
    last = np.zeros(trials, dtype=bool)
    before = np.zeros(trials, dtype=bool)
    for _ in range(n):
        p = np.where(rule(last, before, m), p_high, p_low)  # chosen from the past only
        x = rng.random(trials) < p
        m += x - p
        before, last = last, x
    return m
The solutions script runs four rules, with \(n = 200\) flips, \(t = 20\) and \(10^6\) games each. “When behind” tries to push the martingale up by using the 0.7 coin whenever \(W_{k-1} < 0\). “Always 0.7” is not adaptive at all, so its heads count is \(\mathrm{Bin}(200, 0.7)\) and \(\Pr[W_{200} \ge 20] = \Pr[\text{heads} \ge 160]\) can be computed exactly: \(9.28\times10^{-4}\).



Table 2.3: Tail of the coin-game martingale at \(t = 20\) after 200 flips, under four adaptive rules, with \(10^6\) simulated games per rule and seed 0.









Rule for using the 0.7 coin
Empirical \(\Pr[W_{200} \ge 20]\)




After one head (the chapter’s game)
\(9.13\times10^{-4}\)


After two heads in a row
\(1.10\times10^{-3}\)


When behind (\(W_{k-1} < 0\))
\(1.18\times10^{-3}\)

Azuma bound \(e^{-2t^2/n}\), any rule
\(1.83\times10^{-2}\)


Normal approximation, variance \(200 \times 0.21\)
\(1.01\times10^{-3}\)






The Azuma bound holds for every rule in Table 2.3, with a margin of more than 15 times. (The chapter’s \(1.12\times10^{-3}\) for the first rule came from \(10^5\) games; with about 110 games in the tail, its standard error is about \(1.1\times10^{-4}\), so it is within two standard errors of \(9.13\times10^{-4}\).)
Why the rule does not matter. The proof of Theorem 2.7 used only one fact about each increment: given the past, \(U_k\) has mean zero and lies in an interval of length \(d_k\). Check it for any rule that decides from the past.

The rule fixes \(p_k\) before flip \(k\), so given the past, \(p_k\) is a constant.
Given the past, \(X_k\) is a \(\mathrm{Bern}(p_k)\) flip, so \(U_k = X_k - p_k\) has conditional mean \(p_k - p_k = 0\).
\(U_k\) takes the values \(1 - p_k\) and \(-p_k\), so it lies in \([-p_k, 1 - p_k]\), an interval of length \(d_k = 1\).

Concretely, after the history “heads, heads” the two-heads rule picks \(p_k = 0.7\): \(U_k = +0.3\) with probability 0.7 and \(-0.7\) with probability 0.3, with mean \(0.21 - 0.21 = 0\). After any other history it picks \(0.3\): \(U_k = +0.7\) or \(-0.3\), again with mean 0. With \(d_k = 1\) for all 200 steps, \(\sum_k d_k^2 = 200\) and the bound is \(e^{-2 \cdot 20^2/200}\) whatever the rule. A rule that peeked at flip \(k\) before choosing its coin would break step 2. That is the one thing adaptivity may not do.
Why the simulated tails barely move either. Both coins have the same variance, \(0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.21\). So whatever the rule picks, each increment has conditional variance 0.21, and the martingale’s total variance is \(200 \times 0.21 = 42\). The normal approximation with that variance gives \(1.01\times10^{-3}\), close to every row. Azuma assumes the worst-case per-step variance \(d_k^2/4 = 0.25\) and uses a Chernoff-type exponent, which is why it sits 15 to 20 times above.
Azuma needs only “mean zero and bounded given the past”, which no rule that decides from the past can break.

title: 2  Exercises: Concentration inequalities
text:
2.8 Low-rate estimate

Exercise 8. Low-rate estimate. You observe 3 false positives in 5,000 trials. Give 95% upper bounds on the rate using Hoeffding, Bernstein, the multiplicative Chernoff bound, and the exact Clopper–Pearson interval (scipy.stats.beta.ppf). Explain the ranking. Check: Clopper–Pearson gives \(\approx 0.00155\). (Hoeffding vs variance-aware bounds)







TipSolution





Let \(p\) be the true rate, \(n = 5000\), \(s = 3\) the count, \(\hat p = s/n = 0.0006\), and \(\beta = 0.05\), so \(\ln(1/\beta) = \ln 20 \approx 3.00\). An upper bound needs the lower tail: a candidate rate \(p\) is ruled out when, were \(p\) true, a count as low as 3 would have probability below \(\beta\). The 95% upper bound is the largest \(p\) not ruled out. For a bound of the form “\(\hat p < p - w\) with probability at most \(\beta\)”, that is simply \(\hat p + w\) (Lemma 2.1).

Hoeffding (one-sided, range \([0, 1]\)): \(w = \sqrt{\ln 20/(2 \times 5000)}\), so the upper bound is \(0.0179\).
Bernstein (Theorem 2.6) with \(R = 1\), applied to the lower tail (to \(-X_i\), which has the same variance and range). The plug-in version of Example 2.4, with \(\sigma^2 \approx \hat p(1 - \hat p)\), gives \(\hat p + \sqrt{2\hat p(1-\hat p)\ln 20/n} + 2\ln 20/(3n) = 0.00185\). But a candidate \(p\) above \(\hat p\) has a larger variance \(p(1-p)\), so the plug-in is optimistic. The rigorous version uses each candidate’s own variance: rule out \(p\) when \(\exp\big(-n(p - \hat p)^2/(2p(1-p) + \frac23(p - \hat p))\big) < \beta\). The largest \(p\) not ruled out, found by bisection, is \(0.00256\).
Multiplicative Chernoff (Theorem 2.4), lower tail \(\Pr[S \le (1-r)\mu] \le e^{-r^2\mu/2}\) with \(\mu = np\). At \(s = (1-r)\mu\) the exponent is \(r^2\mu/2 = (\mu - s)^2/(2\mu)\). Rule out \(\mu\) when \((\mu - s)^2 > 2\mu\ln 20\). The boundary is the larger root of \(\mu^2 - 2(s + \ln 20)\mu + s^2 = 0\): \[\mu = s + \ln 20 + \sqrt{(\ln 20)^2 + 2s\ln 20}, \tag{2.6}\] which gives the upper bound \(\mu/n = 0.00224\). With the unsimplified exponent \(\mu[r + (1-r)\ln(1-r)] = \mu - s + s\ln(s/\mu)\), it is \(0.00189\).
Clopper–Pearson. The largest \(p\) with \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(5000, p) \le 3] \ge 0.05\). The script finds it by bisection on the binomial cumulative sum; it equals scipy.stats.beta.ppf(0.95, 4, 4997). The result is \(0.00155\), matching the check value.




Table 2.4: One-sided 95% upper bounds on a rate after 3 events in 5,000 trials (observed rate 0.0006).





Method
95% upper bound on the rate




Hoeffding
0.0179


Bernstein (each candidate’s own variance)
0.00256


Chernoff, \(e^{-r^2\mu/2}\)
0.00224


Chernoff, unsimplified exponent
0.00189


Clopper–Pearson (exact)
0.00155


Bernstein, plug-in \(\hat p(1-\hat p)\) (heuristic)

The ranking in Table 2.4 follows how much each method knows about the count.

Hoeffding knows only the range, so it assumes the variance \(1/4\). The true variance is about \(0.0006\), over 400 times smaller. Its bound is 30 times the observed rate and more than 10 times the exact one.
Bernstein knows the variance. That removes most of the gap, but it pays for the range term \(\frac23 R(p - \hat p)\) with \(R = 1\) and for its constants.
Chernoff knows the whole MGF of a Bernoulli sum, through its Poisson bound. Simplifying the exponent to \(r^2\mu/2\) costs some of that.
Clopper–Pearson uses the binomial distribution itself, with no inequality at all. Nothing valid can be smaller.

The plug-in Bernstein value looks better than the rigorous one, but only because it uses the variance at \(\hat p\), which is too small for the rates it should be ruling in.
Near zero, only variance-aware bounds are usable, and with 3 events even the exact bound is 2.6 times the observed rate.

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.1 Chain rule for KL
Exercises for Divergences, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_divergences.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_divergences.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation and three acronyms: the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, the total variation (TV) distance and the data processing inequality (DPI). \(r = p/q\) is the likelihood ratio and \(L = \ln r\) the log-likelihood ratio, logarithms are natural, and on the die \(P\) is the loaded die and \(Q\) the fair one (Table 3.1).

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
Exercise 1. Chain rule for KL. For joint distributions \(P_{XY}\) and \(Q_{XY}\), show \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{XY}\|Q_{XY}) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_X\|Q_X) + \mathbb E_{x\sim P_X}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y\mid x}\|Q_{Y\mid x})\big]\), and recover additivity as the special case of independent coordinates. Hint: factor \(p(x, y) = p(x)p(y\mid x)\) inside the logarithm. (KL, additivity)







TipSolution






Factor both joints. \(p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y\mid x)\) and \(q(x, y) = q(x)\,q(y\mid x)\), where \(p(x)\), \(q(x)\) are the marginals of \(X\).
The log-likelihood ratio splits into a sum (the logarithm of a product): \[\ln\frac{p(x, y)}{q(x, y)} = \ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} + \ln\frac{p(y\mid x)}{q(y\mid x)}. \tag{3.1}\]
Average the first term under \(P_{XY}\). It depends only on \(x\), so its average is \(\sum_xp(x)\ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_X\|Q_X)\).
Average the second term in two stages: first over \(y\) given \(x\), then over \(x\). For fixed \(x\), \(\sum_yp(y\mid x)\ln\frac{p(y\mid x)}{q(y\mid x)} = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y\mid x}\|Q_{Y\mid x})\). Averaging over \(x \sim P_X\) gives the expected conditional KL.
Add the two averages (linearity of expectation). This is the chain rule.

Additivity. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent under both distributions, then \(p(y\mid x) = p_2(y)\) and \(q(y\mid x) = q_2(y)\) for every \(x\). The conditional KL in step 4 is then \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_2\|Q_2)\) for every \(x\), and its average over \(x\) is the same number. The chain rule becomes Equation 3.3.
Concretely, on the die. Let \(Y\) be the roll and \(X\) its parity. Then \((X, Y)\) carries the same information as \(Y\), so the left side is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.2939\). The parity part is \(0.0823\) (from Table 3.7). Given “even”, the loaded die gives rolls 2, 4, 6 with probabilities \(0.1/0.7, 0.1/0.7, 0.5/0.7 = \frac17, \frac17, \frac57\), and the fair die gives \(\frac13\) each. Given “odd”, both are uniform on 1, 3, 5.

The chain rule says exactly how much the data-processing inequality loses: the KL dropped by keeping only \(X\) is the expected KL of what you threw away.

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.2 Gaussians with different variances

Exercise 2. Gaussians with different variances. Show \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal N(m_0, \sigma_0^2)\|\mathcal N(m_1, \sigma_1^2)) = \ln\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0} + \frac{\sigma_0^2 + (m_0 - m_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} - \frac12\). Check: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal N(0, 1)\|\mathcal N(0, 4)) = \ln2 + \frac18 - \frac12 = 0.3181\). For the Rényi divergence, repeat the proof of Proposition 3.3 and find the condition on \(\alpha\) under which the integral is finite. Hint: the coefficient of \(x^2\) must stay negative: \(\alpha/\sigma_0^2 + (1-\alpha)/\sigma_1^2 > 0\). (Completing the square)







TipSolution





Write \(P = \mathcal N(m_0, \sigma_0^2)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(m_1, \sigma_1^2)\), with means \(m_0, m_1\), and \(s = m_0 - m_1\).
KL.

The log-likelihood ratio. The normal density is \(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x - m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) for mean \(m\), so \[L(x) = \ln\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0} - \frac{(x - m_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2} + \frac{(x - m_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}. \tag{3.2}\] Unlike the equal-variance case, \(L\) is quadratic in \(x\).
Two second moments under \(P\). \(\mathbb E_P(X - m_0)^2 = \sigma_0^2\). For the other, write \(X - m_1 = (X - m_0) + s\); the cross term averages to 0, so \(\mathbb E_P(X - m_1)^2 = \sigma_0^2 + s^2\).
Average \(L\) under \(P\): \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \ln\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0} - \frac12 + \frac{\sigma_0^2 + s^2}{2\sigma_1^2}\), the claimed formula.
Check. For \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\|\mathcal N(0, 4)\): \(\sigma_0 = 1\), \(\sigma_1 = 2\), \(s = 0\), so \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \ln2 + \frac18 - \frac12 = 0.3181\). A numerical integral of \(p\ln(p/q)\) gives 0.3181 as well. In the other direction, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal N(0, 4)\|\mathcal N(0, 1)) = -\ln2 + 2 - \frac12 = 0.8069\): KL is not symmetric here. With \(\sigma_0 = \sigma_1\) the formula reduces to \(s^2/(2\sigma^2)\), as in Equation 3.19.

Rényi, as in the proof of Proposition 3.3.

Constants. \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) has the constant factor \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sigma_0^{-\alpha}\sigma_1^{-(1-\alpha)}\) times \(\exp\big(-\frac12B(x)\big)\), with \[B(x) = w_0(x - m_0)^2 + w_1(x - m_1)^2, \qquad w_0 = \frac{\alpha}{\sigma_0^2},\quad w_1 = \frac{1 - \alpha}{\sigma_1^2}. \tag{3.3}\]
Finiteness. The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \(-\frac12B\) is \(-\frac12(w_0 + w_1)\). If \(w_0 + w_1 \le 0\), the integrand does not decay in at least one direction (it grows like \(e^{cx^2}\), or, when the coefficient is exactly 0, like \(e^{cx}\) or a constant), and the integral is infinite. So the integral is finite exactly when \[w_0 + w_1 = \frac{\alpha}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{1 - \alpha}{\sigma_1^2} > 0 \iff \sigma_\alpha^2 := \alpha\sigma_1^2 + (1 - \alpha)\sigma_0^2 > 0 \tag{3.4}\] (multiply by \(\sigma_0^2\sigma_1^2 > 0\)). Note \(w_0 + w_1 = \sigma_\alpha^2/(\sigma_0^2\sigma_1^2)\).
Complete the square. For weights with \(w_0 + w_1 > 0\), \(w_0(x - m_0)^2 + w_1(x - m_1)^2 = (w_0 + w_1)(x - \bar m)^2 + \frac{w_0w_1}{w_0 + w_1}s^2\) with \(\bar m = \frac{w_0m_0 + w_1m_1}{w_0 + w_1}\). (Expand both sides: the \(x^2\) and \(x\) terms match by the choice of \(\bar m\), and the constant is what is left.) Here \(\frac{w_0w_1}{w_0 + w_1} = \frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{\sigma_0^2\sigma_1^2}\cdot\frac{\sigma_0^2\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_\alpha^2} = \frac{\alpha(1 - \alpha)}{\sigma_\alpha^2}\).
Integrate. \(\int e^{-(w_0 + w_1)(x - \bar m)^2/2}\mathrm dx = \sqrt{2\pi/(w_0 + w_1)} = \sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_0\sigma_1/\sigma_\alpha\). So \[\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,\mathrm dx = \frac{\sigma_0^{1-\alpha}\sigma_1^{\alpha}}{\sigma_\alpha}\exp\left(-\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)s^2}{2\sigma_\alpha^2}\right). \tag{3.5}\]
Take the logarithm and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). The exponent gives \(\frac{\alpha s^2}{2\sigma_\alpha^2}\), as in the equal-variance case. The prefactor gives \(\frac{(1-\alpha)\ln\sigma_0 + \alpha\ln\sigma_1 - \ln\sigma_\alpha}{\alpha - 1} = \ln\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0} + \frac{\ln\sigma_1 - \ln\sigma_\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\). Together, \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \ln\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0} + \frac{1}{2(\alpha - 1)}\ln\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_\alpha^2} + \frac{\alpha s^2}{2\sigma_\alpha^2} \quad\text{if } \sigma_\alpha^2 > 0, \qquad D_\alpha = \infty \text{ otherwise}. \tag{3.6}\]

When is it finite? For \(0 < \alpha < 1\), \(\sigma_\alpha^2\) is a weighted average of two positive numbers, so always positive. For \(\alpha > 1\), \(\sigma_\alpha^2 = \sigma_0^2 + \alpha(\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_0^2)\). If \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_0\) (the second distribution is at least as wide), it is positive for every \(\alpha\). If \(\sigma_1 < \sigma_0\), it is positive only for \[\alpha < \frac{\sigma_0^2}{\sigma_0^2 - \sigma_1^2}. \tag{3.7}\] The reason: \(r^{\alpha-1}\) grows like \(e^{cx^2}\) in the tails when \(Q\) is the narrower one, and for large \(\alpha\) that beats the decay of \(p\).
Checks. As \(\alpha \to 1\), \(\sigma_\alpha^2 \to \sigma_1^2\) and \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_\alpha^2} \to -\frac{\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_0^2}{\sigma_1^2}\) (the derivative of \(-\ln\sigma_\alpha^2\) at \(\alpha = 1\)), so \(D_\alpha \to \ln\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0} + \frac{\sigma_0^2}{2\sigma_1^2} - \frac12 + \frac{s^2}{2\sigma_1^2}\), the KL above. With \(\sigma_0 = \sigma_1\), \(\sigma_\alpha = \sigma\) and only \(\alpha s^2/(2\sigma^2)\) remains, which is Equation 3.19. Table 3.2 compares the formula with a numerical integral.

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.3 Bhattacharyya and Hellinger

Exercise 3. Bhattacharyya and Hellinger. Show \(D_{1/2}(P\|Q) = -2\ln\big(1 - \frac12H^2\big)\) with \(H^2 = \sum(\sqrt p - \sqrt q)^2\), and check it on the die using Table 3.6 and Table 3.4. For the Gaussian pair, show \(D_{1/2} = \mu^2/4\). (Rényi, f-divergences)







TipSolution






\(D_{1/2}\) in terms of the Bhattacharyya coefficient. Put \(\alpha = \frac12\) in the definition: \(D_{1/2} = \frac{1}{-1/2}\ln\sum_xp^{1/2}q^{1/2} = -2\ln\mathrm{BC}\), with \(\mathrm{BC} = \sum_x\sqrt{p(x)q(x)}\).
Expand the Hellinger sum. \((\sqrt p - \sqrt q)^2 = p - 2\sqrt{pq} + q\). Sum over \(x\): \(p\) and \(q\) each sum to 1, so \(H^2 = 2 - 2\,\mathrm{BC}\).
Solve for \(\mathrm{BC}\): \(\mathrm{BC} = 1 - \frac12H^2\). Substitute into step 1: \(D_{1/2} = -2\ln\big(1 - \frac12H^2\big)\).

On the die. Table 3.6 gives \(H^2 = 0.1317\). Then \(\mathrm{BC} = 1 - 0.06585 = 0.9342\) and \(-2\ln0.9342 = 0.1362\), the \(\alpha = 0.5\) entry of Table 3.4 in both directions.
For the Gaussian pair. \(P = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(Q = \mathcal N(s, \sigma^2)\), \(\mu = s/\sigma\).

Step 5 of the proof of Proposition 3.3, at \(\alpha = \frac12\), gives \(\mathrm{BC} = \int\sqrt{pq}\,\mathrm dx = \exp\big(-\frac{\frac12\cdot\frac12 s^2}{2\sigma^2}\big) = e^{-\mu^2/8}\).
So \(D_{1/2} = -2\ln e^{-\mu^2/8} = \mu^2/4\). This is Equation 3.19 at \(\alpha = \frac12\).
As a by-product, \(H^2 = 2\big(1 - e^{-\mu^2/8}\big)\).

At \(\mu = 1/\sqrt2\) (the Gaussian pair with the variance of the Laplace pair at \(t = 1\)) this gives \(D_{1/2} = 0.1250\), the entry in Table 3.5.
Rényi divergence of order \(\frac12\) and squared Hellinger distance carry the same information: each is an increasing function of the other.

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.4 Rejection sampling

Exercise 4. Rejection sampling. In Example 3.6, show in general that \(\mathrm{TV}(P, \tilde P) \le E_\gamma(P\|Q)\). Hint: write \(\min(p, \gamma q) = p - e\) with \(e = (p - \gamma q)_+\), so \(\tilde p = (p - e)/(1 - E_\gamma)\), and use \(e \le p\). (Hockey-stick)







TipSolution





Write \(E = E_\gamma(P\|Q)\) and assume \(E < 1\), so that some proposals are accepted.

The uncovered part. \(\min(p, \gamma q) = p - (p - \gamma q)_+ = p - e\). (Where \(p \le \gamma q\), \(e = 0\) and the min is \(p\); where \(p > \gamma q\), the min is \(\gamma q = p - e\).)
Normalize. \(\sum_xe(x) = E\) by the definition of \(E_\gamma\), so \(\sum_x\min(p, \gamma q) = 1 - E\) and \(\tilde p = (p - e)/(1 - E)\).
The difference \(p - \tilde p\). \(p - \tilde p = \frac{p(1 - E) - p + e}{1 - E} = \frac{e - pE}{1 - E}\).
Use \(e \le p\). Since \(e \le p\) and \(E \ge 0\), \(e - pE \le e - eE = e(1 - E)\). The right side is non-negative, so \((e - pE)_+ \le e(1 - E)\).
Sum, using the form \(\mathrm{TV} = \sum(p - \tilde p)_+\) of Equation 3.30: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, \tilde P) = \frac{1}{1 - E}\sum_x(e - pE)_+ \le \frac{1}{1 - E}\sum_xe(1 - E) = E. \tag{3.8}\]

On the die. Table 3.3 runs the envelope \(\gamma\cdot\)fair over the range \(1 \le \gamma \le 3\). The bound holds everywhere, and both sides reach 0 at \(\gamma = 3 = \max r\).

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.5 DPI for \(E_\gamma\) directly

Exercise 5. DPI for \(E_\gamma\) directly. Without the f-divergence machinery, show \(E_\gamma(PK\|QK) \le E_\gamma(P\|Q)\). Hint: \(PK(B) - \gamma QK(B) = \sum_xK(B\mid x)\big(p(x) - \gamma q(x)\big)\) with \(K(B\mid x) \in [0, 1]\); use the soft-event part of Lemma 3.4. (Lemma 3.4, DPI)







TipSolution





This is Theorem 3.5 for \(E_\gamma\) alone.

Output probabilities of an event. For an output event \(B\), \(PK(B) = \sum_{y\in B}\sum_xp(x)K(y\mid x) = \sum_xp(x)K(B\mid x)\), where \(K(B\mid x) = \sum_{y\in B}K(y\mid x)\) is the probability that input \(x\) lands in \(B\). The same holds for \(Q\). Subtract: \[PK(B) - \gamma QK(B) = \sum_xK(B\mid x)\big(p(x) - \gamma q(x)\big). \tag{3.9}\]
This is a randomized test on the input. \(\phi(x) = K(B\mid x)\) takes values in \([0, 1]\). By the soft-event part of Lemma 3.4, \(\sum_x\phi(x)(p(x) - \gamma q(x)) \le \sum_x(p(x) - \gamma q(x))_+ = E_\gamma(P\|Q)\).
Maximize over \(B\). Step 2 holds for every \(B\). By Definition 3.4 on the output space, \(E_\gamma(PK\|QK) = \max_B[PK(B) - \gamma QK(B)]\), so it is at most \(E_\gamma(P\|Q)\).

On the die, reporting the parity (\(PK = (0.7, 0.3)\), \(QK = (0.5, 0.5)\) for even, odd):

\(\gamma = 1\): \(E_1 = (0.7 - 0.5)_+ = 0.2000\) after processing, against TV \(= 0.3333\) before.
\(\gamma = 1.2\): \((0.7 - 0.6)_+ = 0.1000\), against \(0.5 - 1.2/6 = 0.3000\).
\(\gamma = 2\): \((0.7 - 1)_+ = 0\), against \(0.1667\). The parity bit has likelihood ratios 1.4 and 0.6, so its \(E_\gamma\) is 0 for every \(\gamma \ge 1.4\).

Any processing only lowers the whole \(E_\gamma\) curve, so every statement made through the \(E_\gamma\) curves survives processing.

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.6 Pinsker’s constant is sharp

Exercise 6. Pinsker’s constant is sharp. For \(P = \mathrm{Bern}(\frac12 + \xi)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)\), show \(\mathrm{kl}(\frac12 + \xi\|\frac12)/(2\xi^2) \to 1\) as \(\xi \to 0\). Hint: expand \(\ln(1 \pm 2\xi)\) to second order. (Pinsker)







TipSolution






Write out kl. \(\mathrm{kl}(\frac12 + \xi\|\frac12) = (\frac12 + \xi)\ln\frac{1/2 + \xi}{1/2} + (\frac12 - \xi)\ln\frac{1/2 - \xi}{1/2} = (\frac12 + \xi)\ln(1 + 2\xi) + (\frac12 - \xi)\ln(1 - 2\xi)\).
Expand the logarithms. \(\ln(1 + u) = u - \frac{u^2}2 + O(u^3)\), so \(\ln(1 \pm 2\xi) = \pm2\xi - 2\xi^2 + O(\xi^3)\).
Multiply out, keeping terms up to \(\xi^2\): \[(\tfrac12 + \xi)(2\xi - 2\xi^2) = \xi - \xi^2 + 2\xi^2 + O(\xi^3), \qquad (\tfrac12 - \xi)(-2\xi - 2\xi^2) = -\xi - \xi^2 + 2\xi^2 + O(\xi^3). \tag{3.10}\]
Add. The \(\xi\) terms cancel and the \(\xi^2\) terms give \(2\xi^2\): \(\mathrm{kl}(\frac12 + \xi\|\frac12) = 2\xi^2 + O(\xi^3)\). Divide by \(2\xi^2\): the ratio is \(1 + O(\xi) \to 1\).

Why this makes the constant sharp. Here \(\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \xi\) (one outcome gains \(\xi\), the other loses it). Pinsker says \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \ge 2\,\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)^2 = 2\xi^2\). If some constant \(c > 2\) worked, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \ge c\,\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)^2\), the ratio \(\mathrm{kl}(\frac12 + \xi\|\frac12)/(2\xi^2)\) would stay at least \(c/2 > 1\) for all \(\xi\), which contradicts the limit 1.
How fast. kl is even in \(\xi\) (swapping heads and tails maps \(\xi\) to \(-\xi\)), so the \(O(\xi^3)\) term is in fact zero; carrying the expansion one order further gives the ratio \(1 + \frac23\xi^2 + O(\xi^4)\). Table 3.4 shows it.

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.7 Samples needed for two coins

Exercise 7. Samples needed for two coins. You flip a coin that is either fair or has heads probability 0.6. Use additivity and Pinsker to find how many flips \(n\) are necessary before the TV between \(n\) flips of the two coins can reach 0.8. Check: \(\mathrm{kl}(0.6\|0.5) = 0.02014\), so \(n \ge 2\times0.8^2/0.02014\), that is \(n \ge 64\). Is this a lower or an upper bound on the flips you need? (Additivity, Pinsker)







TipSolution






One flip. \(\mathrm{kl}(0.6\|0.5) = 0.6\ln\frac{0.6}{0.5} + 0.4\ln\frac{0.4}{0.5} = 0.6\ln1.2 + 0.4\ln0.8 = 0.02014\).
\(n\) flips, by additivity (Equation 3.3): \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P^n\|Q^n) = 0.02014\,n\), where \(P\) is the biased coin and \(Q\) the fair one.
Pinsker (Equation 3.44): \(\mathrm{TV}(P^n, Q^n) \le \sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P^n\|Q^n)/2} = \sqrt{0.02014\,n/2}\).
Require TV to reach 0.8. That needs \(\sqrt{0.02014\,n/2} \ge 0.8\), that is \(n \ge 2\times0.8^2/0.02014 = 63.6\). Since \(n\) is an integer, \(n \ge 64\). The check value is right.

Lower or upper bound? A lower bound. Pinsker caps the TV, so with fewer than 64 flips no test can reach TV 0.8. It does not say 64 flips are enough. The exact TV (computed on the number of heads, which is a sufficient statistic, so by the equality case of the DPI it has the same TV as the whole sequence) is only 0.5805 at \(n = 64\), and first reaches 0.8 at \(n = 162\). Pinsker is off by a factor of about 2.5 here, because it is tight only near TV \(= 0\). Bretagnolle–Huber (Equation 3.46) gives the weaker requirement \(n \ge \ln\frac{1}{1 - 0.64}/0.02014\), that is \(n \ge 51\): the KL that Pinsker needs for TV \(= 0.8\) is \(2\times0.8^2 = 1.28\), below the crossover 1.59 of Section 3.9, so Pinsker is the stronger of the two here.
Pinsker turns “KL is small” into “no test can succeed yet”, which is always a statement about necessary, not sufficient, sample sizes.

title: 3  Exercises: Divergences
text:
3.8 Monotonicity of TV over samples

Exercise 8. Monotonicity of TV over samples. Show that \(\mathrm{TV}(P^n, Q^n)\) is non-decreasing in \(n\). Hint: dropping the last sample is a channel. (DPI)







TipSolution






The channel. Let \(K\) map \((x_1, \dots, x_{n+1})\) to \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) with probability 1: \(K(y\mid x) = \mathbf 1[y = (x_1, \dots, x_n)]\). It is a deterministic function, so a channel.
It maps \(P^{n+1}\) to \(P^n\). \(P^{n+1}K(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \sum_{x_{n+1}}p(x_1)\cdots p(x_n)\,p(x_{n+1}) = p(x_1)\cdots p(x_n)\), since \(p\) sums to 1. The same for \(Q\).
Apply the DPI. TV is the f-divergence with \(f(u) = \frac12\lvert u - 1\rvert\) (Table 3.6), so Theorem 3.5 gives \(\mathrm{TV}(P^n, Q^n) = \mathrm{TV}(P^{n+1}K, Q^{n+1}K) \le \mathrm{TV}(P^{n+1}, Q^{n+1})\).

You can also see it directly from the max form of Equation 3.30: any event about the first \(n\) samples is also an event about the first \(n + 1\) (it ignores the last one), so the maximum over the larger family of events is at least as large.
Concretely, with the coins of Exercise 7. One flip: TV \(= 0.6 - 0.5 = 0.1\). Two flips:

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.1 Symmetry of the Gaussian curve
Exercises for Hypothesis testing, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The notation is the chapter’s: \(T = T(P, Q)\) is the trade-off function, \(\Phi\) the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), and the summaries are the total variation (TV), the true positive rate (TPR), the false positive rate (FPR), the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curve (AUC). Every number that is not a one-line hand calculation comes from code/solutions_hypothesis_testing.py, which you run with uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_hypothesis_testing.py.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
Exercise 1. Show that \(T(T(\alpha)) = \alpha\) for Equation 4.8. Hint: use \(1 - \Phi(x) = \Phi(-x)\). Check: at \(\mu = 1\), \(T(0.05) = 0.7405\) and \(T(0.7405) = 0.0500\). (Gaussian trade-off)







TipSolution





Fix \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\). At the ends, \(T(0) = 1\) and \(T(1) = 0\), so \(T(T(0)) = 0\) and \(T(T(1)) = 1\) directly.

Name the threshold. Let \(z = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\). By Equation 4.8, \(\beta = T(\alpha) = \Phi(z - \mu)\).
Compute \(1 - \beta\). By the hint, which holds because the normal density is symmetric about 0, \(1 - \beta = 1 - \Phi(z - \mu) = \Phi(\mu - z)\).
Invert. \(\Phi\) is strictly increasing, so step 2 gives \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta) = \mu - z\).
Apply \(T\) again. By Equation 4.8 at \(\beta\), \(T(\beta) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta) - \mu\big) = \Phi(\mu - z - \mu) = \Phi(-z)\).
Use the hint once more. \(\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z) = 1 - (1 - \alpha) = \alpha\).

The check, step by step. At \(\mu = 1\) and \(\alpha = 0.05\): \(z = 1.6449\), so \(\beta = \Phi(0.6449) = 0.7405\). Then \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - 0.7405) = \Phi^{-1}(0.2595) = -0.6449 = \mu - z\), and \(T(0.7405) = \Phi(-0.6449 - 1) = \Phi(-1.6449) = 0.0500\). The script also evaluates \(|T(T(\alpha)) - \alpha|\) on 999 values of \(\alpha\) for \(\mu = 0.5, 1, 2, 3\): every defect is below \(10^{-9}\), which is rounding error.
Geometrically, the point \((\alpha, \beta)\) is on the curve exactly when \((\beta, \alpha)\) is: the Gaussian curve is symmetric about the diagonal \(\alpha = \beta\). With Exercise 2, this says that swapping which normal is the null hypothesis does not make the problem easier or harder.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.2 Swapping the hypotheses

Exercise 2. Show that if \(T(P, Q)\) is strictly decreasing on \([0, 1]\), then \(T(Q, P)\) is its inverse function. Hint: a test \(\phi\) for \(P\) against \(Q\) with errors \((\alpha, \beta)\) gives the test \(1 - \phi\) for \(Q\) against \(P\) with errors \((\beta, \alpha)\). (Trade-off functions)







TipSolution





Write \(f = T(P, Q)\) and \(g = T(Q, P)\).

The hint. In the problem “\(Q\) against \(P\)”, the null hypothesis is \(Q\) and the alternative is \(P\). By Definition 4.1, the test \(\phi' = 1 - \phi\) has type I error \(\mathbb E_Q[\phi'] = 1 - \mathbb E_Q[\phi] = \beta_\phi\) and type II error \(1 - \mathbb E_P[\phi'] = \mathbb E_P[\phi] = \alpha_\phi\). The map \(\phi \mapsto 1 - \phi\) is a bijection between tests, so the achievable pairs of the swapped problem are exactly the pairs \((\beta, \alpha)\) with \((\alpha, \beta)\) achievable in the original.
What \(f\) looks like. \(f\) is continuous by Theorem 4.2, strictly decreasing by assumption, and \(f(1) = 0\) because \(f(\alpha) \le 1 - \alpha\). So \(f\) maps \([0, 1]\) one-to-one onto \([0, f(0)]\), and for each \(\beta \in [0, f(0)]\) there is exactly one \(\alpha = f^{-1}(\beta)\) with \(f(\alpha) = \beta\).
\(g(\beta) \le \alpha\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, Theorem 4.1, the infimum in Equation 4.5 is attained: some test has errors \((\alpha_\phi, \beta_\phi) = (\alpha, f(\alpha)) = (\alpha, \beta)\) for \(P\) against \(Q\) (for \(\alpha = 0\), the test \(\mathbf 1[p = 0]\) of step 5 of the proof of Theorem 4.2). By step 1, \(1 - \phi\) has type I error \(\beta\) and type II error \(\alpha\) for \(Q\) against \(P\). So \(g(\beta) \le \alpha\).
\(g(\beta) \ge \alpha\). Take any test of the swapped problem with type I error at most \(\beta\). By step 1 it is \(1 - \phi\) for a test \(\phi\) of the original problem with \(\beta_\phi \le \beta\), and its type II error is \(\alpha_\phi\). If \(\alpha_\phi < \alpha\), then \(f(\alpha_\phi) > f(\alpha) = \beta\) because \(f\) is strictly decreasing, while \(f(\alpha_\phi) \le \beta_\phi \le \beta\) by the definition of \(f\) as an infimum. That is a contradiction, so \(\alpha_\phi \ge \alpha\), and taking the infimum, \(g(\beta) \ge \alpha\).
Conclusion. \(g(\beta) = f^{-1}(\beta)\) for every \(\beta \in [0, f(0)]\).

A boundary case. If \(f(0) < 1\) (\(Q\) puts mass where \(P\) has none), \(f^{-1}\) is defined only on \([0, f(0)]\). For \(\beta > f(0)\), the size-0 test of the original problem, flipped, has type I error \(f(0) \le \beta\) and type II error 0, so \(g(\beta) = 0\) there. “\(g\) is the inverse of \(f\)” then means: \(g = f^{-1}\) on \([0, f(0)]\) and \(g = 0\) beyond. When \(f(0) = 1\), as for every pair in the chapter, \(g = f^{-1}\) on all of \([0, 1]\).
Concrete. Take one bit with \(P = (0.5, 0.5)\) and \(Q = (0.2, 0.8)\) on \(\{0, 1\}\), which is not symmetric like the spam example. For \(P\) against \(Q\) the likelihood ratios are \(q/p = 0.4\) at 0 and \(1.6\) at 1, so the likelihood ratio (LR) tests reject nothing, then \(\{1\}\), then everything. For \(Q\) against \(P\) the ratios are \(p/q = 2.5\) at 0 and \(0.625\) at 1, so the LR tests reject nothing, then \(\{0\}\), then everything. The corners of the two curves are in Table 4.1. Each curve is piecewise linear between its corners (Lemma 4.1), and the corners of one are those of the other with the coordinates swapped, so each curve is the reflection of the other across the diagonal.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.3 Laplace total variation

Exercise 3. Compute \(\frac12\int|q - p|\) directly for \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) and \(\mathrm{Lap}(m_1, b)\), with scale \(b\) and shift \(m_1\) as in the chapter, and confirm \(1 - e^{-m_1/(2b)}\). Check: 0.3935 at \(m_1 = b\). (Total variation)







TipSolution






Rescale. Substitute \(x = bu\). The densities are \(p(x) = \frac1{2b}e^{-|x|/b}\) and \(q(x) = \frac1{2b}e^{-|x - m_1|/b}\), and \(\mathrm dx = b\,\mathrm du\), so \(\int|q - p|\,\mathrm dx = \int\big|\tfrac12e^{-|u - \kappa|} - \tfrac12e^{-|u|}\big|\,\mathrm du\) with \(\kappa = m_1/b\). From here on \(b = 1\) and the shift is \(\kappa\).
Where \(q > p\). \(q(u) > p(u)\) exactly when \(|u - \kappa| < |u|\), that is, when \(u\) is closer to \(\kappa\) than to 0: \(u > \kappa/2\). So split the line at \(0\), \(\kappa/2\) and \(\kappa\), where the absolute values change form.
Left tail, \(u \le 0\). Here \(p = \frac12e^u\) and \(q = \frac12e^{u - \kappa}\), so \(p - q = \frac12e^u(1 - e^{-\kappa})\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^0(p - q)\,\mathrm du = \frac12(1 - e^{-\kappa})\).
Right tail, \(u \ge \kappa\). Here \(p = \frac12e^{-u}\) and \(q = \frac12e^{-(u - \kappa)}\), so \(q - p = \frac12e^{-u}(e^\kappa - 1)\) and \(\int_\kappa^\infty(q - p)\,\mathrm du = \frac12e^{-\kappa}(e^\kappa - 1) = \frac12(1 - e^{-\kappa})\).
Middle, \(0 < u < \kappa\). Here \(p = \frac12e^{-u}\) and \(q = \frac12e^{u - \kappa}\). On \((0, \kappa/2)\), \(p > q\) and \[\int_0^{\kappa/2}\tfrac12\big(e^{-u} - e^{u - \kappa}\big)\,\mathrm du = \tfrac12\big[(1 - e^{-\kappa/2}) - (e^{-\kappa/2} - e^{-\kappa})\big] = \tfrac12\big(1 - e^{-\kappa/2}\big)^2. \tag{4.1}\] The substitution \(u \mapsto \kappa - u\) swaps \(p\) and \(q\) and maps \((\kappa/2, \kappa)\) onto \((0, \kappa/2)\), so the integral over \((\kappa/2, \kappa)\) is the same.
Add. With \(c = e^{-\kappa/2}\), so that \(e^{-\kappa} = c^2\), \[\int|q - p| = (1 - c^2) + (1 - c)^2 = 2 - 2c, \qquad \tfrac12\int|q - p| = 1 - e^{-\kappa/2} = 1 - e^{-m_1/(2b)}. \tag{4.2}\]

The check. At \(m_1 = b\), \(\kappa = 1\). Table 4.2 lists the four pieces. Their sum is 0.7869, half of it is 0.3935, and \(1 - e^{-1/2} = 0.3935\). A trapezoid-rule integral of \(\frac12|q - p|\) on 2,000,001 points also gives 0.3935.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.4 Sample size

Exercise 4. How many readings does the drift monitor need for power 0.9 at \(\alpha = 0.01\) when \(h/\sigma = 0.25\)? Rederive the formula, then halve \(h\): by what factor does \(n\) grow? Check: \(n = 209\); halving \(h\) multiplies \(n\) by 4. (Gaussian trade-off, many observations)







TipSolution






Reduce to one Gaussian pair. By Corollary 4.1, the best test on \(n\) readings has the trade-off Equation 4.8 with \(\mu = h\sqrt n/\sigma\).
Write the power target. Power \(1 - \beta'\) at level \(\alpha\) means \(T(\alpha) \le \beta'\), that is, \(\Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu\big) \le \beta'\).
Invert \(\Phi\). \(\Phi\) is increasing, so this is \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu \le \Phi^{-1}(\beta')\). The normal density is symmetric about 0, so \(1 - \Phi(x) = \Phi(-x)\), and applying \(\Phi^{-1}\) gives \(\Phi^{-1}(\beta') = -\Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta')\). So the condition is \[\mu \ge \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) + \Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta'). \tag{4.3}\]
Solve for \(n\). Substitute \(\mu = h\sqrt n/\sigma\) and square both sides (both are positive): \[n \ge \left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) + \Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta')}{h/\sigma}\right)^2. \tag{4.4}\]
Plug in. \(\alpha = 0.01\) and \(\beta' = 0.1\) give \(\Phi^{-1}(0.99) = 2.3263\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(0.9) = 1.2816\). With \(h/\sigma = 0.25\), \(n \ge (3.6079/0.25)^2 = 208.3\), so \(n = 209\). As a check, the power at \(n = 208\) is 0.8996, just short of 0.9, and at \(n = 209\) it is 0.9011.
Halve \(h\). The bound in step 4 is proportional to \((\sigma/h)^2\), so halving \(h\) multiplies it by exactly 4: \(208.3 \to 833.1\), and \(n = 834\). The rounded counts grow by \(834/209 = 3.99\) because each is rounded up separately.

Distinguishability grows like \(\sqrt n\), so the number of readings grows like \(1/h^2\). Detecting half the drift costs four times the data.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.5 A detector that AUC undersells

Exercise 5. Negatives score \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\). Positives score \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) too, except a fraction \(w = 0.05\) that scores \(\mathcal N(6, 1)\). Show that \(\mathrm{AUC} = (1 - w)\frac12 + w\,\Phi(6/\sqrt2)\) and find the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\). Compare with a Gaussian-shift detector of the same AUC. Check: AUC 0.5250 and TPR 0.0509; the equal-AUC shift is \(\mu = 0.0887\), with TPR 0.0013. (AUC, ROC at low FPR)







TipSolution





The AUC.

Ranking probability. By Proposition 4.2, \(\mathrm{AUC} = \Pr[S_+ > S_-]\) for independent \(S_+\) and \(S_-\).
Condition on the component. Let \(J\) be the component of the positive: “bulk” with probability \(1 - w\), “far” with probability \(w\). By the law of total probability, \(\Pr[S_+ > S_-] = (1 - w)\Pr[S_+ > S_- \mid \text{bulk}] + w\Pr[S_+ > S_- \mid \text{far}]\).
Bulk. Given bulk, \(S_+\) and \(S_-\) are independent draws from the same continuous distribution. By symmetry \(\Pr[S_+ > S_-] = \Pr[S_- > S_+]\), and ties have probability 0, so each is \(\frac12\).
Far. Given far, \(S_+ - S_- \sim \mathcal N(6, 2)\), the binormal case of Proposition 4.2. So \(\Pr[S_+ > S_-] = \Phi(6/\sqrt2) = 0.999989\).
Add. \(\mathrm{AUC} = 0.95 \times 0.5 + 0.05 \times 0.999989 = 0.5250\). A simulation with 1,000,000 pairs gives 0.5259, within two standard errors (about 0.0005 each).

The TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\).

Threshold. Negatives are \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), so the threshold with FPR \(10^{-3}\) is \(\tau = \Phi^{-1}(0.999) = 3.0902\).
Split the TPR by component. A bulk positive is distributed like a negative, so it passes with probability \(10^{-3}\). A far positive passes with probability \(\Pr[\mathcal N(6, 1) > \tau] = \Phi(6 - \tau)\). So \[\mathrm{TPR} = (1 - w)\cdot10^{-3} + w\,\Phi(6 - 3.0902) = 0.00095 + 0.04991 = 0.0509. \tag{4.5}\]

The equal-AUC shift detector. A detector whose positives score \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) has \(\mathrm{AUC} = \Phi(\mu/\sqrt2)\) (binormal model with \(\sigma = 1\)). Setting this to 0.5250 gives \(\mu = \sqrt2\,\Phi^{-1}(0.5250) = 0.0887\). Its TPR at the same threshold is \(\Pr[\mathcal N(\mu, 1) > 3.0902] = \Phi(\mu - 3.0902) = 0.0013\).
Comparison. The two detectors have the same AUC, 0.5250, barely above a coin flip. At FPR \(10^{-3}\) the mixture detector catches 0.0509 of the positives and the shift detector 0.0013: 38 times fewer. The mixture’s AUC is low because 95% of its positives are indistinguishable from negatives. Those pairs contribute \(\frac12\) each and swamp the average. A strict threshold ignores them and catches nearly every far positive.
The threshold test is in fact the best possible test here. The likelihood ratio of the positive score against the negative one is \((1 - w) + w\,e^{6s - 18}\), which is increasing in \(s\), so thresholding \(s\) is an LR test, and by Theorem 4.1 it is optimal.
AUC averages over all FPRs. A detector that is excellent on a small subpopulation and blind elsewhere gets an AUC near 0.5 and can still dominate where false alarms must be rare.

4.6 A curve that starts below 1

Exercise 6. For \(P = U[0, 1]\) and \(Q = U[s, 1 + s]\) with \(0 < s < 1\), show that \(T(\alpha) = \max(0, 1 - s - \alpha)\). Which outcomes have \(\Lambda = \infty\), \(\Lambda = 1\) and \(\Lambda = 0\)? Check: at \(s = 0.2\), \(T(0) = 0.8\) and \(\mathrm{TV} = 0.2\). (Neyman–Pearson with \(p = 0\), continuity at 0)







TipSolution





\(p = 1\) on \([0, 1]\) and \(q = 1\) on \([s, 1 + s]\), so the line splits into the three regions of Table 4.3.

The likelihood ratio. \(\Lambda = \infty\) on \((1, 1 + s]\), where only \(Q\) can land; \(\Lambda = 1\) on the overlap \([s, 1]\); and \(\Lambda = 0\) on \([0, s)\), where only \(P\) can land.
\(\alpha = 0\). A size-0 test must have \(\phi = 0\) on almost all of \([0, 1]\), so it can only reject on \((1, 1 + s]\). Rejecting all of it gives power \(s\). So \(T(0) = 1 - s\), which is the value \(T(0) = 1 - \Pr_Q[p = 0]\) of Theorem 4.2.
\(0 < \alpha \le 1 - s\). Take the LR test Equation 4.2 with \(\tau = 1\): reject where \(q > p\), which is \((1, 1 + s]\); on the tie set \(q = p\), which is \([s, 1]\), reject with the constant probability \(\gamma = \alpha/(1 - s) \in (0, 1]\); keep \([0, s)\). Its size is \(\gamma(1 - s) = \alpha\) and its power is \(s + \gamma(1 - s) = s + \alpha\). By Theorem 4.1 it is the most powerful test of level \(\alpha\), so \(T(\alpha) = 1 - s - \alpha\).
\(\alpha > 1 - s\). The test “reject \(x \ge s\)” has size \(1 - s < \alpha\) and power 1, so \(T(\alpha) = 0\).
Combine. Steps 2 to 4 give \(T(\alpha) = 1 - s - \alpha\) for \(\alpha \le 1 - s\) and 0 beyond, which is \(\max(0, 1 - s - \alpha)\).

The check. At \(s = 0.2\), \(T(0) = 0.8\). By Equation 4.13, \(\mathrm{TV} = \frac12\int|q - p| = \frac12(s + s) = s = 0.2\): the two regions where exactly one density is 1. A midpoint-rule integral gives 0.2000. A simulation of the randomized test of step 3 at \(\alpha = 0.3\), with 1,000,000 draws per hypothesis, gives size 0.3004 and power 0.5001, against the exact 0.3 and \(1 - T(0.3) = 0.5\).
Continuity at 0. \(T\) starts at \(1 - s < 1\), but it is continuous there: \(T(\alpha) \to 1 - s = T(0)\) as \(\alpha \to 0\). This is the continuity of Theorem 4.2, and the \(\mathbb E_P[\Lambda\,\mathbf 1[\Lambda > K]]\) term in step 6 of its proof is 0 here because \(\Lambda \le 1\) wherever \(p > 0\). The curve is also a single segment of slope \(-1\), so the advantage \(1 - \alpha - T(\alpha) = s\) at every \(\alpha \le 1 - s\): every point of the segment attains the TV.
Mass that only \(Q\) can produce is free power: a test catches it with no false alarms, so the curve starts at \(1 - \Pr_Q[p = 0]\) instead of 1.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.7 Bayes error and total variation

Exercise 7. Prove that with equal priors the smallest achievable error probability is \(\frac12(1 - \mathrm{TV}(P, Q))\). Check: 0.3085 for the Gaussian pair at \(\mu = 1\). (Bayesian view, best advantage)







TipSolution






Error of a test. With prior \(\pi = \frac12\), a test \(\phi\) errs with probability \(\frac12\alpha_\phi + \frac12\beta_\phi\) (step 2 of the proof of Theorem 4.6).
Rewrite with the advantage. \(\frac12(\alpha_\phi + \beta_\phi) = \frac12\big(1 - (1 - \alpha_\phi - \beta_\phi)\big)\). The error is a decreasing function of the advantage \(1 - \alpha_\phi - \beta_\phi\), so the test with the smallest error is the one with the largest advantage.
Use the best advantage. By Theorem 4.5 the largest advantage over all tests, randomized or not, is \(\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\), attained by rejecting where \(q > p\). So the smallest error is \(\frac12(1 - \mathrm{TV}(P, Q))\), attained by the same test, which is the Bayes rule \(\Lambda(x) > (1 - \pi)/\pi = 1\).

Concrete: the spam example. \(\mathrm{TV} = 0.40\), so the bound is \(\frac12(1 - 0.40) = 0.30\). Of the 16 deterministic tests on \(\{0, 1, 2, 3\}\), the script finds the smallest error 0.30, at the rejection region \(\{2, 3\}\): \(\frac12(0.3 + 0.3) = 0.30\) from Table 4.2.
The check. For the Gaussian pair at \(\mu = 1\), \(\mathrm{TV} = 2\Phi(\frac12) - 1 = 0.3829\), so the smallest error is \(\frac12(1 - 0.3829) = 1 - \Phi(\frac12) = 0.3085\). Minimizing \(\frac12(\alpha + T(\alpha))\) over a grid of 100,001 values of \(\alpha\) gives the same 0.3085. It is also the optimal \(\alpha\) of Figure 4.5: at \(\tau = 1\) the threshold is \(\mu/2\), so \(\alpha = \beta = 1 - \Phi(\frac12)\), and their average is the same number.
With equal priors, the best accuracy is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}\), which is Equation 3.31. TV is exactly what a single balanced decision can extract.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
section: 4.8 Errors decay at the KL rate
text:
4.8 Errors decay at the KL rate

Exercise 8. For \(n\) draws from \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\) and a fixed \(\alpha = 0.05\), the optimal test has \(\beta_n = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(0.95) - \sqrt n)\). Compute \(-\ln(\beta_n)/n\) and compare its limit with \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mu^2/2\) from Divergences. This is the Chernoff–Stein lemma. Check: 0.2740, 0.3796 and 0.4537 at \(n = 10\), 100 and 1,000, approaching 0.5 slowly. (Many observations, Gaussian tails)







TipSolution





Here the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence is \(\mu^2/2 = 0.5\) by Equation 3.19.

Where \(\beta_n\) comes from. By Corollary 4.1, \(n\) draws with \(h = \sigma = 1\) give Equation 4.8 with \(\mu = \sqrt n\). At \(\alpha = 0.05\), with \(z = \Phi^{-1}(0.95) = 1.6449\), that is \(\beta_n = \Phi(z - \sqrt n) = \Phi(-x)\) with \(x = \sqrt n - z\), which is positive for \(n \ge 3\).
Compute. Table 4.4 gives the exact rate. It matches the check: 0.2740, 0.3796, 0.4537.
A lower bound on the rate. The Mills-ratio bound of Concentration inequalities gives \(\Phi(-x) = \Pr[Z \ge x] \le \varphi(x)/x\). Take \(-\ln\): \[-\ln \beta_n \ge \frac{x^2}2 + \ln x + \tfrac12\ln(2\pi). \tag{4.6}\]
An upper bound on the rate. \(\varphi\) is decreasing on \([x, x + 1]\), so \(\Phi(-x) \ge \int_x^{x + 1}\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz \ge \varphi(x + 1)\). Take \(-\ln\): \[-\ln \beta_n \le \frac{(x + 1)^2}2 + \tfrac12\ln(2\pi). \tag{4.7}\]
Divide by \(n\) and let \(n \to \infty\). With \(x = \sqrt n - z\), \(\frac{x^2}{2n} = \frac12 - \frac z{\sqrt n} + \frac{z^2}{2n} \to \frac12\), and \(\frac{(x + 1)^2}{2n} \to \frac12\) the same way. The \(\ln x\) and constant terms divided by \(n\) tend to 0. Both bounds tend to \(\frac12\), so \[\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{-\ln \beta_n}{n} = \frac12 = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q). \tag{4.8}\]
Why so slowly. The leading correction in step 5 is \(-z/\sqrt n\), which shrinks only like \(1/\sqrt n\). At \(n = 1{,}000\) it is \(-1.6449/31.62 = -0.052\), and most of it remains in the gap \(0.5 - 0.4537 = 0.046\). A fixed \(\alpha\) costs a threshold \(z\) that does not shrink with \(n\), and that offset is what slows the approach.

title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.9 Certifying a low rate

Exercise 9. How many negatives with zero false positives do you need to claim FPR \(< 10^{-3}\) at 95% confidence? Check: 2,995. (Clopper–Pearson, rule of three)







TipSolution






The one-sided bound. “FPR below \(u\) at 95% confidence” is a one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound. Rerun the proof of Theorem 4.7 for the upper end alone, with \(\alpha/2\) replaced by \(0.05\): if \(u\) solves \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = 0.05\), then \(\Pr[p \ge u(K)] \le 0.05\).
Zero counts. At \(k = 0\), \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le 0] = (1 - u)^n\), so \(u\) solves \((1 - u)^n = 0.05\).
The requirement. You need \(u \le 10^{-3}\). \((1 - u)^n\) is decreasing in \(u\), so this holds exactly when \((1 - 10^{-3})^n \le 0.05\).
Solve for \(n\). Take logs and divide by \(\ln(1 - 10^{-3}) < 0\), which flips the inequality: \[n \ge \frac{\ln 20}{-\ln(1 - 10^{-3})} = 2{,}994.2, \tag{4.9}\] so \(n = 2{,}995\).
Check both sides. \(0.999^{2994} = 0.05001 > 0.05\) but \(0.999^{2995} = 0.04996 \le 0.05\). The chapter’s two-sided Clopper–Pearson routine at 90% has the same upper end as the one-sided 95% bound. At \(k = 0\) it gives \(1.0001\times10^{-3}\) for \(n = 2{,}994\) and \(9.9974\times10^{-4}\) for \(n = 2{,}995\).

As a hypothesis test. Step 3 is a test of “FPR \(\ge 10^{-3}\)” against “FPR \(< 10^{-3}\)” that rejects the first when it sees no false positive. If the true FPR is at least \(10^{-3}\), it sees none with probability at most \(0.999^n\), its type I error. That is at most 0.05 from \(n = 2{,}995\) on. The rule of three, \(3/10^{-3} = 3{,}000\), is within five of it. If you report the two-sided 95% interval instead, its upper end uses \(0.025\), and you need \(\ln 40/(-\ln 0.999) = 3{,}687.0\), so 3,688 negatives.
Certifying a rate of \(10^{-3}\) needs about \(3/10^{-3}\) clean trials, and that only bounds the rate. Measuring it to within about 20% needs on the order of \(100/10^{-3} = 10^5\), over thirty times more.
