title: 18  Exercises: The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.11 Is it a privacy violation?

Exercise 11. Is it a privacy violation? Apply the three-question test of Section 18.10 to each case, and say what the first question answers and which other question explains the case. (a) A model trained with DP on hospital records predicts that a patient in the training set has diabetes, and she does. (b) A text model trained on a company’s chat logs completes “the door code is” with the code one employee typed once. (c) An insurer raises a smoker’s premium after a published study, which did not include him, finds that smoking causes cancer. (d) A recommender trained on all users suggests baby products to a user who has bought prenatal vitamins from the same shop. (The three-question test)







TipSolution






(a) Not a violation by itself. Ask the first question: would the model predict diabetes for her if her record were left out? A DP model’s prediction can barely depend on one record, and if patients with her features usually have diabetes, a model trained without her says the same. The second question confirms it: the prediction is right because the model is accurate. To check, compare the model’s accuracy on training patients with its accuracy on similar patients outside the training set.
(b) A violation. The first question decides it. No other record makes that particular code likely, so a model trained without the employee’s message would give it no special probability. The completion exists because the model memorized one record, which is what DP prevents.
(c) Not a violation. The first question decides it outright: he was not in the study, so his record cannot have changed its result. This is the population inference of Section 18.9. Preventing it would mean not running the study.
(d) Not a violation in the DP sense. The first question decides it: a recommender trained without her record would make the same suggestion from her purchases, because the pattern is shared by many customers. The third question explains why it still feels invasive: the suggestion uses her own purchase history, which she handed to the shop, as input. Whether such targeting is acceptable is a real question, but it is not one that DP answers.

Only the first question decides a violation in the DP sense. The second and third explain why an inference that feels invasive may still be population inference.

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.1 Majority of three answers
Exercises for Post-processing, group privacy and composition, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_properties.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_properties.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(M\) is a mechanism, \(D \sim D'\) neighbouring datasets, \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), and \(L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\) the privacy loss. Differential privacy (DP) at level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) means \(\Pr_P[S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[S] + \delta\) for every event \(S\) and every ordered neighbouring pair. Randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) reports the true bit with probability \(\frac34\). Logarithms are natural.
crumbs: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
Exercise 1. Majority of three answers. A person gives three randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) each, and only the majority of the three is published. By composition and post-processing it is \(3\ln 3\)-DP. Find its exact \(\varepsilon\). Check: \(\Pr[\text{majority} = 1 \mid \text{bit } 1] = \frac{54}{64}\), so \(\varepsilon = \ln 5.4 = 1.6864\). (Post-processing, composition)







TipSolution






The bound. The three answers are \(3\ln 3\)-DP by Theorem 19.3, and the majority is a deterministic function of them, so it is \(3\ln 3 = 3.2958\)-DP by Theorem 19.1.
Under bit 1 (\(D\)), each answer is 1 with probability \(\frac34\), independently. The majority is 1 when at least two answers are 1: \[\Pr[\text{maj} = 1 \mid 1] = \Big(\frac34\Big)^3 + 3\Big(\frac34\Big)^2\frac14 = \frac{27}{64} + \frac{27}{64} = \frac{54}{64} = 0.84375. \tag{19.1}\]
Under bit 0 (\(D'\)), each answer is 1 with probability \(\frac14\): \[\Pr[\text{maj} = 1 \mid 0] = \Big(\frac14\Big)^3 + 3\Big(\frac14\Big)^2\frac34 = \frac{1}{64} + \frac{9}{64} = \frac{10}{64} = 0.15625. \tag{19.2}\]
The privacy loss of each output. For “majority 1” it is \(\ln\frac{54}{10} = \ln 5.4\). For “majority 0” the probabilities swap (\(\frac{10}{64}\) under bit 1, \(\frac{54}{64}\) under bit 0), so the loss is \(-\ln 5.4\). The exact \(\varepsilon\) is \(\ln 5.4 = 1.6864\).

Majority voting merges transcripts with losses \(3\ln 3\) (three 1s) and \(\ln 3\) (two 1s), and the merged loss is in between. The worst transcript is not reported on its own, so the bound \(3\ln 3\) is loose by almost a factor of 2.

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
section: 19.2 The geometric sum of group privacy
text:
19.2 The geometric sum of group privacy

Exercise 2. The geometric sum of group privacy. Show that \(\delta\sum_{j<k}e^{j\varepsilon} \le k e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta\), that their ratio tends to 1 as \(\varepsilon \to 0\), and that for the alarm mechanism every neighbouring pair is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP as long as \(a_0 \le 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\). Check: for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and \(k = 10\) the two forms are \(2.272 \times 10^{-3}\) and \(9.002 \times 10^{-3}\). (Group privacy)







TipSolution





The inequality.

The sum has \(k\) terms \(e^{0}, e^{\varepsilon}, \dots, e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\). Since \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), each is at most the largest, \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\).
So the sum is at most \(k e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\); multiply by \(\delta\).

The ratio. As \(\varepsilon \to 0\), every term \(e^{j\varepsilon} \to 1\), so the sum tends to \(k\), and \(k e^{(k-1)\varepsilon} \to k\) too. The ratio of simple form to sum tends to 1. At \(k = 10\) the script gives ratios 6.3215, 1.5054 and 1.0456 for \(\varepsilon = 1, 0.1, 0.01\): the simple form is only harmless for small \(\varepsilon\).
The check. With \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(k = 10\): \(\delta\frac{e^{5} - 1}{e^{0.5} - 1} = 2.272 \times 10^{-3}\) and \(10e^{4.5}\delta = 9.002 \times 10^{-3}\).
The alarm mechanism. It outputs “alarm” with probability \(a_c\) on count \(c\), where \(a_c = e^\varepsilon a_{c+1} + \delta\) for \(c < K\), \(a_K = 0\) and \(a_c = 0\) for \(c > K\); so \(a_0 \ge a_1 \ge \dots \ge a_K = 0\). For counts below 0, set \(a_c = a_0\). A neighbouring pair has counts \(c\) and \(c + 1\). With two outputs, the events are \(\emptyset\), \(\{\text{alarm}\}\), \(\{\text{quiet}\}\) and everything; the first and last satisfy the event form trivially. Check the other two in both orders.

Alarm, \(c\) against \(c + 1\): \(a_c \le e^\varepsilon a_{c+1} + \delta\) holds with equality by construction (or trivially when both are 0, or both \(a_0\)).
Alarm, \(c + 1\) against \(c\): \(a_{c+1} \le a_c \le e^\varepsilon a_c + \delta\).
Quiet, \(c\) against \(c + 1\): \(1 - a_c \le 1 - a_{c+1} \le e^\varepsilon(1 - a_{c+1}) + \delta\), since \(a_c \ge a_{c+1}\).
Quiet, \(c + 1\) against \(c\): we need \(1 - a_{c+1} \le e^\varepsilon(1 - a_c) + \delta\). The left side is at most 1, so it suffices that \(1 \le e^\varepsilon(1 - a_c)\), that is \(a_c \le 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\). Since \(a_c \le a_0\), the condition \(a_0 \le 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\) is enough.

For \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and \(K = 10\), \(a_0 = 2.272 \times 10^{-3}\), far below \(1 - e^{-0.5} = 0.3935\). The script computes the exact \(\delta(0.5)\) of every neighbouring pair and finds the largest to be \(1.000 \times 10^{-5}\), attained on “alarm”.
The condition only rules out absurd parameters: \(a_0\) is the probability of an alarm, which must stay well below 1 for the mechanism to be useful at all.

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
section: 19.3 From records to users, then to releases
text:
19.3 From records to users, then to releases

Exercise 3. From records to users, then to releases. Each user contributes at most 5 records, and a mechanism is \((0.2, 10^{-7})\)-DP at the record level. Find the user-level guarantee, then the guarantee of 10 independent runs of the mechanism at the user level. Check: \((1, 7.761 \times 10^{-7})\) per run and \((10, 7.761 \times 10^{-6})\) for ten runs. (Group privacy, composition)







TipSolution






User-level neighbours are at record distance at most 5. Removing one user removes at most 5 records, one at a time, so the two datasets are joined by a path of at most 5 record-level steps.
Group privacy (Theorem 19.2) with \(k = 5\): \[\varepsilon_5 = 5 \times 0.2 = 1, \qquad \delta_5 = 10^{-7}\,\frac{e^{1} - 1}{e^{0.2} - 1} = 10^{-7} \times \frac{1.71828}{0.22140} = 7.761 \times 10^{-7}. \tag{19.3}\] (A user with fewer records is at a shorter distance, and the guarantee only gets better.)
Composition at the user level. Ten runs with fresh noise, each \((1, 7.761 \times 10^{-7})\)-DP for user-level neighbours, are \((10, 7.761 \times 10^{-6})\)-DP by Equation 19.11.

The order matters. Composing first at the record level gives \((2, 10^{-6})\), and group privacy for 5 records then gives \(\varepsilon = 10\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\frac{e^{10} - 1}{e^{2} - 1} = 3.447 \times 10^{-3}\), 444 times worse. Apply group privacy to each run, then compose: group privacy inflates \(\delta\) by powers of the per-step \(\varepsilon\), so apply it where \(\varepsilon\) is smallest.

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.4 Parallel composition under replace

Exercise 4. Parallel composition under replace. For a histogram of \(d\) bins with independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) noise on each, show that the exact pure \(\varepsilon\) is \(1/b\) under add/remove and \(2/b\) under replace (for a replacement that moves a record between bins). Then show that if records are assigned to bins by their position in the dataset, not their value, a replacement costs \(1/b\). Hint: under replace by value, find the output where both bins’ losses take their largest value. (Parallel composition)







TipSolution





Write \(c_i\) for the count in bin \(i\) and \(y_i = c_i + Z_i\) for the released noisy count. For two Laplace densities of scale \(b\) with centres \(c\) and \(c'\), the privacy loss at \(y\) is \(\frac{|y - c'| - |y - c|}{b}\), which lies in \([-\frac{|c - c'|}{b}, \frac{|c - c'|}{b}]\) and reaches each end (Laplace section of Divergences).
Add/remove.

Adding a record raises one count, say \(c_1\), by 1. The other bins have the same distribution under \(D\) and \(D'\).
By Lemma 19.2, \(L(y) = \frac{|y_1 - c_1 - 1| - |y_1 - c_1|}{b} + 0\). Its largest absolute value is \(1/b\), reached for every \(y_1 \le c_1\).

Replace across bins.

Replacing a record in bin 1 by one in bin 2 changes \((c_1, c_2)\) under \(D\) into \((c_1 - 1, c_2 + 1)\) under \(D'\).
\(L(y) = \frac{|y_1 - c_1 + 1| - |y_1 - c_1|}{b} + \frac{|y_2 - c_2 - 1| - |y_2 - c_2|}{b}\).
The first term equals \(1/b\) for every \(y_1 \ge c_1\), the second equals \(1/b\) for every \(y_2 \le c_2\). These regions can occur together, so the largest loss is \(2/b\), and it is never larger than the sum of the two maxima. The exact pure \(\varepsilon\) is \(2/b\).

Replace within a slot. If bin \(i\) holds a noisy version of record \(i\)’s value (one slot per record, values in \(\{0, 1\}\)), then replacing record \(i\) changes slot \(i\) only, by at most 1, and the analysis of add/remove applies: \(\varepsilon = 1/b\).
The script computes the exact pure \(\varepsilon\) of two bins with rounded Laplace noise: for \(b = 1\), \(1.0000\) under add/remove (and within a slot) and \(2.0000\) across bins; for \(b = 2\), \(0.5000\) and \(1.0000\).
Which neighbouring relation the guarantee uses is part of the guarantee. A histogram with \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1/\varepsilon)\) per bin is \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove and \(2\varepsilon\)-DP under replace.
crumbs: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.5 Shared noise

Exercise 5. Shared noise. For the two counts \(c_1(D) + Z\) and \(c_2(D) + Z\) of Proposition 19.2, show that \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = 1\) for every \(\varepsilon\), where \(P\) and \(Q\) are the distributions of the pair under \(D\) and \(D'\). Then find the exact pure \(\varepsilon\) of the pair when the noise is fresh. Check: \(\varepsilon = 1\) with fresh \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise. (Composition, hockey-stick)







TipSolution





Shared noise.

Disjoint supports. The proof of Proposition 19.2 shows that the event \(A = \{(u, v) : u - v = c\}\), with \(c = c_1(D) - c_2(D)\), has \(\Pr_P[A] = 1\) and \(\Pr_Q[A] = 0\).
The hockey-stick is at least 1. \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \max_S[\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[S]] \ge \Pr_P[A] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[A] = 1\).
And at most 1, since \(\sum(p - e^\varepsilon q)_+ \le \sum p = 1\). So it is exactly 1 for every \(\varepsilon\), and the pair is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any \(\delta < 1\).

The script represents the difference \(u - v\) as a point mass at \(c\) under \(D\) and at \(c - 1\) under \(D'\) and gets \(E_{e^\varepsilon} = 1.0000\) at \(\varepsilon = 0, 1, 5, 20\).
Fresh noise. The pair is \((c_1(D) + Z_1, c_2(D) + Z_2)\) with independent \(Z_1, Z_2\).

Removing Alice lowers \(c_1\) by 1 and leaves \(c_2\) unchanged, so the second coordinate has the same distribution under \(D\) and \(D'\).
By Lemma 19.2, the privacy loss is the loss of the first coordinate, a \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) count against its shift by 1, whose largest absolute value is 1.
So the pair is exactly 1-DP; the script gets \(1.0000\) with rounded Laplace noise.

Each count alone is 1-DP in both cases. With shared noise, the pair is not DP at all; with fresh noise, it is 1-DP, and even 2-DP by basic composition if both counts depended on Alice.

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.6 A preview of advanced composition

Exercise 6. A preview of advanced composition. Show that if \(\Pr_{y \sim M(D)}[L_{D,D'}(y) > \varepsilon] \le \delta\) for every ordered neighbouring pair, then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. For \(k\) randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon_0\), use Hoeffding’s inequality on \(L\) to show that \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) + \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}\). Check: for \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(k = 1000\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) this gives \(21.62\), against 100 for basic composition and the exact 19.345. (Composition, concentration)







TipSolution





A tail bound on the loss gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).

The worst event for \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\) is \(B = \{y : p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\} = \{L > \varepsilon\}\), by step 2 of the proof of Lemma 19.1 with \(g\) the indicator of \(B\).
Drop the negative term: \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B] \le \Pr_P[B] = \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\).
This holds for every ordered pair, which is the hockey-stick form of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.

The mean of the loss. For one answer under \(D\) (bit 1), the loss is \(+\varepsilon_0\) with probability \(t = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0}}{1 + e^{\varepsilon_0}}\) and \(-\varepsilon_0\) with probability \(1 - t\). Its mean is \(\varepsilon_0(2t - 1)\), and \[2t - 1 = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} = \tanh(\varepsilon_0/2). \tag{19.4}\] For \(k\) independent answers the losses add (Lemma 19.2), so the mean is \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). At \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(t = 0.5250\) and \(2t - 1 = \tanh(0.05) = 0.04996\), so for \(k = 1000\) the mean is 4.996.
Hoeffding.

\(L = \sum_{i=1}^kL_i\) with independent \(L_i \in [-\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_0]\), each of range \(2\varepsilon_0\). Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration) gives, for \(s > 0\), \[\Pr[L - \mathbb E[L] \ge s] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2s^2}{k(2\varepsilon_0)^2}\Big) = \exp\Big(-\frac{s^2}{2k\varepsilon_0^2}\Big). \tag{19.5}\]
Set the right side to \(\delta\): \(s = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}\).
Combine with the first part: with \(\varepsilon = \mathbb E[L] + s\), \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\). Randomized response is symmetric in the two bits, so the same holds for the reversed pair, and \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.

The check. For \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(k = 1000\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\): \(s = 0.1\sqrt{2000 \ln 10^6} = 16.623\), so \(\varepsilon = 4.996 + 16.623 = 21.62\). The exact tail at that point is \(\Pr_D[L > 21.62] = 5.319 \times 10^{-8}\), well below \(10^{-6}\), which shows how much Hoeffding gives away. The exact \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) is 19.345 and basic composition gives 100.
The bound grows like \(\sqrt k\), not \(k\): the mean grows like \(k\varepsilon_0^2/2\), small when \(\varepsilon_0\) is small, and the fluctuations like \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt k\). Advanced composition proves the same shape for any \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP mechanisms.

text:
19.7 Ask until yes

Exercise 7. Ask until yes. A survey asks a person for randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), one at a time, and stops at the first answer 1 or after 3 answers. Only the number of answers asked is published (1, 2, 3, or “3 and no 1”). Show it is \(3\ln 3\)-DP by adaptive composition, then compute its exact \(\varepsilon\). Check: the exact \(\varepsilon\) is \(\ln 27 = 3.2958\): the basic bound is attained. (Adaptive composition, post-processing)







TipSolution





The bound.

Write it as an adaptive composition of three steps. Step \(i\) looks at the previous answers. If one of them is 1, it outputs “stopped”, which does not depend on the data (0-DP). Otherwise it asks a fresh randomized-response question (\(\ln 3\)-DP). For every fixed previous output, step \(i\) is at most \(\ln 3\)-DP.
Adaptive composition (Theorem 19.3) gives \(3\ln 3\) for the transcript of three steps.
The published count is a function of the transcript, so post-processing keeps \(3\ln 3\).

The exact \(\varepsilon\). Let \(s\) be the probability that one answer is 1: \(s = \frac34\) under bit 1 and \(\frac14\) under bit 0. Stopping after answer \(i\) means \(i - 1\) zeros and then a 1, with probability \((1 - s)^{i-1}s\); no 1 in three answers has probability \((1 - s)^3\). Table 19.1 lists the four outputs.

20.1 A private mean under add/remove
Exercises for the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_laplace_gaussian.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_laplace_gaussian.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Guarantees are differential privacy (DP) guarantees; \(\Delta_1\) and \(\Delta_2\) are the \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) sensitivities; \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\) for the Gaussian mechanism; \(\Phi\) and \(\varphi\) are the standard normal distribution function and density; and \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) - e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\) is the exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism (Equation 20.17).
crumbs: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
Exercise 1. A private mean under add/remove. Records lie in \([0, 1]\) and neighbours differ by adding or removing a record, so \(n\) is private. Release the sum \(s\) and the count \(n\), each with the Laplace mechanism at \(\varepsilon/2\), and estimate the mean as \((s + Z_s)/(n + Z_c)\). Show that the release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP and that the root-mean-square error is approximately \(\frac{2\sqrt2}{n\varepsilon}\sqrt{1 + m^2}\) for true mean \(m\). Check: at \(n = 1000\), \(m = 0.3\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) this is 0.00295 (simulated 0.00296), against 0.00141 for the replace-neighbour mean with \(n\) public. (Sensitivity, basic composition, first-order error)







TipSolution





Privacy.

Sensitivities. Adding or removing a record \(x \in [0, 1]\) changes the count by 1 and the sum by \(x \le 1\). So each query has \(\Delta_1 = 1\).
Each release. \(s + Z_s\) with \(Z_s \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) is the Laplace mechanism with scale \(\Delta_1/(\varepsilon/2)\), so it is \(\frac\varepsilon2\)-DP. The same holds for \(n + Z_c\).
Together. By basic composition (Post-processing, group privacy and composition) the pair is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Equivalently, the vector \((s, n)\) has \(\Delta_1 = 1 + 1 = 2\), and independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) noise on both coordinates is exactly the Laplace mechanism for it.
The estimate. Dividing the two noisy numbers is post-processing, so it costs nothing more.

Error. The noise facts are those of Theorem 20.1: each \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) coordinate has variance \(2b^2\).

Write the error. With \(s = nm\), \[\frac{nm + Z_s}{n + Z_c} - m = \frac{Z_s - mZ_c}{n + Z_c}. \tag{20.1}\]
First order. The noise has scale \(b = 2/\varepsilon\), tiny next to \(n\), so \(n + Z_c \approx n\) and the error is \(\approx (Z_s - mZ_c)/n\).
Variance. \(Z_s\) and \(Z_c\) are independent with variance \(2b^2\) each, so the variance is \(2b^2(1 + m^2)/n^2\). Take the square root and substitute \(b = 2/\varepsilon\): \(\frac{\sqrt2\cdot2}{n\varepsilon}\sqrt{1 + m^2} = \frac{2\sqrt2}{n\varepsilon}\sqrt{1 + m^2}\).
Check. At \(n = 1000\), \(m = 0.3\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(\frac{2\sqrt2}{1000}\sqrt{1.09} = 0.00295\). A million simulated releases give 0.00296.
Compare. Under replace neighbours with \(n\) public, the mean has \(\Delta_1 = 1/n\) and needs only \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/(n\varepsilon))\) noise, with root-mean-square error \(\sqrt2/(n\varepsilon) = 0.00141\). Hiding \(n\) and splitting the budget costs a factor of about 2.

A caveat. Strictly, the ratio has no finite variance: \(n + Z_c\) has a positive density at 0, so the error can be arbitrarily large with probability of order \(e^{-n\varepsilon/2}\), which is \(e^{-500}\) here and never shows up in a simulation. In practice you replace the denominator by \(\max(n + Z_c, 1)\), which is post-processing and removes the problem.
Under add/remove the size of the dataset is itself private, and releasing it costs part of the budget.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
section: 20.2 The Laplace scale cannot be smaller
text:
20.2 The Laplace scale cannot be smaller

Exercise 2. The Laplace scale cannot be smaller. For a count, show that \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise with \(b < 1/\varepsilon\) is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP, by exhibiting an event. Then show that \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) noise is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP for \(\varepsilon' < \varepsilon\) with \(\delta = 1 - e^{-(\varepsilon - \varepsilon')/2}\). Check: \(b = 0.9\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) gives the ratio \(e^{1/0.9} = 3.0377 > e\); with \(b = 1\), \(\delta(0.5) = 0.2212\). (Tightness, hockey-stick of a Laplace pair)







TipSolution





The violating event. The tightness step of Theorem 20.1 already exhibits it: for counts \(f(D) = 0\) and \(f(D') = 1\) and the event \(S = \{y \le 0\}\), the two probabilities are \(\frac12\) and \(\frac12e^{-1/b}\), so their ratio is \(e^{1/b}\), which exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) whenever \(b < 1/\varepsilon\). At \(b = 0.9\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\) the ratio is \(e^{1/0.9} = 3.0377 > e = 2.7183\).
The \(\delta\) curve. Work in units of \(b = 1/\varepsilon\), so the shift is \(t = 1/b = \varepsilon\). Let \(P = \mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{Lap}(t, 1)\).

The privacy loss. \(L(y) = |y - t| - |y|\), which is \(t\) for \(y \le 0\), \(t - 2y\) for \(0 \le y \le t\), and \(-t\) for \(y \ge t\).
The bad event. For \(0 \le \varepsilon' < t\), \(L(y) > \varepsilon'\) exactly when \(y < c\) with \(c = (t - \varepsilon')/2 \in (0, t/2]\).
Its two probabilities. \(\Pr_P[y < c] = 1 - \frac12e^{-c}\) and \(\Pr_Q[y < c] = \frac12e^{-(t - c)}\).
The hockey-stick (Lemma 20.2): \(\delta = \Pr_P[B] - e^{\varepsilon'}\Pr_Q[B] = 1 - \frac12e^{-c} - \frac12e^{\varepsilon' - t + c}\). Since \(\varepsilon' - t = -2c\), the last exponent is \(-c\), and \(\delta = 1 - e^{-c} = 1 - e^{-(\varepsilon - \varepsilon')/2}\).
Check. \(b = 1\) (\(\varepsilon = 1\)) at \(\varepsilon' = 0.5\): \(1 - e^{-0.25} = 0.2212\). At \(\varepsilon' = 0\) the formula gives \(1 - e^{-1/2} = 0.3935\), the total variation distance of the pair, and at \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\) it gives 0.

The Laplace mechanism is exactly \(\varepsilon\)-DP and no better: below \(\varepsilon\) you must pay a \(\delta\) that is not small.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
section: 20.3 The slope of the privacy profile
text:
20.3 The slope of the privacy profile

Exercise 3. The slope of the privacy profile. Show that \(\varphi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) = e^\varepsilon\varphi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\), and deduce \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\varepsilon}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = -e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\). Conclude that \(\delta_\mu\) is strictly decreasing in \(\varepsilon\), and show in the same way that \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\mu}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \varphi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) > 0\). Check: at \(\mu = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) the slope is \(-0.1816\), matching a finite difference. (Differentiating Equation 20.17)







TipSolution





Write \(a = \frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\) and \(c = -\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\), so \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi(a) - e^\varepsilon\Phi(c)\).

The density identity. \(a^2 - c^2 = (a - c)(a + c) = \mu\cdot\big(-\frac{2\varepsilon}\mu\big) = -2\varepsilon\). So \(\varphi(a)/\varphi(c) = e^{-(a^2 - c^2)/2} = e^\varepsilon\). This is the statement that the likelihood ratio at the boundary of the bad event is exactly \(e^\varepsilon\).
Differentiate in \(\varepsilon\). \(\frac{\mathrm da}{\mathrm d\varepsilon} = \frac{\mathrm dc}{\mathrm d\varepsilon} = -\frac1\mu\). By the product and chain rules, \[\frac{\mathrm d\delta_\mu}{\mathrm d\varepsilon} = -\frac{\varphi(a)}\mu - e^\varepsilon\Phi(c) + \frac{e^\varepsilon\varphi(c)}\mu. \tag{20.2}\]
Cancel. By step 1 the first and last terms cancel, leaving \(-e^\varepsilon\Phi(c) < 0\). So \(\delta_\mu\) is strictly decreasing in \(\varepsilon\).
Differentiate in \(\mu\). \(\frac{\mathrm da}{\mathrm d\mu} = \frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dc}{\mathrm d\mu} = -\frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\), so \(\frac{\mathrm d\delta_\mu}{\mathrm d\mu} = \varphi(a)\big(\frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\big) - e^\varepsilon\varphi(c)\big(-\frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\big)\). Replace \(e^\varepsilon\varphi(c)\) by \(\varphi(a)\) (step 1): the \(\varepsilon/\mu^2\) terms cancel and the result is \(\varphi(a) > 0\).
Check. At \(\mu = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(c = -1.5\) and the slope is \(-e\,\Phi(-1.5) = -0.1816\). A central finite difference with step \(10^{-6}\) gives \(-0.1816\) too, and the script evaluates the identity of step 1 to \(0.0\) in floating point. At \(\varepsilon = 0\), \(\delta_1(0) = \Phi(\frac12) - \Phi(-\frac12) = 2\Phi(\frac12) - 1 = 0.3829\), the total variation distance.

The slope \(-e^\varepsilon\Phi(c)\) is the correction term of the bad-event bound, \(e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B]\), so the two terms of the exact \(\delta\) are tied together by one derivative.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.4 Calibrate by hand

Exercise 4. Calibrate by hand. Run bisection on \(\ln\mu\) over \([10^{-3}, 100]\) for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), and compare the result with the classic formula. Check: \(\mu^* = 0.124106\), so \(\sigma^* = 8.0576\,\Delta_2f\), against the classic 10.5976 (a ratio of 1.315). (Analytic calibration)







TipSolution






Why bisection works. By Exercise 3, \(\delta_\mu(0.5)\) is strictly increasing in \(\mu\), so \(\delta_\mu(0.5) = 10^{-6}\) has exactly one root, and at any trial \(\mu\) the sign of \(\delta_\mu(0.5) - 10^{-6}\) says on which side of it you are.
The steps. Take the midpoint in \(\ln\mu\), \(\sqrt{\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\mu_{\mathrm{hi}}}\). If \(\delta_\mu(0.5) > 10^{-6}\) the noise is too small, so the root is below and \(\mu_{\mathrm{hi}}\) moves down; otherwise \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) moves up. The first midpoint is \(\sqrt{10^{-3}\times100} = 0.316228\), where \(\delta\) is too large. Table 20.1 shows the interval after selected steps.

The noise. \(\sigma^* = \Delta_2f/0.124106 = 8.0576\,\Delta_2f\).
The classic formula. \(\sigma = \Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25\times10^6)}/0.5 = 10.5976\,\Delta_2f\), a factor of 1.315 more, or 73% more variance.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.5 Composing Gaussian mechanisms exactly

Exercise 5. Composing Gaussian mechanisms exactly. You answer \(k\) queries, each with \(\Delta_2 = 1\), by adding independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) noise to each. Show that the \(k\) answers together are one Gaussian mechanism with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt k\), so their exact privacy profile is \(\delta_{\sqrt k/\sigma}(\varepsilon)\). Compare with basic composition. Check: \(k = 16\), \(\sigma = 4\) gives \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); basic composition with \(\delta/16\) per query gives \(\varepsilon = 16 \times 1.0864 = 17.3818\). (Lemma 20.1, sensitivity of a concatenation)







TipSolution






Stack the queries. Let \(F(D) = (f_1(D), \dots, f_k(D)) \in \mathbb R^k\) (each \(f_i\) real-valued, or stack the coordinates if they are vectors). The release is \(F(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_k)\), because the noises are independent with the same variance.
Its sensitivity. \(\|F(D) - F(D')\|_2^2 = \sum_i|f_i(D) - f_i(D')|^2 \le k\), so \(\Delta_2F \le \sqrt k\).
Its privacy profile. By Theorem 20.3, the release is \((\varepsilon, \delta_\mu(\varepsilon))\)-DP with \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\) for every \(\varepsilon\), and exactly that when some pair reaches \(\Delta_2F = \sqrt k\).
Check. \(k = 16\), \(\sigma = 4\): \(\mu = 4/4 = 1\). Solving \(\delta_1(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) gives \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\), the value read off Figure 20.3 for \(\sigma/\Delta_2 = 1\).
Basic composition. Each query alone has \(\mu = 1/4\). Spend \(\delta/16 = 6.25\times10^{-7}\) on each: solving \(\delta_{1/4}(\varepsilon) = 6.25\times10^{-7}\) gives \(\varepsilon = 1.0864\) per query, and basic composition adds them to \(\varepsilon = 17.3818\) at total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). That is four times the exact value.

Why. Basic composition adds \(\varepsilon\)’s, so it grows like \(k\). The exact curve depends on \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\), which grows like \(\sqrt k\): sixteen queries cost as much as one query with a quarter of the noise. The same argument holds for adaptively chosen queries, with more care; Advanced and optimal composition and Part 4 develop it.
Gaussian noise composes into Gaussian noise, so for Gaussian mechanisms the exact composed guarantee is a one-line formula.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.6 A private mean of vectors

Exercise 6. A private mean of vectors. Each of \(n\) records is a vector in \(\mathbb R^d\) with \(\|x\|_2 \le 1\), and neighbours replace one record. Find \(\Delta_2\) and an upper bound on \(\Delta_1\) for the mean, and compare the expected squared \(\ell_2\) error of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. Check: at \(d = 100\), \(n = 10{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the root-mean-square \(\ell_2\) errors are 0.02828 (Laplace) and 0.00746 (Gaussian). (Equation 20.3, dense queries)







TipSolution






\(\ell_2\) sensitivity. Replacing \(x\) by \(x'\) moves the mean by \((x' - x)/n\), and \(\|x' - x\|_2 \le \|x\|_2 + \|x'\|_2 \le 2\). So \(\Delta_2 = 2/n\), reached by \(x' = -x\).
\(\ell_1\) sensitivity. By Equation 20.3, \(\Delta_1 \le \sqrt d\,\Delta_2 = 2\sqrt d/n\), reached when \(x\) and \(x'\) are opposite vectors with all coordinates \(\pm1/\sqrt d\).
Laplace error. Each of the \(d\) coordinates has variance \(2b^2\) with \(b = \Delta_1/\varepsilon\), so \(\mathbb E[\|Z\|_2^2] = 2db^2\) and the root-mean-square \(\ell_2\) error is \(\sqrt{2d}\cdot\frac{2\sqrt d}{n\varepsilon} = \frac{2\sqrt2\,d}{n\varepsilon}\).
Gaussian error. \(\mathbb E[\|Z\|_2^2] = d\sigma^2\) with \(\sigma = \Delta_2\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\), so the root-mean-square error is \(\sqrt d\cdot\frac2n\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\).
Check. At \(d = 100\), \(n = 10{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): Laplace gives \(2\sqrt2\times100/10^4 = 0.02828\). With \(\sigma_1(1, 10^{-5}) = 3.7306\), Gaussian gives \(10\times2\times10^{-4}\times3.7306 = 0.00746\). The ratio is 3.79, and it grows like \(\sqrt d\).

Bounding a vector’s \(\ell_2\) norm makes its \(\ell_1\) sensitivity grow like \(\sqrt d\), so for norm-bounded data, such as clipped gradients, Gaussian noise is the right choice.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
section: 20.7 The privacy loss distribution of the Laplace mechanism
text:
20.7 The privacy loss distribution of the Laplace mechanism

Exercise 7. The privacy loss distribution of the Laplace mechanism. A count is released with \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) noise, and its true answers are 0 on \(D\) and 1 on \(D'\). Find the distribution of the privacy loss \(L\) of an output drawn from \(M(D)\): its two atoms, and the density of its continuous part. Check that the total probability is 1, and that the mean loss is \(\varepsilon + e^{-\varepsilon} - 1\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the atoms carry 0.5000 and 0.1839, and the mean loss is 0.3679. (Figure 20.2)







TipSolution






The loss as a function of the output. With \(b = 1/\varepsilon\), the loss is \(L(y) = \varepsilon(|y - 1| - |y|)\). It equals \(\varepsilon\) for \(y \le 0\) and \(-\varepsilon\) for \(y \ge 1\). In between, for \(0 < y < 1\), it is \(\varepsilon(1 - 2y)\), a straight line from \(\varepsilon\) down to \(-\varepsilon\).
The atoms. Under \(M(D)\) the output is \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1/\varepsilon)\). So \(\Pr[y \le 0] = \frac12\) by symmetry, and \(\Pr[y \ge 1] = \frac12e^{-\varepsilon}\), the Laplace tail beyond one unit, which is \(\varepsilon\) scales. These are the atoms at \(+\varepsilon\) and \(-\varepsilon\).
The continuous part. On \(0 < y < 1\) the density of \(y\) is \(\frac\varepsilon2e^{-\varepsilon y}\). Change variables to \(l = \varepsilon(1 - 2y)\), so \(y = (1 - l/\varepsilon)/2\) and \(|\mathrm dy/\mathrm dl| = 1/(2\varepsilon)\). The density of \(L\) on \((-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)\) is \(\frac\varepsilon2e^{-(\varepsilon - l)/2}\cdot\frac1{2\varepsilon} = \frac14e^{(l - \varepsilon)/2}\).
Total probability. The continuous part integrates to \(\frac14 \cdot 2\big(1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\big) = \frac12(1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\). Adding the atoms gives \(\frac12 + \frac12e^{-\varepsilon} + \frac12 - \frac12e^{-\varepsilon} = 1\). The script’s midpoint sum gives 1.0000 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and at \(\varepsilon = 1\).
The mean. The mean of the privacy loss under \(M(D)\) is the Kullback–Leibler divergence of the pair, which for two Laplace densities with centres \(\varepsilon\) scales apart is \(\varepsilon + e^{-\varepsilon} - 1\). The script computes the mean from the atoms and the density: 0.3679 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.1065 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), equal to the formula.

The loss never leaves \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\), which is pure DP, and half the time it sits at the worst value \(\varepsilon\). A Gaussian loss is centred at a much smaller value but has no end points.

21.1 The sharp mean loss
Exercises for Advanced and optimal composition, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_composition.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_composition.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation and its abbreviation for differential privacy (DP). \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), \(L = \ln(p/q)\) is the privacy loss with \(Y \sim P\), \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\), and randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) is truthful with probability \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
Exercise 1. The sharp mean loss. Show that \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \varepsilon^2/2\) and \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) for every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), and that the ratio of the two mean bounds tends to \(\frac12\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the three values are 0.4621, 0.5 and 1.7183. (Lemma 21.3, Theorem 21.3)







TipSolution






\(\tanh u \le u\) for \(u \ge 0\). Both sides are 0 at \(u = 0\), and the derivative of \(\tanh\) is \(1 - \tanh^2 u \le 1\), the derivative of \(u\). So \(\tanh u\) never catches up. With \(u = \varepsilon/2\): \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \varepsilon\cdot\varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon^2/2\).
Against \(\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\). Step 3 of the proof of Proposition 21.1 shows that \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2) = \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}\). The denominator \(e^\varepsilon + 1\) is at least 2, so \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \frac12(e^\varepsilon - 1) \le e^\varepsilon - 1\).
The ratio. By step 2, \(\frac{\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)}{\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)} = \frac{1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}\), which tends to \(\frac12\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\) and decreases as \(\varepsilon\) grows.
Check. Table 21.1 lists the three values.

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.2 When does advanced composition pay?

Exercise 2. When does advanced composition pay? Show that Equation 21.9 is below \(k\varepsilon\) exactly when \(k > 2\ln(1/\delta')/(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2\), for \(\varepsilon < \ln 2\). Check: for \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) the threshold is 28.8, so advanced composition wins from \(k = 29\). (Theorem 21.1)







TipSolution






Write the inequality. \(\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1) < k\varepsilon\).
Divide by \(\varepsilon > 0\) and collect the \(k\) terms: \(\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} < k(2 - e^\varepsilon)\).
Sign. For \(\varepsilon < \ln 2\), \(2 - e^\varepsilon > 0\), so both sides are positive and squaring keeps the inequality: \(2k\ln(1/\delta') < k^2(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2\).
Divide by \(k(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2 > 0\): \(k > 2\ln(1/\delta')/(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2\). (For \(\varepsilon \ge \ln 2\) the right side of step 2 is not positive, and advanced composition never wins.)
Check. \(2\ln 10^5 = 23.03\) and \((2 - e^{0.1})^2 = 0.8948^2 = 0.8007\), so the threshold is 28.8. The script confirms: advanced composition gives 2.8336 at \(k = 28\) (above \(2.8\)) and 2.8891 at \(k = 29\) (below \(2.9\)).

With the \(\tanh\) mean term, the same steps give \(k > 2\ln(1/\delta')/(1 - \tanh(\varepsilon/2))^2\), which is 25.5 at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), so that form wins from \(k = 26\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the original form needs \(k > 186.6\).
Advanced composition is a large-\(k\) tool: below about \(2\ln(1/\delta')\) steps, the \(\delta'\) it spends buys nothing.

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.3 Two rounds by hand

Exercise 3. Two rounds by hand. From Table 21.1, compute \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) for two rounds of randomized response at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), for all \(\varepsilon' \in [0, 2\ln 3]\). Check: \(\delta(0) = \frac12\), \(\delta(\ln 3) = \frac38\), \(\delta(2\ln 3) = 0\). Compare with what basic composition says. (Lemma 21.1, Theorem 21.4)







TipSolution






Which outputs count. By Lemma 21.1, \(\delta(\varepsilon') = \sum_y p(y)(1 - e^{\varepsilon' - L(y)})_+\), and only outputs with \(L(y) > \varepsilon'\) contribute. For \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\), the outputs with \(L = 0\) and \(L = -2\ln 3\) never count. Only \((0, 0)\), with \(p = \frac9{16}\) and \(L = 2\ln 3\), counts, and only while \(\varepsilon' < 2\ln 3\).
The curve. \(\delta(\varepsilon') = \frac9{16}\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon'}/9\big) = \frac{9 - e^{\varepsilon'}}{16}\) for \(0 \le \varepsilon' \le 2\ln 3\), and 0 beyond.
Check. \(\varepsilon' = 0\): \(\frac{8}{16} = \frac12\). \(\varepsilon' = \ln 3\): \(\frac{6}{16} = \frac38\). \(\varepsilon' = 2\ln 3\): \(0\). Enumeration of the four outputs and Equation 21.15 give the same three values.
Compared with basic composition. Basic composition says \((2\ln 3, 0)\), the end point of this curve, and is exact there. For two rounds there is nothing to gain at \(\delta = 0\). What the curve adds is every other point: for example, the pair is \((\ln 3, \frac38)\)-DP. A \(\delta\) of \(\frac38\) is useless for privacy, which is the point: with \(k = 2\) the loss has not had the chance to concentrate.

Composition gains come from many steps. With two steps the worst output has probability \(\frac9{16}\), and you cannot trade it for a small \(\delta\).

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.4 The per-step δ

Exercise 4. The per-step \(\delta\). Prove the identity \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k \le k\delta\) used for advanced composition with \(\delta > 0\), and show that Equation 21.15 is non-trivial only for a target \(\delta_{\mathrm{total}} > 1 - (1 - \delta)^k\). Check: with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), \(\delta = 5\times10^{-8}\), \(k = 100\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{total}} = 10^{-5}\), the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) is 4.4469 and advanced composition gives 5.9926. (Theorem 21.4, Corollary 21.1)







TipSolution






The inequality is a union bound. \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k\) is the probability that at least one of \(k\) independent events of probability \(\delta\) happens: some step shows its flag. The union bound gives at most \(k\delta\). (Or by induction: \((1 - \delta)^{k} \ge (1 - \delta)^{k-1} - \delta \ge 1 - (k - 1)\delta - \delta\).)
The floor of Equation 21.15. \(\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon') \ge 0\), so the right side of Equation 21.15 is at least \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k\) for every \(\varepsilon'\). This floor is attained by the composed four-point pair: the flags have infinite loss. So no finite \(\varepsilon'\) achieves a smaller total \(\delta\), and the script returns \(\varepsilon' = \infty\) for a target of \(4\times10^{-6}\).
Above the floor. For a target \(\delta_{\mathrm{total}} > 1 - (1 - \delta)^k\), solve \(\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon') = \frac{\delta_{\mathrm{total}} - (1 - (1 - \delta)^k)}{(1 - \delta)^k}\), a pure randomized-response problem.
Check. \(1 - (1 - 5\times10^{-8})^{100} = 4.999988\times10^{-6}\), just below \(k\delta = 5\times10^{-6}\). That leaves about \(5\times10^{-6}\) for the randomized-response part, and the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) is 4.4469. Advanced composition with \(\delta' = 10^{-5} - 100 \times 5\times10^{-8} = 5\times10^{-6}\) gives 5.9926, and its \(\tanh\) form 5.4404.

The per-step \(\delta\) is spent outright, step by step; only what is left can be traded against \(\varepsilon'\).

section: 21.5 Which pairs factor through randomized response?
text:
21.5 Which pairs factor through randomized response?

Exercise 5. Which pairs factor through randomized response? For \(P = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\) and \(Q = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5)\), find the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which Equation 21.12 is a valid channel, and write the channel. Hint: a row of \(K\) goes negative exactly where the pair violates \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Check: \(\varepsilon = \ln 2.5 = 0.9163\); the channel rows are then \((0.7, 0.3, 0)\) and \((0, 0.3, 0.7)\). (Theorem 21.2)







TipSolution






Positivity. \(K(y \mid 0) \ge 0\) iff \(e^\varepsilon p(y) \ge q(y)\), and \(K(y \mid 1) \ge 0\) iff \(e^\varepsilon q(y) \ge p(y)\). Together: \(e^\varepsilon \ge \max_y\max(p/q, q/p)\), that is \(\varepsilon \ge \max_y|L(y)|\).
The ratios. \(p/q = 2.5, 1, 0.4\) on the three outputs. The largest \(|\ln(p/q)|\) is \(\ln 2.5 = 0.9163\). So the smallest valid \(\varepsilon\) is \(\ln 2.5\), the pair’s pure-DP level.
The channel. With \(e^\varepsilon = 2.5\), \(K(\cdot \mid 0) = (2.5P - Q)/1.5 = (1.05, 0.45, 0)/1.5 = (0.7, 0.3, 0)\) and \(K(\cdot \mid 1) = (2.5Q - P)/1.5 = (0, 0.3, 0.7)\).
Check. \(t = 2.5/3.5 = 0.7143\), and \(t(0.7, 0.3, 0) + (1 - t)(0, 0.3, 0.7) = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) = P\). Below \(\ln 2.5\) the construction fails: at \(\varepsilon = 0.8\), \(K(\cdot \mid 0) = (0.7448, 0.3, -0.0448)\) has a negative entry, at the third output, where \(q/p = 2.5 > e^{0.8}\).

At the tight level each row of the channel puts zero mass on one output: randomized response’s “report 0” can never produce the output that most favours \(D'\).

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.6 Composing Gaussians exactly

Exercise 6. Composing Gaussians exactly. Show that \(k\) Gaussian mechanisms with noise \(\sigma\) on sensitivity-1 queries, composed non-adaptively, have the same \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) as one Gaussian pair with shift \(\sqrt k/\sigma\). Hint: the privacy loss of each step is normal; use Part 1’s Gaussian pair. Then explain the gap in Figure 21.4 by comparing the mean loss \(k/(2\sigma^2)\) with \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) for the per-step \(\varepsilon_0\) at \(\delta_0 = 5\times10^{-9}\). Check: for \(\sigma = 20\) and \(k = 1{,}000\), the exact \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is 7.511, the true mean loss is 1.25, and \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 29.93\). (Theorem 21.4, Gaussian pair)







TipSolution






One step. The worst pair of a sensitivity-1 Gaussian mechanism is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). With \(\mu = 1/\sigma\), Part 1 (Divergences, the Gaussian pair) shows that its privacy loss under \(P\) is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\).
\(k\) steps. By Lemma 21.2, the total loss is the sum of \(k\) independent such losses: normal with mean \(k\mu^2/2\) and variance \(k\mu^2\).
One pair with shift \(\mu_k = \sqrt k\mu\) has loss with mean \(\mu_k^2/2 = k\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu_k^2 = k\mu^2\): the same distribution.
Same loss, same curve. By Lemma 21.1, \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) depends on the pair only through the distribution of \(L\) under \(P\). So the two curves agree. (The same holds in the other direction by symmetry.)
Check. \(\mu_k = \sqrt{1000}/20 = 1.5811\), and solving the Gaussian \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) by bisection gives \(\varepsilon = 7.511\).
The gap. The true mean loss of the run is \(k\mu^2/2 = 1000/800 = 1.25\). The per-step point at \(\delta_0 = 5\times10^{-9}\) is \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.2453\), and optimal composition must assume the worst mechanism with that \(\varepsilon_0\), randomized response, whose mean loss per step is \(\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). Over \(k\) steps that is \(29.93\), 24 times the truth. The fluctuation term \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\) with the remaining \(\delta' = 5\times10^{-6}\) is 38.32 on top.
Why. A Gaussian step’s loss is rarely as large as \(\varepsilon_0\): \(\varepsilon_0\) was chosen so that it is exceeded only with probability about \(\delta_0\). Randomized response with the same \(\varepsilon_0\) has loss \(\pm\varepsilon_0\) on every output. Replacing each Gaussian step by its worst-case \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) stand-in inflates both the mean and the spread of the total.

The \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) summary of one step is a worst case over a whole class, and composing worst cases compounds the loss. Composing the actual loss distributions avoids it.

21.7 Two different steps

Exercise 7. Two different steps. Compose randomized response at \(\varepsilon_1 = \ln 3\) with randomized response at \(\varepsilon_2 = \ln 2\). List the four outputs with their probabilities and losses, and compute \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) at \(\varepsilon' = 0\), \(\ln\frac32\) and \(\ln 2\). Check: \(\frac12\), \(\frac38\) and \(\frac13\). (Lemma 21.1, Lemma 21.2)







TipSolution






The two steps. The first is truthful with probability \(\frac34\), the second with \(\frac23\).
The four outputs (Table 21.2). On \(D\) the probabilities multiply. On \(D'\) “truthful” and “flipped” swap roles. By Lemma 21.2 the loss adds: \(\pm\ln 3 \pm \ln 2\).

\(\delta(0)\). The outputs with \(e^L > 1\) count: \(\frac12(1 - \frac16) + \frac14(1 - \frac23) = \frac5{12} + \frac1{12} = \frac12\).
\(\delta(\ln\frac32)\). Only \(e^L = 6\) counts: \(\frac12(1 - \frac{3/2}{6}) = \frac12\cdot\frac34 = \frac38\).
\(\delta(\ln 2)\). Again only \(e^L = 6\): \(\frac12(1 - \frac26) = \frac13\). And \(\delta(\ln 6) = 0\), the basic composition point \((\ln 3 + \ln 2, 0)\).

With different \(\varepsilon_i\) the loss takes \(2^k\) distinct values in general, not \(k + 1\). For two steps you can list them; for many, the exact computation is #P-complete, as Murtagh & Vadhan showed.

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.8 Laplace noise in many dimensions

Exercise 8. Laplace noise in many dimensions. One record can move each of \(d\) counts by up to 1. Release each count with its own Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon_0\) and compose the \(d\) steps with the \(\tanh\) form of advanced composition (Equation 21.17) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Show that \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2d\ln(1/\delta)})\) keeps the total at most \(\varepsilon\) when \(\varepsilon \le 8\ln(1/\delta)\), so the error per count grows like \(\sqrt d\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), compare this closed form with the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) the formula allows. Check: at \(d = 1000\) the closed form gives \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.00330\), which spends 0.5054 of the budget, and a root-mean-square error of 429.2; the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) is 0.00645, with error 219.2. (Corollary 21.1, budgeting)







TipSolution






The first term. With \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2d\ln(1/\delta)})\), the term \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2d\ln(1/\delta)}\) is exactly \(\varepsilon/2\).
The drift term. Since \(\tanh y \le y\), the term \(d\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) is at most \(d\varepsilon_0^2/2 = d\varepsilon^2/(16d\ln(1/\delta)) = \varepsilon^2/(16\ln(1/\delta))\). This is at most \(\varepsilon/2\) when \(\varepsilon \le 8\ln(1/\delta)\), which at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) allows any \(\varepsilon\) up to 92.
The error. A \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon_0)\) count has root-mean-square error \(\sqrt2/\varepsilon_0 = 2\sqrt2\sqrt{2d\ln(1/\delta)}/\varepsilon\), which grows like \(\sqrt d\).
Numbers. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(d = 1000\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 1/(2\sqrt{2000\ln 10^5}) = 0.00330\), and advanced composition charges \(0.5054\) for the \(d\) steps: the closed form wastes about half the budget, because its drift term is tiny. Its error is 429.2. The largest \(\varepsilon_0\) that keeps the total at 1, found by bisection, is 0.00645, with error 219.2, the value of Table 21.2. At \(d = 100\) and \(10{,}000\) the closed form gives 135.7 and 1,357.2, against 69.3 and 693.0.

A closed-form budget is easy to state and safe, but it can leave half the budget unused. When the per-step mechanism is fixed, solve for the largest step budget, or better, compute the exact composition.

22.1 The factor 2 is needed
Exercises for Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_selection.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_selection.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A selection problem has \(|\mathcal R|\) candidates with scores \(u(D, r)\) of sensitivity \(\Delta\), and \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) = \max_r u(D, r)\). \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) and \(\mathrm{Gumbel}(\kappa)\) are given by their scales, and logarithms are natural. AboveThreshold is the sparse vector algorithm of Definition 22.2.
crumbs: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
Exercise 1. The factor 2 is needed. Use weights \(e^{\varepsilon u}\) (no 2) with \(\Delta = 1\) on \(|\mathcal R|\) candidates and the neighbours \(u(D) = (1, 0, \dots, 0)\), \(u(D') = (0, 1, \dots, 1)\). Compute the privacy loss of the output “candidate 1” and show that it tends to \(2\varepsilon\) as \(|\mathcal R| \to \infty\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) it is 1.3106 for \(|\mathcal R| = 3\) and 1.9977 for \(|\mathcal R| = 1000\). (Exponential mechanism, the two factors)







TipSolution






The pair is allowed. Every score moves by exactly 1, so \(\Delta = 1\). The scores are not monotone: candidate 1 goes down while all others go up.
On \(D\). Candidate 1 has weight \(e^\varepsilon\) and the other \(|\mathcal R| - 1\) have weight 1, so \(\Pr[1 \mid D] = \dfrac{e^\varepsilon}{e^\varepsilon + |\mathcal R| - 1}\).
On \(D'\). Candidate 1 has weight 1 and the others \(e^\varepsilon\), so \(\Pr[1 \mid D'] = \dfrac{1}{1 + (|\mathcal R| - 1)e^\varepsilon}\).
The ratio splits into the two factors of step 1 of the proof of Theorem 22.1: \[\frac{\Pr[1 \mid D]}{\Pr[1 \mid D']} = \underbrace{e^\varepsilon}_{\text{numerator}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{1 + (|\mathcal R| - 1)e^\varepsilon}{e^\varepsilon + |\mathcal R| - 1}}_{\text{normalizer}}. \tag{22.1}\]
The values. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the script gives a privacy loss of 1.0000 for \(|\mathcal R| = 2\) (the normalizer factor is exactly 1), 1.3106 for \(|\mathcal R| = 3\), 1.7761 for \(|\mathcal R| = 10\) and 1.9977 for \(|\mathcal R| = 1000\). The closed form and the mechanism’s probabilities agree to four decimals.
The limit. Divide numerator and denominator of the normalizer factor by \(|\mathcal R| - 1\): it tends to \(e^\varepsilon/1 = e^\varepsilon\). The ratio tends to \(e^{2\varepsilon}\), so the loss tends to \(2\varepsilon\).

With the correct weights \(e^{\varepsilon u/2}\) the same calculation gives at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\cdot e^{\varepsilon/2} = e^\varepsilon\).
The two factors of the privacy proof are both reached here: candidate 1’s weight drops by \(e^\varepsilon\), and the normalizer, dominated by the \(|\mathcal R| - 1\) competitors, rises by nearly \(e^\varepsilon\). Monotone scores cannot do both at once, which is why only they may drop the 2.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.2 A private median

Exercise 2. A private median. Records take values in \(\{0, 1, \dots, 100\}\). Use the exponential mechanism over \(r \in \{0, \dots, 100\}\) with score \(u(D, r) = -\big|\#\{i : x_i < r\} - \#\{i : x_i > r\}\big|\). Show that \(\Delta u = 1\) under add/remove, and use Equation 22.4 to show that with probability at least 0.95 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the output’s score is within 15.22 of the best score. When some candidate splits the data evenly, this means \(\big|\#\{x_i < r\} - \#\{x_i > r\}\big| \le 15.22\). Hint: \(|\mathcal R| = 101\) and \(t = \ln 20\). (Utility theorem)







TipSolution





Sensitivity.

The argument of step 1 of the proof of Proposition 22.2 does not use that the candidates fill an interval: one record changes the count below \(r\) or the count above \(r\) by 1, or neither, so the imbalance moves by at most 1 and \(\Delta u = 1\) on the grid \(\{0, \dots, 100\}\) too.
The script checks this by brute force on the dataset below: adding a record of every possible value and removing each distinct value, the largest change of any score is 1.

Utility.

There are \(|\mathcal R| = 101\) candidates. With \(t = \ln 20\), \(e^{-t} = 0.05\).
Equation 22.4 gives a gap of at most \(\frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}(\ln |\mathcal R| + t) = 2(\ln 101 + \ln 20) = 2\ln 2020 = 15.22\) with probability at least 0.95.
If some candidate \(r^*\) has as many records below it as above it, \(\mathrm{OPT} = 0\), and the gap is the selected candidate’s \(|a - c|\) itself.

A concrete dataset. Take \(n = 1001\) records \(x_i = \lfloor 100\,(i/1000)^2\rfloor\) for \(i = 0, \dots, 1000\), skewed toward 0. The median is 25. Values repeat (ten records equal 25), so no candidate splits the data evenly: at \(r = 25\), 500 records are below and 491 above, so \(\mathrm{OPT} = -9\). Table 22.1 lists the candidates near the top.



Table 22.1: The median score near the true median 25 for the skewed dataset.

Only candidates 24 and 25 are within the bound of 15.22. The exact probability of any other output is \(4.54\times10^{-5}\), far below the guaranteed 0.05. The mechanism outputs 25 with probability 0.7310, and its expected distance from 25 is 0.2690.
The utility theorem bounds the error in rank, not in value: with heavily repeated values, the candidates adjacent to the median can be far off in score, and the mechanism almost never picks them.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.3 The noisy maximum value

Exercise 3. The noisy maximum value. For independent \(G_r \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\kappa)\), show that \(\max_r(u_r + G_r)\) is Gumbel with scale \(\kappa\) and location \(\kappa\ln\sum_re^{u_r/\kappa}\), so its mean is \(\kappa\big(\ln\sum_re^{u_r/\kappa} + \gamma\big)\) with \(\gamma = 0.5772\) the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Check it on the five scores of Table 22.3 with \(\kappa = 2\). Hint: \(\Pr[\max \le x] = \prod_rF(x - u_r)\). (Gumbel-max)







TipSolution






The maximum is below \(x\) when every term is. The terms are independent, and \(u_r + G_r \le x\) means \(G_r \le x - u_r\). With the Gumbel cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F(g) = \exp(-e^{-g/\kappa})\), \[\Pr\Big[\max_r(u_r + G_r) \le x\Big] = \prod_r\exp\big(-e^{-(x - u_r)/\kappa}\big) = \exp\Big(-e^{-x/\kappa}\sum_re^{u_r/\kappa}\Big). \tag{22.2}\]
Recognize a shifted Gumbel. Write \(\sum_re^{u_r/\kappa} = e^{\ell/\kappa}\), that is \(\ell = \kappa\ln\sum_re^{u_r/\kappa}\). The CDF is \(\exp(-e^{-(x - \ell)/\kappa})\): a Gumbel with scale \(\kappa\) and location \(\ell\).
The mean of a Gumbel. For \(G \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(1)\), substitute \(w = e^{-g}\): \(\mathbb E[G] = \int_0^\infty(-\ln w)\,e^{-w}\,\mathrm dw = -\Gamma'(1) = \gamma\). Scaling and shifting give \(\mathbb E[\max_r(u_r + G_r)] = \ell + \kappa\gamma\).
Check. For scores \((4, 3, 3, 1, 0)\) and \(\kappa = 2\): \(\ell = 2\ln(e^2 + 2e^{1.5} + e^{0.5} + 1) = 5.8890\), and the mean is \(5.8890 + 2\times0.5772 = 7.0434\). A million simulated draws give 7.0430.

The location \(\ell\) is the “soft maximum” of the scores: it lies between \(\max_ru_r = 4\) and \(\max_ru_r + \kappa\ln |\mathcal R| = 4 + 2\ln5 = 7.2189\).
The noisy maximum is a smooth function of all the scores, not of the winner’s alone. Releasing it is a separate numeric query, which needs its own budget; report-noisy-max releases only the index.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.4 Splitting the budget of AboveThreshold

Exercise 4. Splitting the budget of AboveThreshold. With \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_1)\) and \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\), redo the accuracy derivation to get \(\alpha = \max\big(2\Delta\ln(2/\beta)/\varepsilon_1,\ 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)/\varepsilon_2\big)\), and minimize it over \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon\). Check: for \(k = 1000\), \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\Delta = 1\), the equal split gives 84.77 and the best split gives 49.76, with \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.148\). (Laplace tails, union bound)







TipSolution






Threshold noise. \(\Pr[|\rho| \ge \alpha/2] = e^{-(\alpha/2)\varepsilon_1/\Delta}\). This is at most \(\beta/2\) when \(\alpha \ge 2\Delta\ln(2/\beta)/\varepsilon_1\).
Query noise. By the union bound, \(\Pr[\max_i|\nu_i| \ge \alpha/2] \le k\,e^{-(\alpha/2)\varepsilon_2/(2\Delta)}\). This is at most \(\beta/2\) when \(\alpha \ge 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)/\varepsilon_2\).
Both. On the event that both noises are below \(\alpha/2\), which has probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the answers are \(\alpha\)-accurate by step 8 of the proof of Theorem 22.6. So \(\alpha\) is the larger of the two requirements.
Minimize. Write \(a = 2\Delta\ln(2/\beta)\) and \(c = 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)\). As \(\varepsilon_1\) grows, \(a/\varepsilon_1\) falls and \(c/(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_1)\) rises, so the maximum is smallest where they are equal: \(a/\varepsilon_1 = c/\varepsilon_2 = \alpha^*\). Then \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = (a + c)/\alpha^* = \varepsilon\), so \[\alpha^* = \frac{a + c}{\varepsilon} = \frac{2\Delta\ln(2/\beta) + 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \varepsilon_1 = \frac{a}{a + c}\,\varepsilon. \tag{22.3}\]
Numbers. With \(k = 1000\), \(\beta = 0.05\): \(a = 2\ln40 = 7.38\) and \(c = 4\ln40000 = 42.39\). The equal split gives \(\max(14.76, 84.77) = 84.77\), which is Dwork & Roth’s \(8(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta))\). The best split gives \(\alpha^* = 49.76\) with \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.148\) and \(\varepsilon_2 = 0.852\).

The threshold noise is drawn once and the query noise \(k\) times, so the union bound makes the query noise the bottleneck. Giving it 85% of the budget improves the accuracy by 41% at the same privacy.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.5 No query noise

Exercise 5. No query noise. In the two-query counterexample for Algorithm 5 of Table 22.4, with \(\tau = 0\) and \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2)\), compute \(\Pr[\bot\top \mid D]\) and \(\Pr[\bot\top \mid D']\). Check: 0.1967 and 0. (Reading a proof for the step that fails)







TipSolution






On \(D\), \(f = (0, 1)\). The first query says \(\bot\) when \(0 < \rho\), and the second says \(\top\) when \(1 \ge \rho\). So \(\Pr[\bot\top \mid D] = \Pr[0 < \rho \le 1]\).
Laplace CDF. \(\Pr[\rho \le 1] = 1 - \frac12e^{-1/2}\) and \(\Pr[\rho \le 0] = \frac12\), so the probability is \(\frac12(1 - e^{-1/2}) = 0.1967\). A million simulated runs give 0.1968.
On \(D'\), \(f = (1, 0)\). Now \(\bot\) needs \(1 < \rho\) and \(\top\) needs \(0 \ge \rho\). No value of \(\rho\) does both, so the probability is 0. A million simulated runs never produced \(\bot\top\).
Which step fails. Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 22.6 shifts the query noise \(\nu_j\) to keep the \(\top\) consistent after \(\rho\) has been shifted for the \(\bot\)s. Without \(\nu_k\) there is nothing to shift, and the two conditions can become incompatible.

A probability that is positive on one dataset and zero on its neighbour has infinite privacy loss: one observation of \(\bot\top\) proves the data are \(D\), not \(D'\).

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.6 Two candidates

Exercise 6. Two candidates. For two candidates whose scores differ by \(d\), compute the probability that the better one is selected by the exponential mechanism with weights \(e^{u/b}\) and by Laplace report-noisy-max with scale \(b\). Hint: the difference of two independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) variables has \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > x] = \frac12e^{-x/b}(1 + \frac{x}{2b})\) for \(x \ge 0\). Check: at \(d = b\), 0.7311 against 0.7241. Compare with the 50-model example, where Laplace noise did better. (Gumbel-max, Laplace differences)







TipSolution






Exponential mechanism. \(\Pr[\text{better}] = \dfrac{e^{d/b}}{e^{d/b} + 1} = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-d/b}}\), the logistic function of \(d/b\).
The difference of two Laplace variables. \(Z_2\) is symmetric, so \(Z_1 - Z_2\) has the law of \(Z_1 + Z_2\), whose density is the convolution \(\int\frac{1}{4b^2}e^{-|y|/b - |x - y|/b}\,\mathrm dy\). For \(x \ge 0\), split at \(y = 0\) and \(y = x\): the pieces \(y < 0\) and \(y > x\) each give \(\frac b2e^{-x/b}\), and \(0 \le y \le x\) gives \(xe^{-x/b}\). So the density is \(\frac{1}{4b}\big(1 + \frac{|x|}{b}\big)e^{-|x|/b}\).
Its tail. \(\int_x^\infty\big(1 + \frac yb\big)e^{-y/b}\,\mathrm dy = (2b + x)\,e^{-x/b}\), so \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > x] = \frac12e^{-x/b}\big(1 + \frac{x}{2b}\big)\).
Laplace report-noisy-max. The better candidate loses when \(Z_2 - Z_1 > d\), so \(\Pr[\text{better}] = 1 - \frac12e^{-d/b}\big(1 + \frac{d}{2b}\big)\).
Numbers. Table 22.2 compares the two.




Table 22.2: Probability of selecting the better of two candidates.

A million simulated runs at \(d = b\) give 0.7308 for the Gumbel noisy max and 0.7239 for the Laplace one.

Against the 50 models. With two candidates the exponential mechanism is better at every gap in the table. On the 50 models of the chapter, with the same scale \(b = 2\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), Laplace noise picks the best model with probability 0.4241 against 0.3935 and has the smaller expected gap, 1.40 against 1.54.

Neither private argmax dominates the other: which one selects better depends on how many competitors are close to the top. Both have the same privacy guarantee, so the choice is about accuracy on the score profiles you expect.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 22.7 The Laplace mechanism as an exponential mechanism
text:
22.7 The Laplace mechanism as an exponential mechanism

Exercise 7. The Laplace mechanism as an exponential mechanism. Take a query \(f\) with sensitivity \(\Delta = 1\), candidates on the whole real line, and the score \(u(D, h) = -|f(D) - h|\) (Proposition 22.1). Show that the exponential mechanism with the generic weights \(e^{\varepsilon u/2}\) adds \(\mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) noise, that its normalizer does not depend on \(f(D)\), and that its privacy loss is therefore only \(\varepsilon/2\). Then drop the 2 and check that the result is the Laplace mechanism at \(\varepsilon\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\), with \(f(D) = 0\) and \(f(D') = 1\), both normalizers are 4.0000 with the 2 and 2.0000 without; the largest log ratio of the densities is 0.5000 and 1.0000; the root-mean-square errors are 2.8284 and 1.4142. (Exponential mechanism, the normalizer factor)







TipSolution






Without the 2. Proposition 22.1 covers this case: the normalizer is \(2/\varepsilon\) whatever \(f(D)\) is, and the mechanism is the Laplace mechanism at \(\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the script’s numerical integrals give 2.0000 for both datasets and a largest log ratio of 1.0000.
With the 2. The weights \(e^{\varepsilon u/2}\) are the weights of Proposition 22.1 at budget \(\varepsilon/2\), so the density is the \(\mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) density centred at \(f(D)\), and step 3 of that proof with \(\varepsilon/2\) in place of \(\varepsilon\) gives the normalizer \(4/\varepsilon\), again independent of the data. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the script finds 4.0000 for both datasets.
The privacy loss with the 2. The normalizer factor is exactly 1, so only the candidate’s own factor is left, \(e^{\varepsilon(u(D, h) - u(D', h))/2} \le e^{\varepsilon/2}\). The largest log ratio of the two densities, over all \(h\), is 0.5000: the generic recipe spends only half its budget.
What the 2 wastes. Both mechanisms meet the budget \(\varepsilon\), but the generic one has privacy loss at most \(\varepsilon/2\), so it leaves half the budget unused.
The cost of the 2. A \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) variable has root-mean-square size \(\sqrt2\,b\): 2.8284 with the 2 and 1.4142 without.

The factor 2 pays for a normalizer that can move against the candidate. When the scores are a shifted copy of one another, as here, the normalizer cannot move, and the generic recipe adds twice the noise it needs.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.8 Records for a private learner

Exercise 8. Records for a private learner. For the private learner of Equation 22.7, find the number of records each term needs for an excess error of \(\alpha = 0.05\) at \(\beta = 0.05\), for the class of 1,001 thresholds and for a class of \(10^6\). Then find the \(\varepsilon\) below which the privacy term needs more records than the sampling term. Check: 33,913 and 793 records at \(\varepsilon = 1\) for 1,001 thresholds; 56,015 and 1,345 for \(10^6\); privacy dominates below \(\varepsilon = 0.0234\). (Utility of the exponential mechanism, uniform convergence)







TipSolution






The two requirements. Ask each excess term of Equation 22.7 to be at most \(\alpha/2\). The sampling term needs \(2\sqrt{\ln(2|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(2n)} \le \alpha/2\); squaring gives \(\ln(2|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(2n) \le \alpha^2/16\), that is \(n \ge 8\ln(2|\mathcal H|/\beta)/\alpha^2\). The privacy term needs \(2\ln(|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(\varepsilon n) \le \alpha/2\), that is \(n \ge 4\ln(|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(\alpha\varepsilon)\).
1,001 thresholds. \(\ln(2 \times 1001/0.05) = \ln 40{,}040 = 10.598\), so the sampling term asks for \(8 \times 10.598/0.0025 = 33{,}912.4\), that is 33,913 records. \(\ln(1001/0.05) = 9.905\), so the privacy term asks for \(4 \times 9.905/0.05 = 792.4\), that is 793 records at \(\varepsilon = 1\).
\(10^6\) classifiers. The logarithms become 17.50 and 16.81, and the requirements 56,015 and 1,345. A thousandfold larger class costs 1.65 times more records for sampling and 1.70 times more for privacy.
When privacy dominates. The privacy requirement exceeds the sampling one when \(4\ln(|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(\alpha\varepsilon) > 8\ln(2|\mathcal H|/\beta)/\alpha^2\), that is when \(\varepsilon < \alpha\ln(|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(2\ln(2|\mathcal H|/\beta))\). For 1,001 thresholds this is \(0.05 \times 9.905/(2 \times 10.598) = 0.0234\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.01\) the privacy term needs 79,236 records, more than the 33,913 for sampling.

Since the two logarithms are close, privacy dominates roughly when \(\varepsilon < \alpha/2\). At the accuracies machine learning cares about, a few percent, that means strong privacy, \(\varepsilon\) around 0.01; at \(\varepsilon = 1\) privacy is a small surcharge on the records you need anyway.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 22.9 Sparse with basic and advanced composition
text:
22.9 Sparse with basic and advanced composition

Exercise 9. Sparse with basic and advanced composition. For \(k = 1000\) queries, \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), compare the margin of Sparse with basic composition (Equation 22.17) and with advanced composition, as the number \(c\) of answers above grows. Find the smallest \(c\) at which advanced composition gives the smaller margin, and explain where it comes from. Check: advanced composition wins from \(c = 29\) (margins 3,240 against 3,218), and at \(c = 1000\) the margins are 140,035 and 23,691. (Composition of AboveThreshold runs)







TipSolution






Both margins. Each run gets failure probability \(\beta/c\), so both margins are \(8(\ln k + \ln(2c/\beta))/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{run}}\). They differ only in the budget of a run: \(\varepsilon/c\) with basic composition, and the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) whose \(c\)-fold advanced composition is at most \(\varepsilon\) with advanced composition.
The crossover. The script compares the two for \(c = 1, 2, \dots\) and finds that advanced composition first wins at \(c = 29\): the margins are 3,240 (basic) and 3,218 (advanced). At \(c = 28\) they are 3,120 and 3,155.
Why there. For small \(\varepsilon_0\), advanced composition spends about \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2c\ln(1/\delta)}\), so \(\varepsilon_0 \approx \varepsilon/\sqrt{2c\ln(1/\delta)}\). That beats \(\varepsilon/c\) once \(c > 2\ln(1/\delta) = 27.6\), and the drift term \(c\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) pushes the crossover to 29.
Large \(c\). At \(c = 1000\) the margins are 140,035 and 23,691: a factor of 5.9, close to \(\sqrt{c/(2\ln(1/\delta))} = \sqrt{1000/27.6} = 6.0\).

This is the same crossover as for advanced composition in Advanced and optimal composition: composing \(c\) runs pays \(\sqrt c\) instead of \(c\), but only once \(c\) is large compared with \(2\ln(1/\delta)\).

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.10 Many more candidates

Exercise 10. Many more candidates. In the 50-model example at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\Delta = 1\), the tail bound of Theorem 22.2 with \(t = 3\) says the gap exceeds 13.82 with probability at most \(e^{-3}\). By how much does that gap grow if there are \(10^6\) candidates instead of 50, and what does that say about the cost of candidates? Check: 33.63. (Utility of the exponential mechanism)







TipSolution






The gap at 50 candidates. Equation 22.4 with \(\Delta = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(t = 3\) gives \(2(\ln 50 + 3) = 2(3.912 + 3) = 13.82\).
The gap at \(10^6\) candidates. Only \(\ln|\mathcal R|\) changes: \(\ln 10^6 = 13.816\), so the gap is \(2(13.816 + 3) = 33.63\), which is what the chapter’s script prints.
The comparison. The number of candidates grows by a factor of \(10^6/50 = 20{,}000\), and the gap by a factor of \(33.63/13.82 = 2.4\), because it depends on the number of candidates only through its logarithm.
Why the bound does not need few bad candidates. Step 3 of the proof bounds each bad candidate’s probability by \(e^{-\varepsilon a/(2\Delta)}\) and adds at most \(|\mathcal R|\) of them, which is where \(\ln|\mathcal R|\) comes from.

A factor of 20,000 in candidates costs a factor of 2.4 in the gap: selection pays for its candidates in accuracy, logarithmically, and never in privacy.
