title: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
23.1 The halving algorithm
Exercises for Query release and private multiplicative weights, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_query_release.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_query_release.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. The universe has \(N\) possible records, a dataset of \(n\) records is its histogram \(p\), and a linear query \(q\) has answer \(\langle q, p\rangle\). \(\mathcal Q\) is the set of queries, the workload, and \(|\mathcal Q|\) its size. Multiplicative weights with learning rate \(\eta\) (also called the step size) updates each weight by the factor \(1 - \eta\ell\), where \(\ell\) is the expert’s loss, and after \(T\) rounds its regret is at most \(\eta T + \ln N/\eta\) (Equation 23.8). Private multiplicative weights runs \(T\) rounds, each with two steps of budget \(\varepsilon_0\), and its error bound Equation 23.15 contains the term \(L = \ln|\mathcal Q| + 2\ln(2T/\beta)\), where \(\beta\) is the failure probability. Every exercise that needs one uses \(\beta = 0.05\); under approximate differential privacy (DP) it uses \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Logarithms are natural unless written \(\log_2\).
crumbs: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
Exercise 1. The halving algorithm. \(N\) experts predict a yes/no outcome each day, and one of them is always right. You follow the majority of the experts who have never been wrong, and you drop every expert as soon as it errs. Show that you make at most \(\log_2N\) mistakes, whatever the predictions. Check: with 1,024 experts the bound is 10; in 200 simulated runs of 200 days with random experts, the most mistakes was 8. (Potential argument)







TipSolution






The perfect expert survives. It is never wrong, so it is never dropped, and at least one expert always remains.
A mistake halves the survivors. Break ties in the vote either way. You are wrong only when at least half of the surviving experts were wrong. All of those are dropped, so at least half the survivors go.
Count. Start with \(N\) survivors. After \(M\) mistakes at most \(N/2^M\) remain, and by step 1 that is at least 1. So \(2^M \le N\), which is \(M \le \log_2N\).
Numbers. With \(N = 1024\) the bound is \(\log_2 1024 = 10\). In the script’s 200 runs, with random predictions from the other experts, the most mistakes was 8 and the average 4.29.

The days on which you are right cost nothing, and the days on which you are wrong pay for themselves by shrinking the pool. Multiplicative weights replaces “drop” with “shrink the weight”, which is the same argument with the total weight in place of the number of survivors.
crumbs: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
23.2 Weighted majority

Exercise 2. Weighted majority. Now no expert need be perfect, and the best one is wrong \(\mathrm{OPT}\) times. Give every expert weight 1, follow the weighted majority, and halve the weight of every expert that is wrong. Show that you make at most \((\mathrm{OPT} + \log_2N)/\log_2(4/3) \approx 2.41(\mathrm{OPT} + \log_2N)\) mistakes. Check: \(1/\log_2(4/3) = 2.4094\); with 1,024 experts and \(\mathrm{OPT} = 5\) the bound is 36.14, and the most mistakes in 200 simulated runs was 15. (Upper and lower bounds on the total weight)







TipSolution






Lower bound. The best expert’s weight is halved once per mistake, so at the end it is \(2^{-\mathrm{OPT}}\), and the total weight \(W\) is at least that.
Upper bound. When you are wrong, at least half the total weight was on wrong experts, and that half is halved. So the total weight falls to at most \(\frac12 + \frac12\cdot\frac12 = \frac34\) of what it was. After \(M\) mistakes, \(W \le N(3/4)^M\).
Combine. \(2^{-\mathrm{OPT}} \le N(3/4)^M\). Taking \(\log_2\) of both sides, \(-\mathrm{OPT} \le \log_2N - M\log_2(4/3)\), so \(M \le (\mathrm{OPT} + \log_2N)/\log_2(4/3)\).
Numbers. \(\log_2(4/3) = 0.4150\), so the constant is 2.4094. With \(N = 1024\) and \(\mathrm{OPT} = 5\) the bound is \(2.4094 \times 15 = 36.14\). The script’s 200 runs with random experts never exceeded 15 mistakes.

The factor 2.41 in front of \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the price of a deterministic learner: an adversary can make the weighted majority wrong whenever the vote is close. The randomized version of the chapter pays only \(\mathrm{OPT}\) plus a term that grows like the square root of the number of rounds.
crumbs: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights
section: 23.3 The learning rate in the mistake bound
text:
23.3 The learning rate in the mistake bound

Exercise 3. The learning rate in the mistake bound. In the proof of Theorem 23.2, keep a general learning rate \(\eta < \alpha\) instead of \(\alpha/2\). Show that the number of corrections satisfies \(U < \ln N/(\eta(\alpha - \eta))\), and that \(\eta = \alpha/2\) minimizes this bound. Check: for \(N = 256\) and \(\alpha = 0.05\), the bound is 8,872 at \(\eta = 0.025\) and 11,830 at both \(\eta = 0.0125\) and \(\eta = 0.0375\). (Regret to mistakes)







TipSolution






The same two bounds on the regret. As in steps 1 and 2 of Theorem 23.2, each correction has regret more than \(\alpha\), so after \(U\) corrections the total is more than \(\alpha U\). The regret bound Equation 23.8, applied to those \(U\) rounds (\(T = U\)), gives at most \(\eta U + \ln N/\eta\).
Solve for \(U\). \(\alpha U < \eta U + \ln N/\eta\) gives \((\alpha - \eta)U < \ln N/\eta\), so \(U < \ln N/(\eta(\alpha - \eta))\) for \(\eta < \alpha\).
The best learning rate. The bound is smallest when \(\eta(\alpha - \eta)\) is largest. That product is a downward parabola in \(\eta\) with roots at 0 and \(\alpha\), so its maximum is at the midpoint \(\eta = \alpha/2\), where it equals \(\alpha^2/4\). The bound is then \(4\ln N/\alpha^2\).
Numbers. With \(\ln 256 = 5.545\) and \(\alpha = 0.05\): at \(\eta = 0.025\) the bound is \(5.545/(0.025 \times 0.025) = 8872\). At \(\eta = 0.0125\) or \(0.0375\) the product is \(0.0125 \times 0.0375\) in both cases, and the bound is 11,830.

A step that is too small learns slowly from each correction, and a step that is too large pays too much regret on each one. The parabola is symmetric, so the two kinds of error cost the same at equal distances from \(\alpha/2\).
crumbs: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
23.4 The pure-DP sample size

Exercise 4. The pure-DP sample size. Under pure DP each step gets \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(2T)\), and the error bound Equation 23.15 of Theorem 23.3 becomes \(A/\sqrt T + CT\) with \(A = 2\sqrt{\ln N}\) and \(C = 4L/(n\varepsilon)\). The term \(L\) grows with \(T\) only through a logarithm, so treat it as a constant. Find the \(T\) that minimizes the bound, show that the minimum is \(3(4L\ln N/(n\varepsilon))^{1/3}\), and deduce \(n = 108L\ln N/(\alpha^3\varepsilon)\). Check: for \(N = 2^{20}\), \(|\mathcal Q| = 10^6\), \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), a search over \(T\) that lets \(L\) vary needs \(5.14\times10^8\) records, at \(T = 48{,}610\) and \(L = 42.78\). The closed form with that \(L\) gives \(5.12\times10^8\). (Balancing two terms)







TipSolution






The derivative. The derivative of \(A T^{-1/2} + CT\) with respect to \(T\) is \(-\frac A2T^{-3/2} + C\). It is zero at \(T^{3/2} = A/(2C)\), that is \(T = (A/(2C))^{2/3}\), and the function is convex, so this is the minimum.
The minimum. At that \(T\), \(A T^{-1/2} = A(2C/A)^{1/3} = 2^{1/3}A^{2/3}C^{1/3}\) and \(CT = C(A/(2C))^{2/3} = 2^{-2/3}A^{2/3}C^{1/3}\). Since \(2^{1/3} = 2 \times 2^{-2/3}\), the two coefficients add to \(3 \times 2^{-2/3}\), and the sum is \(\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}A^{2/3}C^{1/3}\).
Substitute. \(A^{2/3} = 2^{2/3}(\ln N)^{1/3}\), so the minimum is \(3(\ln N)^{1/3}C^{1/3} = 3\big(4L\ln N/(n\varepsilon)\big)^{1/3}\).
Records. Setting this equal to \(\alpha\) and cubing, \(\alpha^3 = 27 \times 4L\ln N/(n\varepsilon)\), so \(n = 108L\ln N/(\alpha^3\varepsilon)\).
Numbers. The script searches over \(T\), recomputing \(L\) for each, and finds \(5.14\times10^8\) records at \(T = 48{,}610\), where \(L = \ln 10^6 + 2\ln(2 \times 48{,}610/0.05) = 42.78\) with \(\beta = 0.05\). The closed form with that \(L\) gives \(108 \times 42.78 \times \ln 2^{20}/0.05^3 = 5.12\times10^8\). The same search under approximate DP, as in Table 23.4, needs \(1.56\times10^7\) records, about 33 times fewer.

Pure DP pays \(\alpha^{-3}\) where approximate DP (Corollary 23.1) pays \(\alpha^{-2}\), because basic composition charges each round \(1/T\) of the budget, while advanced composition charges only about \(1/\sqrt T\). It is the same \(\sqrt k\) saving as in Advanced and optimal composition.

title: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
23.5 A small dataset by sampling

Exercise 5. A small dataset by sampling. SmallDB rests on a claim: a random sample of \(m = \lceil2\ln(2|\mathcal Q|)/\alpha^2\rceil\) records, drawn from the data, has error at most \(\alpha/2\) on every query with positive probability. Take the chapter’s running example, a table with eight yes/no attributes and 6,560 marginal queries, and \(\alpha = 0.1\). Compute \(m\), and check the claim by drawing samples from the example’s histogram. Check: \(m = 1897\). Over 200 samples, the largest error is 0.0261 on average and at most 0.0451, so every sample is within \(\alpha/2 = 0.05\). With only 200 records per sample, 1% of the samples stay within 0.05. (Hoeffding’s inequality and the union bound)







TipSolution






The size. \(m = \lceil2\ln(2 \times 6560)/0.1^2\rceil = \lceil200\ln 13{,}120\rceil = \lceil1896.4\rceil = 1897\).
Why it works. Lemma 23.3 shows that one query of a sample of \(m\) records is off by more than \(\alpha/2\) with probability at most \(2e^{-m\alpha^2/2}\), by Hoeffding’s inequality. With \(m = 1897\) this is \(2e^{-9.485} = 1.52\times10^{-4}\), and the union bound over 6,560 queries gives at most 0.997, which is below 1.
The check. The script draws 200 samples of 1,897 records from the example’s histogram and computes each sample’s largest error over the 6,560 queries. The average is 0.0261 and the largest is 0.0451, so every sample is within 0.05.
Fewer records. With 200 records instead, the average largest error is 0.0834, and only 1% of samples stay within 0.05.

The union bound only just certifies that a good sample exists, with a failure bound of 0.997. In fact every one of the 200 samples was good. The union bound adds up 6,560 failure probabilities as if the failures never overlapped, but the queries share records, and each query’s own failure probability is far below the Hoeffding bound. SmallDB’s search over all \(N^m\) datasets is where the cost lies, not the existence of a good one.

title: 23  Exercises: Query release and private multiplicative weights
section: 23.6 Where private multiplicative weights overtakes Gaussian noise
text:
23.6 Where private multiplicative weights overtakes Gaussian noise

Exercise 6. Where private multiplicative weights overtakes Gaussian noise. Using Equation 23.4 and the bound of private multiplicative weights with its best number of rounds, find the number of queries at which private multiplicative weights needs fewer records for error 0.05, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Explain why shrinking the universe from \(2^{20}\) to \(2^{10}\) records moves the crossover so little. Check: about \(1.1\times10^9\) queries for \(N = 2^{20}\) and \(5.1\times10^8\) for \(N = 2^{10}\). (Comparing sample complexities)







TipSolution






The two requirements. Gaussian noise on every answer needs \(n = \sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}\,z/(\mu\alpha)\) by Equation 23.4. Here \(\mu\) is a constant fixed by \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), and \(z\), a normal quantile at the tail \(\beta/(2|\mathcal Q|)\), grows only like \(\sqrt{\ln|\mathcal Q|}\), so the requirement grows like \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|\ln|\mathcal Q|}\). Private multiplicative weights needs about \(64\sqrt{\ln N\ln(1/\delta)}\,L/(\alpha^2\varepsilon)\) by Equation 23.20, which grows like \(\ln|\mathcal Q|\) through \(L\).
The crossover. At small \(|\mathcal Q|\) the Gaussian mechanism needs far fewer records (Table 23.4), and its requirement grows faster, so the two curves cross once. A bisection on \(|\mathcal Q|\) in the script finds the crossover at about \(1.1\times10^9\) queries for \(N = 2^{20}\).
A smaller universe. With \(N = 2^{10}\) the factor \(\sqrt{\ln N}\) falls by \(\sqrt{10/20} = 0.71\), so private multiplicative weights needs about 0.71 times as many records. The Gaussian requirement grows like \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}\), up to the slowly growing \(z\), so it reaches a level 0.71 times lower at about \(0.71^2 = 0.5\) times as many queries. The script finds \(5.1\times10^8\). So a universe 1,024 times smaller moves the crossover by only a factor of 2, because the universe enters private multiplicative weights only through \(\sqrt{\ln N}\).

The advantage of private multiplicative weights is real but asymptotic. It needs about a billion queries without structure (queries whose answers one record can all change) at these settings, which is why it matters most for releases such as all marginals of a wide table, where the number of queries grows exponentially with the number of attributes.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.1 Local sensitivity of the mean
Exercises for Beyond global sensitivity, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_sensitivity.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_sensitivity.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Datasets have a fixed size \(n\), neighbours differ in one replaced record, \(d\) is the Hamming distance, and \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) are the parameters of differential privacy (DP). Sorted values are \(x_1 \le \dots \le x_n\) in \([0, \Lambda]\), padded with \(x_i = 0\) for \(i \le 0\) and \(x_i = \Lambda\) for \(i > n\). \(A^{(k)}(D)\) is the largest local sensitivity within distance \(k\) of \(D\), and \(S^*_\beta(D) = \max_k e^{-k\beta}A^{(k)}(D)\). “The ages” are the chapter’s 1,001 synthetic ages (seed 0), with \(\Lambda = 100\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\).

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
Exercise 1. Local sensitivity of the mean. For values in \([0, \Lambda]\) under the replace relation, show \(\mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{mean}}(D) = \max_i\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i)/n\), and deduce \(\Lambda/(2n) \le \mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{mean}}(D) \le \Lambda/n\). Why can smooth sensitivity never gain more than a factor of 2 over global sensitivity for the mean? Check: the 1,001 ages of the chapter include an age clipped to 0, so \(\mathrm{LS} = \Delta = 0.0999\). (Local sensitivity)







TipSolution






One replacement. Replacing \(x_i\) by \(x'\) changes the sum by \(x' - x_i\), and the mean by \((x' - x_i)/n\).
Worst replacement of \(x_i\). Over \(x' \in [0, \Lambda]\), \(|x' - x_i|\) is largest at an endpoint: \(x' = 0\) gives \(x_i\), and \(x' = \Lambda\) gives \(\Lambda - x_i\). So the largest change is \(\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i)/n\).
Worst record. Maximize over \(i\): \(\mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{mean}}(D) = \max_i\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i)/n\).
Bounds. For any \(a \in [0, \Lambda]\), \(\max(a, \Lambda - a) \ge \Lambda/2\) (the two numbers add up to \(\Lambda\), so the larger is at least half), and \(\max(a, \Lambda - a) \le \Lambda\). So \(\Lambda/(2n) \le \mathrm{LS} \le \Lambda/n = \Delta\), the global sensitivity.
At most a factor of 2. Every smooth upper bound satisfies \(S^*_\beta(D) \ge \mathrm{LS}(D) \ge \Lambda/(2n) = \Delta/2\). Noise scaled by \(S^*\) is therefore at least half the global noise, before even paying the \(1/\alpha\) factor of the admissible noise.
The ages. The smallest age is 0 (six ages were clipped to 0), so \(\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i) = 100\) for that record and \(\mathrm{LS} = 100/1001 = 0.0999 = \Delta\).

Local sensitivity helps when the statistic is insensitive on typical data but not in the worst case. For the mean, every dataset is within a factor of 2 of the worst case, so clipping, not smoothing, is the tool.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.2 A sharper Cauchy

Exercise 2. A sharper Cauchy. Show that \(\sup_{u \ge 0}\gamma u^{\gamma-1}/(1 + u^\gamma) = (\gamma - 1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\), so for the Cauchy the sliding constant is 1 rather than \(\gamma = 2\). Redo the pure-DP condition with this constant and find the largest \(\alpha\) for \(\beta = \varepsilon/6\). Check: \(\alpha = \varepsilon/2\), and the noise scale for the median age drops from 0.979 to 0.326. (Admissible noise)







TipSolution






Find the maximum. Let \(g(u) = \gamma u^{\gamma-1}/(1 + u^\gamma)\). It is 0 at \(u = 0\) (for \(\gamma > 1\)) and tends to 0 as \(u \to \infty\), so its maximum is at a critical point. By the quotient rule, \(g'(u) = 0\) when \[(\gamma - 1)u^{\gamma-2}(1 + u^\gamma) = \gamma u^{\gamma-1}\cdot u^{\gamma-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\gamma - 1)(1 + u^\gamma) = \gamma u^\gamma\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u^\gamma = \gamma - 1. \tag{24.1}\]
Evaluate. There \(1 + u^\gamma = \gamma\), so \(g = u^{\gamma-1} = (\gamma - 1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\). A numerical maximum on a fine grid agrees (Table 24.1).




Table 24.1: The sliding constant \(\sup_u \gamma u^{\gamma-1}/(1 + u^\gamma)\) for three tail exponents, against the bound \(\gamma\).

Redo the privacy loss. In step 4 of the proof of Theorem 24.1, the mean value theorem now gives a sliding term of at most \(c_\gamma\alpha\) with \(c_\gamma = (\gamma - 1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\). The scale term (\(\beta\)) and the dilation term (\(\gamma\beta\)) are unchanged. So the condition becomes \(c_\gamma\alpha + (\gamma + 1)\beta \le \varepsilon\).
The Cauchy. With \(\gamma = 2\), \(c_2 = 1\) and \(\beta = \varepsilon/6\): \(\alpha \le \varepsilon - 3\varepsilon/6 = \varepsilon/2\).
The median age. \(S^*_{1/6} = 0.1632\) does not change, since \(\beta\) did not. The noise scale \(S^*/\alpha\) goes from \(6S^*/\varepsilon = 0.979\) to \(2S^*/\varepsilon = 0.326\), three times smaller.

Constants in admissibility lemmas are usually stated for convenience, not optimality. A direct bound on the privacy loss of your one noise distribution can recover a constant factor in the error.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.3 Other quantiles

Exercise 3. Other quantiles. Generalize Equation 24.9 to the \(r\)-th order statistic and compute the smooth sensitivity of the 90th percentile (\(r = 901\)) of the 1,001 ages with \(\beta = 1/6\). Why is it larger than the median’s although its local sensitivity is smaller? Check: \(\mathrm{LS} = 0.0114\), \(S^* = 0.2666\) at \(k = 7\). (Smooth sensitivity)







TipSolution






Local sensitivity. Replacing one record moves the \(r\)-th order statistic to anywhere in \([x_{r-1}, x_{r+1}]\) (Lemma 24.1 with \(k = 1\) and \(j = r\), and the replacements by 0 and by \(\Lambda\) of the proof of Proposition 24.1 attain both ends). So \(\mathrm{LS}_r(D) = \max(x_r - x_{r-1}, x_{r+1} - x_r)\).
Distance \(k\). The proof of Proposition 24.4 used the rank \(m\) only through “exactly \(m\) values are at or below the order statistic”. Replacing \(m\) by \(r\) everywhere gives \[A^{(k)}_r(D) = \max_{0 \le t \le k+1}\big(x_{r+t} - x_{r+t-k-1}\big), \tag{24.2}\] with the same padding: the windows now slide around rank \(r\). The script’s function order_stat_a_profile takes \(r\) as a parameter, and the median is the case \(r = (n + 1)/2\).
Compute. For the ages, \(x_{901} = 55.21\), \(\mathrm{LS} = 0.0114\), and \(S^*_{1/6} = 0.2666\) at \(k = 7\). The median has \(\mathrm{LS} = 0.1386\) but \(S^*_{1/6} = 0.1632\), also at \(k = 7\). With Cauchy noise the 90th percentile gets scale \(6S^*/\varepsilon = 1.599\).
Why the order flips. The local sensitivity is one gap, and a single gap is noisy: the 90th percentile happened to sit between two close values. The smooth sensitivity is governed by \(A^{(7)}\), the span of 8 consecutive values. Near the 90th percentile the data are sparser than near the median (the normal density is lower about 1.2 standard deviations above the mean), so 8 consecutive values span more.

Smooth sensitivity reflects the density of the data around the statistic, not one lucky gap. Quantiles in the tails cost more noise than the median.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.4 Sizing the proposal

Exercise 4. Sizing the proposal. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), how large must \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D)\) be for propose-test-release to answer with probability at least 0.99? For the ages, what is the smallest \(b\) that achieves it? Check: distance 18 (17.73 rounded up), pass probability 0.9924; \(b = A^{(17)} = 0.7892\). (Propose-test-release)







TipSolution






The pass probability. With threshold \(\tau = \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon = 13.82\) and distance \(k \ge \tau\), the test passes when \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) > \tau - k\), which has probability \(1 - \frac12e^{-\varepsilon(k - \tau)}\).
Solve for 0.99. \(\frac12e^{-\varepsilon(k - \tau)} \le 0.01\) means \(k \ge \tau + \ln(50)/\varepsilon = 13.82 + 3.91 = 17.73\).
Round up. The distance counts records, so it is an integer: \(k \ge 18\). At \(k = 18\) the pass probability is \(1 - \frac12e^{-(18 - 13.82)} = 0.9924\).
Translate into \(b\). \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = \min\{k : A^{(k)}(D) > b\}\), and \(A^{(k)}\) is non-decreasing in \(k\). So \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) \ge 18\) exactly when \(A^{(17)}(D) \le b\).
The ages. \(A^{(17)} = 0.7892\), so the smallest proposal that passes with probability 0.99 is \(b = 0.7892\) years; the script confirms \(\operatorname{dist}_{0.7892} = 18\). The chapter’s \(b = 1\) has distance 21, with room to spare.

Propose-test-release needs stability against about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) changes plus a few more for reliability. The proposal has to cover the local sensitivity at that distance, not at distance 1.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.5 The number of blocks

Exercise 5. The number of blocks. Approximate Equation 24.24 by \((\theta B/n)^2 + \theta^2/n + 2(R/(B\varepsilon))^2\) and find the minimizing \(B\) in closed form. Compare with the exact optimum over the divisors of \(n = 10{,}000\). Check: \(B^* = (2R^2n^2/(\theta\varepsilon)^2)^{1/4} = 265.9\); the best divisor is 250. (Bias–variance trade-off)







TipSolution






Where the approximation comes from. The bias \(\theta/(n_b - 1)\) with \(n_b = n/B\) is about \(\theta B/n\) when blocks are large, and the sampling variance \(\operatorname{Var}(z)/B\) is about \(\theta^2/n\), which does not depend on \(B\).
Differentiate \(g(B) = \theta^2B^2/n^2 + 2R^2/(B^2\varepsilon^2)\): \(g'(B) = 2\theta^2B/n^2 - 4R^2/(B^3\varepsilon^2)\).
Set to zero: \(B^4 = 2R^2n^2/(\theta^2\varepsilon^2)\), so \(B^* = \big(2R^2n^2/(\theta\varepsilon)^2\big)^{1/4}\). The second derivative is positive, so this is a minimum.
Numbers. With \(R = 5\), \(n = 10^4\), \(\theta = \varepsilon = 1\): \(B^* = (2 \times 25 \times 10^8)^{1/4} = 265.9\).
Exact optimum. \(B\) must divide \(n\) for equal blocks. Evaluating the exact error Equation 24.24 at every divisor, the best is \(B = 250\) (blocks of 40), with error \(0.0396\). The neighbouring divisors are worse: 200 gives \(0.0421\) and 400 gives \(0.0465\).

At the optimum, bias and noise are of the same size, and \(B^*\) grows like \(\sqrt{n}\): more data buys more, smaller blocks.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.6 Clipping exponential data

Exercise 6. Clipping exponential data. For \(X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)\), show \(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] = e^{-C}\) and, ignoring the sampling term, that the best clipping norm solves \(e^{-2C} = 2C/(n\varepsilon)^2\). Check: \(C^* = 5.692\) for \(n = 1000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\); \(3.616\) for \(n = 100\) and \(7.834\) for \(n = 10{,}000\). (Clipping)







TipSolution






The bias. \(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] = \int_C^\infty(x - C)e^{-x}\,\mathrm dx\). Substitute \(u = x - C\): \(e^{-C}\int_0^\infty ue^{-u}\,\mathrm du = e^{-C}\). (This is memorylessness: given \(X > C\), the excess is again \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\), with mean 1, and \(\Pr[X > C] = e^{-C}\).)
The objective without the sampling term: \(e^{-2C} + 2C^2/(n\varepsilon)^2\).
Differentiate and set to zero: \(-2e^{-2C} + 4C/(n\varepsilon)^2 = 0\), that is \(e^{-2C} = 2C/(n\varepsilon)^2\). The left side falls and the right side rises in \(C\), so there is exactly one root, which bisection finds.
Numbers. For \(n = 1000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(C^* = 5.692\), where the bias is \(e^{-5.692} = 0.0034\), the noise standard deviation \(\sqrt2\,C^*/1000 = 0.0080\), and their combined root-mean-square error \(0.0087\). For \(n = 100\), \(C^* = 3.616\); for \(n = 10{,}000\), \(C^* = 7.834\).
Growth with \(n\). Taking logarithms, \(2C^* = 2\ln(n\varepsilon) - \ln(2C^*)\), so \(C^* \approx \ln(n\varepsilon)\) minus a slowly growing correction: each factor of 10 in \(n\) adds about \(\ln 10 = 2.3\) minus a little, as the three values show.

For a light (exponential) tail, the clipping norm grows only logarithmically with \(n\varepsilon\). For heavier tails, such as the chapter’s log-normal incomes, it grows much faster.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.7 Smoothness at work

Exercise 7. Smoothness at work. For the degenerate pair \(D = (0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) and \(D' = (0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) with \(\beta = 1/6\), compute \(A^{(k)}\) for both and the smooth sensitivities. Check that their ratio is at most \(e^\beta\), and explain why it is exactly \(e^\beta\) here. Check: \(S^*(D) = 84.648\) at \(k = 1\), \(S^*(D') = 100\), ratio \(1.1814 = e^{1/6}\). (Smooth sensitivity)







TipSolution






\(D\), distance 0. \(n = 5\), \(m = 3\), so \(\mathrm{LS}(D) = \max(x_3 - x_2, x_4 - x_3) = \max(0, 0) = 0\).
\(D\), distance \(k \ge 1\). With \(k = 1\) the windows are \(x_3 - x_1 = 0\), \(x_4 - x_2 = 0\) and \(x_5 - x_3 = 100\), so \(A^{(1)} = 100\): replace \(x_4 = 0\) by 100 and the median sits at the bottom of a gap of 100. Since \(A^{(k)} \le \Lambda = 100\), \(A^{(k)} = 100\) for all \(k \ge 1\) (Table 24.2).
\(D'\). Already \(\mathrm{LS}(D') = x_4 - x_3 = 100\), so \(A^{(k)} = 100\) for every \(k\).

Smooth sensitivities. For \(D'\) the maximum of \(e^{-k/6}\times100\) is at \(k = 0\): \(S^*(D') = 100\). For \(D\) the \(k = 0\) term is 0, and the largest of the rest is at \(k = 1\): \(S^*(D) = 100e^{-1/6} = 84.648\).
The ratio is \(100/84.648 = 1.1814 = e^{1/6}\), exactly the largest ratio smoothness allows.
Why it is tight. \(D\)’s largest discounted term is \(D'\) itself, one step away. So \(S^*(D)\) is \(S^*(D')\) discounted by exactly one factor \(e^{-\beta}\), which is step 2 of the proof of Proposition 24.3 holding with equality.

Compare with local sensitivity, which jumps from 0 to 100 on this pair and makes the release on \(D\) deterministic. Smooth sensitivity sees \(D'\) coming and already adds noise of scale 84.6/α on \(D\).

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.8 Inverse sensitivity for a quantile

Exercise 8. Inverse sensitivity for a quantile. Generalize Equation 24.20 from the median to the \(r\)-th order statistic: show that a candidate \(t\) in the gap \((x_i, x_{i+1})\) needs \(r - i\) changes when \(i < r\) and \(i - r + 1\) when \(i \ge r\). Then release the 90th percentile of the ages (\(r = 901\)) with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and compare its median absolute error with the smooth-sensitivity noise scale of Exercise 3. Check: 0.1592 years, against 1.599; for \(r = 501\) the formula gives back the chapter’s 0.0783. (Inverse sensitivity)







TipSolution






Above the target rank. Step 1 of the proof of Proposition 24.5 used the rank \(m\) only as the number of values at or below the target. With \(r\) in its place, a candidate \(t\) in \((x_i, x_{i+1})\) with \(i \ge r\) needs exactly \(i - r + 1\) changes.
Below the target rank. Take \(t\) in \((x_i, x_{i+1})\) with \(i < r\), so \(n - i\) values lie above \(t\). The \(r\)-th smallest equals \(t\) only if at most \(n - r\) values lie above \(t\), and one equals \(t\). So at least \((n - i) - (n - r) = r - i\) changes are needed, and moving one value from above \(t\) to \(t\) and the rest to 0 shows they suffice. For \(r = m\) this is Equation 24.20, without the reflection argument, which needed \(n + 1 = 2m\).
Privacy. Each count is a distance to a set of datasets, so it has sensitivity 1 by Lemma 24.2, and the release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every \(r\) by Theorem 24.4.
The numbers. The script weights each gap by its length times \(e^{-\varepsilon\,\mathrm{len}/2}\), with \(\varepsilon = 1\), and finds the median of the distance from \(x_{901}\) by bisection. The median absolute error is 0.1592 years, against the noise scale 1.599 of smooth sensitivity with Cauchy noise, which is also its median absolute error, since a standard Cauchy variable has median absolute value 1. At \(r = 501\) the same code gives 0.0783, the chapter’s value for the median.

The 90th percentile sits where the ages are sparser than at the median, so its gaps are wider and its error is about twice the median’s. Smooth sensitivity loses by a factor of ten here, as it did at the median.

title: 24  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.9 The stable mode under add/remove

Exercise 9. The stable mode under add/remove. Under add/remove neighbours, one dataset has one more record than the other. Show that \(s(D) = \max(0, g - 1)\), with \(g\) the lead of the mode, works for the stability-based release of the mode, and find the smallest lead that answers with probability 0.95 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Why is it about half the 35 records needed under replacement? Check: a lead of 18 records; at a lead of 20 the release answers with probability 0.9972 under add/remove, and 0.004052 under replacement. (Stability-based release)







TipSolution






Sensitivity. The proof follows that of Proposition 24.6. Adding or removing one record changes one count by 1. The largest and second-largest counts then each move by at most 1, and since only one count changes, at most one of them moves. So the lead moves by at most 1, and so does \(\max(0, g - 1)\).
Zero where the answer can flip. If \(g \ge 2\), one change leaves the old mode ahead by at least \(g - 1 \ge 1\), so the mode cannot change. A dataset whose neighbour has a different mode therefore has \(g \le 1\), where \(s = 0\).
The lead for 0.95. The release answers when \(s + \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) > \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon = 13.82\). For \(s\) above the threshold the probability is \(1 - \frac12e^{-(s - 13.82)}\), which reaches 0.95 at \(s = 13.82 + \ln 10 = 16.12\). So \(g - 1 \ge 17\), and the script confirms that the smallest lead is 18.
At a lead of 20. Add/remove gives \(s = 19\) and probability 0.9972. Replacement gives \(s = \lceil 20/2\rceil - 1 = 9\), below the threshold, and probability 0.004052.

One replacement is one removal and one addition, so it can move the lead by 2 where add/remove moves it by 1. The score must halve the lead, which doubles the lead the release needs.

title: 25  Exercises: Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
25.1 The cost of Algorithm 1
Exercises for Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_discrete_mechanisms.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_discrete_mechanisms.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\) is the discrete Laplace with probability mass function (PMF) \(\frac{1 - r}{1 + r}r^{|z|}\) and \(r = e^{-1/b}\); \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\) is the discrete Gaussian; Algorithms 1–3 are the samplers of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020). Exercise 7 is about differential privacy (DP), and exercise 6 measures the distance between two PMFs in total variation (TV).
crumbs: 25  Exercises: Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms

title: 25  Exercises: Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
Exercise 1. The cost of Algorithm 1. Show that the expected number of uniform draws for \(\mathrm{Bern}(e^{-\lambda})\) is \(e\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}e^{-j} + e^{-n}e^{\lambda - n}\) with \(n = \lfloor\lambda\rfloor\), and that it is below \(\frac{e}{1 - e^{-1}} + 1\) for every \(\lambda\). Check: 3.9414 for \(\lambda = 5/2\). (Theorem 25.2)







TipSolution






One unit coin. For \(\lambda' \le 1\), the loop draws one uniform integer per coin \(I_1, I_2, \dots, I_K\), so it costs \(K\) draws, and \(\mathbb E[K] = e^{\lambda'}\) by Equation 25.6. A coin with \(\lambda' = 1\) costs \(e\) on average.
Which coins run. Write \(\lambda = n + \phi\) with \(n = \lfloor\lambda\rfloor\) and \(0 \le \phi < 1\). The \((j + 1)\)-th of the \(n\) coins with probability \(e^{-1}\) runs only if the first \(j\) all came up 1, which has probability \(e^{-j}\). The final coin, with probability \(e^{-\phi}\), runs only if all \(n\) came up 1, with probability \(e^{-n}\).
Add the expected costs. A coin that runs costs on average what step 1 says, so by linearity of expectation \[\mathbb E[\text{draws}] = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}e^{-j}\cdot e + e^{-n}\cdot e^{\phi}, \tag{25.1}\] which is the claimed formula since \(\phi = \lambda - n\).
The bound. The first sum is below the full geometric series \(e\sum_{j \ge 0}e^{-j} = \frac{e}{1 - e^{-1}} = 4.3003\). For \(n \ge 1\) the last term is \(e^{\phi - n} \le e^{1 - 1} = 1\). For \(n = 0\) the whole cost is \(e^\lambda < e\). Either way the total is below \(4.3003 + 1 = 5.3003\).
Check. For \(\lambda = 5/2\): \(n = 2\), \(\phi = \frac12\), so the cost is \(e(1 + e^{-1}) + e^{-2}e^{1/2} = 3.7183 + 0.2231 = 3.9414\). Over 20,000 coins the script counts 3.9233 draws per coin. At \(\lambda = \frac12\) the formula gives \(e^{1/2} = 1.6487\) (simulated 1.6597) and at \(\lambda = 1\) it gives \(e + e^{-1} = 3.0862\) (simulated 3.0854).

The cost jumps at each integer: just below 1 it is \(e = 2.7183\), at 1 it is 3.0862, because the split always runs a final coin, even for \(\phi = 0\), where that coin costs exactly one draw.

section: 25.2 Discrete Laplace as a difference of geometrics
text:
25.2 Discrete Laplace as a difference of geometrics

Exercise 2. Discrete Laplace as a difference of geometrics. Let \(G_1, G_2\) be independent with \(\Pr[G = g] = (1 - r)r^g\) for \(g \ge 0\). Show that \(G_1 - G_2 \sim \mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\) with \(r = e^{-1/b}\), the integer version of “a difference of exponentials is Laplace” in Probability distributions. Check: \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = 0] = 0.4621\) for \(r = e^{-1}\). (Lemma 25.3, convolution)







TipSolution






Condition on \(G_2\). For \(z \ge 0\), \(G_1 - G_2 = z\) means \(G_1 = g + z\) when \(G_2 = g\), for some \(g \ge 0\). The events for different \(g\) are disjoint, so \[\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = z] = \sum_{g \ge 0}(1 - r)r^{g + z}\cdot(1 - r)r^g = (1 - r)^2r^z\sum_{g \ge 0}r^{2g}. \tag{25.2}\]
Sum the geometric series. \(\sum_gr^{2g} = \frac{1}{1 - r^2} = \frac{1}{(1 - r)(1 + r)}\), so \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = z] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}r^z\).
Negative \(z\). \(G_1 - G_2\) and \(G_2 - G_1\) have the same distribution (swap the names), so \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = -z] = \Pr[G_1 - G_2 = z]\), and the PMF is \(\frac{1 - r}{1 + r}r^{|z|}\) for all \(z\). That is \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\).
Check. At \(r = e^{-1}\), \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = 0] = \frac{1 - e^{-1}}{1 + e^{-1}} = 0.4621\). The script sums the convolution numerically and finds it within \(4.3\times10^{-19}\) of the PMF for every \(|z| \le 10\).

Algorithm 2 builds one geometric and a fair sign instead of two geometrics, because the sign trick needs only one coin; both give the same distribution.

25.3 Variance of the discrete Laplace

Exercise 3. Variance of the discrete Laplace. Show \(\frac{2r}{(1 - r)^2} = \frac{1}{2\sinh^2(1/(2b))}\), deduce that it is below \(2b^2\), and show that \(2b^2 - \operatorname{Var}(Z) \to \frac16\) as \(b \to \infty\). Check: 1.8413 at \(b = 1\) and 199.8334 at \(b = 10\). Hint: \(\sinh x \ge x\) and \(\sinh^2x = x^2 + x^4/3 + O(x^6)\). (Proposition 25.2)







TipSolution





Let \(x = \frac{1}{2b}\), so \(r = e^{-2x}\).

Rewrite. Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(r\): \(\frac{2r}{(1 - r)^2} = \frac{2}{(r^{-1/2} - r^{1/2})^2} = \frac{2}{(e^x - e^{-x})^2} = \frac{2}{4\sinh^2x} = \frac{1}{2\sinh^2x}\).
The bound. \(\sinh x = x + x^3/6 + \dots \ge x\) for \(x \ge 0\), so \(\frac{1}{2\sinh^2x} \le \frac{1}{2x^2} = 2b^2\), with strict inequality for every finite \(b\).
The gap. \(\sinh^2x = x^2(1 + x^2/3 + O(x^4))\), so \(\frac{1}{2\sinh^2x} = \frac{1}{2x^2}\big(1 - \frac{x^2}{3} + O(x^4)\big) = 2b^2 - \frac16 + O(1/b^2)\).

text:
25.4 Accuracy of the geometric mechanism

Exercise 4. Accuracy of the geometric mechanism. Show \(\Pr[|Z| \ge k] = \frac{2r^k}{1 + r}\) for \(k \ge 1\). For a count released at \(\varepsilon = 1\), find the smallest \(k\) with \(\Pr[|Z| > k] \le 0.05\), and compare with the continuous Laplace at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). Check: \(\Pr[|Z| \ge 3] = 0.0728\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), and \(k = 3\). (Definition 25.2, tails)







TipSolution






One tail. \(\Pr[Z \ge k] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\sum_{z \ge k}r^z = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\cdot\frac{r^k}{1 - r} = \frac{r^k}{1 + r}\).
Both tails. By symmetry, \(\Pr[|Z| \ge k] = \frac{2r^k}{1 + r}\) for \(k \ge 1\). (For \(k = 0\) it is 1, not \(\frac{2}{1 + r}\), because 0 is counted once.)
At \(\varepsilon = 1\) (\(b = 1\), \(r = e^{-1}\)): \(\Pr[|Z| \ge 3] = 2e^{-3}/(1 + e^{-1}) = 0.0728\) and \(\Pr[|Z| \ge 4] = 0.0268\). \(\Pr[|Z| > k] = \Pr[|Z| \ge k + 1]\), so the smallest \(k\) with \(\Pr[|Z| > k] \le 0.05\) is \(k = 3\): the released count is within 3 of the truth with probability at least 95%. For the continuous \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\), \(\Pr[|X| \ge 3] = e^{-3} = 0.0498\).
At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) (\(b = 10\)): the script finds the smallest radius is 30. The continuous Laplace has \(\Pr[|X| \ge k] = e^{-k/b} \le 0.05\) for \(k \ge b\ln20 = 29.96\). At large scales the two agree.

At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the comparison with the continuous Laplace is between an integer radius and a real one: the discrete noise can’t be 2.5, so its tail at 3 includes the mass the continuous one puts on \([2.5, 3)\).

25.5 The acceptance rate of Algorithm 3

Exercise 5. The acceptance rate of Algorithm 3. Starting from Equation 25.38, show that \(A \to \sqrt{\pi/2}\,e^{-1/2}\) as \(\sigma \to \infty\). Check: \(A = 0.6629\) at \(\sigma^2 = 4\) and 0.7601 at \(\sigma^2 = 10^4\). Hint: \(\sigma/t \to 1\), and \(\mathcal Z_\sigma/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma) \to 1\) by Equation 25.26. (Theorem 25.7, Lemma 25.4)







TipSolution






The closed form. Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 25.7 averages the acceptance over the \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(t)\) proposal and gives Equation 25.38: \[A = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\,e^{-\sigma^2/(2t^2)}\,\mathcal Z_\sigma, \qquad r = e^{-1/t}. \tag{25.3}\]
Each factor as \(\sigma \to \infty\). \(t = \lfloor\sigma\rfloor + 1\) satisfies \(\sigma < t \le \sigma + 1\), so \(\sigma/t \to 1\) and \(e^{-\sigma^2/(2t^2)} \to e^{-1/2}\). Next, \(\frac{1 - r}{1 + r} = \tanh\frac{1}{2t}\), which is \(\frac{1}{2t}(1 + O(1/t^2))\). Finally Equation 25.26 at \(c = 0\) gives \(\mathcal Z_\sigma = \sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(1 + 2e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2} + \dots)\), so the normalizer is \(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma\) up to an error that vanishes like \(e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2}\).
Multiply. \(A \approx \frac{1}{2t}\cdot e^{-1/2}\cdot\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma \to \frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2}e^{-1/2} = \sqrt{\pi/2}\,e^{-1/2} = 0.7602\).

text:
25.6 Sums of discrete Gaussians

Exercise 6. Sums of discrete Gaussians. Compute the PMF of the sum of two independent \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\) variables and compare it with \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) for \(\sigma^2 = \frac14\), 1 and 4. Show that the sum’s variance is \(2\operatorname{Var}(X)\), and explain why it differs from the variance of \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) at small \(\sigma\). Check: at \(\sigma^2 = \frac14\), \(\Pr[\text{sum} = 0] = 0.6414\) against 0.5641. (Proposition 25.3, Lemma 25.4)







TipSolution






The convolution. \(\Pr[X_1 + X_2 = z] = \frac{1}{\mathcal Z_\sigma^2}\sum_xe^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-(z - x)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), with \(\mathcal Z_\sigma\) the discrete Gaussian normalizer.
Complete the square. \(x^2 + (z - x)^2 = 2(x - z/2)^2 + z^2/2\). So \[\Pr[X_1 + X_2 = z] = \frac{e^{-z^2/(4\sigma^2)}}{\mathcal Z_\sigma^2}\sum_xe^{-(x - z/2)^2/\sigma^2}. \tag{25.4}\] The factor \(e^{-z^2/(4\sigma^2)}\) is the \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) shape. The sum over \(x\) is the lattice sum of Equation 25.26 with variance \(\sigma^2/2\) and shift \(c = z/2\): an integer for even \(z\), a half-integer for odd \(z\).
Why it is not a discrete Gaussian. By Lemma 25.4, the lattice sum is larger at integer shifts. So even \(z\) get a little more weight than \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) gives them, and odd \(z\) a little less. By Equation 25.26, the ratio of the two values is \(\frac{1 + 2e^{-\pi^2\sigma^2} + \cdots}{1 - 2e^{-\pi^2\sigma^2} + \cdots}\), because \(2\pi^2(\sigma^2/2)k^2 = \pi^2\sigma^2k^2\) and \(\cos(2\pi k\cdot\frac12) = (-1)^k\).
Variance. Variances of independent variables add, so \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1 + X_2) = 2\operatorname{Var}(X)\), which is \(2\sigma^2\) minus twice the deficit of Equation 25.33. \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) has its own, much smaller deficit, because the deficit decays like \(e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2}\) and \(\sigma^2\) has doubled.

section: 25.7 The support argument as a test
text:
25.7 The support argument as a test

Exercise 7. The support argument as a test. In the 12-bit toy, the test “say \(D\) when \(y \notin \mathcal Y_{D'}\), and \(D'\) otherwise” never says \(D\) when the data are \(D'\), so its false negative rate is 0. Using the hypothesis-testing form of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, show that the toy sampler is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\) when \(\delta < 0.4791\), and find the bound the reverse test gives. Then show that after snapping to \(\Lambda = 1\) and clamping to \([-10, 10]\), every integer in \([-10, 10]\) is reachable from both inputs. Check: the reverse test gives \(\delta \ge 0.2033\). (Proposition 25.1, Theorem 25.1)







TipSolution






The test. Say “\(D\)” when \(y \in S = \mathcal Y_D \setminus \mathcal Y_{D'}\), and “\(D'\)” otherwise. With the convention of the definition of differential privacy, the false positive rate (FPR) is the chance of saying “\(D'\)” when the data are \(D\), and the false negative rate (FNR) the chance of saying “\(D\)” when they are \(D'\). Here \(\mathrm{FNR} = \Pr[M(D') \in S] = 0\), because \(M(D')\) never lands in \(S\), and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \Pr[M(D) \in S] = 1 - 0.4791\) (Table 25.1).
The constraint. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP makes every test satisfy \(\mathrm{FPR} + e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 - \delta\); this is the hypothesis-testing form in the definition of differential privacy, and also the definition applied to the event \(S\) on which the test says “\(D\)”, as in the proof of Proposition 25.1. With \(\mathrm{FNR} = 0\) the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) multiplies nothing, and the inequality reads \(1 - 0.4791 \ge 1 - \delta\), that is, \(0.4791 \le \delta\). So for \(\delta < 0.4791\) no \(\varepsilon\) works.
The reverse test. Swap the roles: say “\(D'\)” when \(y \in S' = \mathcal Y_{D'} \setminus \mathcal Y_D\), and “\(D\)” otherwise. Its false positive rate is \(\Pr[M(D) \in S'] = 0\) and its true positive rate is \(\Pr[M(D') \in S'] = 0.2033\). DP must hold in both directions, and the other inequality of the hypothesis-testing form, \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\cdot\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\), then gives \(\delta \ge 0.2033\). The direction from \(D\) gives the stronger bound.
Snapping. With \(b = 1\), an output \(k \in \{-9, \dots, 9\}\) arises from input \(f \in \{0, 1\}\) when the rounded noise lands in an interval of width 1 around \(k - f\), which lies in \([-10.5, 9.5]\). The noise magnitudes \(\mathrm{round}(\ln(1/u))\) run from about \(2^{-12}\) up to \(40\ln2 \approx 27.7\), and consecutive ones differ by at most about \(2^{-11}\) of their size (consecutive \(u\) differ by a relative step of at most \(2^{-11}\), and \(\ln\) turns a relative step into an additive one). So every interval of width 1 below 27.7 contains noise values, with either sign. The clamp sends everything beyond \(\pm9.5\) to \(\pm10\), which both inputs reach. So all 21 integers in \([-10, 10]\) are reachable from both inputs, and the script confirms both supports have exactly 21 points with \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = 0\).

The support argument gives a lower bound on \(\delta\) from one single event, without any statistics. Auditing tools use exactly such events, found by search, to refute claimed guarantees.

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
Exercise 1. The forced-response variant. Each person answers truthfully with probability \(s\) and otherwise reports a fair coin. Show that this is randomized response with truth probability \(t = (1 + s)/2\), and find its \(\varepsilon_0\). Check: \(s = \frac12\) gives \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3 = 1.0986\). (Local randomizer)







TipSolution






The report equals the true bit in two ways. Either the person answers truthfully (probability \(s\)), or they toss the coin and it happens to show their bit (probability \((1 - s)\cdot\frac12\)). So \(\Pr[\text{report} = x] = s + \frac{1-s}{2} = \frac{1+s}{2} = t\), for both values of \(x\).
The report is the flipped bit otherwise, with probability \(1 - t = \frac{1-s}{2}\). A mechanism on one bit is determined by these two numbers, so this is randomized response with truth probability \(t\).
Its level. As in the table of output probabilities for randomized response, the largest ratio between the two rows is \(t/(1 - t)\), so \[\varepsilon_0 = \ln\frac{t}{1-t} = \ln\frac{1+s}{1-s}. \tag{26.1}\]
Check. \(s = \frac12\) gives \(t = 0.75\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3 = 1.0986\), the two coins of the forced-response design (Boruch, 1971), the form Dwork & Roth present. \(s = 0.25\) gives \(t = 0.625\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.5108\); \(s = 0.1\) gives \(t = 0.55\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.2007\).

For small \(s\), \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln\frac{1+s}{1-s} \approx 2s\): the truthful fraction is half the privacy level.

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.2 Why \(p = \frac12\)

Exercise 2. Why \(p = \frac12\). Among unary encodings with \(\frac{p(1-q)}{q(1-p)} = e^{\varepsilon_0}\), minimize the rare-value variance \(q(1-q)/(p-q)^2\) over \(p\). Show the minimum is at \(p = \frac12\). Check: at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) the minimum is 3.683, and the symmetric choice gives 3.918. (Debiasing, optimization)







TipSolution





Write \(a = e^{\varepsilon_0}\), and work with odds: \(u = p/(1-p)\) and \(v = q/(1-q)\). The constraint says exactly \(u = av\).

Rewrite both pieces in odds. \(p = u/(1+u)\) and \(q = v/(1+v)\), so \[p - q = \frac{u - v}{(1+u)(1+v)}, \qquad q(1-q) = \frac{v}{(1+v)^2}. \tag{26.2}\]
The variance in one variable. Dividing, the factors \((1+v)^2\) cancel: \[\frac{q(1-q)}{(p-q)^2} = \frac{v(1+u)^2}{(u-v)^2} = \frac{v(1 + av)^2}{(a-1)^2v^2} = \frac{(1 + av)^2}{(a-1)^2\,v}. \tag{26.3}\]
Minimize over \(v > 0\). The derivative of \((1 + av)^2/v\) is \(\big(2av(1 + av) - (1 + av)^2\big)/v^2 = (1 + av)(av - 1)/v^2\). It is negative for \(av < 1\) and positive for \(av > 1\), so the minimum is at \(av = 1\), that is \(u = 1\), that is \(p = \frac12\). Then \(q = v/(1+v) = 1/(a + 1)\): optimized unary encoding.
The minimum value. At \(av = 1\), \((1 + 1)^2/((a-1)^2/a) = 4a/(a-1)^2\), the optimized rare-value variance of Proposition 26.4.
Check at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). \(4e/(e-1)^2 = 3.6827\). A grid search over \(p \in (0.25, 0.75]\) finds the minimum at \(p = 0.5000\) with the same value. Table 26.1 shows the curve around it; it is symmetric in \(p \leftrightarrow 1 - p\) because \((1 + av)^2/v\) takes the same value at \(v\) and at \(1/(a^2v)\). The symmetric choice \(p = e^{1/2}/(e^{1/2} + 1) = 0.6225\) gives 3.9177.

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.3 How many people?

Exercise 3. How many people? At \(\varepsilon = 1\), how many people does randomized response need to estimate a fraction with standard deviation 0.001, and how many does the central Laplace mechanism need? Check: 920,674 local and 1,415 central. (Variance formulas)







TipSolution






Local. By Proposition 26.2 the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{e^\varepsilon/(n(e^\varepsilon - 1)^2)}\). Setting it to at most \(0.001\) and solving for \(n\): \(n \ge \frac{e^\varepsilon}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)^2}\cdot10^6\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the factor is \(e/(e-1)^2 = 0.9207\), so \(n \ge 920{,}674\) (rounding up).
Central. Under replace, the count of ones has sensitivity 1, and \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) on the count gives a fraction with standard deviation \(\sqrt2/(n\varepsilon)\). Setting it to at most \(0.001\): \(n \ge \sqrt2\times1000 = 1414.2\), so \(n \ge 1{,}415\).
Compare. The ratio is about 650. Halving the target standard deviation multiplies the local requirement by 4 but the central one only by 2: the \(\sqrt n\) gap seen from the side of sample sizes.

Local DP turns an error target \(a\) into a sample size of order \(1/(\varepsilon^2a^2)\); central DP into one of order \(1/(\varepsilon a)\).

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.4 Inverting the shuffle bound

Exercise 4. Inverting the shuffle bound. For \(n = 10^6\) and \(\delta = 10^{-8}\), find the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) for which Equation 26.20 gives \(\varepsilon \le 0.5\), and check the theorem’s condition. Check: \(\varepsilon_0 = 5.809\); the condition allows up to 8.093. (Bisection)







TipSolution






The bound increases with \(\varepsilon_0\). Both \(\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\) and the bracket increase with \(\varepsilon_0\), and \(\ln(1 + u)\) is increasing. So the set of allowed \(\varepsilon_0\) is an interval \([0, \varepsilon_0^*]\), and \(\varepsilon_0^*\) solves “bound \(= 0.5\)”.
The condition. \(\ln\big(n/(16\ln(2/\delta))\big) = \ln\big(10^6/(16\times19.11)\big) = 8.093\). The theorem applies only up to there.
Bisect on \([0, 8.093]\): at the upper end the bound exceeds 0.5, at 0 it is 0, so a root lies in between. Bisection gives \(\varepsilon_0^* = 5.809\), where the bound equals 0.5000. This is inside the condition.
Check the pieces. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 5.809\): \(e^{\varepsilon_0} = 333.3\), \(\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} = \tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 0.9940\), \(\ln(4/\delta) = 19.81\), the square-root term \(8\sqrt{333.3\times19.81}/\sqrt{10^6} = 0.6500\) and the \(1/n\) term \(8\times333.3/10^6 = 0.0027\). Their sum times \(0.9940\) is \(u = 0.6487\), and \(\ln(1 + u) = 0.5000\). Using \(u\) itself, the small-\(\varepsilon\) approximation, would overstate \(\varepsilon\) by 30% at this size.

A million users let each report be almost unrandomized (\(e^{\varepsilon_0} \approx 333\)) while the shuffled collection is \((0.5, 10^{-8})\)-DP.
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.5 Sybils in the shuffle

Exercise 5. Sybils in the shuffle. An adversary controls \(m\) of the \(n\) senders. Show that the honest people’s guarantee is Equation 26.20 with \(n - m\) in place of \(n\). With \(n = 10^4\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), compare \(m = 0\) and \(m = 5{,}000\). Check: 0.5009 and 0.6535. (Post-processing)







TipSolution






Split the multiset. The shuffled output is the multiset union of the \(n - m\) honest reports and the \(m\) adversarial ones. The adversary chose its own reports, so it knows them.
The full output is a post-processing of the honest part. Given the honest multiset \(H\), the adversary’s view is \(H \cup A\), where \(A\) is a fixed (or independently random) multiset that does not depend on the honest records. A function of \(H\) and independent randomness is post-processing (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
The honest part is a shuffle of \(n - m\) reports. Its neighbouring datasets replace one honest record, and Theorem 26.2 applies with \(n - m\) people, under its condition with \(n - m\).
So the guarantee for an honest person is Equation 26.20 evaluated at \(n - m\). It cannot be better: the adversary can always remove its own reports, so they hide nobody.
Numbers. With \(m = 0\): \(n = 10{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 0.5009\) (condition: \(\varepsilon_0 \le 3.763\)). With \(m = 5{,}000\): \(5{,}000\) honest people, \(\varepsilon = 0.6535\) (condition: \(\varepsilon_0 \le 3.070\)). With \(m = 9{,}000\) only 1,000 honest people remain, the condition allows only \(\varepsilon_0 \le 1.460\), and the theorem says nothing at \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\).

Halving the honest crowd multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by about \(\sqrt2\) (here 1.30, slightly less because of the logarithm), and too few honest users void the guarantee entirely.
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.6 Splitting Laplace noise

Exercise 6. Splitting Laplace noise. Show that if \(G_i, G'_i\) are independent \(\mathrm{Gamma}(1/n, b)\) (shape \(1/n\), scale \(b\)), then \(\sum_{i=1}^n(G_i - G'_i) \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\). Hint: compare moment generating functions; \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) has \(1/(1 - \lambda^2b^2)\). Check by simulation for \(n = 100\), \(b = 2\). Check: variance \(2b^2 = 8\). (Infinite divisibility)







TipSolution






Gamma moment generating function. For \(G \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(k, b)\) and \(\lambda < 1/b\), \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda G}] = (1 - b\lambda)^{-k}\). For \(-G'\), replace \(\lambda\) by \(-\lambda\): \((1 + b\lambda)^{-k}\).
One client’s share. \(G_i\) and \(G'_i\) are independent, so for \(|\lambda| < 1/b\), \[\mathbb E[e^{\lambda(G_i - G'_i)}] = (1 - b\lambda)^{-1/n}(1 + b\lambda)^{-1/n} = (1 - b^2\lambda^2)^{-1/n}. \tag{26.4}\]
The sum. The \(n\) shares are independent, so the moment generating functions multiply: \(\big((1 - b^2\lambda^2)^{-1/n}\big)^n = 1/(1 - b^2\lambda^2)\), the Laplace one.
Same moment generating function on an interval around 0, same distribution. This is the uniqueness theorem for moment generating functions (for example Billingsley, Probability and Measure, section 30).
Simulation. With \(n = 100\) and \(b = 2\), 200,000 sums give mean \(-0.0077\), variance 8.025 (exact \(2b^2 = 8\)), and \(\Pr[|X| \ge 4] = 0.1361\) against the exact \(e^{-2} = 0.1353\).

Laplace noise can be distributed exactly, so a distributed protocol can give pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP; but Gamma shares are real-valued, and secure aggregation over the integers needs a discrete analogue (differences of Pólya variables split the discrete Laplace the same way).

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.7 Planning for dropouts

Exercise 7. Planning for dropouts. 100 clients calibrate distributed Gaussian noise for \((1, 10^{-6})\) with \(\Delta_2 = \sqrt2\). If 30% drop out after the noise was planned, what \(\varepsilon\) results? How much noise per client keeps \(\varepsilon = 1\) if up to 30% may drop out? Check: \(\varepsilon = 1.212\); per-client \(\sigma = 0.714\) instead of 0.597. (Gaussian calibration)







TipSolution






Planned noise. As in Example 26.8, the exact Gaussian calibration at \((1, 10^{-6})\) and \(\Delta_2 = \sqrt2\) gives total \(\sigma = 5.975\), so each of the 100 clients adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2/100)\), standard deviation 0.597.
Thirty clients drop out. The sum now has 70 shares, total variance \(0.7\sigma^2\), and by Proposition 26.11 the Gaussian mechanism with noise \(\sigma\sqrt{0.7}\) is \((1.212, 10^{-6})\)-DP: about 21% more \(\varepsilon\) than promised. The guarantee falls to \(\varepsilon = 2\) only when the honest fraction drops to 0.279.
Over-provision. To keep total variance \(\sigma^2\) with only 70 shares, each client adds \(\sigma^2/70\): standard deviation \(5.975/\sqrt{70} = 0.714\).
The cost. If nobody drops out, the sum carries \(100/70 = 1.429\) times the variance needed, so the error is \(\sqrt{1.429} = 1.20\) times the central one.

Over-provisioning trades a fixed accuracy loss for a guarantee that survives the worst case you planned for.
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.8 Averaging fresh reports

Exercise 8. Averaging fresh reports. A person reports the same bit every day by randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), with fresh randomness each day. An observer starts with even odds. What is the observer’s probability that the bit is 1 after 7 ones in 10 days, and after 5 ones in 10 days? After how many days is the majority of the reports wrong with probability below 1%? What changes if the report is memoized? Check: 0.9878 and 0.5000; 19 days; memoized, the majority stays wrong with probability 0.25. (likelihood ratios, binomial tails)







TipSolution






The likelihood ratio. By Proposition 26.8, a sequence with \(k\) ones in \(T\) days has likelihood ratio \(e^{\varepsilon_0(2k - T)} = 3^{2k - T}\) between bit 1 and bit 0.
The posterior. Bayes’ rule multiplies the prior odds by the likelihood ratio. With even prior odds and \(k = 7\), \(T = 10\), the odds are \(3^4 = 81\), so the probability is \(81/82 = 0.9878\). With \(k = 5\) the ratio is \(3^0 = 1\), and the probability stays at 0.5000: a balanced sequence says nothing.
The majority. The majority is wrong when more than half of the \(T\) reports are flipped, and a tie is broken by a fair coin. The number of flipped reports is binomial with \(T\) trials and probability \(\frac14\). Computing the tail day by day, it first falls below 0.1 after 7 days, where it is 0.07056. It falls below 0.01 after 19 days, at 0.008903, and below 0.001 after 33 days, at 0.000951.
Memoized. With a memoized report, every day repeats the first report. The majority is then just that report, which is wrong with probability \(1 - t = 0.25\) however many days pass.

Fresh noise on a fixed value is averaged away at an exponential rate, which is why basic composition is tight here and why deployments memoize.

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.9 RAPPOR’s one-report level

Exercise 9. RAPPOR’s one-report level. RAPPOR passes each bit \(x\) of a Bloom filter, set by a number \(H\) of hash functions, through two layers. The permanent layer keeps \(x\) with probability \(1 - \phi\), for a parameter \(\phi\), and otherwise replaces it by a fair coin. The instantaneous layer then sends 1 with probability \(q\) if the permanent bit is 1, and with probability \(p\) if it is 0. Show that a sent bit is 1 with probability \(p^* = \frac\phi2q + (1 - \frac\phi2)p\) when \(x = 0\) and \(q^* = (1 - \frac\phi2)q + \frac\phi2p\) when \(x = 1\), and that one report is \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP with \[\varepsilon_1 = H\ln\frac{q^*(1 - p^*)}{p^*(1 - q^*)}. \tag{26.5}\] Evaluate it for the homepage collection, with \(H = 2\), \(\phi = 0.75\), \(p = 0.5\) and \(q = 0.75\). Then evaluate it for the process-name collection, which differs only in \(\phi = 0.5\), and compare both with \(\varepsilon_\infty\). Check: 0.5343 and 1.0743, against \(\varepsilon_\infty\) of 2.0433 and 4.3944. (composing two randomizers in series)







TipSolution






Through both layers. If \(x = 0\), the permanent bit is 1 with probability \(\frac\phi2\) (the coin came up 1) and 0 otherwise. The sent bit is then 1 with probability \(q\) or \(p\), so by the law of total probability it is 1 with probability \(\frac\phi2q + (1 - \frac\phi2)p = p^*\). If \(x = 1\), the permanent bit is 1 with probability \(1 - \frac\phi2\), which gives \(q^*\) in the same way.
One bit’s ratios. Since \(q > p\), \(q^* > p^*\). A sent 1 has ratio \(q^*/p^*\) between \(x = 1\) and \(x = 0\), and a sent 0 has ratio \((1 - p^*)/(1 - q^*)\) the other way round.
The whole report. Two values set at most \(H\) bits each, so in the worst case \(H\) bits go from 1 to 0 and \(H\) from 0 to 1, and all other bits cancel. As in unary encoding, the worst outcome sends 1 on the bits that only the first value sets and 0 on the bits that only the second value sets, which multiplies \(H\) factors \(q^*/p^*\) and \(H\) factors \((1 - p^*)/(1 - q^*)\). Its logarithm is \(\varepsilon_1\).
The homepage numbers. With \(\phi = 0.75\), \(p^* = 0.375 \times 0.75 + 0.625 \times 0.5 = 0.59375\) and \(q^* = 0.65625\). Then \(\varepsilon_1 = 2\ln\frac{0.65625 \times 0.40625}{0.59375 \times 0.34375} = 0.5343\), the value the RAPPOR paper reports. With \(\phi = 0.5\), \(p^* = 0.5625\), \(q^* = 0.6875\) and \(\varepsilon_1 = 1.0743\), again the paper’s value.
Against \(\varepsilon_\infty\). Equation 26.18 gives \(\varepsilon_\infty = 2.0433\) and \(4.3944\). One report is about four times better protected than all reports of the value together, because the instantaneous layer adds noise that averaging over many reports removes, until only the permanent layer is left.

Two randomizers in series are one randomizer whose probabilities come from the law of total probability, so its level is computed once, from the composed probabilities.

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.10 How many buckets?

Exercise 10. How many buckets? Local hashing has the rare-value variance of Equation 26.14. Find the best integer number of buckets at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), compare its variance with optimized unary encoding and with \(k\)-ary randomized response over \(k = 1{,}000\) values, and say how many bits the bucket takes. Check: \(w = 4\) gives 3.6917 against 3.6827; \(w = 8\) gives 0.7246 against 0.7241; \(k\)-ary randomized response gives 338.9 and 24.6. (optimizing a variance over an integer)







TipSolution






The continuous optimum. Writing \(u = w - 1\), the variance is proportional to \(e^{2\varepsilon_0}/u + 2e^{\varepsilon_0} + u\). This is convex in \(u\), and by Proposition 26.5 it is smallest at \(u = e^{\varepsilon_0}\), so the best real \(w\) is \(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1\).
Round to an integer. A convex function is smallest at one of the two integers around its minimum. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), \(e + 1 = 3.718\), and the variance is 3.7701 at \(w = 3\), 3.6917 at \(w = 4\) and 3.8218 at \(w = 5\). So \(w = 4\), two bits. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), \(e^2 + 1 = 8.389\), and the variance is 0.7246 at \(w = 8\) against 0.7252 at \(w = 9\). So \(w = 8\), three bits.
Against the other oracles. Optimized unary encoding gives 3.6827 and 0.7241, a fraction of a percent better, but with a report of one bit per value. By contrast, \(k\)-ary randomized response over 1,000 values gives 338.9 and 24.6, because it spreads its signal over the whole domain.

Local hashing loses almost nothing to the best oracle, as long as the number of buckets follows \(\varepsilon_0\) rather than the size of the domain.
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 26  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.11 A year of \(\alpha\)-point rounding

Exercise 11. A year of \(\alpha\)-point rounding. Under \(\alpha\)-point rounding with \(m = 1{,}440\) minutes and \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), each person’s daily minutes wobble uniformly by up to \(\pm s\) around their own level, independently each day. What fraction of people change their report at least once in 365 days, for \(s = 15\) and \(s = 60\)? With output perturbation at a flip probability \(\kappa\) of 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3, what does one round cost, and what does each day on which the kept bit changes cost? Check: 0.0126 and 0.0503; one round 0.776, 0.569 and 0.374; per change 2.197, 1.386 and 0.847. (order statistics, the formula for output perturbation)







TipSolution






When a report can change. By item 3 of Proposition 26.10, a person’s report changes only if the two kept bits differ and the threshold \(m - \alpha\) falls between the smallest and largest value they take. The bits differ with probability \(1 - 2e/(e + 1)^2 = 0.6068\). The threshold is uniform on \((0, m]\) and independent of the values, so given the band it falls inside with probability equal to the band’s width divided by \(m\).
The expected width. For \(T\) independent uniforms on \([-s, s]\), the expected largest minus the expected smallest is \(2s(T - 1)/(T + 1)\), because the order statistics of uniforms split the interval into \(T + 1\) gaps of equal expected size. With \(T = 365\) this is \(2s \times 364/366\).
The fractions. For \(s = 15\), \(0.6068 \times 30 \times 364/366 / 1{,}440 = 0.0126\). For \(s = 60\), four times the width gives 0.0503. Over a year, about one person in 80 with a steady habit ever changes their report.
Output perturbation. Equation 26.19 at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) gives 0.776, 0.569 and 0.374 for \(\kappa = 0.1\), 0.2 and 0.3. Each day on which the kept bit changes contributes at most \(\ln((1 - \kappa)/\kappa)\), which is 2.197, 1.386 and 0.847.

A larger \(\kappa\) protects both a single round and the days of change, at the price of a noisier bit and so a less accurate mean.

27.1 Histograms under replace neighbours
Exercises for Lower bounds: what privacy costs, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_lower_bounds.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_lower_bounds.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(M\) is a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, \(\alpha\) an error and \(\beta\) a failure probability, and the random dataset of the fingerprinting section has attribute means \(p_j\) uniform on \([-1, 1]\) and records \(x_i \in \{\pm1\}^d\) with \(\mathbb E[x_{ij} \mid p] = p_j\). The examples use \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\beta = 0.05\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\).
crumbs: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
Exercise 1. Histograms under replace neighbours. Redo the histogram lower bound with datasets of a fixed size \(n\): \(D_0\) is \(n\) copies of an element \(x_0\), and \(D_x\) replaces \(k\) of them by \(x \ne x_0\). Show \(\alpha \ge \frac12\big(\ln((N - 1)(1 - \beta))/\varepsilon - 1\big)\), and show that the Laplace mechanism’s error doubles. Check: at \(N = 10^6\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\beta = 0.05\), the lower bound is still 6.38 and the Laplace error becomes 33.57. (Packing)







TipSolution






The candidates. For each \(x \ne x_0\) there is one dataset \(D_x\), so \(m = N - 1\). Each is \(k\) replacements away from \(D_0\).
Their histograms. \(h(D_x) = (n - k)e_{x_0} + k\,e_x\). For \(x \ne y\), the two histograms agree in bin \(x_0\) and differ by \(k\) in bins \(x\) and \(y\), so \(\|h(D_x) - h(D_y)\|_\infty = k\).
Disjoint regions. As in step 3 of the proof of Theorem 27.1, the \(\ell_\infty\) balls of radius \(\alpha\) around them are disjoint when \(k > 2\alpha\). Take \(k = \lfloor2\alpha\rfloor + 1 \le 2\alpha + 1\).
Lemma 27.1 with \(m = N - 1\): \(2\alpha + 1 \ge \ln((N - 1)(1 - \beta))/\varepsilon\), which rearranges to the claim.
The number. \(\ln(N - 1)\) and \(\ln N\) differ by about \(1/N = 10^{-6}\), so the bound is 6.3821 under both relations.
The upper bound doubles. Replacing a record lowers one count by 1 and raises another by 1, so the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity is 2 and the Laplace scale is \(2/\varepsilon\). Every quantile of the largest noise over the bins scales with it: \(2\times16.79 = 33.57\) (the script computes \(2 \times 16.785\ldots\) before rounding).

The lower bound does not care about the neighbouring relation, because both relations put the packing datasets \(k\) steps from \(D_0\). The upper bound does, because sensitivity depends on it. So under replace neighbours the gap between Laplace and the lower bound is about twice as large.

title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 27.2 What packing can force under approximate DP
text:
27.2 What packing can force under approximate DP

Exercise 2. What packing can force under approximate DP. Starting from Equation 27.1, show that \(m\) disjoint regions force \(m\big(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\big) \le 1\), and that as \(m \to \infty\) this forces only \(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) \le k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), \(\beta = 0.05\) the limit is \(k = 12.26\), so the forced integer group distance is 13 for \(m = 2^{20}\) and for \(m = 2^{1000}\) alike, against \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon = 13.82\). (Group privacy, packing)







TipSolution






The share of each region. Step 1 of the proof of Proposition 27.2, stopped before the last bound \(e^{-\varepsilon} \le 1\), gives \(\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_i] \ge e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\).
Sum over the disjoint regions: \(1 \ge \sum_i\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_i] \ge m\big(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\big)\).
The limit. Call the bracket the floor. If it is positive, step 2 fails for large enough \(m\), so an accurate mechanism must have a \(k\) where the floor is \(\le 0\). As \(m \to \infty\), that is all step 2 says: \(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) \le k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\).
The numbers. Bisection finds the floor’s zero at \(k = 12.26\). At \(k = 12\) the floor is \(0.95e^{-12} - 12e^{-1}\times10^{-6} = 5.83\times10^{-6} - 4.41\times10^{-6} = 1.42\times10^{-6}\), and \(m = 2^{20} \approx 1.05\times10^6\) makes \(m\) times it 1.49, more than 1. So \(k \le 12\) is impossible and \(k \ge 13\) is forced. At \(k = 13\) the floor is already negative, so no larger \(m\), not even \(2^{1000}\), forces more.

Under approximate DP, packing hits a ceiling near \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) that no number of candidates can lift. The ceiling is 12.26 rather than 13.82 because the \(\delta\) term carries the factor \(k\), which costs a further \(\ln k/\varepsilon\).

title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 27.3 The lemma for a shrunk mean
text:
27.3 The lemma for a shrunk mean

Exercise 3. The lemma for a shrunk mean. For \(f = c\,\bar x\) with \(0 \le c \le 1\), show that \(\mathbb E[f\sum_i(x_i - p)] = 2c/3\) exactly, and that the bound in Equation 27.19 is \(\frac23 - 2(1 - c)\mathbb E[|\bar x|]\). Compute \(\mathbb E[|\bar x|]\) for \(n = 1\) and its limit as \(n \to \infty\). Check: for \(n = 5\), \(\mathbb E[|\bar x|] = 0.6\), so \(c = 0.75\) gives correlation 0.5000 against the bound 0.3667. (Fingerprinting lemma)







TipSolution






The correlation. By the equality in Equation 27.19, \(\mathbb E[f\sum_i(x_i - p)] = 2\mathbb E[p\,f] = 2c\,\mathbb E[p\,\bar x]\). Given \(p\), \(\mathbb E[\bar x \mid p] = p\), so \(\mathbb E[p\,\bar x] = \mathbb E[p^2] = \int_{-1}^1\frac{p^2}2\,\mathrm dp = \frac13\). The correlation is \(2c/3\).
The bound. \(|f - \bar x| = |c\bar x - \bar x| = (1 - c)|\bar x|\), so \(\frac23 - 2\mathbb E[|f - \bar x|] = \frac23 - 2(1 - c)\mathbb E[|\bar x|]\).
\(n = 1\). \(\bar x = x_1 \in \{\pm1\}\), so \(\mathbb E[|\bar x|] = 1\).
\(n \to \infty\). \(\bar x \to p\) by the law of large numbers, and \(|\bar x| \le 1\), so \(\mathbb E[|\bar x|] \to \mathbb E[|p|] = \int_{-1}^1\frac{|p|}2\,\mathrm dp = \frac12\). The script gives 0.5050 at \(n = 100\).
\(n = 5\). Summing over the six possible counts of \(+1\) and integrating over \(p\) gives \(\mathbb E[|\bar x|] = 0.6000\). Table 27.1 compares the two sides.

title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
27.4 Padding recovers \(1/\alpha\)

Exercise 4. Padding recovers \(1/\alpha\). Let \(M\) release the means of \(n\) records with \(\ell_\infty\) error \(\alpha\). Pad a dataset of \(n_0\) records with \(n - n_0\) records, half all \(+1\) and half all \(-1\), run \(M\), and rescale. Show that this gives an equally private mechanism for \(n_0\) records with error \(\alpha n/n_0\), choose \(n_0\) so that this error is \(\alpha_0\), and conclude \(n \ge \frac{\alpha_0}{\alpha}\cdot\frac{(2/3 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta)d}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d}\) (up to rounding). Find the best \(\alpha_0\). Check: \(\alpha_0 = \frac16 - \beta\), and the constant \(\alpha_0(\frac23 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta) = (\frac23 - 4\beta)^2/8 = 0.0272\) at \(\beta = 0.05\); at \(d = 10^4\) the bound is 15.8 records for \(\alpha = 0.1\) and 158.4 for \(\alpha = 0.01\). (Fingerprinting, reductions)







TipSolution






The padded dataset. Given a small dataset \(D\) of \(n_0\) records, form \(\tilde D = D \cup P\), where \(P\) has \((n - n_0)/2\) copies of \((+1, \dots, +1)\) and as many of \((-1, \dots, -1)\). The padding sums to 0 in every coordinate, so the mean of \(\tilde D\) is \(\frac{n_0}{n}\bar x_D\).
The new mechanism. \(M'(D) = \operatorname{clip}\big(\frac{n}{n_0}M(\tilde D)\big)\). When \(M\) is within \(\alpha\) of the mean of \(\tilde D\) in every coordinate, \(\frac n{n_0}M(\tilde D)\) is within \(\frac n{n_0}\alpha\) of \(\bar x_D\), and clipping to \([-1, 1]\) cannot move it further away. So \(M'\) has error \(\alpha n/n_0\) with the same failure probability \(\beta\).
The same privacy. Replacing one record of \(D\) replaces one record of \(\tilde D\), and the padding does not depend on \(D\). So \(M'\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP whenever \(M\) is; rescaling and clipping are post-processing.
Choose \(n_0\). Take \(n_0 = \lceil\alpha n/\alpha_0\rceil\), so that the error \(\alpha n/n_0\) is at most \(\alpha_0\). This needs \(\alpha_0 \ge \alpha\), since padding can only add records.
Apply Equation 27.30 to \(M'\) with \(\alpha' = \alpha_0 + 2\beta\): \(n_0 \ge (\frac23 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta)d/R\) with \(R = (e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d\). Since \(n_0 \le \alpha n/\alpha_0 + 1\), ignoring the \(+1\) gives \(n \ge \frac{\alpha_0}\alpha(\frac23 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta)\frac dR\).
The best \(\alpha_0\). \(\phi(\alpha_0) = \alpha_0(\frac23 - 4\beta - 2\alpha_0)\) is a downward parabola with \(\phi'(\alpha_0) = \frac23 - 4\beta - 4\alpha_0 = 0\) at \(\alpha_0 = \frac16 - \beta\). There \(\frac23 - 4\beta - 2\alpha_0 = \frac13 - 2\beta = 2\alpha_0\), so \(\phi = 2(\frac16 - \beta)^2 = (\frac23 - 4\beta)^2/8\). At \(\beta = 0.05\): \(\alpha_0 = 0.1167\) and \(\phi = 0.0272\).
The numbers. At \(d = 10^4\), \(R = 1.7183\times100 + 0.04 = 171.87\). For \(\alpha = 0.1\): \(n \ge 0.0272\times10^4/(0.1\times171.87) = 15.8\). For \(\alpha = 0.01\): ten times more, 158.4.

Padding is a general trick: a lower bound for constant accuracy becomes one for accuracy \(\alpha\) at a cost of a factor \(1/\alpha\) in \(n\). With it the fingerprinting bound has the shape \(\sqrt d/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) of the Gaussian mechanism’s upper bound.

title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 27.5 How many attributes does tracing need?
text:
27.5 How many attributes does tracing need?

Exercise 5. How many attributes does tracing need? Using Equation 27.34 with \(\sigma = 0\), find the number of attributes \(d\) at which the tracing attack has advantage 0.5 for \(n = 100\) and for \(n = 200\). Check: \(d = 5678\) and \(d = 22{,}274\); the ratio \(d/n^2\) is about 0.56 in both cases. (Tracing, normal approximation)







TipSolution






The advantage. With \(m = 2d/(3n)\) and \(s = \sqrt{d(2/15 + 8/(15n))}\), the advantage is \(2\Phi(m/(2s)) - 1\). Setting it to 0.5 gives \(\Phi(m/(2s)) = 0.75\), so \(m/(2s) = \Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 0.6745\).
Solve for \(d\). \(m/s = \frac{2\sqrt d}{3n\sqrt{2/15 + 8/(15n)}}\), so \(\sqrt d = 1.349\times\frac{3n}2\sqrt{2/15 + 8/(15n)}\).
\(n = 100\): \(\sqrt{0.13333 + 0.00533} = 0.3724\), so \(\sqrt d = 1.349\times150\times0.3724 = 75.35\) and \(d = 5678\).
\(n = 200\): \(\sqrt{0.13333 + 0.00267} = 0.3688\), so \(\sqrt d = 1.349\times300\times0.3688 = 149.2\) and \(d = 22{,}274\).
The ratio. \(d/n^2 = 0.5678\) and \(0.5568\). Apart from the small \(8/(15n)\) term, \(d\) is proportional to \(n^2\).

Doubling the number of people quadruples the number of attributes the attacker needs. That is the \(n \approx \sqrt d\) of the fingerprinting bound, read from the attacker’s side.

title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
27.6 Tracing with a reference sample

Exercise 6. Tracing with a reference sample. The attacker does not know \(p\) but has \(m\) fresh records from the population, with mean \(\hat p\). Show that the score \(\langle\bar x, y - \hat p\rangle\) has the same mean gap \(2d/(3n)\) and a variance larger by the factor \(1 + 1/m\) (ignoring terms of order \(1/(nm)\)). Check: at \(n = 50\), \(d = 2000\), \(m = 50\), the predicted advantage is 0.563, and the simulation gives 0.563. (Tracing, robust traceability)







TipSolution





Work with one coordinate and drop the index \(j\). Given \(p\), the dataset, the reference sample and a fresh target are independent.

Non-member mean. \(y\) and \(\hat p\) both have mean \(p\) and are independent of \(\bar x\), so \(\mathbb E[\bar x(y - \hat p)] = \mathbb E[\bar x]\cdot0 = 0\).
Member mean. For \(y = x_i\): \(\mathbb E[\bar x\,x_i] - \mathbb E[\bar x]\,\mathbb E[\hat p]\). The first term is \(\frac1n\mathbb E[x_i^2] + \frac{n - 1}np^2 = \frac1n + \frac{n-1}np^2\); the second is \(p^2\). The difference is \(\frac{1 - p^2}n\), as with a known \(p\). Averaging and summing over coordinates gives the same gap \(2d/(3n)\).
Non-member variance. \(y - \hat p\) has mean 0 and variance \((1 - p^2) + (1 - p^2)/m = (1 - p^2)(1 + \frac1m)\), and it is independent of \(\bar x\). The coordinates are independent, so cross terms vanish, and \(\operatorname{Var} = (1 + \frac1m)\sum_j\mathbb E\big[\bar x_j^2(1 - p_j^2)\big] = (1 + \frac1m)\,d\big(\frac2{15} + \frac8{15n}\big)\), the known-\(p\) variance times \(1 + \frac1m\). (The member’s variance differs from this by terms of order \(d/n\) and smaller, which the normal approximation ignores.)
The numbers. At \(n = 50\), \(d = 2000\): gap 26.67, standard deviation \(16.97\times\sqrt{1.02} = 17.14\), so the predicted advantage is \(2\Phi(26.67/(2\times17.14)) - 1 = 0.563\). The simulation over 200 datasets gives a member mean of 26.15, a non-member standard deviation of 17.11 and an advantage of 0.563.

An estimated population costs the attacker almost nothing: with as many reference records as there are members, the advantage drops only from 0.568 (known \(p\)) to 0.563. This is the robustness that made genomic tracing practical, since public reference panels supply \(\hat p\).
