title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
27.7 Reconstruction implies \(\varepsilon\)

Exercise 7. Reconstruction implies \(\varepsilon\). A reconstruction attack recovers 90% of a database of uniform bits from a release claimed to be \((\varepsilon, 10^{-6})\)-DP. What is the smallest \(\varepsilon\) the claim can have? Check: \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\big((0.9 - 10^{-6})/0.1\big) = 2.1972\); at 99% it is 4.5951. (Bit guessing, Theorem 27.4)







TipSolution






The bound. By Theorem 27.4, recovering a fraction \(r\) of uniform bits from an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP release proves \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{r - \delta}{1 - r}\) (Equation 27.37).
\(r = 0.9\): \(\ln(0.899999/0.1) = \ln 9.0000 = 2.1972\).
\(r = 0.99\): \(\ln(0.989999/0.01) = \ln 99.0 = 4.5951\).
Conversely, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) no attack can recover more than \((e + 10^{-6})/(e + 1) = 0.7311\) of the bits.

Each extra “nine” in the recovery rate adds about \(\ln 10 = 2.3\) to the \(\varepsilon\) the attack proves. The \(10^{-6}\) barely matters here; \(\delta\) would need to be comparable to \(1 - r\) to change the answer.

title: 27  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 27.8 Packing for a mean in many dimensions
text:
27.8 Packing for a mean in many dimensions

Exercise 8. Packing for a mean in many dimensions. Extend Equation 27.17 to normal records in \(d\) dimensions whose mean has length at most \(R\), with error measured by length. Show that some \(m \ge (R/(2\alpha))^d\) candidate means are pairwise more than \(2\alpha\) apart, and conclude that an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism needs \(n \ge \big(d\ln(R/(2\alpha)) + \ln(1 - \beta)\big)/\varepsilon\). Evaluate at \(R = 1000\), \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) for \(d = 1\), 10 and 100, and compare with the capped lemma Equation 27.8 at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Check: 8.47, 85.12 and 851.67 records under pure DP; 8, 11 and 11 under approximate DP. (Packing, volume arguments)







TipSolution






A maximal separated set. Pick means in the ball of radius \(R\) one at a time, each more than \(2\alpha\) from all earlier ones, until no more fit. Then every point of the ball is within \(2\alpha\) of some chosen mean, otherwise it could have been added.
Count them by volume. So the balls of radius \(2\alpha\) around the \(m\) chosen means cover the ball of radius \(R\). Volume in \(d\) dimensions scales like the radius to the power \(d\), so \(m(2\alpha)^d \ge R^d\), that is \(m \ge (R/(2\alpha))^d\).
Disjoint regions. The open balls of radius \(\alpha\) around the chosen means are disjoint, because their centres are more than \(2\alpha\) apart. An estimate within \(\alpha\) of \(\mu_j\) lands in the \(j\)-th of them.
Apply the argument of Equation 27.17. Any two datasets of size \(n\) are within \(n\) replacements, so averaging group privacy over data drawn with mean \(\mu_j\) gives a share of at least \((1 - \beta)e^{-n\varepsilon}\) for each region under a fixed reference dataset. The \(m\) shares fit into 1, so \(n\varepsilon \ge \ln m + \ln(1 - \beta) \ge d\ln(R/(2\alpha)) + \ln(1 - \beta)\).
The numbers. \(\ln(1000/0.2) = 8.517\), so the bound is 8.47, 85.12 and 851.67 records for \(d = 1\), 10 and 100. The capped lemma Equation 27.8, with the same \(\ln m\) and \(\beta\) and \(k = n\), forces only 8, 11 and 11.

Under pure DP, not knowing where a \(d\)-dimensional mean lies costs about \(d\ln(R/\alpha)/\varepsilon\) records. Under approximate DP packing caps that cost near \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), and the shrinking balls of Private mean estimation, an approximate-DP mechanism, pay about \(\sqrt d\ln R/\varepsilon\) records for the range. At \(d = 1\) the volume bound, 8.47, is weaker than the 9.16 of Equation 27.17, because a volume count loses a constant factor inside the logarithm.

title: 28  Exercises: Private mean estimation
text:
28.1 A survey at stronger privacy
Exercises for Private mean estimation, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_mean_estimation.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_mean_estimation.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Datasets have a fixed size \(n\) and neighbours differ in one replaced record. The privacy parameters of differential privacy (DP) are \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\), the failure probability of a “the data lie in this range” statement is \(\beta = 0.05\), and errors are root-mean-square errors (RMSE) around the population mean \(\mu\). For normal data with variance 1, \(\tau = \sqrt{2\ln(2n/\beta)}\) bounds how far the \(n\) records lie from \(\mu\), and the coarse step’s bins have width \(b = 2\tau\). For heavy-tailed data with variance at most \(\sigma^2\), \(\tau_b = \sigma\sqrt{n\varepsilon/(2\sqrt2)}\) is the clipping half-width of Equation 28.15.

title: 28  Exercises: Private mean estimation
text:
Exercise 1. A survey at stronger privacy. Redo the chapter’s survey example at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\): yes/no answers with \(w = 1\) and \(\sigma = 0.5\). How many people does an RMSE of 0.05 need, and of 0.01? Compare each with the simple bound of Equation 28.4 and with the non-private 100 and 2,500. Check: 338 and 3,138 people; the simple bound gives 383 and 3,914. (Sample complexity of a bounded mean)







TipSolution






The quadratic. By Equation 28.3 the squared error is \(\sigma^2/n + 2w^2/(n\varepsilon)^2\). Setting it equal to \(\alpha^2\) and multiplying by \(n^2\) gives \(\alpha^2n^2 - \sigma^2n - 2w^2/\varepsilon^2 = 0\), whose positive root is the first form of Equation 28.4.
Insert the numbers. With \(\sigma^2 = 0.25\), \(w = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the constant term is \(2/0.01 = 200\). For \(\alpha = 0.05\) the root is \((0.25 + \sqrt{0.0625 + 4\times200\times0.0025})/(2\times0.0025) = 337.2\), so 338 people are needed, and the script checks that their RMSE is 0.0499. For \(\alpha = 0.01\) the root is 3,137.5, so 3,138 people are needed, with RMSE 0.0100.
The simple bound. \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2 + \sqrt2\,w/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) gives \(100 + 283 = 383\) and \(2500 + 1414 = 3914\). It overstates the need because the square root of a sum is smaller than the sum of the square roots.
Compare. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) privacy cost 8 extra people at both targets. At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) it costs 238 and 638. The privacy term scales like \(1/\varepsilon\), so it is no longer small next to sampling at the coarser target.

By the simple bound, the privacy term is smaller than the sampling term only while \(\alpha\) is below \(\sigma^2\varepsilon/(\sqrt2\,w)\). At strong privacy and a coarse target, the privacy term dominates.

title: 28  Exercises: Private mean estimation
section: 28.2 The smallest budget for the coarse step
text:
28.2 The smallest budget for the coarse step

Exercise 2. The smallest budget for the coarse step. With \(n = 1000\) normal records and \(R = 10^6\), the coarse step has \(m = 217{,}223\) bins. Find the smallest \(\varepsilon_1\) for which the bound \(m e^{-\varepsilon_1 n/4}\) on its failure probability is at most \(\beta\), and the RMSE of the fine step when it gets the rest of \(\varepsilon = 1\). Check: \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.0611\); the fine RMSE drops from 0.0609 (with \(\varepsilon_2 = 0.75\)) to 0.0523. (Splitting a privacy budget)







TipSolution






Solve the failure bound for \(\varepsilon_1\). Setting \(m e^{-\varepsilon_1 n/4} = \beta\) and taking logarithms gives \(\varepsilon_1 = 4\ln(m/\beta)/n\), the same equation as Equation 28.8 solved for \(\varepsilon_1\) instead of \(n\).
Insert the numbers. \(\ln(217{,}223/0.05) = 15.28\), so \(\varepsilon_1 = 4\times15.28/1000 = 0.0611\), and the script confirms that the bound equals 0.050 there.
The fine step. It gets \(\varepsilon_2 = 1 - 0.0611 = 0.9389\). By Equation 28.7 its RMSE is \(\sqrt{1/n + 18b^2/(n\varepsilon_2)^2}\) with \(b = 9.207\), which is 0.0523 against 0.0609 with \(\varepsilon_2 = 0.75\).

The coarse step needs very little budget once \(n\) is comfortably larger than \(4\ln(m/\beta)\), about 61 here. Sizing it from Equation 28.8, rather than with a fixed quarter of the budget, lowers the error by 14%. The split must still be fixed before looking at the data.

title: 28  Exercises: Private mean estimation
text:
28.3 The Pareto tail

Exercise 3. The Pareto tail. For a Pareto variable with smallest value \(x_m\) and shape \(a > 1\), show that \(\mathbb E[(X - t)_+] = x_m^a t^{1-a}/(a - 1)\) for \(t \ge x_m\). For the chapter’s records (shape 3, variance 1), evaluate it at \(t = \mu + \tau_b\) for \(n = 1000\) and \(n = 100{,}000\), compare it with the exact bias of the clipped mean, and with the bound \(\sigma^2/\tau_b\). Check: 0.001826 against the bound 0.0532 at \(n = 1000\); 0.000021 against 0.0053 at \(n = 100{,}000\). (Clipping bias)







TipSolution






Write the excess as an integral of tails. For a variable \(Y \ge 0\), \(\mathbb E[Y] = \int_0^\infty\Pr[Y > s]\,\mathrm ds\). Applied to \(Y = (X - t)_+\), which exceeds \(s\) exactly when \(X\) exceeds \(t + s\), this gives \(\mathbb E[(X - t)_+] = \int_t^\infty\Pr[X > v]\,\mathrm dv\).
Insert the Pareto tail. \(\Pr[X > v] = (x_m/v)^a\) for \(v \ge x_m\), so the integral is \(x_m^a\int_t^\infty v^{-a}\,\mathrm dv = x_m^a t^{1-a}/(a - 1)\), finite because \(a > 1\).
Only the top is clipped. With \(\mu = 1.7321\) and \(\tau_b = 18.80\) at \(n = 1000\), the lower end \(\mu - \tau_b\) is below the smallest value \(x_m = 1.1547\), so clipping only pulls values down from \(\mu + \tau_b\). The bias is minus the excess at \(t = \mu + \tau_b\).
The numbers. The formula gives 0.001826 at \(n = 1000\) and 0.000021 at \(n = 100{,}000\) (\(\tau_b = 188.03\)), equal to the exact biases the script computes, with the sign reversed. The bound \(\sigma^2/\tau_b\) is 0.0532 and 0.0053.

For shape 3 the excess falls like \(t^{-2}\), while the bound falls like \(t^{-1}\), so the bound is 29 times too large at \(n = 1000\) and about 250 times at \(n = 100{,}000\). That is why the best clipping width for these records is far below \(\tau_b\).

title: 28  Exercises: Private mean estimation
section: 28.4 When does a round shrink the ball?
text:
28.4 When does a round shrink the ball?

Exercise 4. When does a round shrink the ball? Take one round of shrinking balls with \(\|\mu\| \le R = 1000\), budget \(\varepsilon_t = 0.125\) and \(\delta_t = 10^{-6}/3\), the margin \(u = \sqrt{2\ln(4(T + 1)/\beta)}\) for \(T + 1 = 3\) steps, and \(\beta = 0.05\). The noise uses the chapter’s exact Gaussian ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t)\), a number and not the mean. Find the smallest \(n\) for which Equation 28.12 at least halves the radius, for \(d = 10\), 100 and 1000, and explain how it grows with \(d\). Check: 821, 1,699 and 4,556 records. (Shrinking confidence balls)







TipSolution






The new radius. By Equation 28.12, \(r_1 = (\sqrt d + u)/\sqrt n + \sigma_0(\sqrt d + u)\), with \(\sigma_0 = 2(R + \tau_d)/(n\,\mu(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t))\) and \(\tau_d = \sqrt d + \sqrt{2\ln(2n/\beta)}\).
It falls with \(n\). The first term falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), and \(\sigma_0\) falls like \(1/n\) apart from the slowly growing \(\tau_d\). So the condition \(r_1 \le R/2\) holds for all \(n\) above a threshold, which the script finds by bisection.
The numbers. The thresholds are 821, 1,699 and 4,556 records.
The growth. Near the threshold the noise term dominates, and with \(R\) much larger than \(\tau_d\) it is about \(2R\sqrt d/(n\,\mu)\). Halving \(R\) therefore needs \(n\) of about \(4\sqrt d/\mu(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t)\), which grows like \(\sqrt d\). Here \(4/\mu(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t) = 126\), and the ratio \(n/\sqrt d\) is 260, 170 and 144, falling toward 126 as the margin \(u\) matters less next to \(\sqrt d\).

Each round needs about \(\sqrt d/\varepsilon_t\) records to shrink the ball, and the rounds reuse the same records. About \(\ln R\) rounds are needed, so each gets \(\varepsilon_t\) of order \(\varepsilon/\ln R\), and that is where the \(\sqrt d\ln R/\varepsilon\) term of the chapter comes from.

title: 28  Exercises: Private mean estimation
text:
28.5 The fingerprinting bound in length

Exercise 5. The fingerprinting bound in length. The fingerprinting bound Equation 27.30 is for an average error \(\alpha'\) per coordinate on \(\pm1\) data. A mechanism whose error has expected length at most \(\alpha\) has \(\alpha' \le \alpha/\sqrt d\). Apply the bound directly, and then after padding to a per-coordinate error \(\alpha_0 = 1/6\), which needs \(\alpha' \le \alpha_0\), as in Exercise 4 of the lower-bounds chapter, and show that the padded bound is about \(d/(18\alpha(e^\varepsilon - 1))\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), \(\alpha = 1\) and \(d = 1000\), the direct bound is 11.1 records and the padded one 32.3. (Lower bounds, reductions)







TipSolution






From length to coordinates. For a vector \(v\) in \(d\) dimensions, the sum of the absolute values of its coordinates is at most \(\sqrt d\) times its length, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to \(v\) and the all-ones vector. Dividing by \(d\), the average error per coordinate is at most \(\alpha/\sqrt d\).
Direct. Equation 27.30 with \(\alpha' = \alpha/\sqrt d\) gives \(n \ge (2/3 - 2\alpha/\sqrt d)d/((e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d)\), about \(0.39\sqrt d\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\): 11.1 records for \(d = 1000\). It grows only like \(\sqrt d\), because its numerator \(2/3 - 2\alpha'\) is at most \(2/3\), so a smaller per-coordinate error earns nothing in it.
Padded. Padding to \(\alpha_0\) multiplies the bound by \(\alpha_0/\alpha'\) and uses \(\alpha_0\) in place of \(\alpha'\), so \(n \ge (\alpha_0/\alpha')(2/3 - 2\alpha_0)d/((e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d)\). With \(\alpha_0 = 1/6\) the product \(\alpha_0(2/3 - 2\alpha_0) = 1/18\), and with \(\alpha' = \alpha/\sqrt d\) and \(\delta\) negligible the bound is \((\sqrt d/\alpha)\cdot d/(18(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d) = d/(18\alpha(e^\varepsilon - 1))\).
The numbers. At \(d = 100\), 1000 and 10,000 the padded bound is 3.2, 32.3 and 323.2 records, against 2.7, 11.1 and 37.6 directly.

The padded bound grows like \(d/(\alpha\varepsilon)\), the privacy term of the shrinking-balls mechanism. Its constant, \(1/18\), is far from the mechanism’s, but the rate in \(d\) is the point.

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.1 Randomized response at order 2
Exercises for Rényi differential privacy, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_renyi_dp.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_renyi_dp.py. The check values of Exercises 6 and 7 are printed by the chapter’s script, code/part04-privacy-accounting/renyi_dp.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is tracked by the curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) of a mechanism \(M\); \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) are its outputs on neighbours, \(r = p/q\) the likelihood ratio and \(L = \ln r\) the privacy loss. Differential privacy (DP) without qualifier means \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence is the limit of \(D_\alpha\) as \(\alpha \to 1\). Logarithms are natural, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout.

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
Exercise 1. Randomized response at order 2. Show that \(\varepsilon(2) = \ln\big(1 + \chi^2(P\|Q)\big)\) for randomized response with truth probability \(t\), with \(\chi^2(P\|Q) = \frac{(2t - 1)^2}{t(1 - t)}\). Check: 0.8473 for \(t = 0.75\) and 0.1542 for \(t = 0.6\). For \(t = \frac12 + \gamma\) with small \(\gamma\), show \(\varepsilon(2) \approx 16\gamma^2\) and KL \(\approx 8\gamma^2\). (Special orders of the Rényi divergence)







TipSolution






Order 2 is the second moment of the likelihood ratio. By Equation 29.1 at \(\alpha = 2\), \(e^{D_2(P\|Q)} = \mathbb E_Q[r^2]\). Write \(r^2 = 1 + 2(r - 1) + (r - 1)^2\) and use \(\mathbb E_Q[r] = 1\) (Lemma 3.2): \(\mathbb E_Q[r^2] = 1 + \mathbb E_Q[(r - 1)^2] = 1 + \chi^2(P\|Q)\), with \(\chi^2 = \sum_y (p(y) - q(y))^2/q(y)\).
The two outputs of randomized response. From Table 29.2, \(p(y) - q(y) = \pm(2t - 1)\) on the two outputs, and \(q(y)\) is \(1 - t\) on one output and \(t\) on the other. So \[\chi^2 = \frac{(2t-1)^2}{1 - t} + \frac{(2t-1)^2}{t} = \frac{(2t - 1)^2}{t(1-t)}. \tag{29.1}\]
Check. For \(t = 0.75\): \(\chi^2 = 0.25/0.1875 = 1.3333\), and \(\ln 2.3333 = 0.8473\), the value of Table 29.3. For \(t = 0.6\): \(\chi^2 = 0.04/0.24 = 0.1667\), and \(\ln 1.1667 = 0.1542\).
Small \(\gamma\), order 2. With \(t = \frac12 + \gamma\), \(2t - 1 = 2\gamma\) and \(t(1 - t) = \frac14 - \gamma^2\). So \(\chi^2 = \frac{4\gamma^2}{1/4 - \gamma^2} = 16\gamma^2 + O(\gamma^4)\), and \(\ln(1 + x) = x + O(x^2)\) gives \(\varepsilon(2) = 16\gamma^2 + O(\gamma^4)\).
Small \(\gamma\), KL. The KL divergence is \(\mathbb E_P[L] = t\ln\frac{t}{1-t} + (1 - t)\ln\frac{1-t}{t} = (2t - 1)\ln\frac{t}{1-t}\). Here \(\ln\frac{1/2 + \gamma}{1/2 - \gamma} = \ln(1 + 2\gamma) - \ln(1 - 2\gamma) = 4\gamma + O(\gamma^3)\). So KL \(= 2\gamma \cdot 4\gamma + O(\gamma^4) = 8\gamma^2 + O(\gamma^4)\).
Numerically, at \(t = 0.55\) (\(\gamma = 0.05\)): \(\varepsilon(2) = 0.03961\) against \(16\gamma^2 = 0.04000\), and KL \(= 0.02007\) against \(8\gamma^2 = 0.02000\).

For a weak mechanism the curve is about \(\alpha\) times the KL divergence at moderate orders: \(\varepsilon(2) \approx 2\,\)KL. A curve that is linear in \(\alpha\) is what Concentrated DP builds on.

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.2 Composing Laplace mechanisms three ways

Exercise 2. Composing Laplace mechanisms three ways. Run \(k = 100\) Laplace mechanisms with \(b = 10\) (each \(0.1\)-DP) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Compute \(\varepsilon\) by basic composition, by advanced composition with \(\delta' = \delta\), and by RDP with Mironov’s conversion over ORDERS. Check: 10, 5.2981 (with the \(\tanh\) term; 5.8502 with the textbook term) and 5.0705 at \(\alpha = 6.3\). Explain why RDP wins although each Laplace step is pure DP. (Composition, conversion)







TipSolution






Basic composition adds the \(\varepsilon_0 = 1/b = 0.1\) of the steps: \(100 \times 0.1 = 10\), with \(\delta = 0\).
Advanced composition with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(\delta_0 = 0\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) gives \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 5.2981\). With the textbook mean term \(k\varepsilon_0(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\) it is 5.8502.
RDP. Each step has the Laplace curve Equation 29.6 with \(b = 10\). Composition multiplies it by 100 (Equation 29.11). Mironov’s conversion (Equation 29.24), minimized over ORDERS, picks \(\alpha = 6.3\). There a single step has \(\varepsilon(6.3) = 0.02898\), so the composed curve is \(2.8983\), and the tail term is \(\ln(1/\delta)/5.3 = 2.1723\). The total is 5.0705.
Why RDP wins. Pure DP charges every step its worst case, \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), as if the privacy loss were always at its maximum. At order 6.3 the Laplace curve is 0.02898, less than a third of \(\varepsilon_0\): the loss of a Laplace step is usually far below its maximum, and the moderate orders see that. Composition adds these small numbers, and the conversion is paid once.
It does not always win. For \(k = 10\) steps, basic composition gives 1.0000, while RDP gives 1.0090 and advanced composition 1.5674. The RDP order there is 512, the top of the grid, so a longer grid would do a little better (Exercise 5). For \(k = 1000\), basic composition gives 100.0000, advanced composition 20.1701 and RDP 19.6905. RDP’s advantage over advanced composition is small for pure DP mechanisms; its large gains come from mechanisms like the Gaussian whose \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) points hide a whole curve (Table 29.7). An accountant can always report the smallest of the valid bounds.

Composing in RDP and converting once is never much worse than the classical theorems for pure DP steps, and it handles Gaussian and Laplace steps in the same ledger.

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.3 The moments accountant’s tail bound

Exercise 3. The moments accountant’s tail bound. Show that Abadi et al.’s bound \(\delta = \min_\lambda\exp(K(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon)\) is Equation 29.24 solved for \(\delta\). For the Gaussian with \(\sigma = 1\), find the optimal \(\lambda\) for a given \(\varepsilon\) in closed form. Check: at \(\varepsilon = 3\), \(\lambda^* = 2.5\) and \(\delta = 4.394 \times 10^{-2}\). (Change of measure, Chernoff)







TipSolution






Rewrite the moment in RDP terms. By Equation 29.22, \(K(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1)\). With \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\), the exponent is \(K(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon = (\alpha - 1)\big(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon\big)\).
Solve Mironov’s conversion for \(\delta\). At order \(\alpha\), Equation 29.24 says \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). Solving, \(\ln\delta = (\alpha - 1)\big(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon\big)\), which is the exponent of step 1. So at each order the two bounds are the same pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), read in opposite directions.
The two optimizations agree. Abadi et al. fix \(\varepsilon\) and choose \(\lambda\) to make \(\delta\) smallest; Mironov fixes \(\delta\) and chooses \(\alpha\) to make \(\varepsilon\) smallest. Both search the same family of valid pairs. The script checks a round trip: Mironov’s best \(\varepsilon\) for \(\sigma = 1\) is 5.2985 (at \(\alpha = 5.8\)), and the tail bound at that \(\varepsilon\) returns \(\delta = 1.000 \times 10^{-5}\) at \(\lambda = 4.8\), the same order.
The Gaussian in closed form. With \(\sigma = 1\), \(K(\lambda) = \lambda(\lambda + 1)/2\) (Example 29.5 with \(\mu = 1\)). The exponent \(\lambda(\lambda + 1)/2 - \lambda\varepsilon\) has derivative \(\lambda + \frac12 - \varepsilon\), which vanishes at \(\lambda^* = \varepsilon - \frac12\).
Substitute: \(\lambda^*(\lambda^* + 1)/2 - \lambda^*\varepsilon = (\varepsilon - \tfrac12)\big[\tfrac12(\varepsilon + \tfrac12) - \varepsilon\big] = -\tfrac12(\varepsilon - \tfrac12)^2\). So \(\delta = \exp\big(-(\varepsilon - \tfrac12)^2/2\big)\).
Check. At \(\varepsilon = 3\): \(\lambda^* = 2.5\) and \(\delta = e^{-3.125} = 4.394 \times 10^{-2}\); the grid search finds the same \(\lambda\), because \(\alpha = 3.5\) is on the grid. At \(\varepsilon = 4\): \(\lambda^* = 3.5\) and \(\delta = 2.187 \times 10^{-3}\).

The bound \(\delta = e^{-(\varepsilon - 1/2)^2/2}\) is a Gaussian tail in \(\varepsilon\): the Chernoff bound for a normal privacy loss with mean and variance 1/2 and 1.

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
section: 29.4 The weak triangle inequality on three Gaussians
text:
29.4 The weak triangle inequality on three Gaussians

Exercise 4. The weak triangle inequality on three Gaussians. Take \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(R = \mathcal N(0.5, 1)\), \(Q = \mathcal N(1.5, 1)\) and \(\alpha = 3\). Evaluate both sides of Equation 29.15 for \(u = 2\), \(u = 1.5\) and \(u = 3\). Check: left side 3.3750; right sides 3.4375, 4.1562 and 3.5000. Then minimize the right side over \(u\) for the shifts \(s_1\) from \(P\) to \(R\) and \(s_2\) from \(R\) to \(Q\). Check: the best exponent is \(u^* = 1 + \frac{s_2(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha s_1} = 2.3333\), where the right side equals the left side, 3.3750. Explain the equality through the equality case of Hölder’s inequality. (Hölder’s inequality)







TipSolution





Unit-variance normals with shift \(s\) have \(D_\alpha = \alpha s^2/2\) (Equation 3.19). Here \(s_1 = 0.5\), \(s_2 = 1\) and the total shift is \(s_1 + s_2 = 1.5\).

Left side. \(D_3(P\|Q) = 3 \times 1.5^2/2 = 3.3750\).
\(u = 2\), \(v = 2\). The orders are \(u\alpha = 6\) and \(v(\alpha - 1) + 1 = 5\). The right side is \(\frac{3 - 1/2}{2}\cdot\frac{6 \times 0.25}{2} + \frac{5 \times 1}{2} = 1.25 \times 0.75 + 2.5 = 3.4375\).
\(u = 1.5\), \(v = 3\). Orders 4.5 and 7: \(\frac{3 - 2/3}{2}\cdot\frac{4.5 \times 0.25}{2} + \frac{7}{2} = 4.1562\).
\(u = 3\), \(v = 1.5\). Orders 9 and 4: \(\frac{3 - 1/3}{2}\cdot\frac{9 \times 0.25}{2} + \frac{4}{2} = 3.5000\).
The right side as a function of \(u\). With \(v = u/(u - 1)\), \[\mathrm{RHS}(u) = \frac{\alpha u - 1}{u(\alpha - 1)}\cdot\frac{u\alpha s_1^2}{2} + \Big(\frac{u}{u-1}(\alpha - 1) + 1\Big)\frac{s_2^2}{2} = \frac{\alpha(\alpha u - 1)s_1^2}{2(\alpha - 1)} + \Big(1 + \frac{(\alpha - 1)u}{u - 1}\Big)\frac{s_2^2}{2}. \tag{29.2}\]
Minimize. \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d u}\frac{u}{u - 1} = -\frac{1}{(u-1)^2}\), so the derivative is \(\frac{\alpha^2s_1^2}{2(\alpha - 1)} - \frac{(\alpha - 1)s_2^2}{2(u - 1)^2}\). It vanishes at \((u - 1)^2 = \frac{(\alpha - 1)^2s_2^2}{\alpha^2s_1^2}\), that is, \(u^* = 1 + \frac{s_2(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha s_1} = 1 + \frac{2}{1.5} = 2.3333\), with \(v^* = 1.75\). The orders become 7 and 4.5, and the right side is 3.3750, equal to the left side.
Why equality is possible. Hölder’s inequality \(\mathbb E_R[XY] \le (\mathbb E_RX^u)^{1/u}(\mathbb E_RY^v)^{1/v}\) is an equality exactly when \(X^u\) is a constant multiple of \(Y^v\). Here \(X = (p/p_R)^\alpha\) and \(Y = (p_R/q)^{\alpha - 1}\), as in the proof of Lemma 29.1, where \(p_R\) is the density of \(R\). For normals with equal variance, \(\ln(p/p_R)\) and \(\ln(p_R/q)\) are both linear in \(y\), with slopes proportional to \(-s_1\) and \(-s_2\). So \(X^u = cY^v\) holds when the slopes match, \(u\alpha s_1 = v(\alpha - 1)s_2\). With \(v = u/(u - 1)\) this gives \((u - 1)\alpha s_1 = (\alpha - 1)s_2\), the same \(u^*\) as step 6.

The weak triangle inequality loses nothing for Gaussians when \(u\) is tuned to the two shifts. The fixed choice \(u = 2\) is what group privacy uses, and its loss is small (3.4375 against 3.3750 here).

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
section: 29.5 The edge of the order grid
text:
29.5 The edge of the order grid

Exercise 5. The edge of the order grid. For a single Gaussian step at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), find the noise multiplier above which the continuous optimum \(\alpha^*\) of Equation 29.27 exceeds the largest order 512. Check: \(\sigma > 106.5\). At \(\sigma = 200\), how much does the grid lose against the continuous optimum? Check: 0.02893 against 0.02401, a factor 1.205. (Calculus, the order grid)







TipSolution






The threshold. \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\) exceeds 512 when \(\sigma > 511/\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} = 511/4.7985 = 106.5\).
Just below the edge. At \(\sigma = 100\), \(\alpha^* = 480.9\). The grid has no order between 256 and 512, so it uses 512 and gets 0.04813 against the continuous 0.04804, a loss of 0.2%.
Beyond the edge. At \(\sigma = 200\), \(\alpha^* = 960.7\), but the largest order is 512. The converted \(\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) is convex in \(\alpha\) and still decreasing at 512, so the grid’s best is the last order: 0.02893, against 0.02401 at \(\alpha^*\), a factor 1.205.
Remedy. Add larger orders (1024, 2048, …) when the noise is large, or optimize \(\alpha\) continuously when the curve has a closed form. Both converted values are still well above the exact \(\varepsilon = 0.01251\) of this mechanism; that remaining slack is the conversion’s, not the grid’s.

A fixed grid is a convenience for adding curves of different mechanisms. Check that the chosen order is not at the edge of the grid; if it is, the grid is too short.

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.6 Composing two Gaussian curves

Exercise 6. Composing two Gaussian curves. Two Gaussian mechanisms with sensitivity 1 and RDP curves \(\alpha/8\) and \(\alpha/2\) are run on the same dataset. Which single Gaussian mechanism has the same composed curve? Check: noise multiplier \(\sigma = 0.8944\). (Composition, the Gaussian curve)







TipSolution






Read the noise multipliers. By Equation 29.5 a curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) belongs to the noise multiplier \(\sigma\), so \(\alpha/8\) is \(\sigma = 2\) and \(\alpha/2\) is \(\sigma = 1\).
Compose. By Theorem 29.2 the curves add, with equality because the two noises are independent: \[\frac\alpha8 + \frac\alpha2 = \frac{5\alpha}{8}. \tag{29.3}\]
Match one Gaussian. Setting \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2) = 5\alpha/8\) gives \(\sigma^2 = 0.8\), so \(\sigma = \sqrt{0.8} = 0.8944\).
The rule behind it. The curve is proportional to \(1/\sigma^2\), so composing Gaussians adds the values \(1/\sigma^2\): here \(\frac14 + 1 = 1.25 = 1/0.8\). The composed mechanism is less noisy than either step.

Composed Gaussian steps are one Gaussian step whose \(1/\sigma^2\) is the sum of theirs; \(k\) equal steps give \(\sigma/\sqrt k\).

title: 29  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
section: 29.7 Converting one point of a curve
text:
29.7 Converting one point of a curve

Exercise 7. Converting one point of a curve. A mechanism is known only to be \((10, 0.5)\)-RDP. What \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP guarantee does Theorem 29.5 give? Check: \(\varepsilon = 1.7792\). (Conversion)







TipSolution






The tail term. With \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\), and at order 10 the tail term of Equation 29.24 is \(11.5129/9 = 1.2792\).
Add the RDP value. The guarantee is \(\varepsilon = 0.5 + 1.2792 = 1.7792\).
Reading it. The tail term is more than twice the RDP value, so most of the cost is the price of \(\delta\). A mechanism that is also RDP at higher orders, with values not much above 0.5, would convert to a smaller \(\varepsilon\), which is why accountants keep the whole curve.

One point of a curve gives one valid \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair; the whole curve lets the conversion choose the order.

title: 30  Exercises: From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.1 The optimal constant, in general
Exercises for the chapter on converting Rényi differential privacy (DP) to (ε, δ) and to tests, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_rdp_conversions.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_rdp_conversions.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is converted to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy (DP). \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), \(L = \ln(P/Q)\) is the privacy loss, and under \(P\) it is the privacy loss random variable (PRV). \(\alpha\) is always the Rényi order, \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) the RDP curve, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) unless stated otherwise.

title: 30  Exercises: From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
Exercise 1. The optimal constant, in general. The proof of Theorem 30.1 finds the smallest constant \(c^* = \sup_z (1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+ e^{-(\alpha - 1)z}\), attained at \(z^* = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\). Check it numerically at one order, and show that \(\alpha\) times the ratio \(\frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\) of the improved to Mironov’s \(\delta\) tends to \(1/e\). Check: at \(\alpha = 2\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(c^* = 9.196986\times10^{-2}\); \(\alpha\) times the ratio is 0.5000, 0.3874, 0.3697, 0.3681 at \(\alpha = 2, 10, 100, 1000\). (Calculus, majorizing an integrand)







TipSolution






The maximizer and the constant. Steps 2 to 4 of the proof of Theorem 30.1 show that the expression is 0 for \(z \le \varepsilon\), that for \(z > \varepsilon\) it rises and then falls with its maximum at \(z^* = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\), and that its value there is \(c^* = \frac{e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}}{\alpha - 1}(1 - 1/\alpha)^\alpha\). What is new here is the check and the limit.
Check. At \(\alpha = 2\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(z^* = 1 + \ln 2 = 1.6931\) and \(c^* = e^{-1}\cdot\frac14 = 9.196986\times10^{-2}\). The maximum of the expression over a grid of two million points gives the same seven digits.
The ratio. By Corollary 30.1 the ratio of the improved to Mironov’s \(\delta\) is \(c^*/e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon} = \frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\), since both bounds multiply their constant by the same \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\).
The limit. \(\alpha\) times the ratio is \((1 - 1/\alpha)^{\alpha - 1} = \exp\big((\alpha - 1)\ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\big)\). With \(\ln(1 - x) = -x - x^2/2 - \dots\) and \(x = 1/\alpha\), the exponent is \(-(\alpha - 1)/\alpha - O(1/\alpha) \to -1\). The script gives 0.5000, 0.3874, 0.3697 and 0.3681 at \(\alpha = 2, 10, 100, 1000\), approaching \(1/e = 0.3679\).

So at large orders the improved conversion divides Mironov’s \(\delta\) by about \(e\alpha\): the gain is largest in \(\delta\) exactly where it is smallest in \(\varepsilon\), because \(\ln(e\alpha)\) is divided by \(\alpha - 1\).

30.2 Best orders for a linear curve

Exercise 2. Best orders for a linear curve. For \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), solve the conditions of Proposition 30.2 for the best orders of both conversions, and evaluate both at \(\rho = 0.5\) and \(\rho = 0.005\) for \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and \(10^{-10}\). Check: at \(\rho = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), Mironov 7.286 at order 7.786 and improved 6.839 at order 7.483. (Optimization over \(\alpha\))







TipSolution






The conditions. Proposition 30.2 derives both: Mironov’s best order is \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\) with value \(\varepsilon^* = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\), and the improved conversion’s best order solves Equation 30.21. What is left is to solve the second condition and evaluate both.
Solve it. Rewrite as \(\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))/\rho}\) and iterate from Mironov’s \(\alpha^*\). The right side changes slowly with \(\alpha\) (through \(\ln\alpha\)), so the iteration converges; the script’s residual \(\rho(\alpha - 1)^2 - \ln(1/(\alpha\delta))\) is at most \(8.9\times10^{-16}\).
Values. Table 30.1. At \(\rho = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), Mironov gives 7.286 at order 7.786 and the improved conversion 6.839 at order 7.483. Evaluating Mironov’s conversion directly at its \(\alpha^*\) reproduces each \(\varepsilon^*\).

text:
30.3 One order’s boundary at small \(\mathrm{FPR}\)

Exercise 3. One order’s boundary at small \(\mathrm{FPR}\). For a single order \(\alpha\), show from the second inequality of Equation 30.15 that every test has power \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha}\mathrm{FPR}^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\), and that keeping the second term at its value 1 for \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1\) gives the approximation \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} \approx (e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} - 1)^{1/\alpha}\mathrm{FPR}^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\). For the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\), compare both with the exact single-order boundary at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-6}\) for orders 2 and 8, and say when the slope picture of Figure 30.2 is accurate. Check: at order 2, \(1.6487\times10^{-3}\), \(1.3108\times10^{-3}\) and exact \(1.3118\times10^{-3}\); at order 8 all three are \(1.8622\times10^{-4}\). (Test region, asymptotics)







TipSolution






A bound that always holds. The second inequality of Equation 30.15 is \((1 - \mathrm{FNR})^\alpha \mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha} + \mathrm{FNR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{1 - \alpha} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\). The second term is non-negative, so \((1 - \mathrm{FNR})^\alpha \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\mathrm{FPR}^{\alpha - 1}\). Taking the \(\alpha\)-th root gives \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha}\mathrm{FPR}^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\) for every \(\mathrm{FPR}\): on log axes a line of slope \((\alpha - 1)/\alpha\).
The approximation. At small \(\mathrm{FPR}\) the allowed power is small, so \(\mathrm{FNR}\) is near 1 and the second term \(\mathrm{FNR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{1 - \alpha}\) is near 1. Moving it to the right side as 1 gives \((1 - \mathrm{FNR})^\alpha \mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha} \lesssim e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} - 1\), which is the approximation. It is not a bound: \(\mathrm{FNR}^\alpha \approx 1 - \alpha(1 - \mathrm{FNR})\) is a little below 1, so the exact boundary allows slightly more power.
The ratio of the two. The approximation divided by the bound is \((1 - e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)})^{1/\alpha}\), the same at every \(\mathrm{FPR}\). With \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\) it is 0.7951 at order 2, where \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha) = 1\), and 1.0000 at order 8, where \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha) = 28\) and \(e^{-28}\) is negligible.
Against the exact boundary. Table 30.2 compares both with the exact single-order boundary, computed by bisection with both inequalities of Equation 30.15. At order 2 and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-6}\) the bound gives \(1.6487\times10^{-3}\), the approximation \(1.3108\times10^{-3}\) and the exact boundary \(1.3118\times10^{-3}\). At order 8 all three are \(1.8622\times10^{-4}\).

title: 30  Exercises: From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.4 Composing Laplace mechanisms in RDP

Exercise 4. Composing Laplace mechanisms in RDP. Extend Exercise 2 of Rényi DP with the improved conversion. One hundred Laplace mechanisms each with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\): compare basic composition, advanced composition in its textbook form (composition), and the improved conversion of the summed curve, 100 times the Laplace RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big[\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_0} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha\varepsilon_0}\big]\) (Mironov 2017). Check: 10.000, 5.850 and 4.533 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). (Composition in RDP, conversion)







TipSolution






Check the curve. A Riemann sum of \(P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha}\) for \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1/\varepsilon_0)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, 1/\varepsilon_0)\) gives 0.009644 at \(\alpha = 2\) and 0.065854 at \(\alpha = 20\), equal to the formula. For comparison, \(\alpha\varepsilon_0^2/2\) is 0.010000 and 0.100000: the Laplace curve is below the generic \(\varepsilon\)-DP bound of Proposition 30.4.
Basic composition. \(k\varepsilon_0 = 100 \times 0.1 = 10.000\), with \(\delta = 0\).
Advanced composition, textbook form. \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)} + k\varepsilon_0(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1) = 5.850\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
RDP. Composition adds curves, so the total is \(100\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\). The improved conversion over the grid gives 4.533 at order 5.8; Mironov’s gives 5.071 at order 6.3.
Using only the \(\varepsilon\)-DP bound. Replacing the Laplace curve by \(\min(\varepsilon_0, \alpha\varepsilon_0^2/2)\) gives 4.729. That is the Gaussian number of the chapter: \(100 \times \alpha\varepsilon_0^2/2 = \alpha/2\), the RDP curve of a Gaussian with \(\mu = 1\).

RDP beats advanced composition here even with the crude conversion, and the exact Laplace curve gains a further 0.196 over the generic bound.

section: 30.5 How fine must the grid be?
text:
30.5 How fine must the grid be?

Exercise 5. How fine must the grid be? For \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), compute the relative excess of the grid’s improved \(\varepsilon\) over the continuous optimum at \(\rho = 5000\), \(0.005\), \(5\times10^{-5}\) and \(5.556\times10^{-6}\). section: 30.6 When is the improved conversion optimal for one order?
text:
30.6 When is the improved conversion optimal for one order?

Exercise 6. When is the improved conversion optimal for one order? Show that for any pair, the improved bound exceeds the true \(\delta\) by at least \(c^*\,\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\mathbf 1[L \le \varepsilon]]\), and use the worst two-outcome pair to explain why the improved conversion is optimal at large orders and not at small ones. Check: at \(\mu = 1\), improved and optimal are 11.1266 and 10.6680 at order 2, and 5.2141 and 5.2141 at order 8. (Optimal conversion, data processing)







TipSolution






The gap as an expectation. The improved bound is \(c^*e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} \ge c^*\,\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\) by the RDP curve (Equation 30.2). The true \(\delta\) is \(\mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\) (Equation 30.1). So the gap is at least \(\mathbb E_P\big[c^*e^{(\alpha - 1)L} - (1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big]\).
Split by \(L\). Where \(L > \varepsilon\) the integrand is \(\ge 0\), because \(c^*e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\) lies above \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\) everywhere. Where \(L \le \varepsilon\) the second term is 0. Dropping the first part leaves the claimed lower bound \(c^*\,\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\mathbf 1[L \le \varepsilon]]\).
The worst pair cannot avoid it. The optimal conversion for one order is attained by a two-outcome pair (Theorem 30.2). One outcome carries the large loss, near \(z^*\); the other must carry almost all the mass, at a loss near 0, because \(P\) and \(Q\) both sum to 1. That outcome contributes about \(c^* \times 1\) to the gap. So the improved \(\delta\) exceeds the optimal \(\delta\) by about \(c^*\).
Compare \(c^*\) with \(\delta\). At the improved \(\varepsilon\), \(c^*/\delta\) is 0.687 at order 1.5, 0.368 at order 2, 0.002 at order 4 and essentially 0 at order 8 (\(c^* = 6.914\times10^{-18}\)). Since \(c^* \propto e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}/(\alpha - 1)\), it is negligible against \(\delta\) once \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon\) clearly exceeds \(\ln(1/\delta)\).
In \(\varepsilon\). Table 30.4 gives the two conversions for the Gaussian’s single values \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\). The optimal one uses the forward constraint \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) alone, as the improved conversion does. At order 2 the improved conversion gives 11.1266 against the optimal 10.6680; at order 8 both give 5.2141.

31.1 Laplace in a zCDP budget
Exercises for Concentrated differential privacy, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_concentrated_dp.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_concentrated_dp.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zero-concentrated differentially private (\(\rho\)-zCDP) when its Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve satisfies \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for all \(\alpha > 1\); \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy (DP) is the guarantee you report; \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\), and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout, so \(\ell = 11.5129\). Divergences are Kullback–Leibler (KL) or Rényi.

title: 31  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
Exercise 1. Laplace in a zCDP budget. The Laplace mechanism with scale \(b\) on a sensitivity-1 query is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = 1/b\). Using its exact RDP curve (Equation 3.25 with \(t = \varepsilon\)), find numerically the smallest \(\rho\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\), and compare it with \(\varepsilon^2/2\) and with randomized response at the same \(\varepsilon\). Check: the smallest \(\rho\) is the KL divergence \(t + e^{-t} - 1 = 0.3679\), reached as \(\alpha \to 1\). (Pure DP to zCDP, tightness)







TipSolution






The curve. The outputs on neighbours are \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) and \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, b)\), a shift of \(t = 1/b = \varepsilon\) scale units. By Equation 3.25, \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)t} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha t}\right). \tag{31.1}\] The script evaluates it in log space, so large orders do not overflow.
The smallest \(\rho\) is the largest ratio. \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for all \(\alpha\) exactly when \(\rho \ge \sup_{\alpha > 1}\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\). Table 31.1 evaluates the ratio at \(t = 1\).




Table 31.1: The RDP curve of the Laplace mechanism with \(t = \varepsilon = 1\) and its slope from the origin.

The ratio is largest as \(\alpha \to 1\). There \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \to D_{\mathrm{KL}} = t + e^{-t} - 1\) (the KL divergence of the Laplace pair, from Divergences), and \(\alpha \to 1\). On the fine grid of orders the maximum of \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\) is \(0.3679\), equal to the KL divergence \(0.3679\).
Compare. The general bound is \(\varepsilon^2/2 = 0.5000\); randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\) needs \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) = 0.4621\); the Laplace mechanism only \(0.3679\).

The general \(\varepsilon^2/2\) of Theorem 31.2 is a convenient upper bound, not the cost of any mechanism at fixed \(\varepsilon\). Every \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is a post-processing of randomized response (Theorem 21.2), so none needs more than randomized response’s \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) = 0.4621\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (Theorem 31.3). The Laplace mechanism, whose privacy loss reaches \(\pm\varepsilon\) only in its tails, needs \(0.3679\). Charging it \(\varepsilon^2/2\) is safe but overcharges by a factor \(0.5000/0.3679 = 1.36\); the sharp \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) still overcharges by \(0.4621/0.3679 = 1.26\).

title: 31  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.2 Calibrating σ for many steps

Exercise 2. Calibrating \(\sigma\) for many steps. Derive Equation 31.18. Then find the noise multiplier that makes \(k = 100\) Gaussian steps \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP by the simple conversion, and the \(\varepsilon\) that the improved conversion and the exact Gaussian profile give for that \(\sigma\). Check: \(\sigma = 49.01\). (Optimizing over \(\alpha\), inverting a conversion)







TipSolution






Inversion. The simple conversion Equation 31.15 is \(\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\), increasing in \(\rho\). Put \(x = \sqrt\rho \ge 0\): \(x^2 + 2\sqrt\ell\,x = \varepsilon\). Add \(\ell\) to both sides: \((x + \sqrt\ell)^2 = \varepsilon + \ell\). So \(x = \sqrt{\varepsilon + \ell} - \sqrt\ell\) (the other root is negative), and every \(\rho \le x^2\) meets the target. That is Equation 31.18.
The total budget. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\ell = 11.5129\), \(\rho = 0.02082\).
Split it over the steps. Composition adds \(\rho\), so each of the 100 steps may spend \(\rho/100 = 2.0820 \times 10^{-4}\). A Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) spends \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), so \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2\rho/100} = \sqrt{100}/\sqrt{2\rho} = 49.01\).
Check the other conversions. 100 steps at \(\sigma = 49.01\) give back \(\rho = 0.02082\) and \(\varepsilon = 1.0000\) by the simple formula. The improved conversion gives \(0.8118\). The composition of 100 Gaussian steps is itself a Gaussian pair with \(\mu = \sqrt{2\rho}\), whose exact \(\varepsilon\) is \(0.7416\).

Calibrating with the simple formula buys a guarantee that is really about \(\varepsilon = 0.74\). Calibrating with the exact Gaussian profile instead would let you use less noise for the same reported \(\varepsilon\).

title: 31  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.3 Hölder for two steps

Exercise 3. Hölder for two steps. Write out Equation 31.19 for \(m = 2\) and \(\alpha = 2\), and check it on \(P = \mathrm{Bern}(0.2)\), \(Q = \mathrm{Bern}(0.8)\) with \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.4)\) and with \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.5)\). When does it hold with equality? Check: the left side is \(1.1787\); the right side is \(1.1872\) for \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.4)\) and \(1.1787\) for \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.5)\). (Hölder’s inequality, group privacy)







TipSolution






The orders. With group size \(m = 2\) and \(\alpha = 2\): the first order is \(\frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1} = 3\), the coefficient \(\frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1} = \frac43\), and the second order \(m\alpha = 4\): \[D_2(P\|Q) \le \tfrac43D_3(P\|R) + D_4(R\|Q). \tag{31.2}\] The Hölder exponents are \(u = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha(m - 1)} = \frac32\) and \(v = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha - 1} = 3\), and indeed \(\frac23 + \frac13 = 1\).
Evaluate. Each divergence is a two-term sum, \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha-1}\ln\sum_y P(y)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha}\). Table 31.2 lists the values.




Table 31.2: The triangle-like inequality for \(m = 2\), \(\alpha = 2\), \(P = \mathrm{Bern}(0.2)\), \(Q = \mathrm{Bern}(0.8)\).

When equality holds. Hölder’s inequality \(\mathbb E[XY] \le (\mathbb E X^u)^{1/u}(\mathbb E Y^v)^{1/v}\) is an equality when \(X^u\) and \(Y^v\) are proportional. Here \(X = (P/R)^\alpha\) and \(Y = (R/Q)^{\alpha - 1}\), ratios of the densities at an output drawn from \(R\), so \(X^u = (P/R)^3\) and \(Y^v = (R/Q)^3\): equality needs \(\ln(P/R) - \ln(R/Q)\) to be the same for every outcome. For Bernoulli distributions that means the log-odds of \(R\) sit exactly halfway between those of \(P\) and \(Q\). The log-odds of \(0.2\), \(0.4\), \(0.5\), \(0.8\) are \(-1.3863\), \(-0.4055\), \(0.0000\), \(1.3863\), so \(\mathrm{Bern}(0.5)\) is the midpoint and \(\mathrm{Bern}(0.4)\) is not.
The link to the Gaussian. A chain of Gaussians \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathcal N(2, \sigma^2)\) has the same structure: both log-ratios are linear in \(y\) with the same slope, so they differ by a constant. That is why group privacy \(m^2\rho\) is exact for the Gaussian mechanism.

The inequality loses nothing when the middle dataset is “halfway” in the sense of the privacy loss. For the Gaussian mechanism every chain of neighbours is like that.

title: 31  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.4 A mixed pipeline

Exercise 4. A mixed pipeline. A pipeline runs 20 propose-test-release steps, each \((0.25, 10^{-8})\)-DP, and 50 Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 5\). Find its \(\rho\), its \(\delta_a\), and \(\varepsilon\) at total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) with the improved conversion. Check: \(\rho = 1.625\). (Approximate zCDP)







TipSolution






Each stability step. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP step is \(\delta\)-approximately \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP (Proposition 31.3, part 1), so each costs \(\rho = 0.25^2/2 = 0.03125\) and fails with probability \(10^{-8}\).
Each Gaussian step costs \(1/(2 \cdot 25) = 0.020\) and never fails.
Compose. \(\rho = 20 \times 0.03125 + 50 \times 0.020 = 1.6250\) and \(\delta_a = 1 - (1 - 10^{-8})^{20} = 2.0000 \times 10^{-7}\).
Convert. Spend the rest of the \(\delta\) on the conversion: \(\delta' = 10^{-5} - \delta_a\). The improved conversion at \(\rho = 1.625\) and this \(\delta'\) gives \(\varepsilon = 9.463\), at total \(\delta = \delta_a + \delta' = 10^{-5}\) (Proposition 31.3, part 3, which allows \(\delta_a + (1 - \delta_a)\delta' \le 10^{-5}\)).
Compare. Treating the two kinds of steps separately, the Gaussians alone (\(\rho = 1\)) convert to \(\varepsilon = 7.084\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5} - 2 \times 10^{-7} = 9.8 \times 10^{-6}\), and basic composition of the stability steps adds \(20 \times 0.25 = 5\), for \(12.084\).

Twenty steps of \(\varepsilon = 0.25\) cost 5 under basic composition but only \(\rho = 0.625\) in the zCDP ledger, because they compose like Gaussian steps. That is the point of approximate zCDP.

title: 31  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.5 The subsampled Gaussian at order 2

Exercise 5. The subsampled Gaussian at order 2. From Equation 31.27, show \(\varepsilon(2) = \ln\big(1 + q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\big)\), and evaluate it for \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\). Then show that the lower bound Equation 31.28 is positive exactly when \(\alpha > 1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\). Check: \(\varepsilon(2) = 1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\). (Binomial expansion)







TipSolution






The three terms of \(A_2\). In Equation 31.27 with \(\alpha = 2\), \(j = 0\) gives \((1 - q)^2\), \(j = 1\) gives \(2q(1 - q)e^0\), and \(j = 2\) gives \(q^2e^{(4 - 2)/(2\sigma^2)} = q^2e^{1/\sigma^2}\).
Add. \((1 - q)^2 + 2q(1 - q) = (1 - q)(1 + q) = 1 - q^2\), so \(A_2 = 1 - q^2 + q^2e^{1/\sigma^2} = 1 + q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\).
Divide \(\ln A_2\) by \(\alpha - 1 = 1\). For \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\): the closed form and the binomial sum both give \(1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\). Without subsampling, \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\), so subsampling at 1% buys a factor of about 5,800 at this order: \(1/q^2 = 10^4\), divided by \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 = e - 1 = 1.72\).
Where the lower bound turns positive. \(\rho_0\alpha + \frac{\alpha\ln q}{\alpha - 1} > 0\) with \(\rho_0 = 1/(2\sigma^2)\) and \(\alpha > 1\) means \(\frac{\alpha - 1}{2\sigma^2} > \ln(1/q)\), that is \(\alpha > 1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\).
Check. For \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), the threshold is \(10.21\). The bound is \(-0.1169\) at \(\alpha = 10\) and \(0.4343\) at \(\alpha = 11\).

The threshold \(1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\) is where the curve bends in Figure 31.4: below it the rare event “the record is in every sample” is too rare to matter, above it that event dominates.

title: 31  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.6 The tCDP conversion

Exercise 6. The tCDP conversion. Apply the conversion Equation 31.31 of truncated concentrated DP (tCDP) to \(10{,}000\) steps of the running example with \(\omega = 4\) and \(\omega = 8\), saying which branch applies and where the unconstrained best order lies. Check: \(7.469\) and \(8.289\). (Constrained optimization over \(\alpha\))







TipSolution






The rule. By Proposition 31.5, the first branch of Equation 31.31 applies when the unconstrained best order \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\) is at most \(\omega\), that is when \(\ell \le (\omega - 1)^2\rho\). Otherwise the best admissible order is \(\omega\) itself.
\(\omega = 4\). Per step \(\rho = 9.0789 \times 10^{-5}\) (chapter, Table 31.6), so \(10{,}000\) steps give \(\rho = 0.9079\). Then \((\omega - 1)^2\rho = 8.171 < \ell = 11.5129\): second branch, \(\varepsilon = 7.469\). The unconstrained minimizer \(\alpha^* = 4.561\) lies beyond \(\omega\).
\(\omega = 8\). \(\rho = 1.1171\) and \((\omega - 1)^2\rho = 54.736 \ge \ell\): first branch, with \(\alpha^* = 4.210 \le 8\), and \(\varepsilon = 8.289\).

A larger \(\omega\) makes more orders available but forces a larger slope, because the line has to clear the curve on more orders. Here the slope wins, and the smaller truncation point gives the better \(\varepsilon\).

title: 31  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.7 A line for a 5-DP mechanism

Exercise 7. A line for a 5-DP mechanism. A mechanism is \(5\)-DP. Find the \(\rho\) that Theorem 31.2 and Theorem 31.3 charge for it, find the order at which each line \(\rho\alpha\) reaches the pure-DP cap \(\varepsilon = 5\) of Equation 31.7, and say how an accountant should describe the mechanism. Check: \(\rho = 12.5\) and \(4.9331\); the sharp line reaches the cap at \(\alpha = 1.0136\). (Pure DP to zCDP, the cap on the RDP curve)







TipSolution






The general constant. Theorem 31.2 charges \(\varepsilon^2/2 = 25/2 = 12.5\). The line \(12.5\alpha\) is above 5 at every order \(\alpha > 1\), because \(12.5 > 5\) already at \(\alpha = 1\). So it is worse than the cap everywhere.
The sharp constant. Theorem 31.3 charges \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) = 5\tanh(2.5) = 4.9331\). This line starts just below the cap and reaches it where \(4.9331\alpha = 5\), at \(\alpha = 5/4.9331 = 1.0136\).
What the accountant should keep. Above \(\alpha = 1.0136\) the cap \(\varepsilon = 5\) is below both lines, and the exact curve of randomized response, which bounds every \(5\)-DP mechanism (Theorem 31.3), is lower still. Converting either line back gives a worse guarantee than the one you started with. The simple conversion Equation 31.15 returns \(\rho\) plus a positive term, and \(\rho = 4.9331\) is already within \(0.07\) of 5, so the result exceeds 5 for every \(\delta < 1\).

For a large \(\varepsilon\), as in local DP, describe the mechanism by its RDP curve or by \(\varepsilon\) itself, never by a single \(\rho\). A line through the origin cannot follow a curve that flattens almost at once.

title: 32  Exercises: f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.1 The Laplace mechanism is GDP
Exercises for the chapter on differential privacy (DP) as a trade-off curve, f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_gaussian_dp.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_gaussian_dp.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) means the trade-off curve \(G_\mu(\alpha) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu)\). A test has type I error \(\alpha\) and type II error \(\beta\); the chapter writes them \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\), because it needs \(\alpha\) for the order of Rényi divergences. \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), the privacy loss is \(L = \ln(P/Q)\), and Dong, Roth & Su (2022) is cited as Dong et al. Three more acronyms appear: the total variation (TV) distance, the central limit theorem (CLT) for composition, and differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), written DP-SGD.
crumbs: 32  Exercises: f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 32  Exercises: f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
Exercise 1. The Laplace mechanism is GDP. Find the smallest \(\mu\) such that the Laplace mechanism with \(\varepsilon = 1\) is \(\mu\)-GDP, that is \(G_\mu \le T(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1), \mathrm{Lap}(1, 1))\) everywhere. Check numerically that the binding point is on the diagonal, derive the closed form this gives, and prove that it suffices. What \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) does this GDP summary report, and what is the truth? Check: \(\mu = 1.0301\) (the same as Part 1’s Gaussian with equal TV); the GDP summary gives \(\varepsilon = 4.5301\), while the mechanism is \((1, 0)\)-DP. (Ordering trade-off curves, symmetry)







TipSolution





Write \(T_\varepsilon = T(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1/\varepsilon), \mathrm{Lap}(1, 1/\varepsilon))\), Part 1’s Laplace curve with \(\kappa = \varepsilon\).

Both curves are symmetric. \(G_\mu\) is symmetric (Part 1, Exercise 1), and \(T_\varepsilon\) is too: its first and last pieces, \(1 - e^\varepsilon \alpha\) and \(e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \alpha)\), are reflections of each other, and the middle piece \(\beta = e^{-\varepsilon}/(4\alpha)\) is symmetric in \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).
A necessary condition on the diagonal. On the diagonal \(\alpha = \beta\), \(G_\mu(\alpha) = \alpha\) means \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu = \Phi^{-1}(\alpha) = -\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\), so \(\alpha = \Phi(-\mu/2)\). The Laplace curve meets the diagonal on its middle piece: \(\alpha^2 = e^{-\varepsilon}/4\), so \(\alpha = \frac12e^{-\varepsilon/2}\). For \(G_\mu \le T_\varepsilon\) the Gaussian must cross the diagonal no further out, \(\Phi(-\mu/2) \le \frac12 e^{-\varepsilon/2}\), that is \[\mu \ge \mu^* = 2\,\Phi^{-1}\big(1 - \tfrac12e^{-\varepsilon/2}\big). \tag{32.1}\]
It is also sufficient. Both curves are symmetric, so by the duality Theorem 32.2 (step 3 of its proof) each is the upper envelope of its lines \(f_{\varepsilon',\delta(\varepsilon')}\), \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\). Since \(f_{\varepsilon',\delta}\) falls as \(\delta\) grows, \(G_\mu \le T_\varepsilon\) holds as soon as \(\delta_G(\varepsilon') \ge \delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(\varepsilon')\) for every \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\), where \(\delta_G\) is Equation 32.9 at \(\mu = \mu^*\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(\varepsilon') = 1 - e^{(\varepsilon' - \varepsilon)/2}\) for \(\varepsilon' \le \varepsilon\) and 0 beyond (the Laplace profile of Part 3, the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, Exercise 2). Let \(D(\varepsilon') = \delta_G(\varepsilon') - \delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(\varepsilon')\).

At \(\varepsilon' = 0\): \(\delta_G(0) = 2\Phi(\mu^*/2) - 1 = 1 - 2\Phi(-\mu^*/2) = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon/2} = \delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(0)\) by the choice of \(\mu^*\), so \(D(0) = 0\).
The slope. Part 3 (Exercise 3 of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms) showed \(\delta_G'(\varepsilon') = -e^{\varepsilon'}\Phi(v)\) with \(v = -\varepsilon'/\mu^* - \mu^*/2\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}'(\varepsilon') = -\frac12e^{(\varepsilon' - \varepsilon)/2}\) on \([0, \varepsilon]\). So \(D' \ge 0\) exactly when \(h(\varepsilon') = e^{\varepsilon'/2}\Phi(v) \le \frac12e^{-\varepsilon/2} = \Phi(-\mu^*/2) = h(0)\).
\(h\) is non-increasing. \(h'(\varepsilon') = e^{\varepsilon'/2}\big[\frac12\Phi(v) - \varphi(v)/\mu^*\big]\). Since \(v \le -\mu^*/2 < 0\), the Mills-ratio bound \(\Phi(v) < \varphi(v)/|v|\) (Concentration inequalities) gives \(\Phi(v)/\varphi(v) < 1/|v| \le 2/\mu^*\), so \(h' < 0\).
Conclusion. \(h(\varepsilon') \le h(0)\), so \(D' \ge 0\) and \(D \ge 0\) on \([0, \varepsilon]\). Beyond \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{Lap}} = 0 \le \delta_G\). Hence \(G_{\mu^*} \le T_\varepsilon\), and with step 2, \(\mu^*\) is the smallest \(\mu\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\).

The script confirms it numerically. It finds the smallest \(\mu\) with \(G_\mu \le T_\varepsilon\) on a grid of 1,999 values of \(\alpha\) by bisection. For \(\varepsilon = 1\) it gives \(\mu = 1.0301\), equal to the closed form 1.0301, and the two curves come closest (they touch) at \(\alpha = 0.3035\), the grid point next to the diagonal point \(\frac12e^{-1/2} = 0.3033\). For \(\varepsilon = 0.5\): \(\mu = 0.5618\) from both, touching at \(\alpha = 0.3895\), next to \(0.3894\).
The same as matching TV. The diagonal point of a symmetric curve is where the best advantage \(1 - \alpha - \beta = 1 - 2\alpha\) is attained (Part 1). So \(\mu^*\) is the Gaussian shift with the same total variation as the Laplace pair, \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1 = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon/2}\), which Part 1 found to be 1.0301 at \(\kappa = 1\).
What the summary reports. By Equation 32.9, 1.0301-GDP gives \(\varepsilon = 4.5301\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (and 0.5618-GDP gives 2.2706). The Laplace mechanism is \((1, 0)\)-DP.

The GDP summary of a Laplace mechanism is tight at one point, the diagonal, and very loose in the tails: the Laplace privacy loss is bounded by \(\varepsilon\), while every \(G_\mu\) has an unbounded one.

text:
32.2 Group privacy

Exercise 2. Group privacy. Let \(h(\alpha) = 1 - f(\alpha)\) be the largest power at type I error \(\alpha\) that a curve \(f\) allows. Show that if \(T(P, Q) \ge f\) and \(T(Q, R) \ge f\), then \(T(P, R) \ge 1 - h(h(\alpha))\), so an \(f\)-DP mechanism is \(\big(1 - h^{\circ k}\big)\)-DP for groups of \(k\) records (Dong et al., Theorem 2.14). For \(f = G_\mu\), show that \(1 - h^{\circ k} = G_{k\mu}\). What \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) does a 0.5-GDP mechanism give a group of 2 and a group of 4, and what does Part 3’s group property (Equation 19.6) give when applied to the single point \((1.9931, 10^{-5})\) instead? Check: groups of 2 and 4 are 1-GDP and 2-GDP, so \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) and \(9.9973\). From the point, a group of 4 gets \((7.9724, 4.57\times10^{-3})\), while 2-GDP has \(\delta(7.9724) = 5.20\times10^{-4}\). (Trade-off curves as power bounds, GDP)







TipSolution






A curve bounds power. \(T(P, Q) \ge f\) says that every test \(\phi\) with \(\mathbb E_P\phi \le \alpha\) has type II error at least \(f(\alpha)\), that is, power \(\mathbb E_Q\phi \le 1 - f(\alpha) = h(\alpha)\). Since \(f\) is non-increasing, \(h\) is non-decreasing.
Chain the bounds. Take a test \(\phi\) of \(P\) against \(R\) with \(\mathbb E_P\phi \le \alpha\). Read as a test of \(P\) against \(Q\), it has power \(\mathbb E_Q\phi \le h(\alpha)\). Read as a test of \(Q\) against \(R\), its type I error is \(\mathbb E_Q\phi \le h(\alpha)\), so its power is \(\mathbb E_R\phi \le h(\mathbb E_Q\phi) \le h(h(\alpha))\), using that \(h\) is non-decreasing. So its type II error against \(R\) is at least \(1 - h(h(\alpha))\), and \(T(P, R) \ge 1 - h\circ h\).
Groups. Datasets that differ in \(k\) records are joined by a path \(D = D_0 \sim D_1 \sim \dots \sim D_k\). Applying step 2 along the path \(k - 1\) times gives \(T(M(D_0), M(D_k)) \ge 1 - h^{\circ k}\).
The Gaussian case. For \(f = G_\mu\), \(h(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu) = \Phi(\mu - \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\alpha) + \mu)\), using \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) = -\Phi^{-1}(\alpha)\). Each application of \(h\) adds \(\mu\) inside \(\Phi\), so \(h^{\circ k}(\alpha) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\alpha) + k\mu)\) and \(1 - h^{\circ k}(\alpha) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - k\mu) = G_{k\mu}(\alpha)\). The script checks \(1 - h(h(\alpha)) = G_{2\mu}(\alpha)\) at \(\mu = 0.5\) on a grid of 1,999 values of \(\alpha\): the largest difference is \(2.2\times10^{-16}\). For the Gaussian mechanism the bound is tight, because a group of \(k\) shifts the mean by up to \(k\) sensitivities.
The numbers. A 0.5-GDP mechanism is 1-GDP for groups of 2 and 2-GDP for groups of 4, so by Equation 32.9 it gives \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) and \(9.9973\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
Going through one point instead. 0.5-GDP gives \(\varepsilon = 1.9931\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Part 3’s group property turns \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) into \(\big(k\varepsilon, \delta\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\big)\):

32.3 A tensor product by hand

Exercise 3. A tensor product by hand. Show that \(f_{\varepsilon,0}\otimes f_{\varepsilon,0} = \max\big(f_{2\varepsilon,0}, f_{0,\tanh(\varepsilon/2)}\big)\), and read off its privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) for \(0 \le \varepsilon' \le 2\varepsilon\) from the corners. Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta(0) = 0.4621\), \(\delta(1) = 0.3378\), \(\delta(2) = 0\). (Tensor product, duality)







TipSolution





Let \(\pi = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), so randomized response reports the true bit with probability \(\pi\), and note \(2\pi - 1 = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) and \(\pi/(1 - \pi) = e^\varepsilon\).

The product pair. As in Table 32.4, the output pairs 11, 01 or 10, and 00 have likelihood ratios \(Q/P = e^{2\varepsilon}\), \(1\) and \(e^{-2\varepsilon}\), and \(P\)-probabilities \((1 - \pi)^2\), \(2\pi(1 - \pi)\) and \(\pi^2\).
The corners. Adding outcomes in decreasing order of \(Q/P\) gives the corners \((0, 1)\), \(\big((1 - \pi)^2, 1 - \pi^2\big)\), \(\big(1 - \pi^2, (1 - \pi)^2\big)\) and \((1, 0)\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) these are \((0.0723, 0.4656)\) and \((0.4656, 0.0723)\).
First segment. It has slope \(-e^{2\varepsilon}\) and starts at \((0, 1)\): \(\beta = 1 - e^{2\varepsilon}\alpha\). It ends at the second corner because \(e^{2\varepsilon}(1 - \pi)^2 = \pi^2\).
Middle segment. Slope \(-1\) through \(\big((1 - \pi)^2, 1 - \pi^2\big)\): \(\beta = 1 - \pi^2 + (1 - \pi)^2 - \alpha = 1 - (2\pi - 1) - \alpha = 1 - \tanh(\varepsilon/2) - \alpha\).
Last segment. Slope \(-e^{-2\varepsilon}\) through \((1, 0)\): \(\beta = e^{-2\varepsilon}(1 - \alpha)\).
A convex polygon is the maximum of its lines. So the curve is \(\max\big(0, 1 - e^{2\varepsilon}\alpha, e^{-2\varepsilon}(1 - \alpha), 1 - \tanh(\varepsilon/2) - \alpha\big)\). The first three terms make up \(f_{2\varepsilon,0}\) and the last (with 0) is \(f_{0,\tanh(\varepsilon/2)}\), as claimed. On a grid of 1,999 values of \(\alpha\), the two sides differ by at most \(2.2\times10^{-16}\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), where \(\tanh(1/2) = 0.4621\).

The privacy profile. By the duality, \(\delta(\varepsilon') = \max_{\alpha}(1 - f(\alpha) - e^{\varepsilon'}\alpha)\), and for a polygon the maximum is at a corner. The two interior corners, and the midpoint \((1 - \pi, 1 - \pi)\) of the middle segment, give \(1 - \beta - e^{\varepsilon'}\alpha\) equal to \(\pi^2 - (1 - \pi)^2e^{\varepsilon'}\), \(\big(1 - (1 - \pi)^2\big) - (1 - \pi^2)e^{\varepsilon'}\) and \(\pi - (1 - \pi)e^{\varepsilon'}\). For \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\) the first is the largest: it beats the second by \((e^{\varepsilon'} - 1)(1 - \pi^2 - (1 - \pi)^2) = (e^{\varepsilon'} - 1)\,2\pi(1 - \pi) \ge 0\), and the midpoint value is the average of the two. So \[\delta(\varepsilon') = \pi^2 - (1 - \pi)^2e^{\varepsilon'}, \qquad 0 \le \varepsilon' \le 2\varepsilon, \tag{32.2}\] which reaches 0 at \(\varepsilon' = 2\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) (\(\pi^2 = 0.5344\), \((1 - \pi)^2 = 0.0723\)):

32.4 Inverting the duality

Exercise 4. Inverting the duality. Find the largest \(\mu\) such that \(\mu\)-GDP implies \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP. How many full-batch Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\) fit in that budget? How many DP-SGD steps with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) fit in budgets \(\varepsilon = 1, 2, 4\) according to the CLT? Check: \(\mu^* = 0.2681\); 28 full-batch steps; 418, 1463 and 4978 DP-SGD steps. (GDP duality, composition)







TipSolution






\(\delta(\varepsilon)\) grows with \(\mu\). A larger \(\mu\) gives a lower curve, so every supporting line moves down and \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 1 + G_\mu^*(-e^\varepsilon)\) goes up. So the set of \(\mu\) that satisfy \(\delta_\mu(1) \le 10^{-5}\) is an interval \([0, \mu^*]\), found by bisection on Equation 32.9: \(\mu^* = 0.2681\), where \(\delta_{\mu^*}(1) = 1.00\times10^{-5}\).
Full batch. \(T\) Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\) compose to \(\sqrt T/20\)-GDP (Equation 32.11). The budget allows \(\sqrt T/20 \le 0.2681\), so \(T \le (20 \times 0.2681)^2\), and the largest integer is \(T = 28\).
DP-SGD by the CLT. With \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) the budget allows \(T \le (\mu^*/q)^2/(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). With \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\):

text:
32.5 Berry–Esseen for randomized response

Exercise 5. Berry–Esseen for randomized response. Compute \(\mathrm{kl}\), \(\kappa_2\) and \(\bar\kappa_3\) for \(f_{\varepsilon_0,0}\), and show that Equation 32.15 gives \(\mu = 2\sqrt k\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) for \(k\) copies. Check: \(\mathrm{kl} = \varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 0.004996\) at \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\); at \(k = 100\), \(\mu = 1.0004\) and \(\xi = 0.0562\). (CLT functionals)







TipSolution





Let \(t = \tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 2\pi - 1\) with \(\pi = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\).

The privacy loss under \(P\). Randomized response outputs the likely value with probability \(\pi\), where \(L = \ln(\pi/(1 - \pi)) = \varepsilon_0\), and the other value with probability \(1 - \pi\), where \(L = -\varepsilon_0\).
The functionals are moments of \(L\) (Lemma 32.2):

\(\mathrm{kl} = \mathbb E_P L = \varepsilon_0\pi - \varepsilon_0(1 - \pi) = \varepsilon_0 t\);
\(\kappa_2 = \mathbb E_P L^2 = \varepsilon_0^2\);
\(\bar\kappa_3 = \mathbb E_P|L - \varepsilon_0t|^3 = \pi\,\varepsilon_0^3(1 - t)^3 + (1 - \pi)\,\varepsilon_0^3(1 + t)^3\). With \(\pi = (1 + t)/2\) this is \(\frac{\varepsilon_0^3(1 - t^2)}{2}\big((1 - t)^2 + (1 + t)^2\big) = \varepsilon_0^3(1 - t^2)(1 + t^2)\).

The variance. \(\kappa_2 - \mathrm{kl}^2 = \varepsilon_0^2(1 - t^2) = \varepsilon_0^2/\cosh^2(\varepsilon_0/2)\), using \(1 - \tanh^2 = 1/\cosh^2\).
\(\mu\) for \(k\) copies. Equation 32.15 gives \[\mu = \frac{2k\varepsilon_0t}{\sqrt{k\,\varepsilon_0^2/\cosh^2(\varepsilon_0/2)}} = 2\sqrt k\,\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\cosh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 2\sqrt k\,\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2). \tag{32.3}\]
\(\xi\) for \(k\) copies. \(\xi = \frac{0.56\,k\varepsilon_0^3(1 - t^2)(1 + t^2)}{\big(k\varepsilon_0^2(1 - t^2)\big)^{3/2}} = \frac{0.56\,(1 + t^2)\cosh(\varepsilon_0/2)}{\sqrt k}\).
Check. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\): \(\mathrm{kl} = 0.1\tanh(0.05) = 0.004996\). At \(k = 100\): \(\mu = 20\sinh(0.05) = 1.0004\) and \(\xi = 0.0562\), from the closed form and from the general formula alike.

32.6 A sanity limit for the subsampled CLT

Exercise 6. A sanity limit for the subsampled CLT. Put \(q = 1\) in Equation 32.17 and compare with the exact \(\sqrt T/\sigma\). Which way is it off, and why does the derivation not apply? Check: the ratio, the same for every \(T\), is 1.3108 for \(\sigma = 1\), 1.0659 for \(\sigma = 2\) and 1.0101 for \(\sigma = 5\). (Subsampled CLT, expansions)







TipSolution






The formula at \(q = 1\). \(\mu_{\mathrm{CLT}} = \sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\), while full-batch training is exactly \(\sqrt T/\sigma\)-GDP. Their ratio is \(\sigma\sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\), independent of \(T\).
Which way. \(e^x - 1 \ge x\) for all \(x\), so \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) \ge 1\): the formula over-states \(\mu\) at \(q = 1\). As \(\sigma\) grows, \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 \approx 1/\sigma^2\) and the ratio tends to 1.

Why the derivation fails. Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 32.5 expanded \(\ln(1 + qW)\) to second order, which needs \(qW\) small. At \(q = 1\), \(\ln(1 + W) = (y - \frac12)/\sigma^2\) exactly: the loss is Gaussian with variance \(1/\sigma^2\), not \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\). The expansion replaced the variance of \(\ln(1 + W)\) by the variance of \(W\), which is larger, and the gap grows as \(\sigma\) shrinks (Table 32.5).
The regime. The CLT formula is meant for \(q \to 0\) with \(q\sqrt T\) fixed. There \(qW\) is small with high probability and the expansion is accurate, although for small \(\sigma\) the heavy right tail of \(W\) is exactly where it is least accurate.

Formulas derived for a limit regime should be checked at the edges of that regime; here the edge \(q = 1\) is known exactly and shows the formula’s bias.

title: 33  Exercises: Amplification by subsampling

33.1 Subsampling twice
Exercises for Amplification by subsampling, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_subsampling.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_subsampling.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(q\) is the sampling rate, never a density. \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(P_1 = \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) are the outputs of one Gaussian step without and with the record, and \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve of the subsampled step. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise gives differential privacy (DP), and is called DP-SGD.

title: 33  Exercises: Amplification by subsampling
text:
Exercise 1. Subsampling twice. Show that a Poisson sample with rate \(q_2\) of a Poisson sample with rate \(q_1\) is a Poisson sample with rate \(q_1q_2\), and that applying Equation 33.8 twice gives the same \((\varepsilon', \delta')\) as applying it once with \(q_1q_2\). Check: \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(q_1 = q_2 = 0.1\) gives 0.1586 after one stage and 0.01704 after two. (Composition of the amplification map)







TipSolution






The two-stage sample. A record survives the first stage with probability \(q_1\) and, given that, the second with probability \(q_2\), using fresh independent coins. So it survives both with probability \(q_1q_2\), independently of every other record. That is a Poisson sample with rate \(q_1q_2\).
Write the map in terms of \(e^\varepsilon - 1\). Equation 33.8 says \(e^{\varepsilon'} - 1 = q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\). The quantity \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) is simply multiplied by \(q\).
Apply it twice. After the first stage \(e^{\varepsilon_1} - 1 = q_1(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), and after the second \(e^{\varepsilon_2} - 1 = q_2(e^{\varepsilon_1} - 1) = q_1q_2(e^\varepsilon - 1)\). This is the one-stage formula with rate \(q_1q_2\). The \(\delta\) is multiplied by \(q_1\) and then by \(q_2\), so it is also \(q_1q_2\delta\).
Check. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(q_1 = 0.1\), \(\varepsilon_1 = \ln(1 + 0.1(e - 1)) = 0.1586\). With \(q_2 = 0.1\) the second stage gives 0.01704, and the direct formula with \(q = 0.01\) also gives 0.01704.

The amplification map is consistent: in the coordinate \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) it is multiplication by \(q\), so stages of sampling compose by multiplying their rates. This is consistent with Equation 33.8 being exact, though consistency alone does not prove it; exactness comes from randomized response attaining the formula (Theorem 33.1).

33.2 The binomial sum at α = 3

Exercise 2. The binomial sum at \(\alpha = 3\). Write out the four terms of Equation 33.19 for \(\alpha = 3\), \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), and compute \(\varepsilon(3)\). Check: \(\varepsilon(3) = 2.6464 \times 10^{-4}\). Which term carries most of the privacy cost? (Binomial expansion, Gaussian moments)







TipSolution






The terms. By step 7 of the proof of Theorem 33.3, the Gaussian moments are \(\mathbb E_{P_0}[(P_1/P_0)^j] = e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}\), which is \(1, 1, e^{1/\sigma^2}, e^{3/\sigma^2}\) for \(j = 0, 1, 2, 3\). So \[A_3 = (1 - q)^3 + 3q(1 - q)^2 + 3q^2(1 - q)e^{1/\sigma^2} + q^3e^{3/\sigma^2}. \tag{33.1}\]
The numbers are in Table 33.1.
