Sum and convert. \(A_3 = 1.00052942\), and \(\varepsilon(3) = \ln(A_3)/(3 - 1) = 2.6464 \times 10^{-4}\), the same value the chapter’s script computes.
Which term costs. Without the moments, the four coefficients sum to exactly 1 (the binomial theorem for \(((1 - q) + q)^3\)). So the privacy cost is the excess \(3q^2(1 - q)(e - 1) + q^3(e^3 - 1)\). The \(j = 2\) part, \(0.00080733 - 0.00029700 = 0.00051033\) (the term minus its coefficient), dominates the \(j = 3\) part, \(0.00002009 - 0.000001 = 0.00001909\). The \(j = 2\) term carries a share of 0.96 of the cost.

At small orders the whole privacy cost of a subsampled Gaussian step is the \(j = 2\) term, the chance that the record is drawn, squared, times the \(\chi^2\) divergence \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) of the unsubsampled step.

title: 33  Exercises: Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.3 Replace-one under Poisson sampling, exactly

Exercise 3. Replace-one under Poisson sampling, exactly. Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP (\(\delta = 0\)) for add/remove neighbours, and run it on a Poisson sample with rate \(q\). Show that for replace-one neighbours the subsampled mechanism is \(\varepsilon'\)-DP with \(\varepsilon'\) from Equation 33.12, and that the Laplace mechanism on a sum of values in \([-1, 1]\) attains it. Compare with the group-privacy bound \(\ln(1 + q(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1))\) for small and large \(\varepsilon\). Hint: the ratio of two mixtures that share the part \(R\) is largest when one component ratio is as large and the other as small as DP allows. Check: at \(q = 0.01\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), 0.02338 against 0.06193, and 0.01704 for add/remove. (Likelihood-ratio bounds on mixtures)







TipSolution






Condition on the rest of the sample. Let \(D\) hold \(x\) and \(D'\) hold \(x'\) in its place, and let \(\tilde D\) be the Poisson sample of the other records. Given \(\tilde D\), the outputs are \((1 - q)R + qP\) and \((1 - q)R + qP'\), with \(R = M(\tilde D)\), \(P = M(\tilde D \cup \{x\})\) and \(P' = M(\tilde D \cup \{x'\})\).
Bound the component ratios. \(\tilde D \cup \{x\}\) and \(\tilde D\) are add/remove neighbours, and so are \(\tilde D \cup \{x'\}\) and \(\tilde D\). For pure DP the densities then satisfy \(a = P(y)/R(y) \in [e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\) and \(b = P'(y)/R(y) \in [e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\) at every output \(y\).
Bound the mixture ratio. At each \(y\), the ratio of the two mixtures is \(\frac{(1 - q) + qa}{(1 - q) + qb}\). It increases in \(a\) and decreases in \(b\), so it is at most \(\frac{1 - q + qe^\varepsilon}{1 - q + qe^{-\varepsilon}}\). Swapping \(x\) and \(x'\) gives the same bound for the other order.
Average over \(\tilde D\). Each conditional density of the first run is at most \(e^{\varepsilon'}\) times that of the second, with the same weights over \(\tilde D\), so the same holds for the averages. Taking logarithms, \(\varepsilon' = \ln(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)) - \ln(1 - q(1 - e^{-\varepsilon}))\), which is Equation 33.12.
The Laplace mechanism attains it. Let \(M\) add Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) to the sum. Values lie in \([-1, 1]\), so adding or removing one changes the sum by at most 1 and \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Set every other record to 0, \(x = 1\) and \(x' = -1\). Then \(R\), \(P\), \(P'\) are Laplace distributions centred at 0, 1 and \(-1\) for every \(\tilde D\). On the event \(\{Y > 1\}\), \(P(Y > 1) = \frac12\), \(R(Y > 1) = \frac12e^{-\varepsilon}\) and \(P'(Y > 1) = \frac12e^{-2\varepsilon}\). The two mixtures give this event probabilities in the ratio \[\frac{(1 - q)e^{-\varepsilon} + q}{(1 - q)e^{-\varepsilon} + qe^{-2\varepsilon}} = \frac{1 - q + qe^\varepsilon}{1 - q + qe^{-\varepsilon}} \tag{33.2}\] (multiply above and below by \(e^\varepsilon\)). An event with this ratio rules out any smaller \(\varepsilon'\).
Compare (Table 33.2). The script computes the three values and the log-ratio of the Laplace event, which equals the exact value in every row.

text:
33.4 Inverting the accountant

Exercise 4. Inverting the accountant. Find the smallest \(\sigma\) for which DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), 10,000 steps and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) has \(\varepsilon \le 1\) under the RDP accountant with the improved conversion. Hint: \(\varepsilon\) decreases in \(\sigma\); bisect. Check: \(\sigma = 4.126\). (Monotonicity, bisection)







TipSolution






Monotone in \(\sigma\). More noise is post-processing of less noise: \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma_2^2)\) is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma_1^2)\) plus independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma_2^2 - \sigma_1^2)\) for \(\sigma_2 > \sigma_1\). By data processing every \(D_\alpha\) can only fall, so each \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) and hence the converted \(\varepsilon\) is non-increasing in \(\sigma\).
Bracket. At \(\sigma = 0.5\) the accountant reports \(\varepsilon = 47.42\), and at \(\sigma = 10\) it reports 0.377. So the answer lies in \([0.5, 10]\).
Bisect. Halve the interval 20 times, keeping the half where \(\varepsilon \le 1\) starts. Each step computes the RDP curve on the grid of orders, multiplies by 10,000 and converts.
Result (Table 33.3). For \(\varepsilon = 1\) the answer is \(\sigma = 4.126\), and the accountant then reports \(\varepsilon = 1.000\) at the order \(\alpha = 18\).

title: 33  Exercises: Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.5 Fixed-size batches, honestly

Exercise 5. Fixed-size batches, honestly. A team trains with a fresh random batch of exactly 1% of the data at every step, \(\sigma = 1\), for 10,000 steps, and reports the Poisson value 6.71. Using Table 33.2, what is the honest RDP value, and what noise multiplier would make the honest value equal 6.71? Check: 47.42; \(\sigma = 2\). (Matching sampling scheme and neighbouring relation)







TipSolution






Which row. A fresh fixed-size batch at each step is the row “fixed size \(m\) of \(n\)”. Whether the team states add/remove or replace-one neighbours, the base mechanism needs a replace-one guarantee: a clipped sum moves by up to \(2C\) when the record enters the batch and pushes another one out (Lebeda et al. 2024, Proposition 9).
Rescale. Noise \(\sigma C\) against a shift of \(2C\) is the same pair as noise \((\sigma/2)C\) against a shift of \(C\). So the honest accounting is the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian with \(q = 0.01\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma/2 = 0.5\).
Compute. The RDP accountant gives \(\varepsilon = 47.42\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), against the reported 6.71.
Fix. To make the honest value 6.71, the halved noise multiplier must be 1, so the team must train with \(\sigma = 2\). The script confirms that fixed-size batches with \(\sigma = 2\) give 6.71. With \(\sigma = 2\) and Poisson sampling, the same accountant would give 2.35.

Reporting the Poisson number for fixed-size batches is equivalent to claiming you added twice as much noise as you did. The fix is either to sample with Poisson, or to double \(\sigma\), or to report the honest number.

title: 33  Exercises: Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.6 The first direction, exactly

Exercise 6. The first direction, exactly. Show that for any pair \((P_0, P_1)\) and \(e^{\varepsilon'} = 1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), \(E_{e^{\varepsilon'}}((1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\|P_0) = q\,E_{e^\varepsilon}(P_1\|P_0)\), and that the other direction is 0 whenever \(e^{\varepsilon'} \ge 1/(1-q)\). Check it numerically for the subsampled Gaussian with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 2\), both sides equal \(2.09236 \times 10^{-4}\). (Hockey-stick divergence, the mixture lemma with equality)







TipSolution






Expand the event-wise difference. For any event \(A\), \[(1 - q)P_0(A) + qP_1(A) - \big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big)P_0(A) = qP_1(A) - qe^\varepsilon P_0(A) = q\big[P_1(A) - e^\varepsilon P_0(A)\big]. \tag{33.3}\] The \(P_0(A)\) terms cancel except for \(-qe^\varepsilon P_0(A)\).
Maximize over \(A\). The difference is \(q\) times the bracket for every event, so the two maxima agree: \(E_{e^{\varepsilon'}}(\text{mixture}\|P_0) = q\max_A[P_1(A) - e^\varepsilon P_0(A)] = q\,E_{e^\varepsilon}(P_1\|P_0)\). This is step 1 of the proof of Lemma 33.1 with \(P' = R\), where no inequality was needed.
The other direction. The mixture is at least \((1 - q)P_0\) everywhere, so \(P_0/\text{mixture} \le 1/(1 - q)\). If \(e^{\varepsilon'} \ge 1/(1-q)\), then \(P_0 - e^{\varepsilon'}\cdot\text{mixture} \le 0\) everywhere and \(E_{e^{\varepsilon'}}(P_0\|\text{mixture}) = 0\).
Numerically (Table 33.4). For the Gaussian, \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P_1\|P_0)\) is the exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of the Gaussian mechanism. The script integrates both hockey-stick divergences of the mixture on a fine grid.

title: 34  Exercises: Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.1 The PLD of the swapped pair
Exercises for Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_numerical_accounting.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_numerical_accounting.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(P\) and \(Q\) are the output distributions, with densities \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\), because \(q\) is the sampling rate. \(L = \ln(P/Q)\) is the privacy loss, and the privacy loss distribution (PLD) \(\omega\) is its law under \(Y \sim P\). \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E_\omega[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\) (Equation 34.1). The subsampled Gaussian is the one-step pair of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under differential privacy (DP), called DP-SGD, with \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\).

title: 34  Exercises: Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
Exercise 1. The PLD of the swapped pair. Show that if \(\omega\) is the PLD of \((P, Q)\), the PLD of \((Q, P)\) puts mass \(e^{-\ell}\omega(\mathrm d\ell)\) at loss \(-\ell\), plus an atom at \(+\infty\) of size \(1 - \mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}]\). Deduce that the add-direction PLD of the subsampled Gaussian is determined by the remove-direction one, and that the Gaussian pair’s PLD is the same in both directions. Check: tilting the pessimistic remove PLD (\(h = 10^{-5}\)) gives an add-direction \(\delta(0) = 3.830792\text{e-}03\), against the exact 3.829249e-03. (Change of measure)







TipSolution






The swapped loss. For the pair \((Q, P)\) the privacy loss is \(\ln\frac{Q(y)}{P(y)} = -L(y)\), and its PLD is the law of \(-L(Y)\) with \(Y \sim Q\).
The law of \(L\) under \(Q\). Theorem 34.1 gives it: \(e^{-\ell}\omega(\mathrm d\ell)\) on the finite losses, so \(-L\) takes the value \(-\ell\) with that weight.
The rest of \(Q\). The same theorem puts the remaining mass \(1 - \mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}]\) where \(P(y) = 0\), at \(L = -\infty\). There \(Q/P = \infty\), so the swapped loss is \(+\infty\).
The subsampled Gaussian. The add pair \((\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2), \text{mixture})\) is the remove pair (mixture, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\)) swapped. By steps 2 and 3 its PLD is the remove PLD tilted by \(e^{-\ell}\) and reflected. One accountant run can serve both directions.
The Gaussian pair. Tilting \(\mathcal N(\frac{\mu^2}2, \mu^2)\) by \(e^{-\ell}\) and normalizing gives \(\mathcal N(\frac{\mu^2}2 - \mu^2, \mu^2) = \mathcal N(-\frac{\mu^2}2, \mu^2)\): complete the square in \(-\frac{(\ell - m)^2}{2v} - \ell = -\frac{(\ell - m + v)^2}{2v} + \text{const}\). Here \(\mathbb E[e^{-L}] = e^{-m + v/2} = 1\), so the tilt needs no normalization and there is no atom. Reflecting gives \(\mathcal N(\frac{\mu^2}2, \mu^2)\) again.

Concretely. The script applies steps 2 and 3 to the discretized PLDs (Table 34.1).

title: 34  Exercises: Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.2 δ from tail probabilities

Exercise 2. \(\delta\) from tail probabilities. Show that \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\) and that \(\delta(\varepsilon) \ge (1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'})\,\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon']\) for every \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\). Check: for the Gaussian pair with \(\mu = 1\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), the upper bound is 0.3085, \(\delta\) is 0.1269, and the best lower bound is 0.0624, at \(\varepsilon' = 1.504\). (Monotone weight, Markov-style bounds)







TipSolution






The weight is between 0 and an indicator. \(g(\ell) = (1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) is 0 for \(\ell \le \varepsilon\) and in \((0, 1]\) for \(\ell > \varepsilon\). So \(g(\ell) \le \mathbf 1[\ell > \varepsilon]\).
Upper bound. Average step 1 over \(\omega\): \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E[g(L)] \le \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\).
Lower bound. \(g\) is non-decreasing, so for \(\ell > \varepsilon'\), \(g(\ell) \ge g(\varepsilon') = 1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}\). Since \(g \ge 0\) everywhere, \(g(\ell) \ge (1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'})\mathbf 1[\ell > \varepsilon']\).
Average. \(\delta(\varepsilon) \ge (1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'})\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon']\). The first factor grows with \(\varepsilon'\) and the second shrinks, so there is a best \(\varepsilon'\).

Concretely, with \(L \sim \mathcal N(0.5, 1)\), \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(0.5 - \varepsilon)\) (Table 34.2).

title: 34  Exercises: Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.3 The sandwich width

Exercise 3. The sandwich width. Show that, without truncation, \(\varepsilon^\uparrow(\delta) - \varepsilon^\downarrow(\delta) \le kh\), with equality when no loss lies on the grid and \(\varepsilon^\downarrow(\delta) > 0\). When is the width zero? Check: for three-fold randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) at \(\delta = 0.3\), the width is 1.5000 for \(h = 0.5\), 0.3000 for \(h = 0.1\), and 0 for \(h = \ln 3/2\). (Coupling)







TipSolution






The inequality. Part 2 of Theorem 34.4 proves it: coupling the roundings gives totals with \(S^\uparrow \le S^\downarrow + kh\), and since \(g_\varepsilon(\ell) = (1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) satisfies \(g_\varepsilon(s + c) = g_{\varepsilon - c}(s)\), this gives \(\delta^\uparrow(\varepsilon) \le \delta^\downarrow(\varepsilon - kh)\).
Invert. At \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon^\downarrow(\delta) + kh\), step 1 gives \(\delta^\uparrow \le \delta^\downarrow(\varepsilon^\downarrow(\delta)) \le \delta\), so \(\varepsilon^\uparrow(\delta) \le \varepsilon^\downarrow(\delta) + kh\).
Equality. If no loss lies on the grid, \(\lceil x\rceil - \lfloor x\rfloor = 1\) for every loss, so \(S^\uparrow = S^\downarrow + kh\) exactly, the inequality of step 1 is an equality, and the two \(\delta\) curves are shifts of each other. Their crossing points with level \(\delta\) differ by exactly \(kh\), unless the lower one is cut off at \(\varepsilon = 0\).
Zero width. If every loss is on the grid, both roundings return the true PLD and the width is 0. For randomized response, the losses \(\pm\ln 3\) are on the grid when \(h = \ln 3/j\) for an integer \(j\).

title: 34  Exercises: Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.4 Wraparound

Exercise 4. Wraparound. Show that the \(k\)-th power of the discrete Fourier transform on a circular window of \(N\) bins computes the PLD of the total loss reduced modulo \(Nh\) into the window, and that the error in \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is at most the mass of the composed PLD outside the window. Use Chebyshev’s inequality to choose a window for ten Gaussian steps with \(\mu = 1\). Check: a window of width 20 around the mean has mass \(1.57\text{e-}03\) outside it (Chebyshev: 0.1000), and an actual \(\delta(1)\) error of \(9.27\text{e-}06\). (Circular convolution, Chebyshev)







TipSolution






Circular convolution. Proposition 34.2 shows that a window of \(N\) bins reduces the total loss modulo \(Nh\). Placing the window at grid points \(s, \dots, s + N - 1\) means each total loss \(\ell\) lands at the unique point of the window congruent to \(\ell\) modulo \(Nh\).
Mass inside the window is untouched. A total that is already in the window is its own residue, so its mass is in the right place.
Error bound. Write \(\delta = \sum_\ell m_\ell\,g(\ell)\) with \(0 \le g \le 1\). Wraparound moves only the mass \(m_{\text{out}}\) outside the window, and each moved unit changes its weight \(g\) by at most 1 in absolute value. So \(|\delta_{\text{circ}} - \delta| \le m_{\text{out}}\).
Chebyshev. The composed PLD has mean \(k\mu^2/2 = 5\) and variance \(k\mu^2 = 10\). For a window of width \(W\) centred at the mean, \(\Pr_P[|S - 5| \ge W/2] \le 10/(W/2)^2\). For this to be at most \(\tau\) you need \(W \ge 2\sqrt{10/\tau}\). For an error of at most \(\tau = 10^{-5}\), that is \(W \ge 2\sqrt{10/10^{-5}} = 2000\), a hundred times wider than the width 20 that already gives an error of \(9.27\text{e-}06\) (Table 34.4). Chebyshev is safe but very wasteful here.

Concretely, with \(h = 10^{-3}\) (Table 34.4):

PLD of the final release. With sensitivity 1 and \(\sigma = 10\), the Gaussian PLD is \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\) with \(\mu = 0.1\). It is the same for both directions (Exercise 1).

section: 34.6 Why a short window errs upwards
text:
34.6 Why a short window errs upwards

Exercise 6. Why a short window errs upwards. Ten Gaussian steps with \(\mu = 1\) have the PLD \(\mathcal N(5, 10)\). Composed on a circular window from loss 0 to 10 with \(h = 10^{-3}\), they give \(\delta(1) = 0.83478562\), against 0.81891018 with padding. Explain why the wrapped value is too large here, and why the sign of a wraparound error is unknown in general. Check, from the chapter’s script: each tail beyond the window has mass \(\Phi(-5/\sqrt{10}) = 0.0569\), and a share 0.51 of the mass above 10 lies above 11. (Circular convolution, the weight of a loss)







TipSolution






Where the outside mass goes. By Proposition 34.2 the window reduces each total loss modulo 10. A total below 0 lands 10 higher, near the top of the window, and a total above 10 lands 10 lower, near the bottom.
The two tails are equal. The composed PLD has standard deviation \(\sqrt{10} = 3.162\), and the window reaches 5 on either side of the mean. So each tail has mass \(\Phi(-5/\sqrt{10}) = \Phi(-1.581) = 0.0569\).
The lower tail gains weight. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the weight \(g(\ell) = (1 - e^{1 - \ell})_+\) is 0 for every negative total, so these totals counted nothing towards \(\delta(1)\). Most of their mass lies just below 0 and wraps to just below 10, where the weight is close to 1, for example \(1 - e^{-8} = 0.9997\) at \(\ell = 9\). So the window gains nearly the whole 0.0569.
The upper tail loses less. Totals above 10 had weights close to 1. Those between 10 and 11 land between 0 and 1, below \(\varepsilon\), and lose their whole weight. But a share 0.51 of the upper tail lies above 11, lands above 1, and keeps part of its weight. So the window loses less than 0.0569.
The net error. The gain exceeds the loss, so the wrapped \(\delta(1)\) is too large, by \(0.83478562 - 0.81891018 = 0.0159\). This is the error of \(1.59\text{e-}02\) in Table 34.4, below the mass outside the window, as Exercise 4 requires.
The sign in general. The sign depends on how much mass each tail holds and on where it lands relative to \(\varepsilon\). A window placed off the mean, or a different \(\varepsilon\), can make the lost weight exceed the gained weight. So the wraparound error has no known sign and cannot be part of a certified bound.

A wrapped answer can be too large or too small. Only padding, or truncation in the safe directions, keeps the sign of the error known.

Exercises for Amplification by shuffling and by iteration, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_shuffling_iteration.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_shuffling_iteration.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation for differential privacy (DP) and noisy gradient descent (GD). Neighbouring datasets differ in one record’s value (replace-one). Binary randomized response reports the true bit with probability \(p = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\). \(P\) and \(Q\) are the adversary’s views on \(D\) and \(D'\), and \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the larger of the hockey-stick divergences \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\) and \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(Q\|P)\). Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\) is the privacy of a pair of unit-variance Gaussians a distance \(\mu\) apart, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is measured by the Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha\). The one-dimensional iteration is \(\theta_k = c\,\theta_{k-1} + b_k + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), with the two runs’ offsets differing by \(s\) at the steps that use the record. As in the chapter, \(\sigma\) is a noise standard deviation in parameter units, \(G\) a Lipschitz constant (not \(L\), the privacy loss) and \(d_K\) the diameter of the parameter set.

title: 35  Exercises: Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
Exercise 1. Two users. Two users run binary randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) behind a shuffler; the other user holds 0. Write down the distributions of the count on \(D\) and \(D'\), and compute \(\delta(0.5)\). Then show that for every \(n\) the pure-DP level of shuffled randomized response is still \(\varepsilon_0\). Check: \(\delta(0.5) = 0.2534\). (Exact hockey-stick computation)







TipSolution





Here \(p = \frac34\).

The other user’s count. The other user holds 0 and reports 1 with probability \(1 - p = \frac14\): \(b = (\frac34, \frac14)\) on counts \((0, 1)\).
The pair. By Equation 35.1 of the chapter, \(P(y) = \frac34b(y) + \frac14b(y - 1)\) and \(Q(y) = \frac14b(y) + \frac34b(y - 1)\). Table 35.1 lists them.




Table 35.1: Shuffled binary randomized response with two users at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\); the other user holds 0.

\(\frac34\cdot\frac14 + \frac14\cdot\frac34 = \frac6{16}\)
\(\frac14\cdot\frac14 = \frac1{16}\)


\(Q(y)\), you hold 1
\(\frac14\cdot\frac34 = \frac3{16}\)
\(\frac14\cdot\frac14 + \frac34\cdot\frac34 = \frac{10}{16}\)
\(\frac34\cdot\frac14 = \frac3{16}\)

3
0.6
\(\frac13\)







Forward direction at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\). \(e^{0.5} = 1.6487\). Only \(y = 0\) has a ratio above it, so \(E_{e^{0.5}}(P\|Q) = \frac{9 - 3e^{0.5}}{16} = 0.2534\).
Backward direction. \(Q/P\) is \(\frac13\), \(\frac53\) and 3; the last two exceed \(e^{0.5}\), so \(E_{e^{0.5}}(Q\|P) = \frac{(10 - 6e^{0.5}) + (3 - e^{0.5})}{16} = 0.0912\).
So \(\delta(0.5) = 0.2534\), the larger of the two. A single unshuffled report has \(\delta(0.5) = 0.3378\) (chapter, Table 35.1).

Pure DP is not amplified. For any \(n\) with the other users all holding 0, the count \(y = 0\) has \(P(0) = p\,b(0)\) and \(Q(0) = (1 - p)\,b(0)\), with the same \(b(0) = p^{n-1} > 0\). So \(P(0)/Q(0) = p/(1 - p) = e^{\varepsilon_0}\) and \(\delta(\varepsilon) > 0\) for every \(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_0\). The script confirms \(\ln(P(0)/Q(0)) = 1.0986 = \ln 3\) at \(n = 2, 10, 100\), while \(P(0)\) falls from \(5.625\times10^{-1}\) to \(3.207\times10^{-13}\). Since some pair of datasets has this property, the shuffled mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP (with \(\delta = 0\)) for no \(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_0\). It is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP: the bag is a post-processing of the \(n\) independent reports (shuffle them), and changing your data changes only your own report, which is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP while the others’ reports have the same distribution on \(D\) and \(D'\). So the pure-DP level is exactly \(\varepsilon_0\).
Shuffling buys a small \(\delta\) at a smaller \(\varepsilon\); the pure-DP level stays at \(\varepsilon_0\), carried by an outcome whose probability vanishes as \(n\) grows.

title: 35  Exercises: Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.2 How many users?

Exercise 2. How many users? Using the normal approximation Equation 35.3 and the exact Gaussian curve of Theorem 20.3, estimate how many users \(n\) make shuffled randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) reach \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), then check your \(n\) with the exact computation. Hint: find the \(\mu\) whose \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) is 0.1, then solve \(2\sinh(1)/\sqrt n = \mu\). Check: the approximation gives \(n = 7282\); the exact computation needs \(n = 7781\). (Central limit approximation)







TipSolution






Target \(\mu\). The \(\varepsilon\) of \(\mu\)-GDP at fixed \(\delta\) increases with \(\mu\), so bisection on \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi(-\frac\varepsilon\mu + \frac\mu2) - e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\varepsilon\mu - \frac\mu2)\) finds the \(\mu\) with \(\delta(0.1) = 10^{-6}\): \(\mu^* = 0.027545\).
Solve for \(n\). \(2\sinh(1) = 2.3504\), so \(n = (2.3504/\mu^*)^2 = 7281.3\), rounded up: \(n = 7282\).
Check exactly. At \(n = 7282\) the exact \(\varepsilon\) of shuffled randomized response is 0.1037, slightly above the target. Bisection on \(n\) with the exact computation gives the smallest \(n\) with \(\varepsilon \le 0.1\): \(n = 7781\), where \(\varepsilon = 0.1000\).

The approximation undershoots: the exact computation needs 1.069 times as many users. The count of 1-reports is a sum of bits with \(p = 0.8808\), so it is skewed, and at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) the privacy loss is decided far in its tails, where a normal approximation with the right mean and variance is least accurate. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) there are many 1-reports, so the error is small; at \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) and small \(n\) it is large (chapter, Table 35.2).
Use the normal approximation to size a deployment, then confirm with the exact computation, which is cheap.

title: 35  Exercises: Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.3 Clones of a three-valued report

Exercise 3. Clones of a three-valued report. For 3-ary randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 4\) (report the true value with probability \(\frac23\), each other value with probability \(\frac16\)), decompose the report of a user holding value 3 as in Equation 35.6, with \(x^0 = 1\) and \(x^1 = 2\). Then find the largest clone probability \(r\) for which Equation 35.6, with \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) replaced by \(r\), holds for every value \(x\), and compare it with \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\). Check: \(\mathrm{LO}(3) = (\frac1{12}, \frac1{12}, \frac56)\), and \(r = \frac25\) against \(e^{-\varepsilon_0} = \frac14\). (Clone decomposition)







TipSolution






The three report distributions, in 48ths on outputs \((1, 2, 3)\): \(R(1) = (32, 8, 8)\), \(R(2) = (8, 32, 8)\), \(R(3) = (8, 8, 32)\). The largest likelihood ratio is \(\frac{32}{8} = 4 = e^{\varepsilon_0}\), so the randomizer is \(\ln 4\)-DP.
The clone part is \(\frac{e^{-\varepsilon_0}}2\big(R(1) + R(2)\big) = \frac18(40, 40, 16)/48 = (5, 5, 2)/48\).
The leftover mass is \(R(3)\) minus the clone part: \((3, 3, 30)/48\), of total \(\frac{36}{48} = \frac34 = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon_0}\). Dividing by \(\frac34\) gives \(\mathrm{LO}(3) = (\frac1{12}, \frac1{12}, \frac56)\). All entries are non-negative, as Lemma 26.4 guarantees.
The largest clone probability. The decomposition with probability \(r\) needs \(R(x)(y) \ge \frac r2\big(R(x^0)(y) + R(x^1)(y)\big)\) for every output \(y\), that is \(r \le \min_y\frac{2R(x)(y)}{R(x^0)(y) + R(x^1)(y)}\). For \(x = 3\) the binding outputs are 1 and 2: \(\frac{2\cdot8}{32 + 8} = \frac25\). For \(x = 1\) (a user with your \(D\) value) the binding output is 2: \(\frac{2\cdot8}{8 + 32} = \frac25\); \(x = 2\) is symmetric. So \(r = \frac25 = 0.4000\) works for every user, against \(e^{-\varepsilon_0} = 0.2500\).
Why the general argument uses less. The proof of Lemma 26.4 uses only \(R(x) \ge e^{-\varepsilon_0}R(x^0)\) and \(R(x) \ge e^{-\varepsilon_0}R(x^1)\) separately. Averaging two separate lower bounds wastes slack whenever they are not both tight at the same output. For \(k\)-ary randomized response they are never both tight, since \(R(x^0)\) and \(R(x^1)\) peak at different outputs. Binary randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) likewise allows \(r = 0.5000 = 2/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), above \(e^{-\varepsilon_0} = \frac13\).

More clones mean a smaller \(\varepsilon\). Section 4 of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021) gives an analysis for specific randomizers that exploits this.
The clone probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) is what every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer guarantees; a specific randomizer may hide you among more clones.

title: 35  Exercises: Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.4 The best shift schedule

Exercise 4. The best shift schedule. Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 35.4 shows that even payments are the cheapest way to pay off one shift \(z\). Check this on two payments. Check: with \(z = 1\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(\alpha = 2\), the schedule \((0.8, 0.2)\) costs 0.6800 against 0.5000 for \((0.5, 0.5)\). Then let one record be used at steps 1 and 4 of a four-step run of translations (two passes), with shift 1 each time. Show that the even schedule is not allowed and find the best one. Check: \((\frac13, \frac13, \frac13, 1)\), cost 1.3333. (Cauchy–Schwarz, shift reduction)







TipSolution





One use.

The bound. By the Cauchy–Schwarz step of the proof of Theorem 35.4, \(m\) payments that total \(z\) cost at least \(\frac{\alpha z^2}{2m\sigma^2}\), attained by \(a_k = z/m\). With \(z = 1\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(\alpha = 2\) and \(m = 2\) that minimum is 0.5000.
The two schedules. Each payment costs \(\alpha a_k^2/(2\sigma^2) = a_k^2\) here (Equation 35.11). So \((0.5, 0.5)\) costs 0.5000, the minimum, and \((0.8, 0.2)\) costs \(0.64 + 0.04 = 0.6800\).

Two uses. Now \(s_1 = s_4 = 1\), \(s_2 = s_3 = 0\), and Theorem 35.3 needs \(z_t = \sum_{i\le t}(s_i - a_i) \ge 0\) for every \(t\) and \(z_4 = 0\).

The even schedule fails. Paying \(\frac24 = 0.5\) at every step gives \(z = (0.5, 0, -0.5, 0)\). At step 3 more has been paid than has arrived, which the shifted divergence does not allow: you cannot pay off a shift before the record creates it.
The constraint. Since \(z_3 = 1 - (a_1 + a_2 + a_3) \ge 0\), the first three payments total \(S \le 1\), and \(a_4 = 2 - S\).
Optimize. For a given \(S\), the even split of the first three is best (one use), so the cost is \(\frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}\big(\frac{S^2}3 + (2 - S)^2\big)\). Its derivative in \(S\) is \(\frac{2S}3 - 2(2 - S)\), which is negative for all \(S < 1.5\). So the best feasible choice is \(S = 1\): payments \((\frac13, \frac13, \frac13, 1)\), remaining shifts \((0.6667, 0.3333, 0, 0)\), and cost \(\frac13 + 1 = 1.3333\) at \(\alpha = 2\), \(\sigma = 1\).

For translations the exact value is smaller: the final means differ by 2 and the variance is 4, so \(D_2 = 1.0000\). The schedule bound cannot use the noise of steps 1 to 3 against the second shift, because that shift does not exist yet when the noise is added.
A record used again late in training gets little amplification: the last use dominates, as in a single pass.

title: 35  Exercises: Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.5 The hidden-state limit

Exercise 5. The hidden-state limit. Starting from the limit in Equation 35.23, find the number of steps after which full-batch noisy GD with \(c = 0.9\) and \(s/\sigma = 1\) is within 1% of its limit. Show that the number of steps needed grows like \(1/(1 - c)\). Check: the limit is 4.3589, and \(\mu_T\) is within 1% of it from \(T = 44\). (Geometric series)







TipSolution






The ratio to the limit. Step 5 of the proof of Theorem 35.5 writes \(\mu_T\) with the geometric sums \((1 - c^T)/(1 - c)\) and \((1 - c^{2T})/(1 - c^2)\). Using \(1 - c^2 = (1 - c)(1 + c)\), that is \(\mu_T = \frac s\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1 + c}{1 - c}}\cdot\frac{1 - c^T}{\sqrt{1 - c^{2T}}}\), the limit times a correction factor. At \(c = 0.9\) the limit is \(\sqrt{19} = 4.3589\).
The approach. The correction factor is \(g(T) = \frac{1 - c^T}{\sqrt{1 - c^{2T}}} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - c^T}{1 + c^T}}\) (divide \(1 - c^{2T} = (1 - c^T)(1 + c^T)\)). For small \(c^T\), \(g \approx 1 - c^T\). So \(g \ge 0.99\) needs roughly \(c^T \le 0.01\), that is \(T \ge \ln 100/\ln(1/c) \approx 4.61/(1 - c)\), using \(\ln(1/c) \approx 1 - c\) for \(c\) near 1.
Numerically. The script finds the first \(T\) with \(\mu_T \ge 0.99\lim\mu\): 44 steps for \(c = 0.9\) and 458 for \(c = 0.99\) (limit 14.1067). Times \(1 - c\) these are 4.40 and 4.58, close to \(\ln 100 = 4.61\).

The last iterate forgets at the rate the optimizer contracts. After a few multiples of \(1/(1 - c)\) steps, more training costs no more privacy.

title: 35  Exercises: Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.6 Where the plateau starts

Exercise 6. Where the plateau starts. Step 5 of the proof of Proposition 35.2 puts the best window at \(m = d_K/s\), available once \(T \ge d_K/s\). Show that the bound Equation 35.20 nevertheless follows composition until \(T = 4d_K/s\), and evaluate the plateau and that step at \(d_K = 1\), \(s = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 0.1\) and \(\alpha = 2\). Check: plateau 4.0000, starting at \(T = 400\). (Optimizing a schedule)







TipSolution






The plateau. By step 5 of the proof of Proposition 35.2, the best window \(m = d_K/s\) costs \(h(d_K/s) = 4d_Ks\), where \(h(m) = (d_K + ms)^2/m\), so the plateau is \(\frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}\cdot 4d_Ks = \frac{2\alpha d_Ks}{\sigma^2}\), independent of \(T\). Here \(d_K/s = 100\) is an integer, so that window is allowed.
Where it beats composition. The composition term is \(\frac{\alpha Ts^2}{2\sigma^2}\). It equals the plateau when \(Ts^2 = 4d_Ks\), at \(T = 4d_K/s\). For \(d_K/s \le T < 4d_K/s\), the minimum over \(m \le T\) is still \(4d_Ks\), but composition is smaller, so the bound follows composition until \(T = 4d_K/s\).
Numbers. \(m^* = 100\), the plateau is \(2\cdot2\cdot1\cdot0.01/0.1^2 = 4.0000\), and it starts at \(T = 400\). The script gives the bound as 3.9900 at \(T = 399\) (composition), 4.0000 at \(T = 400\), and 4.0000 at \(T = 10{,}000\).

Only the last \(d_K/s\) steps are paid for: the steps before are summarized by a starting point somewhere in the domain.

text:
Exercise 1. Stopping after one step. At \(\alpha = 2\), run randomized response with \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) on one person’s bit, and run a second, identical step only if \(y_1 = 1\); after \(y_1 = 0\) the run stops. List the three transcripts with their \(P\), \(Q\), spend and \(N_T\), check that \(\mathbb E[N_T] = 1\), and compute the joint \(D_2\). Check: \(D_2 = 1.6740\), below \(B = 1.6946\). (Optional stopping, Rényi filter)







TipSolution






The steps. Randomized response with \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) reports the true bit with probability \(e^{\ln 3}/(1 + e^{\ln 3}) = 3/4\). Under \(P\) the bit is 1, under \(Q\) it is 0. Its RDP at \(\alpha = 2\) is \(\ln\big((3/4)^2/(1/4) + (1/4)^2/(3/4)\big) = \ln(9/4 + 1/12) = 0.8473\) (Equation 29.7).
The stopping time. The run takes step 2 only if \(y_1 = 1\). That decision is a function of \(y_1\), so \(T\) is a stopping time (Definition 36.3), and the spend along a path is \(2 \times 0.8473 = 1.6946\) if \(y_1 = 1\) and \(0.8473\) if \(y_1 = 0\). Every path stays within \(B = 1.6946\).
The three transcripts. Multiply the step probabilities along each path, and take \(L = \ln(P/Q)\) and \(N_T = e^{(2-1)(L - \text{spend})}\):

Optional stopping. \(\mathbb E_P[N_T] = 0.5625 \times 1.6531 + 0.1875 \times 0.1837 + 0.25 \times 0.1429 = 1.0000\). For randomized response the conditional moment of each step equals \(e^{(\alpha-1)\varepsilon_t(\alpha)}\) exactly, so \(N\) is a martingale and stopping it keeps its mean at exactly 1.
The divergence. \(D_2(P\|Q) = \ln\sum P^2/Q = 1.6740\), which is at most the budget 1.6946, as the Rényi filter (Equation 36.5) promises. It is above the one-step value 0.8473, because the costly branch carries most of the mass under \(P\).

The table is the derivation of the Rényi filter in miniature: \(\mathbb E[e^{L}] = \mathbb E[N_T e^{\text{spend}}] \le e^{B}\,\mathbb E[N_T] = e^{B}\), and the inequality is strict here only because one branch spends less than \(B\).

section: 36.2 The zCDP route to the DP filter
text:
36.2 The zCDP route to the DP filter

Exercise 2. The zCDP route to the DP filter. Starting from Theorem 36.3, which writes the filter as \(\frac12\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2 \le \rho^*\), show that it allows \(\lfloor 2\rho^*/\varepsilon_0^2\rfloor\) steps of \(\varepsilon_0\), and find the order at which its conversion to DP is attained. Check: at \(\varepsilon_g = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), \(\rho^* = 0.017469\) and 349 steps of \(0.01\). (zCDP conversion)







TipSolution






The rule. By Theorem 36.3, the filter continues exactly while \(\rho = \frac12\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2\) stays at most \(\rho^* = (\sqrt{\ell + \varepsilon_g} - \sqrt\ell)^2\), where \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\); steps 3 to 5 of its proof show that this is the same rule as Equation 36.9.
Count steps. \(k\) steps of \(\varepsilon_0\) have \(\rho = k\varepsilon_0^2/2\), so \(\rho \le \rho^*\) means \(k \le 2\rho^*/\varepsilon_0^2\), and the largest such integer is \(\lfloor 2\rho^*/\varepsilon_0^2\rfloor\).
The order of the conversion. Mironov’s conversion of the line \(\rho\alpha\) is \(\rho\alpha + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\). With \(a = \alpha - 1\) this is \(\rho + \rho a + \ell/a\), whose derivative in \(a\) vanishes at \(a = \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\). So the conversion of Equation 31.15 is attained at the order \(1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\).
Numbers. At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), \(\ell = 13.8155\), and with \(\varepsilon_g = 1\), \(\rho^* = 0.017469\) (converting it back gives 1.0000). For \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.01\), \(2\rho^*/\varepsilon_0^2\) gives 349 steps. The statistic is 0.9994 at \(k = 349\) and 1.0009 at \(k = 350\), so the 350th step is refused. The conversion is attained at the order \(1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho^*} = 29.12\).

Because the halting rule \(\rho \le \rho^*\) does not mention \(\alpha\), the same run is a Rényi filter at every order, which is what lets the conversion pick the order afterwards.

section: 36.3 The Ville boundary is crossed with probability exactly δ
text:
36.3 The Ville boundary is crossed with probability exactly δ

Exercise 3. The Ville boundary is crossed with probability exactly \(\delta\). For Gaussian steps at a fixed order, write \(L_{1:t}\) as Brownian motion with drift in variance time, show with Ville’s inequality (Lemma 36.3) that a standard Brownian motion \(W\) ever crosses the line \(a + bs\) with probability \(e^{-2ab}\), and conclude that the fixed-order Ville boundary of Theorem 36.4 is crossed with probability \(\delta\). Then show that at a single fixed time the crossing probability is at most \(\Phi(-\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)})\). Check: 0.00719 at \(\delta = 0.05\). (Ville, Brownian motion)







TipSolution






One step’s loss. A Gaussian step with shift \(\mu\) (in units of the noise) has privacy loss \(L_t = \mu y_t - \mu^2/2\) with \(y_t \sim \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) under \(P\), so \(L_t \sim \mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\), independent across steps when \(\mu\) is fixed.
Variance time. Let \(s = t\mu^2\). Then \(L_{1:t} = s/2 + W_s\), where \(W\) is a standard Brownian motion observed at the times \(\mu^2, 2\mu^2, \dots\) (sums of independent normals with variance \(\mu^2\) each).
The boundary. At order \(\alpha\), each step spends \(\alpha\mu^2/2\) (Equation 29.5), so the Ville boundary with one order is \(S_t(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1) = \alpha s/2 + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\).
Crossing. Subtracting the drift \(s/2\), \(L_{1:t}\) exceeds the boundary when \(W_s > (\alpha - 1)s/2 + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\): a line \(a + bs\) with \(a = \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) and \(b = (\alpha - 1)/2\).
A martingale for the line. The process \(Z_s = \exp(2bW_s - 2b^2s)\) is non-negative and has mean 1, because the Gaussian moment generating function gives \(\mathbb E[e^{2bW_s}] = e^{(2b)^2s/2} = e^{2b^2s}\). Its increments are independent of the past, so it is a martingale.
Ville’s bound. On the event \(W_s \ge a + bs\), the exponent of \(Z_s\) is at least \(2b(a + bs) - 2b^2s = 2ab\). So crossing the line means \(Z\) reaches \(e^{2ab}\), and Lemma 36.3 bounds the probability by \(e^{-2ab}\).
The bound is attained. A continuous path meets the line exactly, where \(Z = e^{2ab}\), and on paths that never cross, \(Z_s \to 0\), because the exponent \(2bW_s - 2b^2s\) drifts to \(-\infty\). So optional stopping at the crossing holds with equality, and the crossing probability is exactly \(e^{-2ab}\). Here \(2ab = \ln(1/\delta)\), so it is \(\delta\), for every \(\alpha\).
Discrete steps. Watching only at the discrete times can only miss crossings, so Ville’s bound \(\delta\) is attained in the limit of small steps. With \(\alpha = 2\) the script’s formula gives 0.05 at \(\delta = 0.05\) and \(10^{-5}\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and the finite horizon \(s = 1000\) changes neither at the printed precision.
One fixed time. At a fixed \(s\), \(\Pr[W_s > a + bs] = \Phi\big(-(a + bs)/\sqrt s\big)\). The exponent \((a + bs)/\sqrt s = a/\sqrt s + b\sqrt s\) is smallest at \(s = a/b\), where it equals \(2\sqrt{ab} = 2\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/2} = \sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\). So the probability at any single time is at most \(\Phi(-\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)})\): 0.00719 at \(\delta = 0.05\) and \(7.99\times10^{-7}\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).

At a fixed time, Mironov’s conversion overstates the tail by a factor of 7.0 at \(\delta = 0.05\) and 12.5 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). That slack is exactly what makes the same boundary valid at all times at once.

title: 36  Exercises: Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.4 A half-norm record

Exercise 4. A half-norm record. A record whose clipped gradient has norm \(C/2\) at every step, with \(\sigma = 10\). Using Equation 36.15, compute its spend after 100 steps at \(\alpha = 5.8\), its \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) at that order and optimized over the grid, and how many steps the individual filter with \(B = 2.900\) allows it. Check: spend 0.7250, \(\varepsilon = 3.124\) at \(\alpha = 5.8\), 400 steps. (Individual RDP)







TipSolution






Per-step spend. By Equation 36.15 with \(\|\bar g\| = C/2\): \(\alpha(C/2)^2/(2\sigma^2C^2) = \alpha/(8\sigma^2)\), a quarter of the worst case \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\). At \(\alpha = 5.8\) and \(\sigma = 10\) this is \(0.007250\).
After 100 steps. The spends add (the norms here do not even depend on the past): \(100 \times 0.007250 = 0.7250\).
\(\varepsilon\) at the fixed order. Mironov’s conversion (Equation 29.24): \(0.7250 + \ln(10^5)/4.8 = 3.124\), against the worst case 5.299 at the same order.
\(\varepsilon\) with the order optimized. The record’s curve is \(\alpha \times 100/(8\sigma^2)\), a zCDP line with \(\rho = 0.125\); the best order on the grid is 10.6 and gives 2.524. That number would be a guarantee only for a run whose filter was set at order 10.6.
Steps until the filter excludes it. The budget \(B = 2.900\) is the worst-case spend of 100 steps at \(\alpha = 5.8\). At \(0.007250\) per step, the record can take part in \(2.900/0.007250 = 400\) steps, four times as many as a record always at the clip.

A record with half-size gradients can take part in four times as many steps for the same guarantee; the spend scales with the square of the norm.

title: 36  Exercises: Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
section: 36.5 The price of choosing the order late
text:
36.5 The price of choosing the order late

Exercise 5. The price of choosing the order late. For a zCDP spend \(\rho = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), compare the fixed-time conversion over the part’s grid with the Ville odometer over that grid, over the ten orders \(\{1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 32, 64\}\), and at the single order that is optimal for \(\rho = 0.25\). Check: 7.786, 9.137, 8.605 and 9.493. (Union bound, Ville)







TipSolution






Fixed time. For the curve \(\alpha\rho\), Mironov’s conversion over the grid is \(\min_\alpha[\alpha + \ln(10^5)/(\alpha - 1)] = 7.786\), at \(\alpha = 4.4\). Over all real orders it is \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\) (Equation 31.15), also 7.786: the grid is fine enough.
Ville over the grid. Equation 36.12 replaces \(\ln(1/\delta)\) by \(\ln(|\Lambda|/\delta)\) with \(|\Lambda| = 154\), which is the conversion at \(\delta/154\). That gives 9.137; the continuous formula \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(154/\delta)}\) gives 9.136.
Ville over ten orders. With \(|\Lambda| = 10\) the union costs only \(\ln 10\) instead of \(\ln 154\), but the best order on the coarse grid is a little off the optimum. The result, 8.605, is still better than the fine grid.
One order, chosen for the wrong spend. For \(\rho = 0.25\) the best grid order is 7.8. A Ville odometer at that order alone pays no union, but at \(\rho = 1\) it gives \(7.8 + \ln(10^5)/6.8 = 9.493\), worse than both grids.
The trade-off. A single order is free at its design point and poor elsewhere; a fine grid adapts to any spend but pays \(\ln|\Lambda|\). A coarse grid, a few orders per factor of two in spend, gets most of both.

The cost of an odometer over a filter is the union bound over the orders you keep open; Rogers et al.’s lower bound says some such \(\ln\ln\)-type cost is unavoidable.

title: 37  Exercises: Choosing an accountant
text:
37.1 Where RDP’s slack comes from
Exercises for Choosing an accountant, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_choosing_an_accountant.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_choosing_an_accountant.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise gives differential privacy (DP), and is called DP-SGD. \(q\) is the Poisson sampling rate, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(T\) the number of steps, and neighbours are add/remove. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) means the RDP accountant of Amplification by subsampling; the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant is that of Numerical accounting, on the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\); the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) central limit theorem (CLT) is that of f-DP and Gaussian DP. The running example is \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).

title: 37  Exercises: Choosing an accountant
text:
Exercise 1. Where RDP’s slack comes from. For \(T = 1\), 100 and 10,000, split the excess of RDP (improved conversion) over the PLD upper bound into the conversion slack and the curve slack. Explain why the conversion slack dominates at \(T = 1\) by evaluating \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) at the best order. Check: at \(T = 1\), conversion slack 0.4656 and curve slack 0.2905; \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1) = 1.2936\) at \(\alpha = 9.9\); at \(T = 10{,}000\), 0.0000 and 0.4750. (Decomposing a bound)







TipSolution






Three numbers. The improved conversion is an upper bound on what the RDP curve certifies, the optimal conversion is exactly what it certifies, and the PLD upper bound is what the real pair certifies, up to the grid. Always \[\varepsilon_{\text{improved}} - \varepsilon^\uparrow_{\text{PLD}} = \underbrace{(\varepsilon_{\text{improved}} - \varepsilon_{\text{optimal}})}_{\text{conversion slack}} + \underbrace{(\varepsilon_{\text{optimal}} - \varepsilon^\uparrow_{\text{PLD}})}_{\text{curve slack}}, \tag{37.1}\] The conversion slack is non-negative by the first chain of Theorem 37.1. The curve slack is not covered by the theorem, which bounds it only below by \(-Th\) (without truncation). On this example it is non-negative at every \(T\), and the chapter’s script checks it.
The numbers are in Table 37.1.

Why the conversion dominates at \(T = 1\). The improved conversion at order \(\alpha\) is \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\). Its last term contains \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), which does not depend on \(T\) or on the mechanism. At the best order 9.9 it is \(\ln(10^5)/8.9 = 1.2936\), far more than the true \(\varepsilon\), which the PLD puts at 0.1995 (to four decimals). The curve term \(\varepsilon(9.9)\) is tiny for one step. To shrink the fixed cost, the conversion would need a larger order, but at orders above about 10 the subsampled curve explodes (Section 33.4). The improved conversion’s correction terms win back some of this, and the optimal conversion more, but every conversion from the curve must pay for not knowing the distribution beyond its moments.
Why it vanishes at large \(T\). At \(T = 10{,}000\) the best order is 4.1, and the curve \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is large. The optimal conversion then matches the improved one to four decimals, as the conversions chapter found for the Gaussian at every \(\mu\). What remains, 0.4750, is the curve slack: pairs other than the subsampled Gaussian have the same RDP curve and a larger \(\delta\).

For short runs, a better conversion would help; for long runs, only a better summary than the RDP curve helps, and the PLD is that summary.

title: 37  Exercises: Choosing an accountant
text:
37.2 Steps under a budget

Exercise 2. Steps under a budget. With \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and a budget of \(\varepsilon = 3\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), find the largest number of steps each accountant allows: RDP with the improved conversion, the PLD upper bound, and the CLT. Is the CLT’s answer safe? Check: 2195, 2643 and 3009 steps; at 3009 steps the PLD lower bound is 3.1823. (Monotonicity in \(T\), binary search)







TipSolution






Monotonicity in \(T\). No correct accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) decreases as \(T\) grows (Proposition 37.6, property 4). The largest admissible \(T\) is therefore well defined, and binary search over the integers finds it.
RDP. Binary search gives \(T = 2195\): the accountant reports 3.0000 there (to four decimals, and at most 3) and 3.0006 at 2196 steps.
PLD. Binary search with the pessimistic PLD, recomposed at each trial \(T\), gives \(T = 2643\): 2.9995 there and 3.0001 at 2644.
CLT. The CLT has a closed form. Find the \(\mu^*\) whose GDP profile gives \(\varepsilon = 3\) at \(\delta\), then \(q^2T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) \le \mu^{*2}\) gives \(T = \lfloor(\mu^*/q)^2/(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\rfloor = 3009\).
Is 3009 safe? No. At \(T = 3009\) the optimistic PLD, a certified lower bound, is 3.1823. The run is not \((3, 10^{-5})\)-DP.
What the accountant buys. In epochs, RDP allows 21.95 and the PLD 26.43. The tighter accountant buys 20% more training for the same certified budget.

The inverse problems of the chapter come in two flavours, fixed steps and solve for \(\sigma\), or fixed \(\sigma\) and solve for \(T\). Both are monotone, both are solved by bracketing, and in both the CLT’s answer can overshoot the budget.

title: 37  Exercises: Choosing an accountant
text:
37.3 Reporting at a smaller δ

Exercise 3. Reporting at a smaller \(\delta\). Show that a single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee implies nothing at any smaller \(\delta' < \delta\) beyond the trivial, by exhibiting a mechanism that is \((0, \delta)\)-DP but not \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon'\). Then compute the running example at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(10^{-8}\) from the PLD and the RDP curve. Check: PLD upper 6.9574 and 8.2356; RDP 7.4140 and 8.6650. (Privacy profiles)







TipSolution






The mechanism. On a dataset with one record \(x\), output \(x\) with probability \(\delta\) and the symbol \(\bot\) otherwise. On the neighbouring dataset without \(x\), always output \(\bot\). With \(P\) the first output distribution and \(Q\) the second, \(P(\{x\}) = \delta\) and \(Q(\{x\}) = 0\).
It is \((0, \delta)\)-DP. For any event \(S\), \(P(S) - Q(S) \le P(\{x\}) = \delta\), because the two distributions differ only by moving mass \(\delta\) from \(\bot\) to \(x\). In the other direction, \(Q(S) - P(S) \le \delta\) in the same way.
It is not \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP for \(\delta' < \delta\). Take \(S = \{x\}\): \(P(S) = \delta > e^{\varepsilon'} \cdot 0 + \delta'\) for every \(\varepsilon'\). Its privacy profile is \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \delta\) for every \(\varepsilon\), and \(\varepsilon(\delta') = \infty\).
Consequence. From the pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) alone, a reader cannot tell this mechanism from one with a rapidly decaying profile. A report that gives only one pair cannot be re-read at a smaller \(\delta\). That is why NIST SP 800-226 asks for the original parameters of RDP, zero-concentrated DP (zCDP) or GDP guarantees, and why the chapter recommends reporting the profile.
The running example. From the composed PLDs and the RDP curve, Table 37.2.

title: 37  Exercises: Choosing an accountant
text:
37.4 A noise schedule

Exercise 4. A noise schedule. A run uses 5,000 steps at \(\sigma = 1\) and then 5,000 at \(\sigma = 2\), with \(q = 0.01\). Compute \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) with RDP (adding the two curves) and with PLDs (convolving the two phases), and compare with adding the two phases’ \(\varepsilon\). Check: RDP 4.9544; PLD \([4.4981, 4.5981]\); the phases alone are 4.2268 and 1.5024, which add to 5.7292. (Heterogeneous composition)







TipSolution






RDP. Curves add under composition (Equation 29.11), whatever the steps are. The total curve is \(5000\,\varepsilon_{\sigma=1}(\alpha) + 5000\,\varepsilon_{\sigma=2}(\alpha)\). The improved conversion of the sum, minimized over the grid, gives 4.9544.
PLD. The privacy loss of the run is the sum of the per-step losses, so its PLD is the convolution of the two phases’ composed PLDs (Numerical accounting). Convolve direction by direction: the remove-direction PLD of phase 1 with that of phase 2, and the same for add. Then solve for \(\varepsilon\) and take the larger direction. Rounding up in both phases keeps the result an upper bound, and rounding down a lower bound. The bracket is \([4.4981, 4.5981]\), of width \(Th = 10{,}000 \times 10^{-5} = 0.1\) as before.
Adding the phases’ \(\varepsilon\). The phases alone give 4.2268 and 1.5024 (PLD upper). Their sum, 5.7292, is worse than both accountants, and it is not even a guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Basic composition of \((\varepsilon_1, \delta_1)\) and \((\varepsilon_2, \delta_2)\) gives \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2, \delta_1 + \delta_2)\), so the sum is a guarantee only at \(\delta = 2 \times 10^{-5}\).
Comparison with a constant schedule. Ten thousand steps at \(\sigma = 1\) gave 6.2377. Doubling the noise for the second half brings the bound down to 4.5981. The second phase adds only \(4.5981 - 4.2268 = 0.3713\) to the first phase’s bound, much less than its own 1.5024, because composition adds privacy losses, not \(\varepsilon\)’s.

Both RDP and the PLD handle heterogeneous steps without effort. The schedule must be fixed in advance; if the switch depended on the outputs, you would need a filter (Adaptive composition).

title: 37  Exercises: Choosing an accountant
text:
37.5 Whose number is it?

Exercise 5. Whose number is it? Four papers train the running example for 1,000 steps and report \(\varepsilon = 1.62\), 1.83, 2.10 and 2.54 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Identify the accountant behind each, and say which reports are valid DP guarantees. Check: the CLT gives 1.6177, the PLD 1.8332 (lower bound 1.8232), RDP 2.1014 (improved) and 2.5380 (Mironov). (Recomputing a reported guarantee)







TipSolution






Recompute with every accountant. At \(T = 1000\): CLT 1.6177, PLD lower 1.8232, PLD upper 1.8332, RDP improved 2.1014, RDP Mironov 2.5380, and per-step advanced composition 1258.64, which no paper would report.
Match. 1.62 is the CLT, 1.83 the PLD upper bound, 2.10 RDP with the improved conversion, 2.54 RDP with Mironov’s conversion.
Validity. The PLD lower bound 1.8232 is certified: the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least that. So 1.62 is not a valid guarantee; the run is not \((1.62, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The other three are upper bounds and valid. Note that 1.83 must be read as 1.8332 rounded down: a careful report would write 1.84.
Ranking the valid ones. All three describe the same run. The PLD’s number is the most informative: it is within 0.0100 of the truth. Mironov’s is 38% above it (the ratio 1.38 in Table 37.3), purely because of the accountant.

Two reports with different \(\varepsilon\) can describe identical training. Before comparing two private models by their \(\varepsilon\), recompute both with the same accountant.

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.1 Exact against classic calibration
Exercises for Private empirical risk minimization, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_dp_erm.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_dp_erm.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Empirical risk minimization (ERM) picks the parameters \(\theta^*\) that minimize the empirical risk \(\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\). Differential privacy (DP) is required for replace-one neighbours. \(L\) bounds the length of each record’s loss gradient, and \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) is the largest ratio of sensitivity to noise standard deviation for which the Gaussian mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
crumbs: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
text:
Exercise 1. Exact against classic calibration. Output perturbation adds Gaussian noise to the minimizer. Compare the noise the classic formula \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\) prescribes with the exact calibration of Equation 38.2 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.25\), 0.5 and 1. By what factor does the excess risk of output perturbation grow if you use the classic formula? Check: the noise ratio is 1.299 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). (Gaussian calibration)







TipSolution






Classic. \(\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/10^{-5})} = \sqrt{2 \times 11.736} = 4.8448\), so \(\sigma/\Delta_2 f = 4.8448/\varepsilon\): 19.3792, 9.6896 and 4.8448 for the three budgets.
Exact. Solve Equation 38.2 for the largest \(\mu\) with \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le 10^{-5}\) by bisection, then \(\sigma/\Delta_2 f = 1/\mu\). The script gives 13.2855, 7.0318 and 3.7306.
Ratios. \(19.3792/13.2855 = 1.459\), \(9.6896/7.0318 = 1.378\) and \(4.8448/3.7306 = 1.299\). The classic formula is looser at small \(\varepsilon\), where its \(1/\varepsilon\) scaling overshoots the exact curve.
Excess risk. By Equation 38.6 the excess risk is proportional to \(\sigma^2\), so it grows by the square of the ratio: \(1.299^2 \approx 1.69\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(1.459^2 \approx 2.13\) at \(\varepsilon = 0.25\).

The classic formula is valid, but it throws away 30% to 46% of the noise budget, and twice that in excess risk. Since the exact calibration is one bisection, there is no reason not to use it.
crumbs: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.2 Ridge regression on a ball

Exercise 2. Ridge regression on a ball. The squared loss \(\ell(\theta; (x, y)) = \frac12(\langle \theta, x\rangle - y)^2\) has no global gradient bound. Suppose \(\|x\| \le 1\), \(|y| \le 1\), and the minimizer is computed over the ball \(\|\theta\| \le R\). Find a Lipschitz constant \(L\) on the ball and the output-perturbation noise for \(R = 2\), \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(n = 1{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Why does restricting to the ball not break Theorem 6.5? Check: \(L = 3\), sensitivity 0.06, \(\sigma = 0.2238\). (Lipschitz constants on a bounded domain)







TipSolution






The gradient. \(\nabla_\theta\ell = (\langle \theta, x\rangle - y)x\). Its length is \(|\langle \theta, x\rangle - y|\,\|x\|\).
Bound it on the ball. By Cauchy–Schwarz \(|\langle \theta, x\rangle| \le \|\theta\|\|x\| \le R\), so \(|\langle \theta, x\rangle - y| \le R + 1\), and the length is at most \((R + 1) \cdot 1 = 3\) for \(R = 2\).
Sensitivity. Theorem 6.5 gives \(2L/(\lambda n) = 6/100 = 0.06\), and the exact calibration gives \(\sigma = 3.7306 \times 0.06 = 0.2238\).
Why the ball is fine. The argument of Theorem 6.5 works for the minimizer over any convex set: strong convexity still converts a bound on the gradient difference into a bound on the distance between the constrained minimizers, using the first-order optimality condition \(\langle\nabla \mathcal L(\theta^*), v - \theta^*\rangle \ge 0\) for all \(v\) in the set in place of \(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta^*) = 0\). The set must be fixed in advance, not chosen from the data.

Losses without a global gradient bound become Lipschitz on a bounded domain, and the domain’s radius enters the noise. Choosing \(R\) too large costs noise, too small biases the solution: the same trade-off as clipping.
crumbs: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.3 Objective perturbation’s budget

Exercise 3. Objective perturbation’s budget. For logistic regression (\(c = \frac14\)) with \(\lambda = 0.01\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), find the smallest \(n\) for which Equation 38.10 gives \(\varepsilon' > 0\) without extra ridge. Compute \(\varepsilon'\) at that \(n\) and at \(n - 1\), where the extra ridge is used. What is wrong with the rule, and how would you fix it? Check: \(n = 488\); \(\varepsilon' = 0.00008\) at \(n = 488\) but \(0.05000\) at \(n = 487\). (Splitting a privacy budget)







TipSolution






The condition. \(\varepsilon' > 0\) means \(2\ln(1 + c/(n\lambda)) < \varepsilon\), that is \(c/(n\lambda) < e^{\varepsilon/2} - 1\), or \(n > c/(\lambda(e^{\varepsilon/2} - 1))\).
Numbers. \(e^{0.05} - 1 = 0.051271\), so \(n > 0.25/(0.01 \times 0.051271) = 487.6\), and the smallest integer is 488.
At \(n = 488\). The Jacobian takes \(2\ln(1 + 25/488) = 0.09992\) of the budget, so the noise gets \(\varepsilon' = 0.00008\): the noise vector has mean length \(d \cdot 2/\varepsilon' = 25{,}000\,d\), and the output is useless.
At \(n = 487\). Now \(\varepsilon' \le 0\), so the rule adds ridge until the Jacobian takes exactly \(\varepsilon/2\), and the noise gets \(\varepsilon' = 0.05\), with an extra ridge of 0.0103.
The fix. The rule’s switch is in the wrong place. Add extra ridge whenever \(\varepsilon'\) would fall below \(\varepsilon/2\), not only when it would be negative. Then the noise always gets at least half the budget, and one more record never makes the output worse.

A budget split that hands the remainder to the noise can leave it almost nothing. Whenever a guarantee is a sum of two terms, check what happens at the boundary where one of them eats the budget.
crumbs: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.4 Pure against Gaussian noise in \(d\) dimensions
text:
38.4 Pure against Gaussian noise in \(d\) dimensions

Exercise 4. Pure against Gaussian noise in \(d\) dimensions. Output perturbation can use Gaussian noise for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP or noise with density \(\propto e^{-\|b\|\varepsilon/\Delta_2 f}\) for \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Using Lemma 38.1, find the dimension \(d\) above which the Gaussian has smaller mean squared length, at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Repeat at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). Check: \(d = 13\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\); \(d = 9\) at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). (Moments of the gamma distribution)







TipSolution






The two second moments. With \(s = \Delta_2 f/\varepsilon\), Lemma 38.1 gives \(\mathbb E\|b\|^2 = d(d+1)(\Delta_2 f)^2/\varepsilon^2\). The Gaussian gives \(d\sigma^2\), with \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\).
Compare. The Gaussian is smaller when \(d\sigma^2 < d(d + 1)(\Delta_2 f)^2/\varepsilon^2\), that is \(d + 1 > \varepsilon^2\sigma^2/(\Delta_2 f)^2\).
At \(\varepsilon = 1\). \(\sigma^2/(\Delta_2 f)^2 = 3.7306^2 = 13.918\), so \(d + 1 > 13.918\), \(d \ge 13\). At \(d = 12\) the pure noise has 156 against 167.0; at \(d = 13\), 182 against 180.9. At \(d = 100\) it is 10,100 against 1,391.8.
At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). \(\varepsilon^2\sigma^2/(\Delta_2 f)^2 = 9.455\), so \(d \ge 9\).

Pure DP’s noise grows like \(d^2\) in squared length, the Gaussian’s like \(d\). In more than about ten dimensions the small \(\delta\) is worth paying.
crumbs: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.5 Noisy gradient descent with weaker composition
text:
38.5 Noisy gradient descent with weaker composition

Exercise 5. Noisy gradient descent with weaker composition. For noisy gradient descent at \(n = 10{,}000\) with \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-5})\), compute the per-step noise on the mean gradient for \(T = 10\), 100 and 1,000 steps under three accountings: exact composition of Gaussians, as in Theorem 38.3; basic composition, giving each step \((\varepsilon/T, \delta/T)\); and advanced composition, \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2T\ln(1/\delta')} + T\varepsilon_0(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\) with \(\delta' = \delta/2\) and each step \(\delta/(2T)\). Check: at \(T = 100\), exact 0.00746, basic 0.07240, advanced 0.04032. (Composition theorems)







TipSolution






Exact. Each step has sensitivity \(2/n = 2 \times 10^{-4}\), and Equation 38.18 gives \(\sigma = 2 \times 10^{-4}\sqrt T/0.2681\): 0.00236, 0.00746 and 0.02359.
Basic. Each step must be \((1/T, 10^{-5}/T)\)-DP on its own, and the exact single-step calibration gives 0.00726, 0.07240 and 0.72383: 3.08, 9.70 and 30.68 times the exact noise. The ratio grows like \(\sqrt T\), because basic composition adds the \(\varepsilon\)s, while the exact composition adds their squares.
Advanced. Solve for the per-step \(\varepsilon_0\) by bisection and calibrate each step for \((\varepsilon_0, \delta/(2T))\): 0.01194, 0.04032 and 0.13534, that is 5.06, 5.40 and 5.74 times the exact noise. It has the right \(\sqrt T\) growth but a worse constant, and at \(T = 10\) it is worse than basic composition.
In excess risk. The noise floor of Equation 38.19 is proportional to \(\sigma^2\), so at \(T = 100\) advanced composition multiplies it by \(5.40^2 \approx 29\) and basic composition by \(9.70^2 \approx 94\).

The accountant is part of the algorithm. The same noisy gradient descent, accounted for with a loose theorem, needs several times the noise for the same guarantee; Privacy accounting is about closing exactly this gap.
crumbs: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.6 A sharper Jacobian bound

Exercise 6. A sharper Jacobian bound. In step 5 of the proof of Theorem 38.2, \(K = \alpha\tilde x'\tilde x'^\top - \beta\tilde x\tilde x^\top\), where the curvatures \(\alpha = \psi''(m')\) and \(\beta = \psi''(m)\) of the arriving and leaving records lie in \([0, c]\). Show that \(K\) has at most one positive and at most one negative eigenvalue, and conclude that \(\det(I + K)\) lies in \([1/(1 + a), 1 + a]\) with \(a = c/(n\lambda)\) once both directions are considered. So the Jacobian costs only \(\ln(1 + a)\), half of what Equation 38.10 charges. Check the bound on random instances. Check: over 2,000 random instances (\(d = 5\), \(n = 20\), \(\lambda = 0.05\)) the largest \(|\ln\det|\) is 0.9759 times \(\ln(1 + a)\); an extreme instance attains 1.0000. (Eigenvalue interlacing)







TipSolution






At most one positive eigenvalue. \(K \preceq \alpha\tilde x'\tilde x'^\top\), because the difference \(\beta\tilde x\tilde x^\top\) is positive semi-definite. By the Courant–Fischer characterization, the second-largest eigenvalue of \(K\) is at most that of \(\alpha\tilde x'\tilde x'^\top\), which is 0. So only the largest eigenvalue \(\kappa_1\) can be positive, and it is at most \(\alpha\|\tilde x'\|^2 \le c/(n\lambda) = a\).
At most one negative eigenvalue. The same argument applied to \(-K \preceq \beta\tilde x\tilde x^\top\) gives one negative eigenvalue \(\kappa_2 \ge -a\) at most.
The determinant. \(\det(I + K) = (1 + \kappa_1)(1 + \kappa_2)\) with \(\kappa_1 \in [0, a]\) and \(\kappa_2 \in [-a, 0]\), so it lies in \([1 - a, 1 + a]\). Exchanging \(D\) and \(D'\) bounds the reciprocal the same way, so \(\det(I + K) \ge 1/(1 + a)\), which is larger than \(1 - a\). Hence \(|\ln\det(I + K)| \le \ln(1 + a)\).
Check. The script draws 2,000 random instances with curvatures in \([0, c]\) and features of length at most 1. The largest \(|\ln\det|\) is 0.9759 times \(\ln(1 + a)\), and an instance where the other records add no curvature and the new record adds \(c\) along an axis attains it exactly, 1.0000.
What it buys. In the chapter’s one-dimensional example (\(n = 5\), \(\lambda = 0.1\)), \(\ln(1 + a) = \ln 1.5 = 0.4055\) instead of 0.8109, so the noise could get \(\varepsilon' = 1 - 0.4055 = 0.5945\) instead of 0.1891, three times as much, and the noise length would shrink threefold.

Bounds that charge each of two terms its worst case separately are safe but can be loose when the two worst cases point in opposite directions. Here the record that leaves and the record that arrives push the determinant in opposite directions, and only one can win.

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.7 How tight must an approximate minimizer be?
text:
38.7 How tight must an approximate minimizer be?

Exercise 7. How tight must an approximate minimizer be? Using Equation 38.9, find the largest gradient tolerance \(\tau\) for which an approximate minimizer’s sensitivity is within 10% of the exact \(2L/(\lambda n)\). Evaluate it for \(n = 10{,}000\), \(L = 1\). Does it depend on \(\lambda\)? Check: \(\tau = 10^{-5}\). (Strong convexity: small gradient, close to the minimizer)







TipSolution






The condition. The extra term \(2\tau/\lambda\) must be at most \(0.1 \times 2L/(\lambda n)\).
Solve. Multiply both sides by \(\lambda/2\): \(\tau \le 0.1L/n\). The \(\lambda\) cancels.
Numbers. \(\tau = 0.1/10{,}000 = 10^{-5}\).
Interpretation. The tolerance shrinks like \(1/n\): the more data, the more precisely you must solve. For Newton’s method this is cheap, a few extra steps; for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) it can be the dominant cost.

An approximate solver changes the sensitivity, not just the accuracy. Stop on a gradient check at a tolerance tied to \(L/n\), and the privacy proof survives.
crumbs: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.8 Privacy noise as gradient variance

Exercise 8. Privacy noise as gradient variance. Noisy projected gradient descent without a ridge (Equation 38.22) runs on \(n = 1{,}000\) records in \(d = 10\) dimensions, in the ball of radius \(R = 5\), with \(L = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and the step rule \(T = \lceil n^2\mu^2/(4d)\rceil\). Compute the noise \(\sigma\), the extra second moment \(d\sigma^2\) that the noise adds to each gradient, and the bound Equation 38.23. Compare it with the bound \(RL/\sqrt T\) that the same number of noiseless steps would have. Why is the ratio close to \(\sqrt2\), and does it depend on \(n\)? Check: \(T = 1{,}797\), \(d\sigma^2 = 1.0004\), bounds 0.1668 and 0.1179, ratio 1.4144. (Second moments of unbiased gradients)







TipSolution






The noise. With \(\mu = 0.2681\), the rule gives \(T = \lceil 1{,}000^2 \times 0.2681^2/40\rceil = 1{,}797\), and Equation 38.22 gives \(\sigma = (2/1{,}000)\sqrt{1{,}797}/0.2681 = 0.3163\).
The extra second moment. By step 3 of the proof of Theorem 38.4, the noise adds \(d\sigma^2 = 10 \times 0.3163^2 = 1.0004\) to the noiseless \(L^2 = 1\), so \(G^2 = 2.0004\).
The two bounds. Theorem 6.2 gives \(RG/\sqrt T = 5\sqrt{2.0004/1{,}797} = 0.1668\). Without noise, \(G = L\) and the bound is \(5/\sqrt{1{,}797} = 0.1179\).
The ratio. It is \(\sqrt{G^2/L^2} = \sqrt{2.0004} = 1.4144\). The rule chooses \(T\) so that the noise term \(4d/(n^2\mu^2)\) equals \(1/T\), which is the same as saying that \(d\sigma^2 = L^2\). So the noise doubles the second moment, and the bound grows by \(\sqrt2\), at every \(n\). The rounding up of \(T\) is why the ratio is 1.4144 rather than exactly \(\sqrt2\).

The optimizer cannot tell privacy noise from sampling noise: both only raise the second moment of its gradients. The step rule spends exactly as much second moment on privacy as the gradient itself has.

title: 38  Exercises: Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.9 How many steps without a ridge?
text:
38.9 How many steps without a ridge?

Exercise 9. How many steps without a ridge? In Equation 38.23 the noise term does not depend on \(T\), so more steps only help. Find the smallest \(T\) for which the bound is within 10% of its limit \(2RL\sqrt d/(n\mu)\), for \(d = 10\), \(R = 5\), \(L = 1\), \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-5})\) and \(n = 1{,}000\) and \(10{,}000\). How many per-record gradient evaluations do these full-batch runs take, and how does that compare with the \(n^2\) steps of one record each that Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014) use? Check: \(T = 8{,}554\) and \(855{,}374\); \(8.55 \times 10^6\) and \(8.55 \times 10^9\) evaluations, against \(10^6\) and \(10^8\). (Trading steps for accuracy)







TipSolution






The condition. Write \(a = 4d/(n^2\mu^2)\). The bound is \(RL\sqrt{1/T + a}\) and its limit is \(RL\sqrt a\). Being within 10% means \(\sqrt{1/T + a} \le 1.1\sqrt a\), that is \(1/T \le (1.1^2 - 1)a = 0.21a\), so \(T \ge 1/(0.21a)\).
Numbers. For \(n = 1{,}000\) the script gives \(T = 8{,}554\), with bound 0.1298 against the limit 0.1180. For \(n = 10{,}000\), \(a\) is a hundred times smaller, so \(T = 855{,}374\), with bound 0.0130 against 0.0118.
Cost. Each full-batch step evaluates \(n\) gradients, so the runs cost \(8.55 \times 10^6\) and \(8.55 \times 10^9\) evaluations. The number of steps grows like \(n^2\) and each costs \(n\), so the cost grows like \(n^3\).
One record per step. Bassily, Smith & Thakurta take about \(n^2\) steps that each touch one random record, \(10^6\) and \(10^8\) evaluations. Each step then uses a gradient estimated from one record, and amplification by subsampling lets each step use less noise; the guarantee is of the same order up to logarithms. At \(n = 10{,}000\) that saves a factor of about 85 in computation.

Without a ridge, accuracy costs computation rather than privacy: the steps are free in budget, and the rate is reached when the optimization error falls below the noise term. Sampling records instead of passing over all of them is what makes that affordable, and it is one of the two ideas behind DP-SGD.
