title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
text:
39.1 When does the signal beat the noise?
Exercises for the chapter on differential privacy (DP) in stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_dp_sgd.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_dp_sgd.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. To give differential privacy (DP), stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is run with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, as DP-SGD. \(C\) is the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(q\) the Poisson sampling rate, \(B = qn\) the expected batch size, \(T\) the number of steps, \(\eta\) the learning rate and \(d\) the number of parameters \(\theta\). The running example has \(n = 10{,}000\), \(d = 3{,}329\), \(q = 0.01\) and \(C = 0.5\), and its averaged clipped gradient has length about 0.026 during training. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is the accountant’s currency.

title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
text:
Exercise 1. When does the signal beat the noise? In the running example the averaged clipped gradient has length about 0.026. Using the argument of Example 39.1, compute the length of the noise on the averaged gradient and the number of steps after which accumulated signal exceeds accumulated noise, at \(\varepsilon = 8\), 4 and 1 (\(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(T = 10{,}000\)). Check: 104, 228 and 2,100 steps. (Drift against random walk)







TipSolution






The noise multipliers. From the accountant, \(\sigma = 0.917\), 1.36 and 4.13 for the three budgets (Table 39.2).
Noise length. The noise on the averaged gradient has standard deviation \(\sigma C/B\) per coordinate and length about \(\sigma C\sqrt d/B\): \(0.917 \times 0.5 \times \sqrt{3{,}329}/100 = 0.265\), then 0.392 and 1.191.
Accumulation. Over \(t\) steps a signal of roughly constant direction adds up to length \(0.026t\), and independent noise to about \(\sqrt t\) times its per-step length. They are equal when \(\sqrt t = \text{noise}/0.026\), so \(t = (\text{noise}/0.026)^2\).
Numbers. \((0.265/0.026)^2 = 104\), \((0.392/0.026)^2 = 228\) and \((1.191/0.026)^2 = 2{,}100\).

At \(\varepsilon = 1\) a run of 10,000 steps contains only about five break-even intervals; at \(\varepsilon = 8\) it contains about a hundred. This is a rough measure, since the signal’s direction changes as the model learns, but it explains why accuracy collapses below some budget instead of declining smoothly.

title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
section: 39.2 Dividing by the realized batch size
text:
39.2 Dividing by the realized batch size

Exercise 2. Dividing by the realized batch size. Under Poisson sampling the batch size \(|S|\) is random, with mean \(B = qn\). For \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(q = 0.01\), compute its relative standard deviation, the probability that the batch is empty, and (by a normal approximation) the probability that it is less than half its mean. Repeat for \(n = 1{,}000\). Why does dividing by \(|S|\) break the proof even when these probabilities are tiny? Check: relative standard deviation 0.0995 and 0.3146. (Binomial batch sizes)







TipSolution






The distribution. \(|S|\) is a sum of \(n\) independent coins with probability \(q\), so it is binomial with mean \(nq\) and variance \(nq(1 - q)\).
Relative spread. \(\sqrt{nq(1 - q)}/(nq) = \sqrt{(1 - q)/(nq)}\): \(\sqrt{0.99/100} = 0.0995\) for \(n = 10{,}000\), and \(\sqrt{0.99/10} = 0.3146\) for \(n = 1{,}000\).
Empty batch. \((1 - q)^n\): \(10^{-43.6}\) for \(n = 10{,}000\), and \(10^{-4.36}\), about 1 in 23,000, for \(n = 1{,}000\).
Less than half. The normal approximation gives \(\Phi(-\frac{B/2}{\sqrt{nq(1-q)}})\): \(2.5 \times 10^{-7}\) for \(B = 100\), and 0.056 for \(B = 10\).
Why it breaks the proof anyway. Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 39.1 needs the update to be a function of the noisy sum \(G_t\) alone. Dividing by \(|S_t|\) uses a second data-dependent quantity, which changes by one when the target record is drawn. The accountant has not paid for releasing it, and the sensitivity of \(G_t/|S_t|\) is no longer \(C\) divided by a constant. A proof does not hold “with high probability” unless it was written that way.

Small batch sizes vary a lot, and a correct implementation divides by the public \(B\); the update is then unbiased (Equation 39.6), at the price of a step length that varies a little with \(|S_t|\).

title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
section: 39.3 Adam does not see the clipping norm
text:
39.3 Adam does not see the clipping norm

Exercise 3. Adam does not see the clipping norm. Suppose every per-example gradient is clipped, so each noisy sum is \(C\) times a quantity that does not depend on \(C\) (Proposition 39.2). Show that Adam’s update is then independent of \(C\) up to its small constant \(c_{\text{Adam}}\) in the denominator, so with Adam the clipping norm does not even need to be matched by the learning rate. Check numerically with 20 random gradients, \(C = 0.01\) and \(C = 10\). Check: the updates agree to a relative difference of \(7.3 \times 10^{-5}\). (Scale invariance of adaptive optimizers)







TipSolution






Adam’s update. Adam keeps running averages \(m_t\) of the gradients and \(v_t\) of their squares, coordinate by coordinate, corrects them for their start at zero, and steps by \(-\eta\hat m_t/(\sqrt{\hat v_t} + c_{\text{Adam}})\).
Scale the gradients by \(C\). Every gradient is multiplied by \(C\), so \(m_t\) is multiplied by \(C\) and \(v_t\) by \(C^2\). The bias corrections do not depend on the gradients.
The ratio. \(\hat m_t/\sqrt{\hat v_t}\) is unchanged, since \(C/\sqrt{C^2} = 1\). Only \(c_{\text{Adam}}\) breaks the invariance, and only when \(\sqrt{\hat v_t}\) is comparable to it.
Check. With 100 coordinates, 20 standard normal gradients scaled by 0.01 and by 10, and \(c_{\text{Adam}} = 10^{-8}\), the summed updates differ by at most \(7.3 \times 10^{-5}\) relative to their size. At \(C = 0.01\) the gradients have entries of about 0.01, and \(10^{-8}\) is a relative perturbation of about \(10^{-6}\) per step, which accumulates over the 20 steps.

With Adam, DP-SGD’s clipping norm only decides which gradients are clipped, not the step length. This is one reason DP training with Adam is less sensitive to \(C\). Privacy is unaffected: Adam is post-processing of the noisy sums.

title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
text:
39.4 Where ghost clipping stops paying

Exercise 4. Where ghost clipping stops paying. For a dense layer from \(d_{\text{in}}\) to \(d_{\text{out}}\) applied to sequences of length \(N\), the number of tokens, ghost norms store \(2BN^2\) numbers and explicit per-example gradients \(Bd_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\). Find the sequence length above which explicit gradients are cheaper, for \(768 \to 768\), \(768 \to 3{,}072\) and \(4{,}096 \to 4{,}096\). Check: 543, 1,086 and 2,896 tokens. (Comparing costs)







TipSolution






The condition. Explicit gradients are cheaper when \(Bd_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}} < 2BN^2\), that is \(N > \sqrt{d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}/2}\). The batch size cancels.
Numbers. \(\sqrt{768^2/2} = 768/\sqrt2 = 543\); \(\sqrt{768 \times 3{,}072/2} = 1{,}086\); \(4{,}096/\sqrt2 = 2{,}896\).
Reading it. Wider layers favour ghost norms up to longer sequences. In a transformer, the projections inside the feed-forward block, \(768 \to 3{,}072\), stay ghost-friendly up to twice the sequence length of the attention projections, \(768 \to 768\).

The choice is per layer and per sequence length; implementations that make it automatically, such as the mixed ghost clipping of Bu, Mao & Xu (2022), use exactly this comparison.

title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
section: 39.5 The small-q law for the noise multiplier
text:
39.5 The small-q law for the noise multiplier

Exercise 5. The small-q law for the noise multiplier. Approximate the composed RDP curve of DP-SGD by a line, \(\rho\alpha\), and convert it with \(\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\) (the zero-concentrated DP conversion of Concentrated differential privacy). Find \(\rho\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Then compute \(\sigma\) for \(q = 0.01\), \(T = 10{,}000\) in two ways, from \(Tq^2/(2\sigma^2) = \rho\) and from \(Tq^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)/2 = \rho\), and compare with the accountant. Repeat for \(q = 0.001\), \(T = 100{,}000\). Check: \(\rho = 0.2977\); \(\sigma = 1.296\) and 1.463 against the accountant’s 1.36; at \(q = 0.001\), 0.410 and 0.718 against 0.704. (Approximating an accountant)







TipSolution






Solve for \(\rho\). With \(s = \sqrt\rho\) and \(c = \ln(10^5) = 11.513\), \(s^2 + 2s\sqrt c - 4 = 0\), so \(s = -\sqrt c + \sqrt{c + 4} = 0.5456\) and \(\rho = 0.2977\).
Quadratic law. \(\sigma^2 = Tq^2/(2\rho) = 10{,}000 \times 10^{-4}/0.5954 = 1.680\), so \(\sigma = 1.296\).
With the exact factor. \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 = 2\rho/(Tq^2) = 0.5954\), so \(1/\sigma^2 = \ln 1.5954 = 0.4671\) and \(\sigma = 1.463\).
Compare at \(q = 0.01\). The accountant’s 1.36 lies between the two. The quadratic law ignores the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) = 1.33\) and needs too little noise; the second estimate includes it but uses a looser conversion than the accountant’s, and needs too much.
At \(q = 0.001\). The required \(\sigma\) is near 0.7, where the factor is about 3: the quadratic law gives 0.410, far too small, while the second estimate, 0.718, is within 2% of the accountant’s 0.704.

The quadratic law is good for orientation at large \(\sigma\) and wrong by almost a factor of two at small \(\sigma\). Use it to see trends, and the accountant for numbers.

title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
section: 39.6 How ε grows with the number of steps
text:
39.6 How ε grows with the number of steps

Exercise 6. How \(\varepsilon\) grows with the number of steps. With \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), compute \(\varepsilon\) after 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 steps, and the number of steps at which \(\varepsilon\) first reaches 1, 2 and 4. Explain the shape. Check: 1.21, 2.10, 6.71 and 27.23; 5, 882 and 3,859 steps. (Composition in RDP)







TipSolution






The values. The accountant gives \(\varepsilon = 1.21\), 2.10, 6.71 and 27.23.
The thresholds. Bisection over \(T\) gives 5 steps for \(\varepsilon = 1\), 882 for 2 and 3,859 for 4.
Why the first steps cost so much. The conversion of Equation 39.5 adds \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) and related terms at any order, about 1 for the orders that are best for short runs. Even a few steps report \(\varepsilon \approx 1\), because the conversion, not the composition, dominates. The first step alone has \(\varepsilon = 0.96\) by this accountant.
The middle. From 1,000 to 10,000 steps, \(\varepsilon\) grows by a factor of 3.2, close to \(\sqrt{10}\), as in the quadratic regime: the composed RDP is \(T\) times a curve linear in \(\alpha\), and the conversion of a linear curve grows like the square root of its slope for small slopes.
The end. From 10,000 to 100,000 steps the factor is 4.1, more than \(\sqrt{10}\): the best order falls toward 1, where the curve is no longer linear and the conversion grows faster.

Privacy cost is not proportional to training time. It is front-loaded by the conversion, grows like \(\sqrt T\) over the useful range, and faster for very long runs.

title: 39  Exercises: DP-SGD
text:
39.7 What microbatches cost

Exercise 7. What microbatches cost. Microbatched DP-SGD (Equation 39.16) clips the mean gradient of groups of \(m\) records fixed in advance, and adds noise \(2\sigma C\) to keep the accountant’s \(\varepsilon\). For the running example (\(q = 0.01\), \(B = 100\), \(C = 0.5\), \(\sigma = 1\), 10,000 steps, \(\varepsilon = 6.71\)), find by what factor microbatches of \(m = 2\) and \(m = 4\) multiply the noise on the averaged update. Per-example DP-SGD with that much more noise would have what \(\varepsilon\)? Explain the factor 2 in the sensitivity with a two-record example. Check: factors 4 and 8; per-example DP-SGD with \(\sigma = 4\) and 8 has \(\varepsilon = 1.035\) and 0.481. (Sensitivity of clipped means)







TipSolution






The factor. By Proposition 39.5 the noise per coordinate is \(2m\) times that of per-example clipping, which is 4 for \(m = 2\) and 8 for \(m = 4\).
The same noise, spent per example. Per-example DP-SGD with noise multiplier 4 or 8 has exactly as much noise on its averaged update as these microbatched runs. The accountant gives it \(\varepsilon = 1.035\) and 0.481. So microbatches of 4 buy the accuracy of a run at \(\varepsilon \approx 0.5\) while paying \(\varepsilon = 6.71\).
The factor 2. Take a microbatch with one other record whose gradient is \(Cu\) for a unit vector \(u\), and add a record whose gradient is \(-3Cu\). The mean changes from \(Cu\) to \(-Cu\), both of length \(C\) after clipping, so the clipped mean moves by \(2C\). Under per-example clipping the added record contributes its own clipped term, \(-Cu\), and the sum moves by only \(C\).

Microbatches make clipping cheaper by making it coarser, and the privacy accounting charges for that twice: fewer clipped terms carry the signal, and each moves by up to \(2C\). Vectorized per-example gradients give the speed without the charge.

title: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.1 Composition is nearly tight at large orders
Exercises for Hyperparameter tuning and private selection, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_hyperparameter_tuning.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_hyperparameter_tuning.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A run \(Q\) is a private training algorithm, satisfying differential privacy (DP), that outputs a model and a score; the best-of-\(K\) mechanism \(M\) runs it \(K\) times and releases the best output, and \(f(x) = \mathbb E[x^K]\) is the generating function of \(K\). Guarantees are Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curves \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), with \(D_\alpha\) the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\), which Papernot & Steinke write \(\lambda\). A geometric number of runs stops after each run with a probability \(\omega\), and a Poisson number of runs is described by its mean \(\mathbb E[K]\). Randomized response with parameter \(\varepsilon\) is the run with two outcomes, “good” and “bad”, where a run is bad with probability \(s = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) on \(D\) and \(1 - s\) on its neighbour \(D'\). The running example trains with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and noise, DP-SGD, at a sampling rate \(q\) of 0.01.
crumbs: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
Exercise 1. Composition is nearly tight at large orders. For randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and the best of \(k = 5\) runs, compute the exact Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha(M(D)\|M(D'))\) at orders 2, 10 and 100, and compare it with the lower bound \(k\varepsilon - k\ln(1 + e^{-\varepsilon})/(\alpha - 1)\) of Proposition 40.1 and with composition, \(k\) times one run’s divergence. Check: at order 2 the three numbers are 0.6763, 0.1296 and 1.1367; at order 10, 2.2366, 2.2366 and 2.2367. (Rényi divergence of discrete distributions)







TipSolution






The two distributions. The best of 5 is bad only if all five runs are bad. On \(D\) that has probability \(s^5\) with \(s = e^{0.5}/(1 + e^{0.5}) = 0.6225\), on \(D'\) probability \((1 - s)^5\); the good outcome takes the rest.
The divergence. \(D_\alpha = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big[(s^5)^\alpha((1 - s)^5)^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - s^5)^\alpha(1 - (1 - s)^5)^{1 - \alpha}\big]\). At order 2 this is 0.6763, at order 10 it is 2.2366 and at order 100 it is 2.4761.
The lower bound. Proposition 40.1 with \(k = 5\) gives \(5 \times 0.5 - 5\ln(1 + e^{-0.5})/(\alpha - 1)\), which is 0.1296 at order 2, 2.2366 at order 10 and 2.4761 at order 100.
Composition. Five times one run’s divergence (Equation 40.8): 1.1367 at order 2, 2.2367 at order 10 and 2.4761 at order 100.
Reading it. At low orders the good outcome contributes most of the sum, so the lower bound is loose and composition overstates the exact value by 68%. At high orders the bad outcome, with its likelihood ratio \(e^{5\varepsilon}\), dominates the sum, and all three agree.

The best of a fixed number of runs is as expensive as all the runs exactly where conversions to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at small \(\delta\) look: at the large orders that weight rare events.

title: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.2 Geometric stopping on randomized response

Exercise 2. Geometric stopping on randomized response. Run randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) a geometric number of times, stopping after each run with probability \(\omega\), and release the best outcome. Using Lemma 40.1, show that the log ratio of the probabilities of “bad” is \(\varepsilon + \ln\frac{\omega + (1 - \omega)s}{\omega + (1 - \omega)(1 - s)}\), find its limits as \(\omega \to 1\) and \(\omega \to 0\), and evaluate it for \(\omega = 0.5\), 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001. Check: 0.6636, 0.9063, 0.9897 and 0.9990, approaching \(2\varepsilon = 1\). (Generating functions)







TipSolution






The probability of “bad”. The best is bad only if every run is bad, so by Equation 40.2 \(\Pr[M = \text{bad}] = f(\Pr[\text{run is bad}])\) with the geometric generating function \(f(x) = \omega x/(1 - (1 - \omega)x)\).
The ratio. On \(D\) the argument is \(s\), on \(D'\) it is \(1 - s\): \[\frac{f(s)}{f(1 - s)} = \frac{s}{1 - s}\cdot\frac{1 - (1 - \omega)(1 - s)}{1 - (1 - \omega)s} = e^\varepsilon\cdot\frac{\omega + (1 - \omega)s}{\omega + (1 - \omega)(1 - s)}, \tag{40.1}\] using \(s/(1 - s) = e^\varepsilon\) and \(1 - (1 - \omega)x = \omega + (1 - \omega)(1 - x)\).
Limits. As \(\omega \to 1\) the second factor tends to 1, and the log ratio to \(\varepsilon\): one run. As \(\omega \to 0\) it tends to \(s/(1 - s) = e^\varepsilon\), and the log ratio to \(2\varepsilon\).
Numbers. With \(\varepsilon = 0.5\): 0.6636, 0.9063, 0.9897 and 0.9990. The good outcome has a smaller log ratio, so these are the exact \(\varepsilon\) of the release, as the script confirms.

Two outcomes give only \(2\varepsilon\), as the chapter said: the good outcome has nothing better than it, so one of the three factors of Equation 40.9 cannot move. The third factor of Liu and Talwar’s \(3\varepsilon\) needs an outcome with something above and something below it.

title: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.3 The expected quantile of the best run
text:
40.3 The expected quantile of the best run

Exercise 3. The expected quantile of the best run. If one run’s score has a continuous distribution, its quantile \(U\) (the fraction of runs it beats) is uniform on \([0, 1]\), and the best of \(K\) runs has quantile \(\max(U_1, \dots, U_K)\). Show that its expectation is \(\mathbb E[K/(K + 1)] = 1 - \int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm dx\), and evaluate it for four distributions with mean 8: fixed \(K = 8\), Poisson, geometric and logarithmic. Check: 0.8889, 0.8750, 0.8034 and 0.7360. (Order statistics and generating functions)







TipSolution






Fixed \(k\). The maximum of \(k\) uniforms is at most \(x\) with probability \(x^k\), so its mean is \(\int_0^1(1 - x^k)\,\mathrm dx = 1 - \frac{1}{k + 1} = \frac{k}{k + 1}\).
Random \(K\). Average over \(K\): \(\mathbb E[K/(K + 1)] = 1 - \mathbb E\int_0^1x^K\,\mathrm dx = 1 - \int_0^1\mathbb E[x^K]\,\mathrm dx = 1 - \int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm dx\), exchanging the expectation and the integral because the integrand is non-negative.
Fixed 8. \(8/9 = 0.8889\).
Poisson. \(\int_0^1e^{\mathbb E[K](x - 1)}\,\mathrm dx = (1 - e^{-\mathbb E[K]})/\mathbb E[K]\), so the expected quantile is \(1 - (1 - e^{-8})/8 = 0.8750\), almost that of a fixed 8.
Geometric and logarithmic. Numerical integration of their generating functions gives 0.8034 (geometric, \(\omega = 1/8\)) and 0.7360 (logarithmic, \(\omega = 0.0363\)).

Papernot and Steinke use this measure of utility. Poisson random search is nearly as good as running a fixed 8, while the skewed distributions, which the chapter showed are cheaper in privacy, lose a lot: the logarithmic distribution’s best run is, on average, at the 74th percentile instead of the 89th.

title: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.4 The Poisson theorem for a pure-DP run
text:
40.4 The Poisson theorem for a pure-DP run

Exercise 4. The Poisson theorem for a pure-DP run. An \(\varepsilon\)-DP run is \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP with \(\hat\varepsilon = \varepsilon\) and \(\hat\delta = 0\). Find the largest order \(\alpha^*\) at which Equation 40.17 applies with \(\hat\delta = 0\), and show that the bound there is \(\varepsilon(\alpha^*) + (e^\varepsilon - 1)\ln\mathbb E[K]\). Evaluate it for randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\mathbb E[K] = 100\), and compare it with the exact divergence and with composition of 100 runs at the same order. Check: \(\alpha^* = 10.5083\); bound 0.5299, exact 0.0729, composition 4.5556. (Applying a theorem’s side condition)







TipSolution






The side condition. Equation 40.17 needs \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\). With \(\hat\varepsilon = \varepsilon\) this is \(\alpha - 1 \le \frac{1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\), so \(\alpha^* = 1 + \frac{1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\); for \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), \(\alpha^* = 10.5083\).
The bound. With \(\hat\delta = 0\), \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha^*) \le \varepsilon(\alpha^*) + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\alpha^* - 1} = \varepsilon(\alpha^*) + (e^\varepsilon - 1)\ln\mathbb E[K]\).
Numbers. Randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) has \(\varepsilon(10.5083) = 0.0456\), and \((e^{0.1} - 1)\ln 100 = 0.1052 \times 4.6052 = 0.4843\), so the bound is 0.5299.
Compare. The exact divergence of the best of a Poisson number of runs, from Equation 40.2, is 0.0729 at this order; composition of 100 runs gives \(100 \times 0.0456 = 4.5556\). The bound is about nine times below composition and seven times above the exact value.

For very private runs the Poisson bound is excellent, because the condition \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + 1/(\alpha - 1)\) allows large orders. For a DP-SGD run with \(\varepsilon\) of several units, the same condition forces either small orders or a \(\hat\delta\) at a small \(\hat\varepsilon\), which is why the Poisson bound grows almost linearly in Table 40.4.

title: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.5 Calibrating the noise of a search
text:
40.5 Calibrating the noise of a search

Exercise 5. Calibrating the noise of a search. You want to tune the running example’s DP-SGD runs of 10,000 steps with \(q = 0.01\) over about 10 configurations, and the whole search must satisfy \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the budget of one run at \(\sigma = 1\). Find the noise multiplier each run needs under composition of 10 runs, and with a Poisson, geometric or logarithmic number of runs with mean 10. Check: 2.45, 1.65, 1.47 and 1.31. (Inverting an accountant)







TipSolution






The total as a function of \(\sigma\). For each \(\sigma\) the accountant gives one run’s RDP curve, \(10{,}000\,\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\). Composition multiplies it by 10 (Equation 40.8); the random-\(K\) bounds transform it by Equation 40.17 or Equation 40.21, with the best second order \(\hat\alpha\); Equation 30.8 converts the result.
Monotonicity. More noise lowers the curve at every order, and each of the transformations is increasing in the curve, so the total \(\varepsilon\) falls as \(\sigma\) grows. Bisection over \(\sigma\) (to three significant digits, rounding up) finds the smallest \(\sigma\) within budget.
Numbers. Composition needs \(\sigma = 2.45\) (as in Table 40.1); Poisson 1.65; geometric 1.47; logarithmic 1.31.
Reading it. With the logarithmic distribution each run is only 31% noisier than the untuned run, against 145% more noise for composition. Whether that buys accuracy depends on how often the skewed distribution stops early (Exercise 3).

Search and noise are one budget. Fix the search procedure first, then solve for the noise multiplier that keeps the whole procedure within the target.

title: 40  Exercises: Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.6 How large a validation set?

Exercise 6. How large a validation set? You select among the fixed candidates in \(\mathcal R\), the candidate set, with the exponential mechanism at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), scoring each candidate by its number \(u\) of correct predictions on \(m\) private validation records. Using the tail bound \(\Pr[\text{gap} \ge \frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln|\mathcal R| + t)] \le e^{-t}\) of Selection (Theorem 22.2), find the smallest \(m\) that keeps the accuracy gap below 0.5 percentage points with probability at least 0.95, for \(|\mathcal R| = 8\) and \(|\mathcal R| = 1{,}000\). Check: 4,061 and 7,923 records. (Utility of the exponential mechanism)







TipSolution






From counts to accuracy. With \(\Delta u = 1\) the gap in correct predictions exceeds \(\frac{2}{\varepsilon}(\ln|\mathcal R| + t)\) with probability at most \(e^{-t}\). Dividing by \(m\), the accuracy gap exceeds \(\frac{2(\ln|\mathcal R| + t)}{\varepsilon m}\) with probability at most \(e^{-t}\).
Choose \(t\). A failure probability of 0.05 means \(t = \ln 20 = 2.9957\).
Solve for \(m\). \(\frac{2(\ln|\mathcal R| + \ln 20)}{\varepsilon m} \le 0.005\) gives \(m \ge \frac{2(\ln|\mathcal R| + \ln 20)}{0.5 \times 0.005}\). For \(|\mathcal R| = 8\): \(2 \times (2.0794 + 2.9957)/0.0025 = 4{,}060.1\), so 4,061. For \(|\mathcal R| = 1{,}000\): \(2 \times (6.9078 + 2.9957)/0.0025 = 7{,}922.8\), so 7,923.
Reading it. A 125-fold increase in candidates needs less than twice the validation data, because the cost is logarithmic in \(|\mathcal R|\).

Private selection among fixed candidates is cheap in data. The chapter’s running example has a validation set of 5,000 records, enough for eight candidates at this precision; what tuning costs is the training of the candidates, not the choice among them.

title: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.1 When does the tree beat independent noise?
Exercises for the chapter on differential privacy (DP) with follow the regularized leader (FTRL) and matrix factorization, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_matrix_mechanisms.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_matrix_mechanisms.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. To train with differential privacy (DP) without sampling, a run releases the prefix sums \(S_t = x_1 + \dots + x_t\) of the clipped gradient sums, the workload \(Ax\) with \(A\) the \(T \times T\) lower-triangular matrix of ones. A matrix mechanism factors \(A = LR\) and releases \(L(Rx + z)\); its sensitivity \(\Delta_2 R\) is the largest column length of the encoder \(R\) for one participation, and its error per unit of privacy at step \(t\) is \(e_t = \Delta_2 R\|\ell_t\|\), with \(\ell_t\) the \(t\)-th row of the decoder \(L\) (Equation 41.7). Column \(\tau\) of \(R\) is \(r_\tau\), and the square-root factorization has coefficients \(c_k = \binom{2k}k4^{-k}\) (Theorem 41.3). The follow the regularized leader (FTRL) algorithm run on prefix sums released by a binary tree is DP-FTRL. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping, Gaussian noise and Poisson sampling is DP-SGD, and its accountant works with Rényi differential privacy (RDP).
crumbs: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization

title: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
Exercise 1. When does the tree beat independent noise? Compute the root-mean-square error per unit of privacy, \(\big(\frac1T\sum_te_t^2\big)^{1/2}\), of the binary tree and of independent noise on each step, for \(T = 8\) by hand. Then find the smallest \(T\) for which the tree is better. Check: 2.550 against 2.121 at \(T = 8\); the tree first wins at \(T = 28\). (Comparing factorizations by their error)







TipSolution






Independent noise. \(R = I\), so \(\Delta_2 R = 1\), and row \(t\) of \(L = A\) has \(t\) ones, so \(e_t = \sqrt t\). The mean of \(e_t^2\) over \(t = 1, \dots, 8\) is \((1 + 2 + \dots + 8)/8 = 36/8 = 4.5\), and the root-mean-square error is \(\sqrt{4.5} = 2.121\).
The tree. With \(T = 8\) there are \(\lceil\log_28\rceil + 1 = 4\) levels, so each step is in 4 nodes and \(\Delta_2 R = 2\) (Equation 41.12). Prefix \(t\) uses one node per 1 in its binary expansion: the popcounts of \(1, \dots, 8\) are \(1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1\), with mean \(13/8\). So \(e_t^2 = 4\operatorname{popcount}(t)\) has mean \(6.5\), and the root-mean-square error is \(\sqrt{6.5} = 2.550\).
Why the tree loses. Every step pays for being in 4 nodes, a factor of 2 in noise, while the prefix sums are too short for the saving in the number of noise terms to make up for it.
The crossover. Computing both errors for each \(T\), the tree is first better at \(T = 28\): 3.789 against 3.808. From there on independent noise grows like \(\sqrt{T/2}\) and the tree like \(\log_2T\), and the gap widens quickly, to 70.71 against 9.84 at \(T = 10{,}000\) (Table 41.2).

The tree is a long-run device. For a few dozen steps, plain independent noise is as good; the square-root factorization beats both at every length.

title: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.2 The square root at T = 4

Exercise 2. The square root at T = 4. Write down the \(4 \times 4\) square-root encoder \(R\) of Equation 41.13, check that \(R^2 = A\), and compute \(\Delta_2 R\) and the error of the last prefix sum per unit of privacy. Then write the noise added to step 4’s gradient, \((R^{-1}z)_4\), in terms of \(z_1, \dots, z_4\), and compute its standard deviation relative to the noise scale. Check: \(\sum_{k<4}c_k^2 = 1.4883\), \(\Delta_2 R = 1.2200\); the step-4 noise has standard deviation 1.1267 times the noise scale. (Power series and Toeplitz matrices)







TipSolution






The encoder, \(R^2 = A\), sensitivity and last error. These are Example 41.4: \(R\) is the lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix with first column \((1, \frac12, \frac38, \frac5{16})\), its square is \(A\) by Lemma 41.1, and its first column has squared length \(\frac{381}{256} = 1.4883\), so \(\Delta_2 R = 1.2200\). The last row of \(L = R\) holds the same four numbers in reverse order, so \(e_4 = 1.2200^2 = 1.4883\), against \(\sqrt4 = 2\) for independent noise.
The step noise. By Theorem 41.3, \(R^{-1}\) is the Toeplitz matrix of \((1 - u)^{1/2}\), with coefficients \(1, -\frac12, -\frac18, -\frac1{16}\). So \((R^{-1}z)_4 = z_4 - \frac12z_3 - \frac18z_2 - \frac1{16}z_1\).
Its spread. The \(z\)’s are independent, so by Equation 41.3 the variance is the noise scale squared times \(1 + \frac14 + \frac1{64} + \frac1{256} = \frac{325}{256} = 1.2695\), a standard deviation of 1.1267 times the noise scale.

Each step’s noise is only 13% larger than independent noise of the same scale, yet the prefix sums are much more accurate, because the step noises are negatively correlated and partly cancel when summed.

title: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 41.3 The optimal factorization for two steps
text:
41.3 The optimal factorization for two steps

Exercise 3. The optimal factorization for two steps. For \(T = 2\), every encoder with columns of length 1 has \(X = R^\top R = \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho\\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\) for some \(\rho \in (-1, 1)\), and the best decoder gives \(\|L\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1})\). Find the \(\rho\) that minimizes it, and compare the minimum with independent noise, the square root and the lower bound Equation 41.9 (in squared form, \((\Delta_2 R)^2\|L\|_F^2 \ge \|A\|_*^2/T\)). Check: \(\rho = 0.3820\), minimum \(2.6180 = (3 + \sqrt5)/2\); independent noise 3, square root 2.8125, bound 2.5. (Optimizing a factorization)







TipSolution






The objective. \(A^\top A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(X^{-1} = \frac1{1 - \rho^2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & -\rho\\ -\rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\), so \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1}) = \frac{2 - \rho - \rho + 1}{1 - \rho^2} = \frac{3 - 2\rho}{1 - \rho^2}\).
Minimize. The derivative vanishes when \(-2(1 - \rho^2) + 2\rho(3 - 2\rho) = 0\), that is \(\rho^2 - 3\rho + 1 = 0\), whose root in \((-1, 1)\) is \(\rho = (3 - \sqrt5)/2 = 0.3820\).
The minimum. Substituting, \(\frac{3 - 2\rho}{1 - \rho^2} = 2.6180 = (3 + \sqrt5)/2\). The fixed-point iteration of Theorem 41.4 finds the same \(X_{12} = 0.3820\) and \(\|L\|_F^2 = 2.6180\).
Independent noise. \(\rho = 0\) gives \(3 = \|A\|_F^2\).
The square root. \(R = L = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ \frac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}\): \((\Delta_2 R)^2 = 1 + \frac14 = 1.25\) and \(\|L\|_F^2 = 2.25\), product 2.8125. Its columns have unequal lengths, 1.25 and 1 squared, which wastes privacy on the short one.
The bound. The singular values of \(A\) are \(1.6180\) and \(0.6180\) (the golden ratio and its reciprocal), so \(\|A\|_* = \sqrt5\) and \(\|A\|_*^2/T = 2.5\).

So \(2.5 \le 2.6180 \le 2.8125 \le 3\): even at two steps the optimum is close to the bound, and the square root sits between it and independent noise. The optimal encoder’s columns are positively correlated, \(\rho > 0\): noise put into the first step’s quantity is partly reused for the second prefix sum.
crumbs: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization

title: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 41.4 How close is the square root to the lower bound?
text:
41.4 How close is the square root to the lower bound?

Exercise 4. How close is the square root to the lower bound? Compute the trace-norm lower bound Equation 41.9 and the square root’s root-mean-square error per unit of privacy for \(T = 100\), 1,000 and 10,000. By how much does each grow per tenfold increase of \(T\)? Check: bound 2.178, 2.902, 3.634; square root 2.371, 3.102, 3.836; ratio 1.089, 1.069, 1.056. (Lower bounds from singular values)







TipSolution






The bound. By Theorem 41.2, the singular values of \(A\) are \(1/(2\sin\frac{(2k-1)\pi}{4T + 2})\); summing them and dividing by \(T\) gives 2.178, 2.902 and 3.634.
The square root. Its error per unit of privacy at step \(t\) is \(\Delta_2 R\|\ell_t\| = \big(\sum_{k<T}c_k^2\big)^{1/2}\big(\sum_{k<t}c_k^2\big)^{1/2}\); the root mean square over \(t\) is 2.371, 3.102 and 3.836.
The ratios. 1.089, 1.069 and 1.056: the square root’s excess over the bound shrinks, in relative terms, as \(T\) grows.
Growth per decade. The bound grows by 0.724 and 0.732 per decade, the square root by 0.731 and 0.734. Both approach \(\ln(10)/\pi = 0.733\) per decade, the growth of \(\frac1\pi\ln T\): for small \(k\), \(\sin\frac{(2k-1)\pi}{4T+2} \approx \frac{(2k-1)\pi}{4T}\), so the \(k\)-th singular value is \(\nu_k \approx \frac{2T}{\pi(2k-1)}\), and the sum of \(\frac{2}{\pi(2k - 1)}\) over \(k\) up to about \(T\) grows like \(\frac1\pi\ln T\).

No factorization can make the error stop growing: the lower bound itself grows like \(\ln(T)/\pi\), and the square root matches that rate with a constant overhead of about 0.2.
crumbs: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization

title: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 41.5 Two participations under the square root
text:
41.5 Two participations under the square root

Exercise 5. Two participations under the square root. With \(T = 200\) and a record in steps 1 and 101 (separation 100), use Equation 41.21 to compute the square-root encoder’s sensitivity from the two columns’ lengths and their inner product. Compare with the banded encoder that keeps the first 100 coefficients. Check: \(\|r_1\|^2 = 2.7524\), \(\|r_{101}\|^2 = 2.5314\), cross term 1.1211, sensitivity 2.5308; banded 2.2500. (Sensitivity under several participations)







TipSolution






The two columns. Column 1 of the \(200 \times 200\) square-root encoder holds \(c_0, \dots, c_{199}\), with squared length 2.7524. Column 101 holds \(c_0, \dots, c_{99}\) starting in row 101, with squared length 2.5314.
Their inner product. In rows 101 to 200 the first column holds \(c_{100}, \dots, c_{199}\) and the second \(c_0, \dots, c_{99}\), so twice the inner product is \(2\sum_{k<100}c_kc_{k+100} = 1.1211\).
Sensitivity. The entries are nonnegative, so the worst case aligns the two gradients, and \((\Delta_2 R)^2 = 2.7524 + 2.5314 + 1.1211 = 6.4048\), a sensitivity of 2.5308. Starting the record at step 1 is the worst offset; the script’s maximum over offsets agrees.
Banded. Cutting the encoder to its first 100 diagonals leaves column 1 with \(c_0, \dots, c_{99}\) in rows 1 to 100 and column 101 with the same in rows 101 to 200: no overlap, no cross term, so \((\Delta_2 R)^2 = 2 \times 2.5314\) and the sensitivity is \(2.2500 = \sqrt2 \times 1.591\).
Reading it. The cross term adds 21% to the squared sensitivity of the full square root (1.1211 out of 5.2838). With more participations the cross terms multiply: at 20 epochs the full square root’s sensitivity is 17.191 against the banded 7.115 (Table 41.3).

Correlated noise makes a record’s repeated contributions pile up in the same noisy quantities. Banding with a band no wider than the separation keeps them apart, so participations compose as in independent noise.
crumbs: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization

title: 41  Exercises: DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 41.6 How much amplification would DP-SGD need?
text:
41.6 How much amplification would DP-SGD need?

Exercise 6. How much amplification would DP-SGD need? For one epoch of the running example (\(T = 100\), batch 100) at \(\varepsilon = 2\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the chapter reports the standard deviation of the noise in the final prefix sum: 8.27 for DP-SGD with Poisson sampling, 19.94 for fixed-order independent noise and 5.05 for the square root, in units of \(C\). Derive the first two from the noise multipliers. Then find the noise multiplier DP-SGD would need to match the square root’s final noise, and the \(\varepsilon\) it would then have. Check: \(\sigma = 0.505\), \(\varepsilon = 7.82\). (Comparing mechanisms at equal privacy)







TipSolution






DP-SGD. The RDP accountant gives \(\sigma = 0.827\) for \(q = 0.01\), 100 steps and \(\varepsilon = 2\). The final prefix sum carries 100 independent noises of standard deviation \(\sigma\), so \(0.827\sqrt{100} = 8.27\).
Independent noise without sampling. One participation, sensitivity 1, \(\mu(2, 10^{-5}) = 0.502\), so the noise scale is \(1/0.502 = 1.994\) and the final prefix noise is \(1.994 \times 10 = 19.94\).
The square root. Its sensitivity is 1.591, so its noise scale is \(1.591/0.502 = 3.172\), and its last decoder row has length 1.591, giving \(3.172 \times 1.591 = 5.05\).
Matching it with DP-SGD. DP-SGD’s final noise is \(\sigma\sqrt{100}\), so it would need \(\sigma = 5.05/10 = 0.505\). At that noise multiplier the accountant reports \(\varepsilon = 7.82\) for 100 steps at \(q = 0.01\).

To carry as little noise in its final model as the square root does at \(\varepsilon = 2\), DP-SGD would have to spend nearly four times the budget, even with amplification. For a single short pass, correlated noise beats sampling; over many epochs at small \(\varepsilon\) the comparison turns, as Table 41.4 shows.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.1 The failure probability of a Laplace vote
Exercises for the chapter on private prediction with private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) and in-context learning, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_private_prediction.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_private_prediction.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. To give differential privacy (DP) to predictions, \(k\) teachers are trained on disjoint shards of the private data and each query is answered by a noisy vote: LNMax adds \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise to every vote count, GNMax adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), and only the label with the largest noisy count is released. The gap \(g\) is the difference between the top two counts, \(Q\) the number of answered queries, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Costs are measured in Rényi differential privacy (RDP) of order \(\alpha\); one GNMax answer is \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP (Theorem 42.1). Private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) trains a student on public inputs labelled this way.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
Exercise 1. The failure probability of a Laplace vote. Show that if \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) are independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\), then for \(t \ge 0\), \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > t] = \frac14(2 + t/b)e^{-t/b}\). Use it to compute the probability that LNMax with \(b = 5\) returns the runner-up on a two-label query with gap 10, and compare with GNMax at the same noise standard deviation, using Equation 42.5. Repeat for a gap of 30. Check: 0.1353 (simulated 0.1356) against 0.1587; at gap 30, \(4.96 \times 10^{-3}\) against \(1.35 \times 10^{-3}\). (Convolution of densities)







TipSolution






Condition on \(Z_2\). \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > t] = \mathbb E\big[\Pr[Z_1 > t + Z_2 \mid Z_2]\big]\), and for a Laplace variable \(\Pr[Z_1 > s] = \frac12e^{-s/b}\) when \(s \ge 0\) and \(1 - \frac12e^{s/b}\) when \(s < 0\).
Split the integral at \(Z_2 = -t\). For \(z \ge -t\), \(t + z \ge 0\) and the inner probability is \(\frac12e^{-(t + z)/b}\). Integrating against the density \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\) over \(z \in [-t, 0]\) gives \(\frac14e^{-t/b}\cdot\frac tb\), and over \(z \ge 0\) gives \(\frac14e^{-t/b}\cdot\frac12\).
The rest. For \(z < -t\), the inner probability is \(1 - \frac12e^{(t + z)/b}\); the density there integrates to \(\frac12e^{-t/b}\), and the second part contributes \(-\frac14e^{t/b}\int_{-\infty}^{-t}\frac1be^{2z/b}dz = -\frac18e^{-t/b}\). Together, \(\frac12e^{-t/b} - \frac18e^{-t/b} = \frac38e^{-t/b}\).
Add. \(\frac14\frac tbe^{-t/b} + \frac18e^{-t/b} + \frac38e^{-t/b} = \frac14(2 + t/b)e^{-t/b}\). At \(t = 0\) this is \(\frac12\), as symmetry requires.
Numbers. With \(t = 10\) and \(b = 5\): \(\frac14 \times 4 \times e^{-2} = e^{-2} = 0.1353\), and a simulation with a million draws gives 0.1356. The Laplace standard deviation is \(\sqrt2b = 7.07\); GNMax with \(\sigma = 7.07\) fails with probability \(\Phi(-10/(\sqrt2 \times 7.07)) = \Phi(-1) = 0.1587\). At a gap of 30, Laplace gives \(\frac14 \times 8 \times e^{-6} = 4.96 \times 10^{-3}\), Gaussian \(\Phi(-3) = 1.35 \times 10^{-3}\).

At small gaps the two are close, the Laplace slightly better; at large gaps the Laplace tail, which falls like \(e^{-t/b}\) rather than \(e^{-t^2/(4\sigma^2)}\), is much heavier. This is the Laplace failure bound that Papernot et al. (2017) use in their data-dependent analysis, and one reason GNMax replaced it.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.2 The gap a reliable answer needs
text:
42.2 The gap a reliable answer needs

Exercise 2. The gap a reliable answer needs. GNMax answers 1,000 queries at \(\varepsilon = 4\). Using Equation 42.3 and Equation 42.5, find the gap at which a two-label answer returns the plurality with probability 0.9 and 0.99, and the fraction of 250 teachers that must agree for that gap. Compare with Table 42.3. Check: \(\sigma = 51.8\); gaps 93.8 and 170.3; fractions 0.688 and 0.841. (Inverting a normal probability)







TipSolution






The noise. By Equation 42.3, \(\sigma = \sqrt{1{,}000/0.3731} = 51.8\).
Invert Equation 42.5. \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma)) = p\) gives \(g = \sqrt2\sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(p)\). With \(\Phi^{-1}(0.9) = 1.2816\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(0.99) = 2.3263\): \(g = 93.8\) and \(g = 170.3\).
Agreement. If \(a\) of the 250 teachers agree, the gap is \(250a - 250(1 - a) = 250(2a - 1)\), so \(a = (250 + g)/500\): 0.688 and 0.841.
Compare. With 250 teachers, the median gap on the running example is 0.408 of 250, about 102, so the median query is answered correctly with probability a little above 0.9; a substantial share of queries has much smaller gaps.

Reliable answers need strong agreement: more than 84% of the teachers on one side for 99% reliability at this noise. Teachers that each learn the task well are worth more than many teachers that each learn it a little.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.3 Where Gaussian noise overtakes Laplace noise
text:
42.3 Where Gaussian noise overtakes Laplace noise

Exercise 3. Where Gaussian noise overtakes Laplace noise. For a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) spread over \(Q\) answers, compare the noise standard deviation LNMax needs (\(\sqrt2b\), each answer charged as a \((2/b)\)-DP step through the randomized-response curve) with GNMax’s \(\sigma\). Find the smallest \(Q\) at which Gaussian noise is smaller, and repeat for \(\varepsilon = 4\). Explain why Laplace wins for a single answer. Check: from 5 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\), from 6 at \(\varepsilon = 4\). (Composition of pure and Gaussian mechanisms)







TipSolution






One answer. A single LNMax answer is \((2/b)\)-DP by Theorem 42.1, so \(\varepsilon = 1\) needs \(b\) close to 2; the accountant, which goes through the randomized-response curve and Equation 42.2, gives \(b = 2.02\), a standard deviation of 2.85. A single GNMax answer needs \(\sigma = 5.72\) (Table 42.2). A Gaussian has no pure-DP guarantee: for one release, its \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is set by how far into its tail the privacy loss must be controlled, which takes a lot of noise.
Many answers. The pure-DP curve of each Laplace answer is bounded by \(\varepsilon_0\) and, at small orders, behaves like \(\alpha\varepsilon_0^2/2\); summed over \(Q\) answers, the conversion trades between these. The Gaussian curve is the line \(\alpha/\sigma^2\), which composes exactly. As \(Q\) grows, the Laplace cost per unit of noise variance is worse than the Gaussian’s, and the ratio of standard deviations tends to about 2 (Table 42.2).
The crossover. Scanning \(Q = 1, 2, \dots\) with the accountant, Gaussian noise is smaller from \(Q = 5\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and from \(Q = 6\) at \(\varepsilon = 4\).

Use Laplace for a handful of answers and Gaussian beyond. The same pattern holds for any pure-DP versus Gaussian comparison: pure DP is cheap for few releases, Gaussian noise for many.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.4 Small failure probabilities are nearly free
text:
42.4 Small failure probabilities are nearly free

Exercise 4. Small failure probabilities are nearly free. Show that the right side of Equation 42.9 has derivative \(\big(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_0} + (\alpha - 1)e^{\varepsilon_0} - \alpha\big)/(\alpha - 1)\) at \(\beta = 0\), and is therefore about \(\beta\) times this constant for small \(\beta\). Evaluate it for \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\) at \(\alpha = 8\) and \(\alpha = 32\), and compare \(0.001\) times the slope with the bound at \(\beta = 0.001\). Check: slopes 0.2500 and 0.7890; \(2.50 \times 10^{-4}\) against \(2.50 \times 10^{-4}\), and \(7.89 \times 10^{-4}\) against \(7.80 \times 10^{-4}\). (First-order expansion)







TipSolution






The bracket. Let \(x = e^{\varepsilon_0}\) and \(f(\beta) = (1 - \beta)^\alpha(1 - x\beta)^{1 - \alpha} + \beta x^{\alpha - 1}\), so the bound is \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln f(\beta)\) and \(f(0) = 1\).
Differentiate at 0. The first term’s derivative at \(\beta = 0\) is \(-\alpha + (\alpha - 1)x\) (product rule, with \((1 - x\beta)^{1 - \alpha}\) contributing \((\alpha - 1)x\)); the second term’s is \(x^{\alpha - 1}\). So \(f'(0) = x^{\alpha - 1} + (\alpha - 1)x - \alpha\).
The logarithm. \(\ln f(\beta) \approx f'(0)\beta\) near \(\beta = 0\), since \(f(0) = 1\). Dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives the slope. It is non-negative: \(x \ge 1\) makes \(x^{\alpha - 1} \ge 1\) and \((\alpha - 1)x \ge \alpha - 1\).
Numbers. At \(\alpha = 8\): \((e^{0.7} + 7e^{0.1} - 8)/7 = (2.0138 + 7.7362 - 8)/7 = 0.2500\). At \(\alpha = 32\): \((e^{3.1} + 31e^{0.1} - 32)/31 = 0.7890\). At \(\beta = 0.001\) the bound is \(2.50 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(7.80 \times 10^{-4}\), against the linear approximations \(2.50 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(7.89 \times 10^{-4}\): the approximation is exact to three digits at the lower order and 1% high at the higher, where the curvature of \(f\) matters sooner.

An answer that the noise almost never overturns costs almost nothing, in proportion to the chance of overturning it. That is the whole mechanism behind data-dependent accounting; the data-independent cost at \(\alpha = 8\) is 0.0367, about 150 times the cost at \(\beta = 0.001\).

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.5 The budget of Confident-GNMax

Exercise 5. The budget of Confident-GNMax. In Table 42.8, 459 of 1,000 queries pass the check with \(\sigma_1 = 150\) and are answered with \(\sigma_2 = 40\). Split the RDP slope of Equation 42.11 into the check and the answers, convert the total to \(\varepsilon\), and compare with plain GNMax answering all 1,000 queries with \(\sigma = 40\). For which \(\sigma_1\) would the check cost as much as the answers? Check: slopes 0.0222 and 0.2869; \(\varepsilon = 3.59\) against 5.38; \(\sigma_1 = 41.7\). (Accounting for a two-step mechanism)







TipSolution






The check. By Proposition 42.3 each check has slope \(1/(2 \times 150^2)\), and 1,000 of them \(1{,}000/45{,}000 = 0.0222\).
The answers. 459 GNMax answers with \(\sigma_2 = 40\): \(459/1{,}600 = 0.2869\).
Convert. The total line has slope 0.3091, which converts to \(\varepsilon = 3.59\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) by Equation 42.2.
Plain GNMax. 1,000 answers with \(\sigma = 40\) have slope \(1{,}000/1{,}600 = 0.625\) and \(\varepsilon = 5.38\).
Equal costs. \(1{,}000/(2\sigma_1^2) = 0.2869\) gives \(\sigma_1 = \sqrt{1{,}000/0.5738} = 41.7\).

Skipping 541 queries saves almost half of the slope, and the check costs less than a tenth of what it saves. The check can afford much more noise than the answers because it only has to tell strong consensus from weak, not pick a label. The accounting is valid because the budget is fixed in advance: the number of answered queries is random, and only a filter makes a random number of RDP costs compose as if it were fixed.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.6 One teacher can move every query’s cost
text:
42.6 One teacher can move every query’s cost

Exercise 6. One teacher can move every query’s cost. With \(\sigma = 40\) at order 8, compute the data-dependent cost of Equation 42.10 for a two-label query with gap \(g\) and with gap \(g - 2\), the gap after one teacher switches sides, for \(g = 150\), 200 and 250. Why does this make the total data-dependent cost of \(Q\) queries hard to release with noise calibrated to global sensitivity? Check: ratios 1.096, 1.130 and 1.165; at \(g = 150\), 0.00123 against 0.00135. (Local sensitivity of a sum)







TipSolution






One query. With \(\tilde\beta = \frac12\operatorname{erfc}(g/80)\), Equation 42.10 gives 0.00123 at \(g = 150\) and 0.00135 at \(g = 148\), a ratio of 1.096. At \(g = 200\) the ratio is 1.130, and at \(g = 250\), 1.165: the relative change grows with the gap, because the cost falls faster than exponentially in the gap.
All queries. One record changes one teacher, and that teacher may switch sides on every query, so every term of the sum can move at once. The local sensitivity of the total, how much it changes for this dataset’s neighbours, is a sum of \(Q\) such changes, each small in absolute terms.
Global sensitivity. Over all datasets, the worst case includes histograms near a tie, where the answer is decided by one teacher and the cost jumps between nearly 0 and the full \(\alpha/\sigma^2\). The global sensitivity of the total is then close to the data-independent total itself, and noise of that size would make the released \(\varepsilon\) useless.
The fix. Smooth sensitivity (Beyond global sensitivity) scales the noise to how much the total can change near the actual dataset, discounted with distance, which on a dataset with strong consensus is small. This is what Papernot et al. (2018) do; in the chapter’s example, switching all of one teacher’s votes on 1,000 queries moves the data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) only from 4.375 to 4.389.

A data-dependent cost is a statistic of the private data like any other. It is cheap to release only because its local behaviour is tame, and that has to be proved and paid for, not assumed.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.7 Subsampling in private in-context learning

Exercise 7. Subsampling in private in-context learning. In Table 42.10, 1,000 queries at \(\varepsilon = 1\) use \(\sigma = 7.39\) with Poisson sampling rate 0.04. Compute \(\varepsilon\) for the same \(\sigma\) and \(Q\) without subsampling, and the \(\sigma\) that 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\) need without subsampling. How many queries does each record take part in, on average? Check: \(\varepsilon = 1.00\) against 45.8; \(\sigma = 180.9\); 40 queries. (Amplification by subsampling)







TipSolution






With subsampling. By Theorem 42.6 the curve is 1,000 times the subsampled-Gaussian curve with rate 0.04 and noise multiplier \(7.39/\sqrt2\), which converts to \(\varepsilon = 1.00\).
Without. Every record is in every query’s exemplars, each answer is \((\alpha, \alpha/7.39^2)\)-RDP, and 1,000 of them convert to \(\varepsilon = 45.8\).
The noise without subsampling. By Equation 42.3, \(\sigma = \sqrt{1{,}000/0.0306} = 180.9\), about 24 times more.
Participation. A record is drawn with probability 0.04 per query, so it takes part in \(1{,}000 \times 0.04 = 40\) queries on average.

Subsampling helps for two reasons: each record takes part in only 40 of the 1,000 answers, and when it does not, its absence is hidden among the random draws. But the noise must still be compared with the vote gaps of an ensemble of only 25 voters, which is why the stand-in’s accuracy falls anyway. With a large language model, whose votes agree far more, the same noise costs much less accuracy.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.8 Distance to instability and the threshold
text:
42.8 Distance to instability and the threshold

Exercise 8. Distance to instability and the threshold. Compute the distance to instability of Equation 42.12 for the two-label votes 0–0, 5–4, 6–4, 7–4, 55–45 and 135–115, and say for each why one more changed teacher would or would not be safe. Then find the threshold \(\tau\) of Equation 42.13 at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) and \(\delta_{\text{bad}} = 5 \times 10^{-6}\) for pools of 1,000 and 10,000 queries, and the smallest gap whose distance reaches it. Why does a tenfold larger pool raise \(\tau\) by about \(4\ln 10\)? Check: distances 0, 0, 0, 1, 4, 9; \(\tau = 74.8\) and 84.0; gaps 151 and 171; \(4\ln 10 = 9.2\). (Distances to a set; union bounds)







TipSolution






The distances. The gaps are 0, 1, 2, 3, 10 and 20, so Lemma 42.2 gives 0, 0, 0, 1, 4 and 9 (0 for a tie). With 5–4, one teacher moving from the leader to the other label makes it 4–5, and the leader changes. With 6–4, one move makes it 5–5, a tie that the argmax may break either way, so the distance is still 0. With 7–4, one move gives 6–5 and the leader stays strictly on top, but a second move gives 5–6. In general each move costs the leader 2 votes of gap.
The thresholds. Bisection on \(Q_{\mathrm{pool}}\cdot\Pr[\nu - \xi > \tau] \le 5 \times 10^{-6}\), with \(\nu \sim \mathrm{Lap}(4)\) and \(\xi \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2)\), gives \(\tau = 74.8\) for \(Q_{\mathrm{pool}} = 1{,}000\) and \(\tau = 84.0\) for \(Q_{\mathrm{pool}} = 10{,}000\).
The gaps. The distance must be at least \(\tau\), so at least \(\lceil \tau\rceil\), which needs \(\lceil g/2\rceil \ge \lceil \tau\rceil + 1\), that is \(g \ge 2\lceil \tau\rceil + 1\): gaps of 151 and 171.
The pool size. For large \(\tau\) the tail is dominated by its slower term, about \(\frac23e^{-\tau\varepsilon_0/4}\). Multiplying the pool by 10 requires the tail to fall by 10, so \(\tau\) grows by \(4\ln 10/\varepsilon_0 = 9.2\), which matches \(84.0 - 74.8\).

The threshold protects every query of the pool at once, so it grows with the logarithm of the pool, and it is measured in teachers. An ensemble whose typical gap is smaller than about \(2\tau\) cannot use stable aggregation, however good its teachers are.

title: 42  Exercises: Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.9 What stable aggregation needs

Exercise 9. What stable aggregation needs. You want 1,000 exact labels from stable aggregation with a cutoff of \(c = 20\) unstable answers, a pool of 10,000 queries and \(\delta_{\text{bad}} = \delta' = 5 \times 10^{-6}\). Compute the budget and the smallest passing gap at \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.5\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). Suppose a share \(f\) of the queries is unstable, in the sense that the test says so. How small must \(f\) be for 20 unstable answers to leave 1,000 labelled queries on average? What does that say about the number of teachers? Check: \(\varepsilon = 9.93\) with gap 339, and 20.00 with gap 171; \(f \le 0.0196\). (Sparse vector; planning a budget)







TipSolution






Budgets. Twenty runs of \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP AboveThreshold compose by Theorem 42.5 to \(\varepsilon = 9.93\) at \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.5\) and 20.00 at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). At this scale the composition is almost linear, about \(20\varepsilon_0\).
Gaps. The thresholds are \(\tau = 168.1\) and 84.0, so by Exercise 8 the plurality must lead by at least 339 and 171 votes.
The share of unstable queries. Before each unstable answer the procedure labels on average \((1 - f)/f\) stable queries, so \(c\) unstable answers leave about \(c(1 - f)/f\) labels. Setting this to at least 1,000 gives \(f \le c/(c + 1{,}000) = 20/1{,}020 = 0.0196\).
Teachers. Fewer than 2% of the queries may fall short of a lead of 171 votes at \(\varepsilon = 20\), or of 339 votes at \(\varepsilon = 9.93\). Since the gap cannot exceed the number of teachers, that takes several hundred teachers, nearly unanimous on 98% of the queries. The running example’s 500 teachers clear a distance of 84 on only 0.3923 of the pool.

Stable aggregation buys a budget fixed in advance and exact labels, and it pays with a demand on consensus that few tasks meet. Measure the share of queries that clear the threshold on public or held-out data before choosing it.

title: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.1 Counting the adapter’s weights
Exercises for Public data and private fine-tuning, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_public_data.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_public_data.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Models are trained with differential privacy (DP) by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD. \(p\) is the number of weights, \(d\) the number of trainable weights, \(C\) the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(B\) the expected batch size, \(s = \sigma C/B\) the noise standard deviation per coordinate on the averaged gradient, \(\eta\) the learning rate and \(T\) the number of steps. The running example has \(n = 10{,}000\) private records, \(p = 3{,}329\), \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\); its student is pretrained on a related public task, and the last layer has \(d = 65\) weights.
crumbs: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
Exercise 1. Counting the adapter’s weights. A low-rank adapter of rank \(r\) on a \(d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}\) matrix trains \(r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) weights (Equation 43.12). For a \(768 \times 768\) projection, compute the number of adapter weights, their share of the matrix’s weights, and the factor by which the noise on the averaged gradient is shorter than for the full matrix at the same \(\sigma\), for \(r = 1\), 8 and 64. Repeat for the running example’s first layer, \(51 \to 64\), at \(r = 4\). At which rank does the adapter stop saving anything? Check: 1,536, 12,288 and 98,304 weights; noise 19.60, 6.93 and 2.45 times shorter; 2.66 times for the running example. (Counting dimensions)







TipSolution






Counts. \(r(768 + 768) = 1{,}536r\): 1,536, 12,288 and 98,304. The matrix has \(768^2 = 589{,}824\) weights, so the shares are 0.0026, 0.0208 and 0.1667.
Noise. By Equation 43.1 the noise length is \(s\sqrt d\), so the ratio of full to adapter is \(\sqrt{589{,}824/d}\): 19.60, 6.93 and 2.45.
The running example. \(4 \times (51 + 64) = 460\) of 3,264 weights, a share of 0.1409, and a noise ratio of \(\sqrt{3{,}264/460} = 2.66\). The small layer leaves less to save: the share \(r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})/(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}})\) falls with the layer’s size.
Break-even rank. The adapter has fewer weights than the matrix while \(r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}) < d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\), that is \(r < d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}/(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\): 384 for the square \(768 \times 768\) matrix, and \(3{,}264/115 = 28.4\) for the running example.

The saving grows with the layer’s width, which is why adapters matter most for large models. Counting weights gives the noise length; Section 43.1 says the cost depends on the effective dimension, which can be much smaller for both.

title: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.2 The noise cost of a finite run
text:
43.2 The noise cost of a finite run

Exercise 2. The noise cost of a finite run. In Equation 43.2, a direction of curvature \(h\) reaches the share \(1 - (1 - \eta h)^{2T}\) of its steady-state noise cost after \(T\) steps. (a) Compute this share for \(h = 10^{-5}\), \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-3}\) and \(0.1\), with \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\). (b) For the spectra \(h_j = 0.7\,j^{-a}\), \(j = 1, \dots, 3{,}329\), with \(a = 1\), 1.5 and 2, compute the trace, \(d_{\text{eff}}\) and the bound \(2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H\) of Equation 43.3. Check: (a) 0.0198, 0.1813, 0.8647 and 1.0000; (b) \(d_{\text{eff}} = 2{,}079\), 286 and 65. (Geometric sums and spectra)







TipSolution






Why this share. Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 43.1 gives the variance after \(T\) steps as the steady-state variance \(\eta^2s^2/(1 - (1 - \eta h)^2)\) times \(1 - (1 - \eta h)^{2T}\), the partial sum of a geometric series with ratio \((1 - \eta h)^2\).
(a) With \(\eta T = 1{,}000\): \(h = 10^{-5}\) gives \(1 - (1 - 10^{-6})^{20{,}000} \approx 1 - e^{-0.02} = 0.0198\); \(h = 10^{-4}\) gives \(1 - e^{-0.2} = 0.1813\); \(h = 10^{-3}\) gives \(1 - e^{-2} = 0.8647\); \(h = 0.1\) gives \(1 - 0.99^{20{,}000}\), which is 1 to four decimals. The threshold \(2\eta hT = 1\) sits at \(h = 5 \times 10^{-4}\), between the second and the third.
(b) Traces. \(0.7\sum_jj^{-a}\): 6.081 for \(a = 1\) (a harmonic sum, about \(0.7\ln 3{,}329\) plus a constant), 1.804 for \(a = 1.5\) and 1.151 for \(a = 2\) (close to \(0.7\pi^2/6 = 1.151\)).
(b) Effective dimension. Summing the shares: \(d_{\text{eff}} = 2{,}079\), 286 and 65. Roughly, \(d_{\text{eff}}\) counts the eigenvalues above \(5 \times 10^{-4}\): \(0.7j^{-a} > 5 \times 10^{-4}\) when \(j < 1{,}400^{1/a}\), that is \(j < 1{,}400\), 125 and 37, plus the partial contributions of the smaller ones.
(b) The bound. \(2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H = 2{,}000\operatorname{tr}H\): 12,163, 3,609 and 2,302, all larger than \(d_{\text{eff}}\) by a factor between 6 and 35, and the first two larger than \(p\) itself.

How fast the spectrum decays decides what full fine-tuning costs: with \(a = 2\), all 3,329 weights cost as much noise as 65 weights would at their steady state. The trace bound is valid but loose, because it charges every direction as if it were flat.

title: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.3 A private linear probe without clipping
text:
43.3 A private linear probe without clipping

Exercise 3. A private linear probe without clipping. The last layer of the running example is logistic regression on 65 frozen features, each in \((-1, 1)\) or equal to 1, so every per-record gradient has length at most \(L = \sqrt{65}\) (Section 43.2). Train it privately by full-batch noisy gradient descent, the method of Private empirical risk minimization with replace-one neighbours, per-step noise \(\sigma = 2L\sqrt T/(n\mu)\) on the mean gradient and \(\mu = 0.2681\) for \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-5})\), learning rate 1, from the pretrained last layer, with \(T = 100\) and 400 steps: once with \(L = \sqrt{65}\) and no clipping, once clipping each gradient to \(C = 1\). Check: per-step noise 0.0602 and 0.0075 at \(T = 100\); accuracy 0.9383 without clipping, 0.9410 with. (Lipschitz bound against clipping)







TipSolution






The bound. By Proposition 43.1 the gradient is \(\ell'(u)y\phi(x)\), with \(u\) the margin and \(|\ell'(u)| < 1\), so it is shorter than \(\|\phi(x)\| < \sqrt{65} = 8.062\). On the private records the largest feature norm is 7.035, so the bound is not far from attained in norm, but \(|\ell'(u)|\) is small for most records.
Noise without clipping. \(\sigma = 2 \times 8.062 \times \sqrt{100}/(10{,}000 \times 0.2681) = 0.0602\) per coordinate, a noise vector of length \(0.0602 \times \sqrt{65} = 0.4850\) on the mean gradient. With \(T = 400\), \(\sqrt T\) doubles it: 0.1203 and 0.9700.
Noise with clipping at 1. The sensitivity uses \(C = 1\) in place of 8.062, so the noise is 8.062 times smaller: 0.0075 at \(T = 100\) (length 0.0602) and 0.0149 at \(T = 400\).
Accuracy. On the report half of the private test set, the unclipped probe reaches 0.9383 at \(T = 100\) and 0.9361 at \(T = 400\); the clipped one 0.9410 and 0.9454. More steps help the clipped version, whose noise is small enough for the extra progress to outweigh the extra noise, and hurt the unclipped one.
Why clipping wins. Clipping at 1 changes only the gradients of records with \(|\ell'(u)|\,\|\phi(x)\| > 1\), the few badly classified ones, and divides the noise by 8. The bias it introduces is smaller than the noise it removes.

A known Lipschitz constant makes clipping unnecessary for privacy, not useless for accuracy. Both runs are below the chapter’s DP-SGD probe at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (0.9497): each full-batch step of noisy gradient descent uses every record, so it gets none of the amplification that Poisson sampling gives DP-SGD, and the replace-one relation doubles the sensitivity to \(2L/n\).

title: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.4 The adapter’s first step

Exercise 4. The adapter’s first step. Start a rank-4 adapter on the running example’s first layer from \(U = 0\) and a random \(V\), at the pretrained weights. Take one noisy step on a batch of 100 private records with \(\sigma = 4.13\), \(C = 0.5\) and step \(\eta/B\) applied to both factors. Show that the change \(W' - W\) of the matrix has rank at most 4, and that its rows lie in the span of the columns of \(V\) up to a term of relative size about \((\eta/B)\,\|\xi_V\|/\|V\|\). Check numerically for \(\eta/B = 0.001\) (the chapter’s learning rate 0.1 with \(B = 100\)), 0.003 and 1. Check: rank 4 each time; parts outside the span of relative size 0.016, 0.041 and 0.97. (Low-rank updates)







TipSolution






The step and its rank. Step 5 of the proof of Proposition 43.2 gives, from \(U = 0\), \(G_V = \xi_V\) and \(W' - W = -\frac\eta BG_UV^\top + \frac{\eta^2}{B^2}G_U\xi_V^\top\), a \(64 \times 4\) matrix times a \(4 \times 51\) one, so its rank is at most 4. Numerically it is 4 in all three cases.
Span. The first term’s rows are combinations of the columns of \(V\). The second is smaller by a factor of about \(\frac\eta B\|\xi_V\|/\|V\|\). Here \(\xi_V\) has \(51 \times 4 = 204\) entries of standard deviation \(\sigma C = 2.065\), so \(\|\xi_V\| \approx 2.065\sqrt{204} = 29.5\), and \(V\) has entries of standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{51}\), so \(\|V\| \approx 2\). For \(\eta/B = 0.001\) the ratio is about \(0.001 \times 29.5/2 = 0.015\), close to the measured 0.016; for 0.003 about 0.044 against 0.041. At \(\eta/B = 1\) the second term dominates and 0.97 of the change lies outside the span.
Reading it. In realistic training, the adapter’s first steps are the private gradient of \(W\) projected onto the random input subspace spanned by \(V\), plus noise inside that subspace. The subspace then turns, slowly, as \(U\) grows and \(\nabla_V\) stops being zero.

Starting from \(U = 0\) makes the model start exactly at the pretrained one, but it also means the first steps can only move \(W\) within a random subspace. Initializing \(V\) from public data, for example from the top principal directions of public inputs to the layer, is one way to make those first steps count.

title: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.5 How related must the public data be?
text:
43.5 How related must the public data be?

Exercise 5. How related must the public data be? Rebuild the public task with four degrees of mismatch between the public and the private teacher: shift and rotation \((0, 0)\), \((0.15, 0.3)\) (the chapter’s), \((0.5, 1.0)\) and \((1.0, \pi/2)\). For each, pretrain the student, and report the public teacher’s agreement with the private labels, the pretrained student’s accuracy on the private task, and the accuracy after private last-layer fine-tuning at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (learning rate 0.3). Compare with training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 0.9246 (Table 43.5). Check: agreements 1.0000, 0.9004, 0.6378 and 0.4866; after fine-tuning 0.9749, 0.9507, 0.9054 and 0.8586. (Distribution shift)







TipSolution






Identical teachers. The public task is the private task with five times more data and no privacy. The pretrained student reaches 0.9784 on the private test inputs, more than any private method in the chapter; fine-tuning its last layer privately gives 0.9749, slightly worse. There is nothing left to learn, and the noise can only move the model away.
The chapter’s mismatch. Agreement 0.9004, pretrained 0.9035, fine-tuned 0.9507: the features are good, the readout is wrong, and the private last layer fixes most of it.
Large mismatch. At \((0.5, 1.0)\) the public labels agree with the private ones on only 0.6378 of the inputs, and the pretrained student is at 0.6334; the private probe lifts it to 0.9054, which is still below training from scratch at the same budget (0.9246). The features are partly relevant, but their ceiling is too low.
Unrelated. At \((1.0, \pi/2)\) the public teacher is close to independent of the private one (agreement 0.4866, about chance), and the probe reaches 0.8586: random-ish features of a tanh network still support a mediocre linear classifier, but pretraining has bought nothing.
The pattern. The value of public data is set by how much the private task shares with it, not by how much public data there is: the four public sets are equally large. Below some level of relatedness, a strategy that freezes the features loses to training from scratch.

Before relying on a public model, measure how well its frozen features do on the private task’s distribution, using public data that resemble it if you can, or a small private budget if you cannot. Evaluations in which public and private data come from nearly the same distribution flatter the method.
crumbs: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 43  Exercises: Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.6 A record in both datasets

Exercise 6. A record in both datasets. A fine-tuning run is \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP with respect to the private dataset. (a) Bound the true positive rate of any test of whether a given record was in the private dataset, at false positive rates 0.001 and 0.01. (b) The record appears twice in the private dataset. What does group privacy guarantee? (c) The record appears once in the private dataset and once in the public pretraining data. What is guaranteed now? Check: (a) 0.00273 and 0.02719; (b) \((2, 5.44 \times 10^{-5})\). (What the guarantee covers)







TipSolution






(a) An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism makes every test between neighbouring datasets satisfy \(\text{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\text{FPR} + \delta\) (Theorem 18.3). With \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(e \times 0.001 + 10^{-5} = 0.00273\) and \(e \times 0.01 + 10^{-5} = 0.02719\).
(b) Removing both copies changes the dataset by two records. Group privacy (Theorem 19.2) for a group of two gives \((2\varepsilon, 2e^\varepsilon\delta) = (2, 5.44 \times 10^{-5})\), using its bound \(\delta_k \le ke^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta\): the test’s power bound becomes \(e^2\,\text{FPR} + 5.44 \times 10^{-5}\), weaker but finite.
(c) The guarantee compares the private dataset with and without the record, the public data held fixed (Theorem 43.2). Whether the record is in the public data is not something the mechanism randomizes over: the pretrained weights depend on it without noise. So nothing bounds a test that targets the public copy, such as a membership inference attack on the pretrained model. The private copy is still covered by (a).
Comparison. A duplicate inside the private dataset weakens the guarantee by a known factor; a copy in the public data removes it for that person, as far as the theorem goes.

Deduplicate the private dataset against the public data before fine-tuning, and when that is not possible, do not describe the people in the overlap as protected.

title: 44  Exercises: User-level differential privacy
text:
44.1 Group privacy at a small δ
Exercises for User-level differential privacy, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_user_level.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_user_level.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A guarantee of differential privacy (DP) is example-level when neighbouring datasets differ in one record and user-level when they differ in all the records of one user. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise is DP-SGD; \(q\) is its Poisson sampling rate, \(\sigma\) its noise multiplier, \(C\) its clipping norm and \(T\) its number of steps. A user has \(k\) records, and \(H \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, q)\) of them land in a batch. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is the accountant’s currency. The running example’s model is example-level \((6.71, 10^{-5})\)-DP, from \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), and its population has 1,000 users with between 1 and 348 records each.

title: 44  Exercises: User-level differential privacy
text:
Exercise 1. Group privacy at a small \(\delta\). A mechanism is example-level \((1, 10^{-6})\)-DP. Using Equation 44.2, give the user-level guarantee for users with 2, 5 and 10 records. For which of them is the guarantee meaningful if the dataset has 10,000 users? Check: \(\delta_2 = 3.718 \times 10^{-6}\), \(\delta_5 = 8.579 \times 10^{-5}\), \(\delta_{10} = 0.01282\). (The geometric sum of group privacy)







TipSolution






The formula. By Proposition 44.1, a user with \(k\) records gets \(\varepsilon_k = k\varepsilon\) and \(\delta_k = \delta(e^{k\varepsilon} - 1)/(e^\varepsilon - 1)\).
\(k = 2\). The user gets \(\varepsilon_2 = 2\) and \(\delta_2 = 10^{-6}(e^2 - 1)/(e - 1) = 10^{-6}(1 + e) = 3.718 \times 10^{-6}\).
\(k = 5\). The user gets \(\varepsilon_5 = 5\) and \(\delta_5 = 10^{-6}(e^5 - 1)/(e - 1) = 8.579 \times 10^{-5}\).
\(k = 10\). The user gets \(\varepsilon_{10} = 10\) and \(\delta_{10} = 10^{-6}(e^{10} - 1)/(e - 1) = 0.01282\).
Which are meaningful. \(\delta\) is the probability that the guarantee fails outright, so for \(U = 10{,}000\) users it should be well below \(1/U = 10^{-4}\). Only \(k = 2\) satisfies that comfortably; \(k = 5\) is just below \(10^{-4}\), and \(k = 10\) allows a failure for about one user in 78.

The \(\delta\) of group privacy grows like \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), so a guarantee designed for records must start from a much smaller \(\delta\) to survive the step to users.

title: 44  Exercises: User-level differential privacy
text:
44.2 When group privacy gives nothing

Exercise 2. When group privacy gives nothing. The running example’s accountant can convert its RDP curve to \((\varepsilon_{\text{rec}}, \delta_{\text{rec}})\) at any \(\delta_{\text{rec}}\). For \(\delta_{\text{rec}} = 10^{-5}\), \(10^{-10}\), \(10^{-20}\), \(10^{-50}\) and \(10^{-100}\), compute \(\varepsilon_{\text{rec}}\) and the user’s \(\delta_k\) from Equation 44.2 for \(k = 2\), 5 and 10. Explain why group privacy yields a user-level \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\) guarantee for \(k = 2\) and 5 but none for \(k = 10\). Check: \(\varepsilon_{\text{rec}} = 6.71\), 9.78, 14.31, 24.94 and 41.02; for \(k = 10\), \(\log_{10}\delta_{10}\) grows from 21.2 to 60.3. (A race between \(\delta\) and \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\))







TipSolution






The record-level guarantees. The accountant gives \(\varepsilon_{\text{rec}} = 6.71\), 9.78, 14.31, 24.94 and 41.02 at the five values of \(\delta_{\text{rec}}\). A smaller \(\delta\) costs a larger \(\varepsilon\), roughly through the term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) of the conversion.
The user’s \(\delta\). \(\delta_k \approx \delta_{\text{rec}}e^{(k-1)\varepsilon_{\text{rec}}}\), so \(\log_{10}\delta_k \approx \log_{10}\delta_{\text{rec}} + (k - 1)\varepsilon_{\text{rec}}/\ln 10\). The script gives, in powers of 10:




Table 44.1: The user’s δ from group privacy, as a function of the record-level δ at which the accountant is converted. Values above 1 are no guarantee.
