Who wins the race. Going from \(\delta_{\text{rec}} = 10^{-50}\) to \(10^{-100}\) lowers \(\log_{10}\delta_{\text{rec}}\) by 50 and raises \(\varepsilon_{\text{rec}}\) by 16.08, so \((k - 1)\varepsilon_{\text{rec}}/\ln 10\) rises by \(6.98(k - 1)\). For \(k = 2\) and 5 the rise, 7.0 and 27.9, is less than 50 and \(\delta_k\) falls; it crosses \(10^{-5}\) for \(\delta_{\text{rec}}\) between \(10^{-5}\) and \(10^{-10}\) when \(k = 2\), and between \(10^{-20}\) and \(10^{-50}\) when \(k = 5\). For \(k = 10\) the rise is 62.8, more than 50, and \(\delta_{10}\) grows at every step of the table: it never comes near \(10^{-5}\).
Why. At small \(\delta_{\text{rec}}\) the conversion uses orders close to 1, where \(\varepsilon_{\text{rec}}\) grows almost in proportion to \(\ln(1/\delta_{\text{rec}})\), with a slope that the table puts at about \(16.08/(50\ln 10) = 0.14\). The user’s \(\ln\delta_k\) then changes by \((k - 1) \times 0.14 - 1\) per unit of \(\ln(1/\delta_{\text{rec}})\), positive once \(k - 1 > 7\).

This is why the chapter’s group-privacy column reads “none” from \(k = 10\): generic group privacy cannot turn this RDP curve into any user-level guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The direct accountant, which knows the mechanism, gives \(\varepsilon = 146.20\).

title: 44  Exercises: User-level differential privacy
section: 44.3 The second moment and the rate-kq rule
text:
44.3 The second moment and the rate-kq rule

Exercise 3. The second moment and the rate-kq rule. At order \(\alpha = 2\), Equation 44.7 says \(A_2 = \mathbb E[e^{H_1H_2/\sigma^2}]\) for two independent copies of \(H \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, q)\). Compute \(\varepsilon(2) = \ln A_2\) for \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(k = 2\), 5 and 10, and compare with Equation 44.12’s single record at rate \(kq\), \(\ln(1 + (kq)^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1))\). Explain the result for \(k = 10\). Check: ratios 1.0177, 1.0793 and 469. (Moments of a mixture)







TipSolution






Exact. The moment is a double sum over the possible numbers \(a\) and \(b\) of drawn records in two independent batches, \(A_2 = \sum_{a,b}b_ab_be^{ab/\sigma^2}\) with \(b_m = \binom km q^m(1 - q)^{k-m}\). It gives \(\varepsilon(2) = 6.992273 \times 10^{-4}\) for \(k = 2\), \(4.626224 \times 10^{-3}\) for \(k = 5\) and \(7.990343\) for \(k = 10\), the same values as the chapter’s numerical integral for \(k = 2\) and 5.
Rate \(kq\). \(\ln(1 + (kq)^2(e - 1))\) gives \(6.870766 \times 10^{-4}\), \(4.286504 \times 10^{-3}\) and \(1.703686 \times 10^{-2}\).
Ratios. 1.0177, 1.0793 and 469. For \(k = 2\) and 5 the rule is good to 2% and 8%: the terms it drops, with \(ab \ge 2\), have probability of order \((kq)^3\) or smaller.
What breaks at \(k = 10\). The term \(a = b = k\), both batches drawing all of the user’s records, has probability \(q^{2k}\) and factor \(e^{k^2/\sigma^2}\). For \(k = 10\) that is \(10^{-40}e^{100} \approx e^{7.90}\), larger than everything else together: the exact \(\ln A_2 = 7.99\) is almost entirely this one term. A tiny probability cannot cancel a factor that grows like \(e^{k^2}\).
Consequence. At \(\sigma = 1\), low orders of the user’s curve are dominated by the rare steps that draw all of a heavy user’s records together. The accountant then moves to orders close to 1, as Table 44.2 shows (best order 1.3 for \(k = 10\)).

The all-records-drawn term \(q^{2k}e^{k^2/\sigma^2}\) exceeds 1 when \(k^2/\sigma^2 > 2k\ln(1/q)\), that is \(k > 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\), which is 9.2 for \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\). Well below that size the rate-\(kq\) rule is a good quick estimate; near or above it only the accountant is reliable.

title: 44  Exercises: User-level differential privacy
text:
44.4 Per-record clipping inside user-level sampling

Exercise 4. Per-record clipping inside user-level sampling. User-level DP-SGD with \(q = 0.1\), \(T = 1{,}000\) and per-user clipping needs \(\sigma = 3.78\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Instead, you clip each record to \(C\) and sum at most \(k\) records per user. Using Equation 44.14, what noise multiplier gives the same guarantee for \(k = 2\) and \(k = 5\)? Verify numerically at \(\alpha = 3\). Check: 7.56 and 18.9. (Rescaling a Gaussian mechanism)







TipSolution






The effective noise. By Proposition 44.3, per-record clipping with a cap of \(k\) has the curve of noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\), given by Equation 44.14.
Match the guarantee. To be as private as per-user clipping with \(\sigma = 3.78\), the noise multiplier must satisfy \(\sigma/k = 3.78\): \(\sigma = 7.56\) for \(k = 2\) and \(18.9\) for \(k = 5\).
Check. At \(\alpha = 3\), the binomial sum with \(k = 2\) and \(\sigma = 7.56\), and with \(k = 1\) and \(\sigma = 3.78\), both give \(1.094286 \times 10^{-3}\); so does \(k = 5\) with \(\sigma = 18.9\).

Summing clipped records costs a factor \(k\) in noise, where clipping the user’s average costs nothing. Per-record clipping is convenient when the code for per-example gradients already exists, but its noise grows with the cap.

title: 44  Exercises: User-level differential privacy
text:
44.5 Averaging or summing before clipping

Exercise 5. Averaging or summing before clipping. Three users have 1, 10 and 348 records, and every record of every user has the same gradient \(g\) with \(\|g\| = 0.01\). With \(C = 0.5\), compute the length of each user’s clipped contribution when the per-user vector is (i) the average of the user’s gradients and (ii) their sum. Relate the answers to Equation 44.15. Check: (i) 0.01 for all three; (ii) 0.01, 0.1 and 0.5. (Weights in the expected update)







TipSolution






Average then clip. Every user’s average is \(g\), of length \(0.01 < C\), so nothing is clipped and each user contributes 0.01. Every user has the same weight, whatever their size.
Sum then clip. The sums have lengths 0.01, 0.1 and 3.48. The first two are below \(C\) and are kept; the third is clipped to 0.5.
Weights. With averaging, the expected update is Equation 44.15: each user counts \(1/U\). With summing, users below the clip count in proportion to their records, as in example-level training, and users above it count \(C/\|g\|\) records’ worth: here the 348-record user counts as 50 records, not 348.
Privacy. Both are valid user-level DP-SGD: each user’s vector is computed from their own records and clipped to \(C\), so the guarantee is the same.

Between equal weights per user and equal weights per record there is a continuum, set by how a user’s vector is formed and by \(C\). It is a modelling choice, made inside the per-user computation, and it costs no privacy.

title: 44  Exercises: User-level differential privacy
text:
44.6 Capping contributions to a count

Exercise 6. Capping contributions to a count. You release the number of records in the running example’s population, \(n = 10{,}000\), with user-level \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Cap each user at \(k\) records, so the true capped count is \(n_k = \sum_u\min(n_u, k)\) and its user-level sensitivity is \(k\), and add Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(k\) times the noise for sensitivity 1. Taking the error of the estimate of \(n\) as \(\sqrt{(n - n_k)^2 + \text{noise variance}}\), find the best cap. Check: noise 3.731 per unit of sensitivity; best \(k = 158\) with error 698.6; no cap (\(k = 348\)) gives 1,298.3. (The bias–variance trade-off of Amin et al.)







TipSolution






The noise. The exact calibration of the Gaussian mechanism for \((1, 10^{-5})\) and sensitivity 1 gives standard deviation 3.731, so a cap of \(k\) needs \(3.731k\).
The bias. Capping at \(k\) removes \(n - n_k\) records, all from users with more than \(k\). In the population, \(n_k = 1{,}000\) at \(k = 1\), a bias of \(-9{,}000\), and 5,063 at \(k = 10\). It rises to 8,437 at \(k = 50\) and 9,214 at \(k = 100\), and then to 9,756 at \(k = 200\) and 10,000 at \(k = 348\).
The error. The error \(\sqrt{(n - n_k)^2 + (3.731k)^2}\) is 9,000 at \(k = 1\) and 1,574.1 at \(k = 50\). It falls to 870.0 at \(k = 100\) and 785.0 at \(k = 200\). At \(k = 348\) the bias vanishes, and the error is the noise standard deviation, 1,298.3.
The best cap. Scanning every \(k\) gives \(k = 158\), with \(n_k = 9{,}625\) and error 698.6. Below it, each extra unit of \(k\) removes more bias than it adds noise, because many users still have more records; above it, only a few heavy users gain and the noise keeps growing in proportion to \(k\).

The best cap is set by the tail of the distribution of user sizes, as Amin et al. (2019) show in general. Choosing it from the data, as here, is itself a release that should use public information or be made privately.

title: 45  Exercises: Disparate impact
text:
45.1 Upweighting does not survive clipping
Exercises for Disparate impact, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_disparate_impact.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_disparate_impact.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Training with differential privacy (DP) runs stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD. \(C\) is the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(q\) the Poisson sampling rate, \(B = qn\) the expected batch size, \(T\) the number of steps and \(\eta\) the learning rate. A group \(g\) has a share \(s_g\) of the \(n\) training records, and its clipping weight \(w_g\) is the average of \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\) over its records. The running example uses \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(T = 10{,}000\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); at \(\varepsilon = 4\) the noise multiplier is \(\sigma = 1.36\) and the noise on the averaged gradient has standard deviation \(\tau = \sigma C/B = 0.0068\) per coordinate.

title: 45  Exercises: Disparate impact
text:
Exercise 1. Upweighting does not survive clipping. A common fix for an under-represented group is to multiply its records’ losses by a factor \(u > 1\). Take the chapter’s two-dimensional example: 95 majority records with gradient \((0.2, 0)\) and 5 minority records with gradient \((0, 4)\), clipped at \(C = 0.5\). Define the minority’s share of the update as its component divided by the sum of the two components. Compute it without clipping, and with clipping for \(u = 1\), 4 and 20. Then compute the effective share of Equation 45.5 when the majority keeps weight 1 and the minority has weight \(C/4 = 0.125\). Check: 0.5128 without clipping; 0.1163 with clipping for every \(u\); effective share 0.0065. (Clipping as reweighting)







TipSolution






Without clipping. The average gradient is \((0.95 \times 0.2, 0.05 \times 4) = (0.19, 0.2)\), and the minority’s share is \(0.2/0.39 = 0.5128\): five records with large gradients pull as hard as ninety-five with small ones.
With clipping, \(u = 1\). The majority’s gradients have length \(0.2 < C\) and are untouched. The minority’s have length 4 and are rescaled to length 0.5, so the average is \((0.19, 0.05 \times 0.5) = (0.19, 0.025)\), and the share is \(0.025/0.215 = 0.1163\).
Upweighting. Multiplying the minority’s loss by \(u\) multiplies its gradient by \(u\), to \((0, 4u)\). Its length \(4u\) is still above \(C\), so clipping rescales it back to length 0.5, pointing the same way. The clipped average is again \((0.19, 0.025)\), and the share 0.1163, for \(u = 4\) and for \(u = 20\) alike.
Effective share. Equation 45.5 gives \(0.05 \times 0.125/(0.05 \times 0.125 + 0.95 \times 1) = 0.00625/0.95625 = 0.0065\). This is the minority’s share of the records, weighted by how much of each record’s gradient survives; step 2’s 0.1163 is larger because the minority’s gradients were twenty times longer to begin with.

Clipping bounds each record’s pull at \(C\) whatever the loss says, so a weight on the loss is undone exactly for records that are clipped. To give a group more pull you must give it more records in the batch (oversampling, which costs privacy) or a larger share of the clipping budget.

title: 45  Exercises: Disparate impact
text:
45.2 The noise floor, exactly

Exercise 2. The noise floor, exactly. In the quadratic model of Section 45.3, each of a group’s \(d_g\) weights follows \(x \leftarrow (1 - a)x - \eta\tau\xi\) with \(a = \eta s_g\lambda\) and \(\xi\) standard normal. Use the stationary variance of Lemma 45.1, without the small-\(a\) approximation, to evaluate the group’s excess loss \(\frac\lambda2d_g\operatorname{Var}x\) for \(d_g = 51\), \(\lambda = 1\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(\tau = 0.0068\) and shares \(0.95\) and \(0.05\). Compare with the approximation \(d_g\eta\tau^2/(4s_g)\). Check: \(4.069 \times 10^{-4}\) against \(3.103 \times 10^{-4}\) for the majority, \(5.970 \times 10^{-3}\) against \(5.896 \times 10^{-3}\) for the minority. (Stationary variance of a linear recursion)







TipSolution






The stationary variance. The recursion is that of Lemma 45.1 with noise variance \(\omega^2 = \eta^2\tau^2\), so the variance of \(x\) settles at \(V = \eta^2\tau^2/(a(2 - a))\), with no approximation.
The majority, \(s_g = 0.95\). \(a = 0.5 \times 0.95 = 0.475\), so \(V = 0.25 \times 0.0068^2/(0.475 \times 1.525) = 1.596 \times 10^{-5}\), and the excess loss is \(0.5 \times 51 \times V = 4.069 \times 10^{-4}\). The approximation \(51 \times 0.5 \times 0.0068^2/(4 \times 0.95) = 3.103 \times 10^{-4}\) is 24% low, because \(2 - a = 1.525\) is far from 2.
The minority, \(s_g = 0.05\). \(a = 0.025\), \(V = 2.341 \times 10^{-4}\), excess loss \(5.970 \times 10^{-3}\); the approximation gives \(5.896 \times 10^{-3}\), 1% low.
The ratio. Exactly, the minority’s floor is \(5.970 \times 10^{-3}/4.069 \times 10^{-4} = 14.7\) times the majority’s, against \(0.95/0.05 = 19\) from the approximation. The exact form is Equation 45.11.

The approximation is accurate for small groups, the case that matters, and overstates the gap between a small group and a large one by the factor \((2 - a_{\text{major}})/(2 - a_{\text{minor}})\).

title: 45  Exercises: Disparate impact
section: 45.3 Why waiting does not help a small group
text:
45.3 Why waiting does not help a small group

Exercise 3. Why waiting does not help a small group. By Equation 45.7, a drift that is a fraction \(s_g\) of the population’s needs \(1/s_g^2\) times as many steps to emerge from the noise. Evaluate the factor for \(s_g = 0.2\), 0.05 and 0.01. Then explain why training longer at a fixed \(\varepsilon\) does not fix this. Check: 25, 400 and 10,000. (Drift against random walk)







TipSolution






The factors. \(1/0.2^2 = 25\), \(1/0.05^2 = 400\), \(1/0.01^2 = 10{,}000\).
What they mean. In the running example the population’s signal emerges after about 228 steps at \(\varepsilon = 4\). A group with 1% of the records, pulling with its share only, would need about \(2.3\) million steps, two hundred times the whole run.
Why more steps do not help. At a fixed budget, more steps need more noise per step. In the regime of the DP-SGD chapter, \(\varepsilon\) stays fixed when \(Tq^2/\sigma^2\) does, so multiplying \(T\) by \(m\) multiplies \(\sigma\) by \(\sqrt m\) and the per-step noise variance by \(m\). The break-even count \((\text{noise}/\text{signal})^2\) also grows by \(m\): the run gets longer and the target moves away at the same rate.
What does help. A larger share of the signal (more records from the group, or a larger effective share after clipping), less noise per unit of signal (larger batches, Equation 39.9), or a starting point that already serves the group (a public pretrained model).

The \(1/s_g^2\) law is about directions the rest of the data does not teach. Where the minority’s task overlaps the majority’s, the majority’s gradient does part of the work, and the penalty is smaller.

title: 45  Exercises: Disparate impact
section: 45.4 How many test records does a gap need?
text:
45.4 How many test records does a gap need?

Exercise 4. How many test records does a gap need? A model has accuracy 0.70 on 100 minority test records. Give the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval. Then, with the majority measured on 9,500 test records at accuracy 0.95, find the smallest number of minority test records for which the normal 95% interval of the gap, Equation 45.14, excludes zero when the minority’s true accuracy is 0.90, and when it is 0.85. Check: \([0.600, 0.788]\); 140 and 50 records. (Binomial intervals)







TipSolution






The interval. With \(k = 70\) correct of \(m = 100\), the lower end solves \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(100, l) \ge 70] = 0.025\) and the upper end \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(100, u) \le 70] = 0.025\). Bisection gives \([0.600, 0.788]\), about 19 points wide.
The gap’s standard error. The two accuracies are measured on disjoint test records, so their variances add: \(\mathrm{se}^2 = 0.95 \times 0.05/9{,}500 + p(1 - p)/m\). The first term is \(5 \times 10^{-6}\) and negligible.
Minority at 0.90. The gap is 0.05. The interval excludes zero when \(1.96\sqrt{5 \times 10^{-6} + 0.09/m} < 0.05\), that is \(0.09/m < 6.46 \times 10^{-4}\), so \(m \ge 140\).
Minority at 0.85. The gap is 0.10, and \(1.96\sqrt{5 \times 10^{-6} + 0.1275/m} < 0.10\) needs \(m \ge 50\).
Reading it. The number of minority records you need grows like one over the gap squared. A test split that is 5% minority and has 1,000 records holds 50 of them: enough to see a 10-point gap, not a 5-point one.

This is the expected gap at the true accuracies; with an observed gap the same calculation gives the interval to report. Disjoint groups make the variances add; the majority’s term almost never matters.

title: 45  Exercises: Disparate impact
text:
45.5 What oversampling costs

Exercise 5. What oversampling costs. Sampling the minority’s records at rate \(vq\) instead of \(q\) gives them more pull, but their privacy is that of a subsampled Gaussian at rate \(vq\) (Equation 45.17). With \(\sigma = 1.36\), \(q = 0.01\), \(T = 10{,}000\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), compute the minority records’ \(\varepsilon\) for \(v = 2\), 4 and 8, and the noise multiplier that brings them back to \(\varepsilon = 4\). Check: \(\varepsilon = 8.92\), 20.96 and 53.04; \(\sigma = 2.44\), 4.71 and 9.31. (Amplification by subsampling)







TipSolution






Whose privacy changes. By Proposition 45.5, minority records sampled at rate \(vq\) have the privacy of the subsampled Gaussian at rate \(vq\), majority records keep rate \(q\), and the guarantee of the whole algorithm is the minority’s.
The accountant. At \(\sigma = 1.36\) and rate \(vq\) the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant gives \(\varepsilon = 8.92\) for \(v = 2\), 20.96 for \(v = 4\) and 53.04 for \(v = 8\), against 4 at \(v = 1\).
Paying it back. To keep every record at \(\varepsilon = 4\), the noise multiplier must be 2.44, 4.71 and 9.31. The number of steps is fixed, and in the small-\(q\) regime of the DP-SGD chapter \(\varepsilon\) stays fixed when \(Tq^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) does. For large \(\sigma\) that is \(Tq^2/\sigma^2\), so \(\sigma\) grows in proportion to the rate: \(1.36v\) would be 2.72, 5.44 and 10.88. The accountant needs a little less, because at \(\sigma = 1.36\) the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) is still well above 1 and at the larger \(\sigma\) it is not.
Who gains. The minority’s pull grows by \(v\), and the noise by \(\sigma(vq)/\sigma(q)\): for \(v = 4\), by \(4.71/1.36 = 3.46\). The minority’s signal-to-noise ratio improves by \(4/3.46 = 1.16\); the majority’s falls by 3.46.

Oversampling is honest only if the accountant uses the largest sampling rate. Paid for that way, it buys the minority little and costs the majority much; the chapter’s experiment shows the same.

title: 45  Exercises: Disparate impact
section: 45.6 Global scaling is a large clipping norm
text:
45.6 Global scaling is a large clipping norm

Exercise 6. Global scaling is a large clipping norm. Global scaling multiplies every per-example gradient by \(C/C_{\max}\), where \(C_{\max}\) is an upper bound on all gradient norms, and adds noise \(\sigma C\) to the sum. Proposition 45.4 shows that if no gradient exceeds \(C_{\max}\), one step equals a DP-SGD step with the clipping norm set to \(C_{\max}\), noise multiplier \(\sigma\) and learning rate \(\eta C/C_{\max}\). Check the identity numerically on 200 records of the running example at initialization with \(C = 0.5\), \(C_{\max} = 50\) and the same noise draw. Check: the two updates differ by at most \(1.7 \times 10^{-18}\). (Scale invariance)







TipSolution






The identity. Proposition 45.4 proves it: factoring \(C/C_{\max}\) out of the noisy scaled sum leaves DP-SGD’s step with the clipping norm set to \(C_{\max}\), which clips nothing when no gradient is longer than \(C_{\max}\), and learning rate \(\eta C/C_{\max}\). Both steps have sensitivity-to-noise ratio \(1/\sigma\), so the same accountant applies.
Check. At initialization the 200 gradient norms are well below 50. With the same noise draw, the two computed updates agree to \(1.7 \times 10^{-18}\), which is rounding error.

Global scaling does not escape the trade-off of the clipping norm: it is the point where nothing is clipped, so the update is unbiased in direction, and the noise is as large relative to the signal as it can be. Esipova et al.’s adaptive variant moves \(C_{\max}\) during training to sit just above most gradient norms.

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
text:
46.1 What an audit can prove
Exercises for Choosing ε, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_choosing_epsilon.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_choosing_epsilon.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A mechanism satisfies differential privacy (DP) with parameters \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), or is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, when one record changes the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) plus \(\delta\). A membership test has a false positive rate (FPR) and a true positive rate (TPR). The running example is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, with a sampling rate \(q\) of 0.01 and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps on 10,000 records, at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); its noise multipliers come from the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant.

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
text:
Exercise 1. What an audit can prove. An audit measures a membership test’s FPR and TPR on a trained model. Using Equation 46.1, find the smallest \(\varepsilon\) consistent with a measurement, as a function of TPR, FPR and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Evaluate it for TPR 0.05 at FPR \(10^{-3}\), and then for the best tests against the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 8\) run read off Table 46.4 and Table 46.5 (upper ends of the brackets): TPR 0.0589 at FPR \(10^{-3}\), 0.2092 at \(10^{-2}\) and 0.5901 at \(10^{-1}\). What does this say about audits? Check: 3.912, 4.076, 3.041 and 1.775. (Inverting the testing bound)







TipSolution






Invert the line. Every test satisfies \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\), so a measured pair is possible only if \(e^\varepsilon \ge (\mathrm{TPR} - \delta)/\mathrm{FPR}\), that is \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}\).
The first measurement. \(\ln\frac{0.05 - 10^{-5}}{10^{-3}} = \ln 49.99 = 3.912\). A model claimed to be \((3, 10^{-5})\)-DP would be refuted by it; one claimed \((4, 10^{-5})\)-DP would not.
The best possible tests against the \(\varepsilon = 8\) run. \(\ln(58.89) = 4.076\) at FPR \(10^{-3}\), \(\ln\frac{0.2092 - 10^{-5}}{0.01} = 3.041\) at \(10^{-2}\) and \(\ln\frac{0.5901 - 10^{-5}}{0.1} = 1.775\) at \(10^{-1}\).
Reading it. These are the largest lower bounds that any audit of this run can reach at these FPRs, even with the optimal attack and exact error rates, and they are far below the run’s true \(\varepsilon\) of about 7.3. The reason is Theorem 46.1: the line \(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) touches the curve of DP-SGD only at an FPR of at most \(e^{-\varepsilon}Q[L > \varepsilon]\), so an audit can certify the accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) only by measuring at FPRs of that order.

Tight audits need very low false positive rates, hence many trials and very exposed canaries; Auditing private training takes this up. An audit that compares its measurement with the whole curve, rather than with one line, can be much more informative.

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
text:
46.2 The advantage of Gaussian DP

Exercise 2. The advantage of Gaussian DP. The largest advantage \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) against \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) versus \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) is \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) (Corollary 4.2). Evaluate it for the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) approximations of the \(\varepsilon = 4\) and \(\varepsilon = 8\) runs, \(\mu = 0.847\) and 1.511 (Table 46.3), and find the \(\varepsilon\) of randomized response, whose advantage is \((e^\varepsilon - 1)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), with the same advantage. Check: 0.3281 and 0.5501; randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.681\) and 1.237. (Total variation of two Gaussians)







TipSolution






The best test. By Theorem 4.5 the largest advantage is the total variation of the two Gaussians, and Corollary 4.2 evaluates it as \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\): the best test thresholds the output at \(\mu/2\), where the two densities cross.
Numbers. \(2\Phi(0.4235) - 1 = 0.3281\) and \(2\Phi(0.7555) - 1 = 0.5501\). The chapter’s script prints 0.3280 for the first, from the unrounded \(\mu\).
Randomized response. Solving \((e^\varepsilon - 1)/(e^\varepsilon + 1) = A\) for \(\varepsilon\) gives \(e^\varepsilon = (1 + A)/(1 - A)\): \(\ln(1.3281/0.6719) = 0.681\) and \(\ln(1.5501/0.4499) = 1.237\).

Measured by advantage alone, the \(\varepsilon = 8\) run of DP-SGD is about as private as randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 1.24\). The comparison is fair only at that one point of the curve: at low FPR the Gaussian curve rises above the randomized-response line, which is why a single summary number never suffices.

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
section: 46.3 When can a flag be trusted?
text:
46.3 When can a flag be trusted?

Exercise 3. When can a flag be trusted? An attacker with prior \(p = 0.01\) wants a test whose flags are right at least half the time. Using Equation 46.11, find the largest FPR at which the pair \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\) allows a precision of 1/2, for \(\varepsilon = 1\), 4 and 8. Check: \(1.04\times10^{-7}\), \(2.25\times10^{-7}\), and every FPR at \(\varepsilon = 8\). (Base rates)







TipSolution






The condition. Precision at least 1/2 means \(p(e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta) \ge (1 - p)\mathrm{FPR}\), with \(\mathrm{FPR}\) the false positive rate: the flagged members at least as many as the flagged non-members.
Solve for \(\mathrm{FPR}\). \(\mathrm{FPR}\big((1 - p) - pe^\varepsilon\big) \le p\delta\). If \((1 - p) > pe^\varepsilon\), this is \(\mathrm{FPR} \le p\delta/\big((1 - p) - pe^\varepsilon\big)\). If not, every \(\mathrm{FPR}\) works.
Numbers. At \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(0.01 \times 10^{-5}/(0.99 - 0.0272) = 1.04\times10^{-7}\). At \(\varepsilon = 4\): \(10^{-7}/(0.99 - 0.546) = 2.25\times10^{-7}\). At \(\varepsilon = 8\): \(0.01e^8 = 29.8 > 0.99\), so the pair allows even odds at every FPR.
Reading it. For \(\varepsilon \le 4\), the only way the pair allows a trustworthy flag at this prior is through \(\delta\), at FPRs around \(10^{-7}\), where at most a fraction \(\delta\) of members can be flagged.

At small priors DP limits confident identification much more than the advantage suggests; but the pair at \(\varepsilon = 8\) limits nothing, which is why the chapter reads the actual curve instead.

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
text:
46.4 A family in the data

Exercise 4. A family in the data. Three members of one family are in the training set, one record each, and the privacy unit is a record. Group privacy says that a mechanism that is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for one record is \((k\varepsilon, ke^{(k - 1)\varepsilon}\delta)\)-DP for \(k\) records. Compute the family’s guarantee for \((1, 10^{-5})\) and for \((4, 10^{-5})\), and the largest posterior that the family took part, from a prior of 0.01, when the loss is at most \(3\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\). Check: \((3, 2.22\times10^{-4})\), posterior 0.1687; \((12, 0.0894)\). (Group privacy)







TipSolution






Why group privacy. Datasets that differ in \(k\) records are joined by a chain of \(k\) neighbouring steps, and Theorem 19.2 chains the definition along it to give \((k\varepsilon, ke^{(k - 1)\varepsilon}\delta)\).
At \(\varepsilon = 1\). \((3 \times 1, 3e^2 \times 10^{-5}) = (3, 2.22\times10^{-4})\).
Posterior. Equation 46.10 with \(3\) in place of \(\varepsilon\): \(0.01e^3/(0.01e^3 + 0.99) = 0.1687\), against 0.0267 for one person.
At \(\varepsilon = 4\). \((12, 3e^8 \times 10^{-5}) = (12, 0.0894)\): a \(\delta\) of almost 9% means no meaningful guarantee for the family through this route.

Group privacy is a worst-case bound, and the actual curve of three records in DP-SGD is better, because their gradients share the noise; but a per-record guarantee should never be presented as protecting families or users. That needs a different unit (User-level differential privacy).

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
section: 46.5 Two ways to add up the Census budget
text:
46.5 Two ways to add up the Census budget

Exercise 5. Two ways to add up the Census budget. The 2020 Census redistricting data spent \(\rho = 2.56\) of zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) on persons and \(\rho = 0.07\) on housing units. Using Equation 46.16 at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), convert each separately and add the two \(\varepsilon\), then convert the total \(\rho\) once. Which is the valid and tighter statement of the combined guarantee? Check: \(17.915 + 2.609 = 20.524\) against 18.194. (Composition in zCDP)







TipSolution






Separately. \(\ln(10^{10}) = 23.026\). Persons: \(2.56 + 2\sqrt{2.56 \times 23.026} = 17.915\). Housing: \(0.07 + 2\sqrt{0.07 \times 23.026} = 2.609\). Sum: 20.524, at \(\delta = 2 \times 10^{-10}\) by basic composition of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees.
Together. zCDP composes by adding \(\rho\), so the combined release is \(2.63\)-zCDP, and one conversion gives \(2.63 + 2\sqrt{2.63 \times 23.026} = 18.194\) at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\).
Which is better. Both are valid. The second is smaller and has the smaller \(\delta\), because the conversion’s square root is concave: \(\sqrt{\rho_1} + \sqrt{\rho_2} \ge \sqrt{\rho_1 + \rho_2}\), so converting once wastes less.

This is the same lesson as the chapter’s, in another form: keep the guarantee in its richest form (here \(\rho\), there the curve) as long as possible, and convert to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end. The Census Bureau’s own 17.14 and 2.47 come from a tighter conversion than Equation 46.16.

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
text:
46.6 Retraining every month

Exercise 6. Retraining every month. A team retrains the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 2\) configuration (noise multiplier 2.28) every month on the same data and publishes every model. What is the total \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) after 1, 3 and 12 months under RDP composition, and under basic composition of the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees? Check: RDP 1.998, 3.675, 8.185; basic 2, 6, 24. (Composition over releases)







TipSolution






RDP composition. Each run’s RDP curve is \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\), and by Theorem 29.2 \(k\) runs on the same data add up to \(kT\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\), exactly one run of \(kT\) steps. Converting at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) gives 1.998, 3.675 and 8.185.
Basic composition. Adding \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) gives \(2k\) at \(\delta = k \times 10^{-5}\): 2, 6 and 24, at a larger \(\delta\).
Reading it. A year of monthly releases at “\(\varepsilon = 2\)” is an \(\varepsilon \approx 8\) guarantee for the year, by the tightest of the two accountings. The budget in the model card must be the budget for the period the data are used, not for one run.

State the period with the budget, and account for every release that touched the data, including discarded runs and hyperparameter searches (Hyperparameter tuning).

title: 46  Exercises: Choosing ε
text:
46.7 From actions to users

Exercise 7. From actions to users. The Facebook URLs release adds Gaussian noise with \(\sigma = 22\) to the counts of likes, one count per URL and group of users, and sets \(k = 5\), the 99th percentile of URLs a user likes. Each like moves one count by 1. Find the zCDP parameter \(\rho\) and the \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for one like, for a user with 5 likes, and for a user with 10 likes. Use the release’s conversion \(\varepsilon = \rho + \sqrt{4\rho\ln(\sqrt{\pi\rho}/\delta)}\), and compare it with Equation 46.16. Check: \(\varepsilon = 0.190\), 0.447 and 0.647; Equation 46.16 gives 0.219, 0.493 and 0.700. (Composition in zCDP, user-level units)







TipSolution






One like. The Gaussian mechanism with noise \(\sigma\) on a count that one action moves by 1 is \(\rho\)-zCDP with \(\rho = 1/(2\sigma^2) = 1/968 = 0.00103\). The conversion gives \(\varepsilon = 0.190\).
A user with \(k\) likes. Each like is on a different URL, so it moves a different count by one. zCDP composes by adding \(\rho\), so the user is \(k/(2\sigma^2)\)-zCDP: \(\rho = 0.00517\) for \(k = 5\), which converts to \(\varepsilon = 0.447\), the release’s user-level target of about 0.45.
A heavier user. With 10 likes, \(\rho\) doubles to 0.01033 and \(\varepsilon\) rises to 0.647. It does not double, because \(\varepsilon\) grows roughly like \(\sqrt\rho\) when \(\rho\) is small.
The two conversions. Equation 46.16 gives 0.219, 0.493 and 0.700. Both conversions are valid bounds. The release’s conversion is tighter because it keeps a factor \(\sqrt{\pi\rho}\) inside the logarithm, which is below 1 for small \(\rho\).

A per-action guarantee becomes a per-user one only for users whose number of actions you have bounded. Above the bound, the guarantee weakens smoothly rather than failing, and a privacy statement should say how.

title: 47  Exercises: Auditing private training
text:
47.1 Both inequalities
Exercises for Auditing private training, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_auditing.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_auditing.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. An audit tests whether a training algorithm \(M\) satisfies differential privacy (DP) as claimed. It trains with a canary record, on the dataset written \(D'\), and without it, on \(D\), and an attack says “canary in” when its score passes a threshold. The attack’s true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of runs with the canary that it flags, and its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of runs without the canary that it flags.
The training algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD. Each step samples a fraction \(q\) of the records, the sampling rate, and adds noise with multiplier \(\sigma\). The run takes \(T\) steps. The running example has \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\). For it the accountant claims a privacy level \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), at a slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Every bound holds with probability \(1 - \beta = 95\%\), where \(\beta\) is the failure probability. Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\) is the trade-off curve of two unit-variance normals at distance \(\mu\).

title: 47  Exercises: Auditing private training
text:
Exercise 1. Both inequalities. For three attacks with exactly known rates, (FPR, TPR) \(= (0.05, 0.95)\), \((0.001, 0.05)\) and \((0.5, 0.999)\), compute the two lower bounds on \(\varepsilon\) that Equation 47.2 gives at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and say which one matters for each attack and why. Check: 2.94 and 2.94; 3.91 and 0.05; 0.69 and 6.21. (Reading the privacy region)







TipSolution






The two bounds. Equation 47.2 gives \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}\) (the direct form, from “canary in” events) and \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{1 - \mathrm{FPR} - \delta}{1 - \mathrm{TPR}}\) (the mirror form, from “canary out” events).
A symmetric attack. At \((0.05, 0.95)\), both are \(\ln(0.95/0.05) = \ln 19 = 2.94\), up to the \(\delta\): the attack errs equally often in both directions.
A low-FPR attack. At \((0.001, 0.05)\), the direct form is \(\ln(0.05/0.001) = \ln 50 = 3.91\), and the mirror form \(\ln(0.999/0.95) = 0.05\). The attack is confident when it says “in” and useless when it says “out”, so the direct form carries the information.
An attack that rarely misses. At \((0.5, 0.999)\), the direct form is \(\ln(0.999/0.5) = 0.69\) and the mirror form \(\ln(0.5/0.001) = 6.21\). The attack almost never misses a present canary, so its “out” verdicts are confident: when it says “out”, the canary was absent with odds of about 500 to 1.

An audit that only computes the direct form throws away attacks of the third kind. The certified version, Equation 47.4, applies Clopper–Pearson bounds to both forms.

title: 47  Exercises: Auditing private training
text:
47.2 The ceiling of an audit

Exercise 2. The ceiling of an audit. A perfect attack with \(n\) trials per hypothesis certifies the exact ceiling of Corollary 47.1, about \(\ln(n/\ln(2/\beta))\). Compare the approximation with the exact value for \(n = 100\), 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000, and estimate the number of trials needed to certify the running example’s 6.71. Check: 3.28 against 3.30, 5.60 against 5.60, 7.90 against 7.91, 10.21 against 10.21; 3,038 trials exactly, 3,035 by the approximation. (The rule of three)







TipSolution






The two formulas. Corollary 47.1 gives the exact ceiling \(\ln\frac{(\beta/2)^{1/n} - \delta}{1 - (\beta/2)^{1/n}}\), and its proof approximates it by \(\ln(n/\ln 40)\) at \(\beta = 0.05\), using \(e^{-x} \approx 1 - x\) for the small exponent \(x = \ln(2/\beta)/n\).
Numbers. The exact values are 3.28, 5.60, 7.90 and 10.21, against 3.30, 5.60, 7.91 and 10.21 from the approximation. The approximation is a little high at \(n = 100\), where the exponent is largest and \(e^{-x} \approx 1 - x\) is cruder.
Inverting. Setting \(\ln(n/\ln 40) = 6.71\) gives \(n = e^{6.71}\ln 40 = 3{,}035\), and the exact search gives 3,038.

Each unit of \(\varepsilon\) multiplies the trials by \(e\). The ceiling is reached only by an attack that never errs; real audits need many more trials (Section 47.3).

title: 47  Exercises: Auditing private training
text:
47.3 Where ε lives

Exercise 3. Where \(\varepsilon\) lives. For a \(\mu\)-GDP mechanism, Proposition 47.1 gives the false positive rate at which the line \(\mathrm{TPR} = e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) touches the trade-off curve. Evaluate it at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for \(\mu = 1.3108\) (the running example), 0.5 and 3, and compute how many trials without the canary are needed to see ten false positives there. Check: \(\varepsilon = 6.01\), FPR \(8.1\times10^{-8}\), \(1.2\times10^{8}\) trials; \(\varepsilon = 1.99\), \(1.1\times10^{-5}\), \(8.8\times10^{5}\); \(\varepsilon = 16.68\), \(8.4\times10^{-13}\), \(1.2\times10^{13}\). (Duality between \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and trade-off curves)







TipSolution






The touching point. By Proposition 47.1, the line touches the curve at the threshold with \(\mathrm{FPR}^* = \Phi(-\varepsilon/\mu - \mu/2)\) and \(\mathrm{TPR}^* = \Phi(-\varepsilon/\mu + \mu/2)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function and \(\varepsilon\) is the curve’s value at \(\delta\). That \(\varepsilon\) comes from the Gaussian privacy profile, Corollary 32.1, solved for \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
The running example. \(\mu = 1.3108\) gives \(\varepsilon = 6.01\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) through the Gaussian privacy profile, and then \(\mathrm{FPR}^* = 8.1\times10^{-8}\), \(\mathrm{TPR}^* = 4.3\times10^{-5}\). Ten false positives at that rate need \(10/(8.1\times10^{-8}) = 1.2\times10^{8}\) trials.
The other two. \(\mu = 0.5\) gives \(\varepsilon = 1.99\), \(\mathrm{FPR}^* = 1.1\times10^{-5}\), \(\mathrm{TPR}^* = 9.3\times10^{-5}\) and \(8.8\times10^{5}\) trials. \(\mu = 3\) gives \(\varepsilon = 16.68\), \(\mathrm{FPR}^* = 8.4\times10^{-13}\), \(\mathrm{TPR}^* = 2.5\times10^{-5}\) and \(1.2\times10^{13}\) trials.

In all three the touching TPR is between 2.5 and 10 times \(\delta\): at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the optimal test detects the canary only a few times in \(10^5\), and its false positive rate is smaller still. Auditing the full \(\varepsilon\) at a small \(\delta\) is a measurement in the extreme tail, which is why the audits of the chapter stop short.

title: 47  Exercises: Auditing private training
section: 47.4 What the sum of projections loses
text:
47.4 What the sum of projections loses

Exercise 4. What the sum of projections loses. By Theorem 47.2, for a white-box Dirac canary the likelihood-ratio statistic of Equation 47.9 behaves like \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) and the sum of projections like \(\mu_{\mathrm{sum}} = q\sqrt T/\sigma\). Compute their ratio for \(\sigma = 0.5\), 1, 2 and 4, and how many times more steps the sum would need to reach the likelihood ratio’s \(\mu\). Explain why the ratio tends to 1 for large \(\sigma\). Check: 3.661, 1.311, 1.066, 1.016; step factors 13.40, 1.72, 1.14, 1.03. (Linearizing a likelihood ratio)







TipSolution






The ratio. \(\mu/\mu_{\mathrm{sum}} = \sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\cdot\sigma\), since \(q\) and \(\sqrt T\) cancel.
Numbers. \(0.5\sqrt{e^4 - 1} = 3.661\); \(\sqrt{e - 1} = 1.311\); \(2\sqrt{e^{0.25} - 1} = 1.066\); \(4\sqrt{e^{1/16} - 1} = 1.016\).
Steps. Both \(\mu\) grow like \(\sqrt T\), so matching them needs the ratio squared in steps: 13.40, 1.72, 1.14 and 1.03.
Large \(\sigma\). \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 = 1/\sigma^2 + 1/(2\sigma^4) + \dots\), so the ratio is \(\sqrt{1 + 1/(2\sigma^2) + \dots} \to 1\). In words: when the noise is large compared with the canary’s shift of 1, each step’s log-likelihood ratio \(\ln(1 - q + qe^{(x - 1/2)/\sigma^2})\) is nearly linear in \(x\) over the range where \(x\) falls, so summing the \(x_t\) is nearly optimal. At small \(\sigma\) the exponential is strongly curved and a single large \(x_t\) outweighs many moderate ones.

Small noise multipliers are where DP-SGD leaks most per step, and where a naive statistic wastes most of the evidence: at \(\sigma = 0.5\) the sum would need thirteen times as many steps.

title: 47  Exercises: Auditing private training
section: 47.5 How many canaries one run needs
text:
47.5 How many canaries one run needs

Exercise 5. How many canaries one run needs. In a one-run audit where every one of \(m = r\) guesses is correct, find the smallest \(m\) that certifies the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 6.71\): first for pure DP with Equation 47.15, then with the \(\delta\) correction of Equation 47.18 at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(10^{-5}\). Give the bound for 2,000, 2,500 and 5,000 canaries at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Check: 2,467; 2,483 and 2,648; 6.45, 6.66 and 7.28. (Binomial tails)







TipSolution






Pure DP. All \(m\) guesses correct has probability at most \(p^m\) under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, with \(p = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\). The claim is rejected when \(p^m < \beta\), that is \(m > \ln\beta/\ln p\).
Numbers. At \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), \(1 - p = 1/(1 + e^{6.71})\) is about \(1.2\times10^{-3}\). Since \(\ln p \approx -(1 - p)\) for \(p\) near 1, the condition is about \(m > \ln(1/\beta)(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), with \(\ln(1/\beta) = \ln 20 = 3.00\); the smallest integer that satisfies the exact condition is 2,467.
With \(\delta\). The correction term of Equation 47.18 grows with the number of guesses \(m\). At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) it barely matters, and 2,483 canaries suffice; at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the requirement rises to 2,648.
The bounds. 2,000 perfect guesses certify 6.45, 2,500 certify 6.66 and 5,000 certify 7.28 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).

Two and a half thousand canaries, every one guessed right, just to reach the claim. A real attack errs, and Table 47.4 shows that 1,000 white-box Dirac canaries certify 2.22. In one run as in many, the bound grows like the logarithm of the number of trials.

title: 47  Exercises: Auditing private training
text:
47.6 Randomized response meets the bound

Exercise 6. Randomized response meets the bound. Suppose each of 100 guesses is produced by \(\varepsilon\)-randomized response on the true inclusion bit: it reports the true bit with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and the other one otherwise. At \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), compute the expected number of correct guesses, check it by simulation, and compute the one-run p-value (Equation 47.15 with \(\delta = 0\)) of 75 and of 85 correct guesses. What does this say about the tightness of Equation 47.15? Check: 75; simulated mean 75.01; p-values 0.553 and 0.0111. (Tightness of a stochastic-dominance bound)







TipSolution






Randomized response is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Its two output distributions differ by a factor of \(e^\varepsilon\) on each output, by construction.
Its correct guesses. Each guess is right with probability \(p = 3/(1 + 3) = 0.75\), independently, so the count is \(\mathrm{Bin}(100, 0.75)\), with mean 75. Simulating 100,000 audits gives a mean of 75.01.
The p-values. Equation 47.15 bounds \(\Pr[W \ge v]\) by \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(100, 0.75) \ge v]\): 0.553 for \(v = 75\) and 0.0111 for \(v = 85\).
Tightness. For randomized response, \(W\) is the binomial, so the inequality holds with equality: no smaller bound is valid for every \(\varepsilon\)-DP algorithm. Seeing 75 correct guesses is entirely consistent with \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) (p-value 0.553), and is what this mechanism produces on average; seeing 85 would reject \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) at the 5% level.

The one-run bound is exact for randomized response and conservative for mechanisms whose trade-off curve is smooth, like the Gaussian. This is why one-run audits of DP-SGD fall further short of the accountant than many-run audits.

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.1 How many point queries break a sample
Exercises for Adaptive data analysis, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_adaptive_data_analysis.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/solutions_adaptive_data_analysis.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. The data are a sample of \(n\) records, the dataset \(D\), drawn independently from a distribution \(\mathcal D\). A statistical query \(q\) maps a record to \([0, 1]\). Its empirical value \(q(D)\) is its average over the sample, and its population value \(q(\mathcal D)\) is its average over the distribution. A mechanism answers \(k\) queries, possibly chosen adaptively, and \(a_j\) is its answer to query \(j\).
Privacy is differential privacy (DP) with privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\), under the replace-one relation, where a neighbour \(D^{(i)}\) replaces record \(x_i\) by a fresh draw \(x_i'\). Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) with parameter \(\rho\) converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{48.1}\]

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
text:
Exercise 1. How many point queries break a sample. In the point-query attack of Section 48.1, the records are uniform on \(N\) values and the final query asks whether a record’s value occurs in the sample. Show that the final query’s expected population value is \(1 - (1 - 1/N)^n\) and that it is at most \(n/N\). For \(n = 1{,}000\), find the smallest \(N\) for which the final query’s expected error exceeds \(\frac12\), and compare it with \(n/\ln 2\). Check: \(N = 1{,}444\), so 1,445 queries, against \(n/\ln 2 = 1{,}442.7\). (Counting, and the inequality \(1 - x \le e^{-x}\))







TipSolution






The population value. The final query is 1 on a value exactly when that value occurs in the sample. A fresh record has each value with probability \(1/N\), so the population value is the fraction of the \(N\) values that the sample covers.
Its expectation. A given value is missed by one draw with probability \(1 - 1/N\), and by all \(n\) independent draws with probability \((1 - 1/N)^n\). So it is covered with probability \(1 - (1 - 1/N)^n\), and by linearity of expectation the expected covered fraction is the same number.
The upper bound. Step 3 of the proof of Proposition 48.1 shows that the covered fraction is at most \(n/N\) for every sample, so it is also at most \(n/N\) on average.
The error. The final query’s empirical value is 1, so its expected error is \((1 - 1/N)^n\). This exceeds \(\frac12\) when \(n\ln(1 - 1/N) > -\ln 2\).
Solve. For large \(N\), \(\ln(1 - 1/N) \approx -1/N\), so the condition is about \(N > n/\ln 2 = 1{,}442.7\). The script checks every \(N\) and finds that the smallest is \(N = 1{,}444\). With \(N = 2{,}000\) the expected population value is 0.3935 and the error 0.6065, and with \(N = 10{,}000\) the error is 0.9048.

So 1,445 queries, of which only the last is adaptive, are enough to make one answer off by more than a half on 1,000 records. Exact empirical answers need \(n\) to grow linearly with the number of queries.

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
section: 48.2 The reverse direction, and a selection from one record
text:
48.2 The reverse direction, and a selection from one record

Exercise 2. The reverse direction, and a selection from one record. (a) Prove the second inequality of the transfer lemma, \(\mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[q_W(D)] + \delta\), by applying DP from \(D^{(i)}\) to \(D\). (b) Take \(n = 1\) record, a uniform bit \(x_1\). The algorithm \(W\) keeps the bit with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flips it otherwise, which gives a bit \(y\), and outputs the query \(q(x) = \mathbf 1[x = y]\). Show that \(W\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP and that its selection bias is \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)/2\), about \(\varepsilon/4\). Compare it with the lemma’s bounds. Check: at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), a bias of 0.02498 against the sharper bound 0.05259 and the lemma 0.10517. (Transfer lemma; randomized response)







TipSolution





(a)

DP in the other direction. Hold \(D\) and \(x_i'\) fixed. The samples \(D^{(i)}\) and \(D\) are neighbours, and the replace-one relation is symmetric. So Equation 48.7, the bound of Lemma 19.1 on averages, applied to \(f(q) = q(x_i)\), gives \(\mathbb E_W[q_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_W[q_{W(D)}(x_i)] + \delta\).
Average. Averaging over \(D\) and \(x_i'\) keeps the inequality. Averaging over \(i\) turns the right side into \(e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[q_W(D)] + \delta\), by step 1 of the proof of Lemma 48.1.
The left side. By the swap of Lemma 7.1, as in step 2 of the proof of Lemma 48.1, \(\mathbb E[q_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)] = \mathbb E[q_{W(D)}(x_i')] = \mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)]\), because \(x_i'\) is a record that \(W\) never saw. This gives the claim.

(b)

Privacy. The output is determined by \(y\). Changing \(x_1\) changes the probability of each value of \(y\) from \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) to \(1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) or back, a ratio of \(e^\varepsilon\). This is randomized response, which is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
The empirical value. With one record, \(q_W(D) = \mathbf 1[x_1 = y]\), which is 1 exactly when the bit was kept. Its expectation is \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).
The population value. A fresh uniform bit equals \(y\) with probability \(\frac12\), whatever \(y\) is, so \(q_W(\mathcal D) = \frac12\).
The bias. The difference is \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon) - \frac12 = (e^\varepsilon - 1)/(2(e^\varepsilon + 1)) = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)/2\). For small \(\varepsilon\), \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \approx \varepsilon/2\), so the bias is about \(\varepsilon/4\).
Numbers. At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the bias is 0.02498, against the sharper bound \((e^\varepsilon - 1)\cdot\frac12 = 0.05259\) and the lemma’s \(e^\varepsilon - 1 = 0.10517\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) it is 0.23106, against 0.85914 and 1.71828.

A selection bias linear in \(\varepsilon\) is possible, so the lemma’s order cannot be improved. Its constant is loose by a factor of 2 against the sharper form here, and by 8 for the exponential mechanism of the chapter’s example.

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.3 Why the complements are needed

Exercise 3. Why the complements are needed. In the proof of Theorem 48.1, suppose you skip step 1 and let \(W\) choose, among the original \(k\) queries only, the one with the largest signed error \(q_j(\mathcal D) - a_j\). What does the proof then bound? Why is adding the complements simpler than running the proof a second time for answers that are too high? (Post-processing)







TipSolution






Without complements. The same steps bound \(\mathbb E[\max_j(q_j(\mathcal D) - a_j)]\), the largest error in one direction only: answers that are too low. Answers that are too high, with \(a_j > q_j(\mathcal D)\), are invisible to this \(W\). In Table 48.2, \(W\) would pick \(q_2\) with error 0.05 and miss \(q_1\), whose answer is 0.12 too high.
A second selector. One could instead run the proof again with a selector that maximizes \(a_j - q_j(\mathcal D)\), but that needs the lemma for queries of the form \(1 - q\). That is exactly what the complements provide, in one pass.
What the complements cost. Nothing. Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 48.1 computes the complement answers from the original ones, so by post-processing they cost no privacy. Step 4 uses that a complement’s error on the sample equals the original’s, so they cost no accuracy either.
The complement is a statistical query. \(1 - q_j\) maps each record to \([0, 1]\), so Lemma 48.1 applies to it, and one selector over the \(2k\) queries covers both directions.

The complements are a bookkeeping trick: they let one private choice carry the largest error in either direction, at no cost in privacy or accuracy.

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.4 Gaussian noise for 1,000 queries

Exercise 4. Gaussian noise for 1,000 queries. Corollary 48.1 says that the Gaussian mechanism with the transfer theorem reaches an expected largest error \(\alpha\) with about \(n = 8\sqrt{k\ln(2k)\ln(1/\delta)}/\alpha^2\) records, which is \(4\sqrt{4k\ln(2k)\ln(1/\delta)}/\alpha^2\). Evaluate it for \(k = 1{,}000\), \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(\delta = 0.0019\), and compare it with the exact optimum of Table 48.4. At that optimum, compute \(\rho\) from \(\sigma\). Check: the formula gives 697,435 records against 764,337; at the optimum \(\sigma = 0.00620\), \(\rho = 2.224\times10^{-5}\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.0236\). (zCDP composition and conversion)







TipSolution






The formula. Corollary 48.1 balances the noise term \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)}\) of Equation 48.17 against the leading part of its transfer term, \(\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}/(n\sigma)\). Its size \(8\sqrt{k\ln(2k)\ln(1/\delta)}/\alpha^2\) equals \(4\sqrt{4k\ln(2k)\ln(1/\delta)}/\alpha^2\), because \(4\sqrt4 = 8\).
Numbers. With \(k = 1{,}000\), \(\ln(2k) = 7.601\), and with \(\delta = 0.0019\), \(\ln(1/\delta)\) is about 6.27. The formula gives 697,435 records.
Against the optimum. The exact minimization of Equation 48.17 needs 764,337 records. The formula is about 9% low because it drops the \(\rho\) term of the conversion, the \(\delta\) term and the curvature of \(e^\varepsilon\), all of which add to the bound.
The parameters at the optimum. There \(\sigma = 0.00620\), so \(\rho = 1{,}000/(2 \times 764{,}337^2 \times 0.00620^2) = 2.224\times10^{-5}\). The conversion with \(\delta = 0.0019\) gives \(\varepsilon = 0.0236\). The noise term is 0.0242 and the transfer term 0.0258, almost equal, as the balancing argument predicts.

The rate grows like \(\sqrt k\), but the constant is large: three quarters of a million records for 1,000 queries at an error of 0.05.

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.5 Rounds of adaptivity

Exercise 5. Rounds of adaptivity. An analysis asks \(k\) queries in \(r\) rounds. The queries of each round are fixed before any of that round’s answers are seen. Show that splitting the sample into \(r\) parts, one per round, gives an expected largest error of at most \(\sqrt{r\ln(2k)/(2n)}\). For \(k = 1{,}000\) and \(\alpha = 0.05\), compute the records needed for \(r = 1\), 10 and 1,000, and explain why splitting is linear in \(k\) when every query is its own round. Check: 1,521, 15,202 and 1,520,181 records. (Conditioning; the maximal inequality)







TipSolution






One round. Fix the parts used by earlier rounds. The queries of round \(\ell\) are then fixed, and part \(\ell\), of \(n/r\) records, is independent of them. This is the situation of step 1 of the proof of Proposition 7.3, with \(n/r\) records per part, so each query’s error has a moment generating function at most \(e^{\lambda^2r/(8n)}\).
All rounds. That proof finishes with the maximal inequality over the \(2k\) signed errors, which never needs them to be independent and never counts parts. With \(n/r\) in place of \(n/k\), it gives \(\sqrt{r\ln(2k)/(2n)}\): only the factor in front of \(\ln(2k)\) changes.
Records needed. Setting this equal to \(\alpha\) gives \(n = r\ln(2k)/(2\alpha^2) = r \times 7.601/0.005\). That is 1,521 records for \(r = 1\), 15,202 for \(r = 10\) and 1,520,181 for \(r = 1{,}000\), after rounding up.
Why linear in \(k\). When every query is chosen from the previous answers, each query is its own round, so \(r = k\) and the cost is \(k\ln(2k)/(2\alpha^2)\). Each record answers one query only, so the data must grow with the number of queries.

The number of rounds, not the number of queries, sets the cost of splitting. That is why a single final test set is cheap, and why a long sequential search is expensive.

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.6 The boosting attack’s approximation

Exercise 6. The boosting attack’s approximation. Derive the chapter’s approximation \(\sqrt{k/(2n)}/\pi\) for the overfitting of the boosting attack, and check it by simulation for \(n = 1{,}000\), \(k = 100\) and for \(n = 4{,}000\), \(k = 400\). Check: the approximation is 0.0712 in both cases; the script’s simulations, over 40 runs each, give 0.0681 ± 0.0021 and 0.0715 ± 0.0012. (Normal approximation)







TipSolution






One submission. A random labelling’s holdout accuracy is \(\frac12 + Z\), where \(Z\) is approximately normal with mean 0 and standard deviation \(s = 1/(2\sqrt n)\). Its average agreement with each holdout label is also \(\frac12 + Z\), by symmetry between the records.
The kept submissions. Given \(Z > 0\), the mean of \(Z\) is \(s\sqrt{2/\pi}\), the mean of a half-normal. So a kept submission agrees with each holdout label with probability about \(\frac12 + s\sqrt{2/\pi}\). About \(k/2\) are kept.
The vote on one record. Each kept submission votes \(+1\) for the right label or \(-1\), with mean \(2s\sqrt{2/\pi}\). The sum of \(k/2\) votes has mean \(k s\sqrt{2/\pi}\) and standard deviation about \(\sqrt{k/2}\), since each vote has variance close to 1.
The ratio. Mean over standard deviation is \(k s\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sqrt{k/2} = 2s\sqrt k/\sqrt\pi = \sqrt{k/n}/\sqrt\pi\), using \(2s = 1/\sqrt n\).
The accuracy. For a small ratio \(z\), a normal sum is positive with probability about \(\frac12 + z/\sqrt{2\pi}\). So the overfitting is about \(\sqrt{k/n}/(\sqrt\pi\sqrt{2\pi}) = \sqrt{k/(2n)}/\pi\).
Numbers. Both cases have \(k/n = 0.1\), so the approximation is \(\sqrt{0.05}/\pi = 0.0712\). The simulations give 0.0681 ± 0.0021 and 0.0715 ± 0.0012, within about one and a half standard errors. The chapter’s 20 runs at \(n = 1{,}000\), \(k = 100\) gave 0.0739.

The overfitting depends on \(k\) and \(n\) only through \(k/n\): ten times more holdout records buy ten times more submissions at the same overfitting, not a hundred times.

title: 48  Exercises: Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.7 Thresholdout’s budget

Exercise 7. Thresholdout’s budget. In the chapter’s experiment, the queries are correlations with sensitivity \(\Delta = 2/n\), and Thresholdout uses the Laplace noise scale \(b = 1/\sqrt n\) with \(n = 2{,}000\). How many overfitting detections fit within \(\varepsilon = 1\)? How large must the holdout set be to afford 300 detections at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) with the same \(b = 1/\sqrt n\)? Check: 11 detections; \(n = 1.44\times10^8\). (Sparse vector technique; basic composition)







TipSolution






The cost of one detection. By Equation 48.21, one detection costs \(2\Delta/b = 2 \cdot (2/n) \cdot \sqrt n = 4/\sqrt n\). At \(n = 2{,}000\) that is 0.0894.
The budget. Detections compose by adding their costs, so \(\varepsilon = 1\) allows \(\lfloor 1/0.0894\rfloor = 11\) detections.
The experiment. The chapter’s runs recorded 325.8 detections on average, so their total cost was \(\varepsilon = 29.1\), far above 1.
A larger holdout set. With \(B\) detections, \(\varepsilon = 4B/\sqrt n\). Setting \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(B = 300\) gives \(\sqrt n = 4 \times 300/0.1 = 12{,}000\), so \(n = 1.44\times10^8\) records.

Thresholdout’s guarantee makes agreeing answers free, but each disagreement costs a fixed amount. A careless analyst who triggers many detections exhausts the formal budget quickly, which is why the experiment’s good behaviour lies outside its theorem.
